For what is near to that is also of such a nature. Since there is naturally no offense regarding what belongs to different families in different places, the statement 'no offense' is said with reference to what belongs to a single family in different places. Because what was undertaken was interrupted, it is said, 'he is allowed to eat again on one day'. Although 'odissā' is stated generally, it should be taken to mean only bhikkhus, thus he said, 'only for bhikkhus'. First.

2. Gaṇabhojanasikkhāpadaṃ

2. The Training Rule on Taking Meals in a Group.

209. Dutiye pahīnalābhasakkārassa hetuṃ dassento āha “so kirā”tiādi. Soti devadatto. “Ahosī”ti ca “pākaṭo jāto”ti ca yojetabbo. Ajātasattunāti ajātasseyeva piturājassa sattubhāvato ajātasattunā, “mārāpetvā”tipade kāritakammaṃ. Rājānanti bimbisārarājaṃ, “mārāpetvā”tipade dhātukammaṃ. Abhimāreti abhinilīyitvā bhagavato māraṇatthāya pesite dhanudhare. Gūḷhapaṭicchannoti guhito hutvā paṭicchanno. Parikathāyāti pariguhanāya kathāya. “Rājānampī”tipadaṃ “mārāpesī”tipade dhātukammaṃ. Pavijjhīti pavaṭṭesi. Tatoti tato vuttato paraṃ uṭṭhahiṃsūti sambandho. Nagare nivasantīti nāgarā. Rājāti ajātasatturājā. Sāsanakaṇṭakantisāsanassa kaṇṭakasadisattā sāsanakaṇṭakaṃ. Tatoti nīharato. Upaṭṭhānampīti upaṭṭhānampi, upaṭṭhānatthāyapi vā. Aññepīti rājato aññepi. Assāti devadattassa. Kiñci khādanīyabhojanīyaṃ “dātabba”nti iminā yojetabbaṃ. Kiñci vā abhivādanādi “kātabba”nti iminā sambandho. Kulesu [M 0.0061] viññāpetvā bhuñjanassa hetuṃ dassento āha “mā me”tiādi. Posento hutvā bhuñjatīti sambandho.

209. In the second, explaining the reason for the loss of gains and honor, he says, 'so kirā', and so on. 'So' refers to Devadatta. The phrases 'ahosī' and 'pākaṭo jāto' should be connected. 'Ajātasattunā' means by Ajātasattu, because he was an enemy of his own father the king before he was born; in the phrase 'mārāpetvā', it is the agent of the causative action. 'Rājānaṃ' refers to King Bimbisāra; in the phrase 'mārāpetvā', it is the object of the root verb. 'Abhimāreti' refers to the archers who were sent, lying in wait, for the purpose of killing the Blessed One. 'Gūḷhapaṭicchanno' means having been hidden and concealed. 'Parikathāya' refers to talk of concealment. The word 'rājānaṃ'pi' is the object of the root verb in the word 'mārāpesī'. 'Pavijjhī' means he instigated. 'Tato' means after what was said; the connection is 'they arose from that'. 'Those who live in the city' are citizens. 'Rājā' refers to King Ajātasattu. 'Sāsanakaṇṭakaṃ' means a thorn in the teaching, because he is like a thorn to the teaching. 'Tato' means from removing him. 'Upaṭṭhānaṃ'pi' means also attendance, or for the purpose of attendance. 'Aññe'pi' means others besides the king. 'Assa' refers to Devadatta. 'Kiñci khādanīyabhojanīyaṃ' should be connected with 'dātabbaṃ', meaning 'something should be given'. Alternatively, 'kiñci vā abhivādanādi' is connected with 'kātabbaṃ', meaning 'something should be done'. Explaining the reason for eating after requesting from families, he says, 'mā me', and so on. The connection is: 'he eats while supporting himself'.

211. Bhattaṃ anadhivāsentānaṃ kasmā cīvaraṃ parittaṃ uppajjatīti āha “bhattaṃ agaṇhantāna”ntiādi.

211. Why does a limited amount of robe-cloth arise for those who do not consent to meals? He said, 'for those not taking a meal', and so on.

212. Cīvarakārake [V 1.0051] bhikkhū bhattena kasmā nimantentīti āha “gāme”tiādi.

212. Why are the bhikkhus who are making robes invited with a meal? He said, 'In the village', etc.

215. Nānāverajjaketi ettha rañño idaṃ rajjaṃ, visadisaṃ rajjaṃ virajjaṃ, nānappakāraṃ virajjaṃ nānāvirajjaṃ. Nānāvirajjehi āgatā nānāverajjakā. Majjhe vuddhi hotīti āha “nānāvidhehi aññarajjehi āgate”ti. Aññarajjehīti rājagahato aññehi rajjehi. Rañjitabbanti rañjanti vutte niggahitassa anāsanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “nānāverañjakeitipi pāṭho”ti.

215. Here, regarding 'nānāverajjakā': the king's realm is 'rajjaṃ'; a dissimilar realm is 'virajjaṃ'; a 'virajjaṃ' of various kinds is 'nānāvirajjaṃ'. Those who come from various 'virajjaṃ' are 'nānāverajjakā'. He says 'there is vowel strengthening in the middle', referring to 'those who come from other realms of various kinds'. 'Aññarajjehi' means from realms other than Rājagaha. 'Rañjitabbaṃ' means 'to be delighted in'; when 'rañjanti' (they delight) is said, it is said with reference to the non-destruction of attachment; this explains the statement: 'There is also a variant reading, nānāverañjake'.

218. Gaṇabhojaneti gaṇassa bhojanaṃ gaṇabhojanaṃ, gaṇabhojanassa bhojanaṃ gaṇabhojanaṃ, tasmiṃ gaṇabhojane pācittiyanti attho. “Rattūparato”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.10; ma. ni. 1.293) viya ekassa bhojanasaddassa lopo daṭṭhabbo. Nanu uposathe viya dve tayo gaṇo nāmāti āha “idha gaṇo nāma cattāro”tiādi. Tena dve tayo gaṇo nāma na honti, cattāro pana ādiṃ katvā taduttari gaṇo nāmāti dasseti. Taṃ panetanti ettha etasaddo vacanālaṅkāro dvīsu sabbanāmesu pubbasseva yebhuyyena padhānattā. Pasavatīti vaḍḍhati, jāyatīti attho. Vevacanena vāti “bhattena nimantemi, bhojanena nimantemī”ti pariyāyena vā. Bhāsantarena vāti mūlabhāsāto aññāya bhāsāya vā. Ekato nimantitā bhikkhūti sambandho. Hīti saccaṃ, yasmā vā. Pamāṇanti kāraṇaṃ. “Cattāro”ti liṅgavipallāsaṃ katvā “vihāre”tipadena yojetabbaṃ. Ṭhitesuyevāti padaṃ niddhāraṇasamudāyo. Eko nimantitoti sambandho.

218. Regarding 'gaṇabhojane': 'gaṇabhojana' is a meal of a group, or the eating of a group meal; the meaning is that there is a Pācittiya offense in that group meal. As in phrases like 'restrained at night' (rattūparato), the elision of one word 'bhojana' should be understood. One might ask, 'Is not a group two or three, as on the Uposatha day?' He says, 'Here, a group means four,' and so on. Thus, he shows that two or three do not constitute a group, but four and upwards, beginning from that number, constitutes a group. Here, in 'taṃ panetaṃ', the word 'etaṃ' is an embellishment of the sentence, because among two pronouns, the former is usually the principal one. 'Pasavati' means 'increases' or 'arises'. 'By synonym' means by an alternative expression, such as 'I invite with a meal, I invite with food'. 'By a different language' means by a language other than the original language. The connection is 'bhikkhus invited together'. 'Hi' means 'truly' or 'because'. 'Pamāṇaṃ' means 'reason'. 'Cattāro' (four) should be connected with the word 'vihāre' (in the monastery), altering the gender. 'Ṭhitesuyeva' (only while they are present) is a phrase of specification. The connection is 'one is invited'.

Cattāro [M 0.0062] bhikkhū viññāpeyyunti sambandho. Pāṭekkanti patiekassa bhāvo pāṭekkaṃ, visunti attho. Ekato vā nānāto vā viññāpeyyunti sambandho.

The connection is: ‘Four monks should inform.’ ‘Pāṭekkaṃ’ means the state of being for each one, that is, separately. The connection is: ‘They should inform together or separately.’

Chavisaṅkhātato bāhiracammato abbhantaracammassa thūlattā “mahācammassā”ti vuttaṃ. Phālaṃ etesaṃ pādānaṃ sañjātanti phālitā, uppādentīti sambandho. Pahaṭamatte satīti yojanā. Lesena kappanti pavattaṃ cittaṃ lesakappiyaṃ.

Because the inner skin is thicker than the outer skin, which is designated ‘chavi,’ it is called ‘mahācamma’ (great skin). ‘Phālitā’ (split) means that a split has arisen in these feet, or they produce it—this is the connection. The construction is: ‘when merely struck.’ ‘Lesakappiyaṃ’ means a mind that proceeds by way of a pretext, making something allowable.

Suttañcāti sūcipāsapavesanasuttañca. Nanu visuṃ cīvaradānasamayo viya cīvarakārasamayopi atthi, kasmā “yadā tadā”ti vuttanti āha “visuṃ hī”tiādi. Hīti saccaṃ, yasmā vā. Visuṃ cīvaradānasamayo viya cīvarakārasamayo nāma yasmā natthi, tasmā [V 1.0052] “yadā tadā”ti mayā vuttanti adhippāyo. Tasmā yo bhikkhu karoti, tena bhuñjitabbanti yojanā. Sūciveṭhanakoti sibbanatthāya dve pilotikakhaṇḍe sambandhitvā sūciyā vijjhanako. Vicāretīti pañcakhaṇḍasattakhaṇḍādivasena saṃvidahati. Chindatīti satthakena vā hatthena vā chindati. Moghasuttanti muyhanaṃ mogho, atthato gahetabbachaṭṭetabbaṭṭhāne muyhanacittaṃ, tassa chindanaṃ suttanti moghasuttaṃ. Āgantukapaṭṭanti dupaṭṭacīvare mūlapaṭṭassa upari ṭhapitapaṭṭaṃ. Paccāgatanti paṭṭacīvarādīsu labbhati. Bandhatīti mūlapaṭṭena āgantukapaṭṭaṃ. Bandhati. Anuvātanti cīvaraṃ anupariyāyitvā vīyati bandhīyatīti anuvātaṃ, taṃ chindati. Ghaṭṭetīti dve anuvātante aññamaññaṃ sambajjhati. Āropetīti cīvarassa upari āropeti. Tatthāti cīvare. Suttaṃ karotīti sūcipāsapavesanasuttaṃ vaṭṭeti. Valetīti vaṭṭitvā suttaveṭhanadaṇḍake āvaṭṭeti. Pipphalikanti satthakaṃ. Tañhi piyampi phāletīti pipphali, sāyeva pipphalikanti katvā pipphalikanti vuccati, taṃ niseti nisānaṃ karotīti attho. Yo pana katheti, etaṃ ṭhapetvāti yojanā.

‘Suttaṃ’ means the thread for inserting into the needle-eye. One might ask, ‘Is there not a separate time for making robes, just as there is a separate time for giving robes? Why then is “whenever” said?’ To this, he says, ‘Because truly,’ and so on. ‘Hi’ means ‘truly’ or ‘because.’ The intention is: ‘Since there is no separate time for making robes, unlike the time for giving robes, therefore I said “whenever.”’ Therefore, the construction is: ‘The monk who makes it should be the one to use it.’ ‘Sūciveṭhanako’ means one who pierces with a needle, having joined two pieces of cloth for sewing. ‘Vicāreti’ means he arranges it in five or seven sections, and so on. ‘Chindati’ means he cuts with a knife or by hand. ‘Moghasuttaṃ’ (useless thread): ‘mogha’ means confusion; it refers to a confused mind regarding what should be taken or discarded. The cutting of that is ‘moghasuttaṃ.’ ‘Āgantukapaṭṭaṃ’ (additional patch) means a patch placed over the original patch in a double-layered robe. ‘Paccāgataṃ’ (returned) is obtained in the case of patchwork robes, and so on. ‘Bandhati’ means he binds the additional patch with the original patch. He binds. ‘Anuvātaṃ’ (the seam): the robe is stitched by passing the thread around, thus it is called ‘anuvātaṃ’; he cuts it. ‘Ghaṭṭeti’ means he joins two seam-ends together. ‘Āropeti’ means he places it over the robe. ‘Tattha’ (there) means on the robe. ‘Suttaṃ karoti’ means he twists the thread for inserting into the needle-eye. ‘Valeti’ means, having twisted it, he winds it around the thread-winding stick. ‘Pipphalika’ means a small knife. Indeed, it splits even what is dear, hence it is called ‘pipphali’; that itself, having been made ‘pipphalika,’ is called ‘pipphalika.’ The meaning is that he hones it. The construction is: ‘But whoever says this, setting this aside.’

Addhānamaggassa dvigāvutattā “addhayojanabbhantare gāvute”ti vuttaṃ. Abhirūḷhena bhuñjitabbanti sambandho. Yatthāti yasmiṃ kāle. “Sannipatantī”ti bahukattuvasena vuttaṃ. Akusalaṃ parivajjetīti paribbājako[M 0.0063], pabbajjavesaṃ vā pariggahetvā vajati gacchati pavattatīti paribbājako. Vinā bhāvapaccayena bhāvatthassa ñātabbato paribbājakabhāvo paribbājako, taṃ samāpannoti paribbājakasamāpanno. Atha vā paribbājakesu samāpanno pariyāpannoti paribbājakasamāpanno. “Etesa”ntipadaṃ “yena kenacī”tipade niddhāraṇasamudāyo.

Because a long road is two gāvutas, it is said, ‘within half a yojana, a gāvuta.’ The connection is: ‘He should eat having ascended.’ ‘Yattha’ means ‘at which time.’ ‘Sannipatanti’ (they assemble) is said in the sense of many. ‘Paribbājaka’ (wanderer) means one who avoids the unwholesome; or, having taken up the guise of one gone forth, one who proceeds, goes, or carries on, is a wanderer. Since the meaning of a state of being is to be understood without the suffix indicating a state of being, ‘paribbājaka’ means the state of being a wanderer; one who has attained that is ‘paribbājakasamāpanna.’ Alternatively, one who is included or counted among wanderers is ‘paribbājakasamāpanna.’ The word ‘etesaṃ’ in the phrase ‘yena kenaci’ specifies the group.

220. Yepi bhikkhū bhuñjantīti sambandho. Tatthāti “dve tayo ekato”tivacane. Animantito catuttho yassa catukkassāti animantitacatutthaṃ, animantitena vā catutthaṃ animantitacatutthaṃ. Eseva nayo aññesupi catutthesu. Idhāti imasmiṃ sāsane. Nimantetīti akappiyanimantanena nimanteti. Tesūti catūsu bhikkhūsu. Soti upāsako. Aññanti nāgatabhikkhuto aññaṃ, nimantitabhikkhuto vā. Taṅkhaṇappattanti tasmiṃ pucchanakathanakkhaṇe pattaṃ. Hīti vitthāro. Tatthāti tasmiṃ ṭhāne, gehe vā. Tehīti karaṇabhūtehi bhikkhūhi.

220. The connection is: ‘And those monks who are eating.’ ‘Tattha’ (there) refers to the utterance ‘two or three together.’ ‘Animantitacatutthaṃ’ (the uninvited fourth) means the fourth of that group of four who is uninvited; or it means the fourth by the uninvited one. The same method applies to the other fourths. ‘Idha’ (here) means in this dispensation. ‘Nimanteti’ (he invites) means he invites with an improper invitation. ‘Tesu’ (among them) means among the four monks. ‘So’ (he) refers to a lay follower. ‘Aññaṃ’ (another) means another other than the monk who arrived, or other than the invited monk. ‘Taṅkhaṇappattaṃ’ (arrived at that moment) means arrived at that moment of questioning or speaking. ‘Hi’ indicates elaboration. ‘Tattha’ (there) means in that place, or in the house. ‘Tehi’ (by them) means by the monks who are the instruments.

Soti piṇḍapātiko. Anāgacchantampīti sayaṃ na āgacchantampi. Lacchathāti labhissatha.

‘So’ (he) refers to one who lives on alms. ‘Anāgacchantaṃ pi’ (even if he does not come) means even if he himself does not come. ‘Lacchatha’ (you will receive) means ‘you will obtain.’

Sopīti sāmaṇeropi, na piṇḍapātikoyevāti attho.

‘Sopi’ (he too) refers to even a novice, not just an alms-goer—that is the meaning.

Tatthāti [V 1.0053] gilānacatutthe, tesu catūsu vā. Gilāno itaresaṃ pana gaṇapūrako hotīti yojanā.

‘Tattha’ (there) means in the group of four with a sick person, or among those four. The construction is: ‘The sick one, however, completes the quorum for the others.’

Gaṇapūrakattāti samayaladdhassa gaṇapūrakattā. Catukkānīti cīvaradānacatutthaṃ cīvarakāracatutthaṃ addhānagamanacatutthaṃ nāvābhiruhanacatutthaṃ mahāsamayacatutthaṃ, samaṇabhattacatutthanti cha catukkāni. Purimehi missetvā ekādasa catukkāni veditabbāni. Eko paṇḍito bhikkhu nisinno hotīti sambandho. Tesūti tīsu bhikkhūsu, gatesu gacchatīti yojanā. Bhutvā āgantvā ṭhitesupi anāpattiyeva. Kasmā sabbesaṃ anāpatti, nanu cattāro bhikkhū ekato gaṇhantīti āha “pañcannaṃ hī”tiādi. Hīti saccaṃ, yasmā vā. Bhojanānaṃyevāti na yāgukhajjakaphalāphalādīnaṃ. Tāni cāti yehi bhojanehi visaṅketaṃ natthi, tāni ca bhojanāni. Tehīti catūhi bhikkhūhi[M 0.0064]. Tānīti yāguādīni. Itīti tasmā anāpattinti yojanā.

‘Gaṇapūrakattā’ (because of completing the group) means because of completing the group at the proper time. ‘Catukkāni’ (groups of four) refers to: the group of four for robe-giving, the group of four for robe-making, the group of four for traveling a journey, the group of four for boarding a boat, the group of four for a great occasion, and the group of four for a meal for ascetics—these are the six groups of four. Mixed with the previous ones, eleven groups of four should be understood. The connection is: ‘One wise monk is seated.’ ‘Tesu’ (among them) means among those three monks; the construction is: ‘when they have gone, he goes.’ Even if they return after eating and are standing, there is still no offense. Why is there no offense for all of them? Is it not that four monks are taking it together? To this, he says, ‘Because of the five,’ and so on. ‘Hi’ means ‘truly’ or ‘because.’ ‘Bhojanānaṃ yeva’ (only of staple foods) means not of gruel, snacks, fruits, and so on. ‘Tāni ca’ (and those) refers to those staple foods for which there is no prior arrangement. ‘Tehi’ (by them) means by the four monks. ‘Tāni’ (those) refers to gruel, and so on. ‘Iti’ (thus); the construction is: ‘therefore, there is no offense.’

Koci pesito apaṇḍitamanusso vadatīti yojanā. Kattukāmena pesitoti sambandho. Bhattaṃ gaṇhathāti vāti vāsaddo “odanaṃ gaṇhatha, bhojanaṃ gaṇhatha, annaṃ gaṇhatha, kuraṃ gaṇhathā”ti vacanānipi saṅgaṇhāti. Nimantanaṃ sādiyantīti nemantanikā. Piṇḍapāte dhutaṅge niyuttāti piṇḍapātikā. Punadivase bhanteti vutteti yojanā. Haritvāti apanetvā. Tatoti tato vadanato paranti sambandho. Vikkhepanti vividhaṃ khepaṃ. Teti asukā ca asukā ca gāmikā. Bhanteti vutteti yojanā. Sopīti apaṇḍitamanussopi, na gāmikāyevāti attho. Kasmā na labhāmi bhanteti vutteti yojanā. Evaṃ “kathaṃ nimantesuṃ bhante”ti etthāpi. Tatoti tasmā kāraṇā. Esāti eso gāmo. Tanti bhūmatthe cetaṃ upayogavacanaṃ, tasmiṃ gāme carathāti hi attho. Kiṃ etenāti etena pucchanena kiṃ payojanaṃ. Etthāti pucchane. Mā pamajjitthāti vadatīti sambandho. Dutiyadivaseti nimantanadivasato dutiyadivase. Dhuragāmeti padhānagāme, antikagāme vā. Bhāvo nāma kiriyattā ekoyeva hoti, tasmā kattāraṃ vā kammaṃ vā sambandhaṃ vā apekkhitvā bahuvacanena na bhavitabbaṃ, tena vuttaṃ “na dubbacehi bhavitabba”nti. Tesūti gāmikesu bhojentesūti sambandho. Asanasālāyanti bhojanasālāyaṃ. Sā hi asati bhuñjati etthāti asanā, salanti pavisanti assanti sālā, asanā ca sā sālāceti asanasālāti atthena “asanasālā”ti vuccati.

The construction is: ‘Some foolish person who has been sent says.’ The connection is with ‘sent by one who wishes to do.’ The word ‘vā’ (or) in ‘Take the meal’ also includes the expressions: ‘take the rice,’ ‘take the food,’ ‘take the grain,’ ‘take the sour gruel.’ Those who accept an invitation are called ‘nemantanikā.’ Those devoted to the ascetic practice of alms-gathering are called ‘piṇḍapātikā.’ The construction is: ‘When on the next day it is said, “Venerable sirs…”’ ‘Haritvā’ means having removed. The connection is: ‘after that,’ meaning after that speech. ‘Vikkhepanti’ means a various scattering. ‘Te’ refers to such and such villagers. The construction is: ‘When it was said, “Venerable sirs…”’ ‘Sopi’ means even that foolish person, not just the villagers—this is the meaning. The construction is: ‘When it was said, “Why do I not receive, venerable sir?”’ Likewise also here: ‘How were they invited, venerable sir?’ ‘Tato’ means for that reason. ‘Esā’ means this village. ‘Taṃ’ is a functional expression here in the sense of location, for the meaning is indeed ‘you should walk in that village.’ ‘Kiṃ etena’ means what is the purpose of this question? ‘Ettha’ means in the question. The connection is: ‘He says, “Do not be negligent.”’ ‘Dutiyadivase’ means on the second day from the day of invitation. ‘Dhuragāme’ means in the main village, or in a nearby village. The state of being, since it is an action, is singular; therefore, it should not be plural with respect to the agent, the object, or the relation. For that reason it is said: ‘One should not be difficult to admonish.’ The connection is: ‘Tesu’ means among the villagers while they are providing food. ‘Asanasālāyaṃ’ means in the dining hall. For ‘asanā’ is so called because one sits and eats there; ‘sālā’ is so called because they go and enter into it; an ‘asanā’ that is a ‘sālā’ is an ‘asanasālā.’ By this meaning it is called ‘asanasālā.’

Atha panāti tato aññathā pana. Apādānattho hi athasaddo. Tattha tatthāti tasmiṃ tasmiṃ [V 1.0054] ṭhāne antaravīthiādīsūti attho. Paṭikaccevāti paṭhamaṃ katvā eva. Bhikkhūsu gāmato anikkhantesu pagevāti vuttaṃ hoti. Na vaṭṭatīti “bhattaṃ gaṇhathā”ti pahiṇattā na vaṭṭati. Ye pana manussā bhojentīti sambandho. Nivattathāti vuttapadeti “nivattathā”ti vutte kiriyāpade. Yassa kassaci [M 0.0065] hotīti yassa kassaci atthāya hotīti yojanā. Nivattituṃ vaṭṭatīti “bhattaṃ gaṇhathā”ti avuttattā nivattituṃ vaṭṭati. Sambandhaṃ katvāti “nivattatha bhante”ti bhantesaddena abyavahitaṃ katvā. Nisīdatha bhante, bhattaṃ gaṇhathāti bhantesaddena byavahitaṃ katvā vutte “nisīdathā”tipade nisīdituṃ vaṭṭati. Atha bhantesaddena byavahitaṃ akatvā “nisīdatha, bhattaṃ gaṇhathā”ti sambandhaṃ katvā vutte nisīdituṃ vaṭṭati. Iccetaṃ nayaṃ atidisati “eseva nayo”tiimināti. Dutiyaṃ.

'Now, then' (atha pana) means otherwise from that. For the word 'atha' has the meaning of separation. 'Here and there' means in each and every place, such as along the road, etc.—this is the meaning. 'Paṭikaccevā' means having done it first. It is said that the monks had not yet left the village, beforehand. It is not proper—because it was sent with the message 'Take the meal,' it is not proper. The connection is with 'but those people who offer food.' Regarding the word 'turn back' (nivattatha), it refers to the verb when 'turn back' is spoken. The connection is 'for anyone' means for the sake of anyone. It is proper to turn back—because 'Take the meal' was not said, it is proper to turn back. 'Having made a connection' means by making it uninterrupted by the word 'bhante,' as in 'Turn back, venerable sirs.' If it is said with interruption by the word 'bhante,' such as 'Sit down, venerable sirs, take the meal,' then it is proper to sit down regarding the word 'sit down.' But if it is said without interruption by the word 'bhante,' connecting it as 'Sit down, take the meal,' then it is proper to sit down. By this, 'this is the very method,' he extends this principle. The second.

3. Paramparabhojanasikkhāpadaṃ

3. The Training Rule on Successive Meals.

221. Tatiye “na kho…pe… karontī”tipāṭhassa atthasambandhaṃ dassento āha “yena niyāmenā”tiādi. Tattha “yena niyāmenā”tiiminā “yathayime manussā”ti ettha yathāsaddassa yaṃsaddatthabhāvaṃ dasseti. Tenāti tena niyāmena. Iminā yathāsaddassa niyamaniddiṭṭhabhāvaṃ dasseti. “Ñāyatī”tiiminā kiriyāpāṭhasesaṃ dasseti. “Sāsanaṃ vā dānaṃ vā”tipadehi idaṃsaddassa atthaṃ dasseti. Buddhappamukhe saṅgheti sampadānatthe cetāni bhummavacanāni, buddhappamukhassa saṅghassa dānaṃ vāti attho. “Paritta”ntiiminā orakasaddassa atthaṃ dasseti. “Lāmaka”ntiiminā parittasaddassa parivāratthaṃ nivatteti. Kiro eva patibhāve niyutto kirapatikoti atthaṃ dassento āha “kirapatikoti etthā”ti ādi. Soti kirapatiko. Kammaṃ kāretīti sambandho. Upacāravasenāti vohāravasena, upalakkhaṇavasena, padhānavasena vāti attho. Na kevalaṃ badarāyeva, aññepi pana bahū khādanīyabhojanīyā paṭiyattāti adhippāyo. Badarena misso badaramisso, badarasāḷavoti āha “badarasāḷavenā”ti. Badaracuṇṇena misso madhusakkharādi “badarasāḷavo”ti vuccati.

221. In the third passage, explaining the connection of meaning in the text “na kho…pe… karontī,” he said, “by which method,” etc. Here, by “by which method” he indicates that “yathā” in “just as these people” has the meaning of “yaṃ.” “By that” means by that method. By this, he shows the defining nature of the word “yathā.” By “ñāyatī” he indicates the remaining verbal portion. By the words “sāsanaṃ vā dānaṃ vā” he conveys the meaning of “idaṃ.” “Buddhappamukhe saṅghe”—these are locative terms in the sense of giving, meaning “a gift to the Sangha headed by the Buddha.” By “paritta” he conveys the meaning of “oraka.” By “lāmaka” he negates the meaning of “surrounding” for “paritta.” To explain the meaning that a kirapatika is one appointed as a substitute, he said, “kirapatiko means here,” etc. “So” means the kirapatika. The connection is with “kammaṃ kāretī.” “Upacāravasena” means by way of common usage, by way of indication, or by way of emphasis. The intended meaning is that not only jujube fruits, but also many other hard and soft foods were prepared. Mixed with jujube is “badaramisso,” and “badarasāḷavo”—thus he said, “badarasāḷavena.” “Badarasāḷavo” is said of something mixed with jujube powder, honey, sugar, etc.

222. Uddhaṃ [M 0.0066] sūro uggato asmiṃ kāleti ussūroti vutte atidivākāloti āha “atidivā”ti.

222. When it is said 'ussūro,' meaning 'the sun has risen high in this time,' he says 'atidivā,' meaning 'it is past midday.'

226. Ayaṃ bhattavikappanā nāma vaṭṭatīti yojanā. Pañcasu sahadhammikesūti niddhāraṇasamudāyo, itthannāmassāti sambandho. Yadi pana sammukhāpi vikappituṃ vaṭṭati, tadā attanā [V 1.0055] saha ṭhitassa bhagavato kasmā na vikappetīti āha “sā cāya”ntiādi. Sā ayaṃ vikappanā saṅgahitāti sambandho. Kasmā bhagavato vikappetuṃ na vaṭṭatīti āha “bhagavati hī”tiādi. Hīti saccaṃ, yasmā vā. Saṅghena katanti sambandho.

226. The explanation is: 'This modification of the meal is permissible.' 'Among five fellow practitioners'—this is the determination of a group; 'of such and such a name'—this is the connection. If it is permissible to modify even in his presence, then why did he not modify it for the Blessed One standing with him? Hence he said, 'And this...' 'And this modification is included'—this is the connection. Why is it not permissible to modify for the Blessed One? He said, 'Because in the Blessed One...' 'For' signifies truth, or because. 'Done by the Sangha'—this is the connection.

229. “Dve tayo nimantane”tipadāni liṅgavipallāsānīti āha “dve tīṇi nimantanānī”ti. Nimantitabbo etehīti nimantanāni bhojanāni bhuñjatīti sambandho. Dve tīṇi kulāni ākirantīti yojanā. Sūpabyañjananti sūpo ca byañjanañca sūpabyañjanaṃ. Anāpatti ekato missitattāti adhippāyo. Mūlanimantananti paṭhamanimantanaṃ bhojanaṃ. Antoti heṭṭhā. Ekampi kabaḷanti ekampi ālopaṃ. Yathā tathā vāti yena vā tena vā ākārena. Tatthāti tasmiṃ bhojane. Rasaṃ vāti khīrato aññaṃ rasaṃ vā. Yena khīrarasena ajjhotthataṃ bhattaṃ ekarasaṃ hoti, taṃ khīraṃ vā taṃ rasaṃ vā ākirantīti yojanā. Yaṃsaddo hi uttaravākye ṭhito pubbavākye taṃsaddaṃ avagamayati. Khīrena saṃsaṭṭhaṃ bhattaṃ khīrabhattaṃ. Evaṃ rasabhattaṃ. Aññepīti khīrabhattarasabhattadāyakato aññepi. Anāpatti bhattena amissitattāti adhippāyo. “Bhuñjantenā”tipadaṃ “bhuñjitu”ntipade bhāvakattā. Sappipāyāsepīti sappinā ca pāyāsena ca kate bhattepi.

229. The phrases 'dve tayo nimantane' are due to gender inversion, hence it is said, 'dve tīṇi nimantanāni.' The connection is that 'nimantanāni' are meals by which one is invited, and one eats them. 'Two or three families contribute'—this is the explanation. 'Soup and curry' means soup and curry together. The intent is that there is no offense because they are mixed together. 'The original invitation' refers to the first meal offered. 'Below' means at the bottom. 'Even a single morsel' means even a single bite. 'In whatever way' means by any means. 'There' refers to that meal. 'Or flavor' means a flavor other than milk. The explanation is that they mix that milk or that flavor by which the rice, soaked in the milk-flavor, becomes of one taste. The word 'which' in the latter clause refers back to the word 'that' in the former clause. Rice mixed with milk is called milk-rice. Similarly, flavored rice. 'Others' refers to others besides those who give milk-rice or flavored rice. The intent is that there is no offense because it is not mixed with the meal. The word 'bhuñjantena' (by one eating) is in the sense of the agent for the word 'bhuñjituṃ' (to eat). 'Even in ghee and milk-rice' means even in a meal prepared with ghee and milk-rice.

Tassāti mahāupāsakassa. Āpattīti ca vaṭṭatīti ca dvinnaṃ aṭṭhakathāvādānaṃ yuttabhāvaṃ mahāpaccarivādena dassetuṃ vuttaṃ “mahāpaccariya”ntiādi. Dve aṭṭhakathāvādā hi sandhāyabhāsitamattameva visesā, atthato pana ekā. Mahāpaccariyaṃ vuttanti sambandho. Ekovāti kumbhiyā ekova. Paramparabhojananti parassa parassa bhojanaṃ[M 0.0067]. Nimantitamhāti ahaṃ nimantito amhi nanūti attho. Āpucchitvāpīti mahāupāsakaṃ āpucchitvāpi.

'His' refers to the great lay devotee. To show the suitability of the two commentary views, 'there is an offense' and 'it is permissible,' it is stated, 'The Mahāpaccariya...' etc., by means of the Mahāpaccari tradition. The two commentary views differ only in their mode of expression; in meaning, however, they are one. 'It is stated in the Mahāpaccariya'—this is the connection. 'Only one' means only one in the cooking pot. 'Successive meals' means the meal of one after another. 'Invited' means, 'I have been invited, have I not?'—this is the meaning. 'Even after asking permission' means even after asking permission of the great lay devotee.

Soti anumodako bhikkhu. Tanti bhikkhuṃ. Aññoti aññataro. Kinti kasmā. Nimantitattāti nimantitabhāvato.

'He' refers to the monk who gives thanks. 'Him' refers to the monk. 'Another' means a certain one. 'Why?' means for what reason. 'Because of being invited' means from the state of having been invited.

Sakalena gāmena nimantitopi ekato hutvāva nimantitassa kappati, na visuṃ visunti āha “ekato hutvā”ti. Pūgepīti samādapetvā puññaṃ karontānaṃ samūhepi. “Nimantiyamāno”tipadassa nimantanākāraṃ dassento āha “bhattaṃ gaṇhā”ti. Yadaggenāti yaṃ aggena yena koṭṭhāsenāti attho. Dvīsu theravādesu mahāsumattheravādova yuttoti so pacchā vuttoti. Tatiyaṃ.

Even when invited by the entire village, it is permissible for one invited only if they have come together, not separately—thus it is said, 'having come together.' 'Even in a group' means even in a group of those who perform meritorious deeds after being exhorted. Showing the manner of the invitation for the word 'being invited,' he says, 'take the meal.' 'By whatever portion' means by which best part, by which share. Among the two Theravāda views, the view of the great elder Sumana is the more appropriate—thus it is stated later. The third.

4. Kāṇamātāsikkhāpadaṃ

4. The Training Rule on Kāṇamātā.

230. Catutthe [V 1.0056] “nakulamātāti”ādīsu (a. ni. 1.266; a. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.266) nakulassa bhagavato mātā nakulamātāti ca nakulañca bhagavato taṃ mātā cāti nakulamātāti ca attho sambhavati, “uttaramātāti”ādīsu uttarāya mātā uttaramātāti atthoyeva sambhavati. Tesu “uttaramātā”tipadasseva “kāṇamātā”tipadassa kāṇāya mātā kāṇamātāti atthoyeva sambhavatīti āha “kāṇāya mātā”ti. Tassā dhītuyā “kāṇā”tināmena vissutabhāvaṃ dassento āha “sā kirā”tiādi. Sāti dārikā vissutā ahosīti sambandho. Assāti mahāupāsikāya. Ye yeti purisā. “Rāgena kāṇā hontī”tiiminā kaṇanti nimilanti rāgena purisā etāyāti kāṇāti atthaṃ dasseti. Tassāti kāṇāya. Āgatanti ettha bhāvatthe toti āha “āgamana”nti. Adhippāyoti “kismiṃ viyā”tipadassa, kāṇamātāya vā adhippāyo[M 0.0068]. Rittāti tucchā, suññāti attho. “Asmiṃ gamane”tiiminā bāhiratthasamāsaṃ dasseti. “Ariyasāvikā”tiādinā ariyānaṃ bhikkhūhi apaṭivibhattabhogaṃ dasseti. Na kevalaṃ kiñci parikkhayaṃ agamāsi, atha kho sabbanti āha “sabbaṃ parikkhayaṃ agamāsī”ti. Kāṇāpīti pisaddo na kevalaṃ mātāyeva maggaphalabhāginī ahosi, atha kho kāṇāpi sotāpannā ahosīti dasseti. Sopi purisoti kāṇāya patibhūto sopi puriso. Pakatiṭṭhāneyevāti jeṭṭhakapajāpatiṭṭhāneyeva.

230. In the fourth section, in phrases such as 'Nakulamātā' (AN 1.266; AN-a 1.1.266), the meaning is possible as 'Nakula’s mother', and also as 'Nakula and she who is the mother of the Blessed One'. In phrases such as 'Uttaramātā', only the meaning 'mother of Uttarā' is possible. For the word 'Kāṇamātā', just as for 'Uttaramātā', only the meaning 'mother of Kāṇā' is possible; thus he says, 'mother of Kāṇā'. To show that her daughter was famous by the name 'Kāṇā', he says, 'She, it is said,' and so on. The connection is that the girl was famous. 'Her' refers to the great laywoman. 'Whoever' refers to the men. The phrase 'they are blinded by lust' indicates the meaning that men are blinded by lust on account of her, and thus she is called 'Kāṇā'. 'Her' refers to Kāṇā. In 'āgatan'ti', the suffix 'to' is in the sense of an abstract noun; thus he says 'āgamanaṃ'. 'The intention' refers to the intention of the phrase 'in what way?' or the intention of Kāṇā’s mother. 'Rittā' means empty, that is, void. The phrase 'on this journey' indicates a compound with an external referent. The phrase 'a noble female disciple' indicates that the possessions of noble ones are undivided with the bhikkhus. It was not that just something was exhausted, but rather everything; thus he says, 'everything was exhausted'. The particle 'pi' in 'Kāṇāpi' indicates that not only did the mother become a partaker of the path and its fruit, but Kāṇā also became a stream-enterer. 'That man also' refers to that man, Kāṇā’s husband. 'In the normal position' means in the position of the chief wife.

231. Imasmiṃ pana vatthusminti imasmiṃ pūvavatthusmiṃ. Etanti pātheyyavatthuṃ. Ariyasāvakattāti ariyabhūtassa sāvakassa bhāvato, ariyassa vā sammāsambuddhassa sāvakabhāvato.

231. ‘But in this matter’ means in this matter concerning the cakes. ‘This’ refers to the matter of provisions. ‘Ariyasāvakatta’ means from the state of being a disciple who has become noble, or from the state of being a disciple of the noble Perfectly Enlightened One.

233. Paheṇakapaṇṇākārasaddānaṃ aññamaññavevacanattā vuttaṃ “paheṇakatthāyāti paṇṇākāratthāyā”ti. Idhāti “pūvehi vā”tipade, sikkhāpade vā. Baddhasattūti madhusakkharādīhi missetvā baddhasattu. Thūpīkatanti thūpīkataṃ katvā.

233. Since the words 'paheṇaka' and 'paṇṇākāra' are synonyms, it is said, '“for the purpose of paheṇaka” means “for the purpose of paṇṇākāra.”' 'Here' refers to the phrase 'or with cakes' or to the training rule. 'Baddhasattu' means flour mixed and bound with honey, sugar, and so on. 'Thūpīkataṃ' means having made it into a heap.

“Dvattipattapūre”tipadassa visesanuttarabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ vuttaṃ “pūre patte”ti. Dve vā tayo vā pattāti dvattipattā, vāsaddatthe saṅkhyobhayabāhiratthasamāso, tisaddaparattā dvissa ca akāro hoti, dvattipattā ca te pūrā cāti dvattipattapūrā, te dvattipattapūre gahetvāti yojanā. “Ācikkhitabba”nti vuttavacanassa ācikkhanākāraṃ dassento āha “atra mayā”tiādi. Tenāpīti [V 1.0057] dutiyenāpi. Paṭhamabhikkhu ekaṃ gahetvā dutiyabhikkhussa ārocanañca dutiyabhikkhu ekaṃ gahetvā tatiyabhikkhussa ārocanañca atidisanto āha “yenā”tiādi. Tattha yenāti paṭhamabhikkhunā. Paṭikkamanti bhuñjītvā etthāti paṭikkamananti vutte asanasālāva gahetabbāti āha “asanasāla”nti. Yatthāti yassaṃ asanasālāyaṃ. Mukholokanaṃ na vaṭṭatīti āha “attano”tiādi. Aññatthāti paṭikkamanato aññattha. Assāti bhikkhussa.

To show that the word 'dvattipattapūre' is a descriptive compound with a subsequent qualifier, it is said, 'pūre patte' (full bowls). 'Dve vā tayo vā pattā' (two or three bowls) becomes 'dvattipattā'; in the sense of 'vā' (or), it is a compound with an external referent involving two numerals. Because the word 'ti' (three) follows, the 'i' of 'dvi' (two) becomes 'a'. 'Dvattipattā' (two or three bowls) and those are full—thus, 'dvattipattapūrā' (two or three full bowls). The construction is: 'having taken those two or three full bowls'. To show the manner of declaration for the stated phrase 'should be declared', he says, 'here by me,' and so on. 'Tenāpi' means 'by the second one as well'. Extending the principle whereby the first monk, having taken one, informs the second monk, and the second monk, having taken one, informs the third monk, he says, 'by whom,' and so on. Here, 'by whom' means by the first monk. A place where 'they return' (paṭikkamanti) after eating is a 'paṭikkamana'; when 'paṭikkamana' is mentioned, the refectory should be understood. Thus, it is said, 'asanasāla' (refectory). 'Yattha' means 'in which refectory'. 'Looking at faces is not proper'; thus, it is said, 'one’s own,' and so on. 'Aññattha' means 'elsewhere,' that is, other than from the place of return. 'Assa' means 'of the monk'.

“Saṃvibhajitabba”nti [M 0.0069] vuttavacanassa saṃvibhajanākāraṃ dassetuṃ vuttaṃ “sace tayo”tiādi. Yathāmittanti yassa yassa mittassa. Akāmāti na kāmena. Kāraṇatthe cetaṃ nissakkavacanaṃ.

To show the manner of sharing indicated by the phrase 'saṃvibhajitabbaṃ' (it is to be shared), it is said, 'sace tayo' (if there are three), etc. 'Yathāmittaṃ' means 'to whichever friend'. 'Akāmā' means 'not through desire'. And this is an ablative case in the sense of a cause.

235. Antarāmaggeti maggassa antaro antarāmaggo, sukhuccāraṇatthaṃ majjhe dīgho, tasmiṃ. Bahumpi dentānaṃ etesaṃ ñātakapavāritānaṃ bahumpi paṭiggaṇhantassāti yojanā. Aṭṭhakathāsu pana vuttanti sambandho. Aṭṭhakathānaṃ vacanaṃ pāḷiyā na sametīti. Catutthaṃ.

235. 'Antarāmagge' means within the path; for ease of pronunciation, the vowel in the middle is lengthened; 'in that'. The construction is: 'of one who is receiving much, even from these invited relatives who are giving much'. The connection is that it is said in the commentaries. The statement of the commentaries does not agree with the Pāli text. The fourth section is concluded.

5. Paṭhamapavāraṇasikkhāpadaṃ

5. The First Training Rule on Invitation

236. Pañcame pavāritāti ettha vassaṃvutthapavāraṇā, paccayapavāraṇā, paṭikkhepapavāraṇā, yāvadatthapavāraṇā cāti catubbidhāsu pavāraṇāsu yāvadatthapavāraṇā ca paṭikkhepapavāraṇā cāti dve pavāraṇā adhippetāti dassento āha “brāhmaṇenā”tiādi. Brāhmaṇena pavāritāti sambandho. Sayanti tatiyantanipāto “pavāritā”tipadena sambandho. Casaddo aññattha yojetabbo yāvadatthapavāraṇāya ca paṭikkhepapavāraṇāya cāti. Paṭimukhaṃ attano gehaṃ visanti pavisantīti paṭivissakāti vutte āsannagehavāsikā gahetabbāti āha “sāmantagharavāsike”ti.

236. In the fifth section, concerning 'pavāritā', it is shown that among the four kinds of invitation—namely, the invitation after completing the rains retreat, the invitation for requisites, the invitation of refusal, and the invitation for as much as one needs—the two intended are the invitation for as much as one needs and the invitation of refusal. To show this, it is said, 'by the brahmin,' etc. The connection is 'invited by the brahmin'. 'Sayaṃ' is a particle that functions as an instrumental and is connected with the word 'pavāritā'. The word 'ca' should be connected elsewhere, namely, to 'the invitation for as much as one needs' and to 'the invitation of refusal'. When 'paṭivissakā' is said, which means 'they enter their own homes facing them', those dwelling in neighboring houses are to be understood. Thus, it is said, 'sāmantagharavāsike' (those dwelling in nearby houses).

237. Uddhaṅgamo ravo oravo, soyeva saddo oravasaddo, kākānaṃ oravasaddo kakoravasaddoti dassento āha “kākāna”ntiādi.

237. An upward-going sound is 'orava'; that same sound is 'oravasadda'. Showing that the 'oravasadda' of crows is 'kakoravasadda', it is said, 'of the crows,' etc.

239. Tavantupaccayassa atītatthabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ vuttaṃ “tattha cā”tiādi. Tatthāti “bhuttavā”tipade. Yasmā yena bhikkhunā ajjhoharitaṃ hoti, tasmā so “bhuttāvī”ti saṅkhyaṃ gacchatīti [V 1.0058] yojanā. Saṅkhāditvāti dantehi cuṇṇaṃ katvā. Tenāti tena hetunā. Assāti “bhuttāvī”tipadassa. Pavāreti paṭikkhipatīti pavārito bhikkhūti dassento āha “katapavāraṇo”ti. Sopi cāti so paṭikkhepo ca hotīti sambandho. Assāti “pavārito”tipadassa. Tatthāti “asanaṃ paññāyatī”tiādivacane. Yasmā [M 0.0070] bhuttāvītipi saṅkhyaṃ gacchati, tasmā na passāmāti yojanā. “Asanaṃ paññāyatī”ti padabhājaniyā “bhuttāvī”ti mātikāpadassa asaṃsandanabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ vuttaṃ “asanaṃ paññāyatīti iminā”tiādi. Yañcāti yañca bhojanaṃ. Dirattādīti ettha ādisaddena pañcādivacanaṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Etanti “bhuttāvī”tipadaṃ.

239. To show the past tense meaning of the suffix 'tavantu', it is said, 'and there,' etc. Here, 'tattha' refers to the word 'bhuttavā'. The construction is: 'Because it has been ingested by a monk, therefore he is counted as ‘bhuttāvī’ (one who has eaten)'. 'Saṅkhāditvā' means 'having crushed with the teeth'. 'Tena' means 'for that reason'. 'Its' refers to the word 'bhuttāvī'. Showing that 'pavāreti' means 'he refuses', and thus 'pavārito' means 'a monk who has refused', he says, 'katapavāraṇo' (one who has made a refusal). The connection is that 'sopi ca' means 'that refusal also occurs'. 'Its' refers to the word 'pavārito'. 'Tattha' refers to the phrase 'food is evident,' etc. The construction is: 'Because one is also counted as ‘bhuttāvī’, therefore we do not see it'. To show the lack of correspondence between the phrase 'food is evident' in the word-analysis (padabhājaniyā) and the headword (mātikāpada) 'bhuttāvī', it is said, 'by this "food is evident," etc.'. 'Yañca' means 'whatever food'. Here, by the word 'ādi' in 'dirattādi' (two nights, etc.), five nights, etc., are included. 'Etaṃ' refers to the word 'bhuttāvī'.

“Asanaṃ paññāyatī”tiādīsu vinicchayo evaṃ veditabboti sambandho. “Paññāyatī”ti ettha ñādhātuyā khāyanatthaṃ dassetuṃ vuttaṃ “dissatī”ti. “Hatthapāse”tipadassa dvādasahatthappamāṇo hatthapāso nādhippetoti āha “aḍḍhateyyahatthappamāṇe”ti. Vācāya abhiharaṇaṃ nādhippetaṃ. Tenāha “kāyenā”ti. Abhiharatīti abhimukhaṃ harati. Tanti bhojanaṃ. Etanti pañcaṅgabhāvaṃ, “pañcahi…pe… paññāyatī”ti vacanaṃ vā.

The connection is that the determination in phrases like 'asanaṃ paññāyatī' (food is evident) should be understood thus. To show that the root 'ñā' in 'paññāyatī' has the meaning of 'appearing', it is said, 'dissatī' (is seen). The word 'hatthapāse' (within arm’s reach) does not refer to a distance of twelve hands; thus, it is said, 'aḍḍhateyyahatthappamāṇe' (a measure of two and a half hands). Bringing near by speech is not intended. Therefore, it is said, 'kāyena' (by body). 'Abhiharati' means 'he brings near'. 'Taṃ' means 'that food'. 'Etaṃ' refers to the state of being five-fold, or the statement 'pañcahi…pe… paññāyatī' (by five…etc…is evident).

Tatrāti “asanaṃ paññāyatī”tiādivacane. Asnātīti kīyādigaṇattā, tassa ca ekakkharadhātuttā sakāranakārānaṃ saṃyogo daṭṭhabbo. Tanti bhojanaṃ. Undati pasavati bhuñjantānaṃ āyubalaṃ janetīti odano. Yavādayo pūtiṃ katvā katattā kucchitena masīyati āmasīyatīti kumāso. Sacati samavāyo hutvā bhavatīti sattu. Byañjanatthāya māretabboti maccho. Mānīyati bhuñjantehīti maṃsaṃ. Tatthāti odanādīsu pañcasu bhojanesu. Sāro assatthi aññesaṃ dhaññānanti sālī. Vahati bhuñjantānaṃ jīvitanti vīhi. Yavati amissitopi missito viya bhavatīti yavo. Gudhati pariveṭhati milakkhabhojanattāti godhumo. Sobhanasīsattā kamanīyabhāvaṃ gacchatīti kaṅgu. Mahantasīsattā, madhurarasanāḷattā ca varīyati patthīyati janehīti varako. Koraṃ rudhiraṃ dūsati bhuñjantānanti kudrūsako. Nibbatto odano nāmāti sambandho. Tatthāti sattasu dhaññesu. Sālītīti ettha itisaddo nāmapariyāyo. Sālī nāmāti attho. Eseva nayo “vīhītī”tiādīsupi.

Therein, in the phrase “asanaṃ paññāyatī” (food is evident), etc. “Asnāti” belongs to the kīyādi group of roots, and since it is a single-syllable root, the combination of the letters ‘s’ and ‘n’ should be understood. “Taṃ” means “that food.” Because it moistens (undati) or produces (pasavati), generating life and strength for those who eat it, it is “odano” (cooked rice). Grains like barley, when made rotten and then prepared, are poorly mashed or kneaded—thus, “kumāso” (fermented gruel). Because it adheres (sacati), coming together to exist, it is “sattu” (flour). It is to be killed for the purpose of a relish—thus, “maccho” (fish). It is esteemed by those who eat it—thus, “maṃsaṃ” (meat). “Tattha” refers to these five kinds of food: cooked rice, etc. “Sālī” (fine rice) means it has essence among other grains. “Vīhi” (common rice) means it sustains the life of those who eat it. “Yavo” (barley) means even when unmixed, it appears as if mixed. “Godhumo” (wheat) means it is wrapped up, being the food of barbarians. “Kaṅgu” (millet) means because of its beautiful head, it becomes desirable. “Varako” (a type of grain) means because of its large head and sweet stalk, it is desired by people. “Kudrūsako” (a type of grain) means it corrupts the blood of those who eat it. The connection is that what is produced (nibbatto) is called cooked rice. “Tattha” refers to these seven grains. In “sālīti,” the word “iti” is a synonym for “name.” The meaning is “named sālī.” The same method applies to phrases like “vīhīti,” etc.

Etthāti [M 0.0071] tiṇadhaññajātīsu. Nīvāro sāliyā anulomo, varakacorako varakassa anulomo. Ambilapāyāsādīsūti ettha ādisaddena khīrabhattādayo saṅgaṇhanti. Odhīti avadhi, mariyādoti attho. So hi avahīyati cajīyati asmāti odhīti vuccati.

Here, in “tiṇadhaññajātīsu,” it refers to types of grass-grain. Nīvāra (wild rice) is similar to sālī (fine rice), and varakacoraka (a type of grain) is similar to varaka (another type of grain). In “ambilapāyāsādīsu” (in sour milk-rice, etc.), the word “ādi” (etc.) includes milk-rice, etc. “Odhī” means “avadhi” (limit) or “mariyāda” (boundary). For it is left behind (avahīyati) or relinquished from it—thus it is called “odhī” (boundary).

Yopi [V 1.0059] pāyāso vā yāpi ambilayāgu vā odhiṃ na dasseti, so pavāraṇaṃ na janetīti yojanā. Payena khīrena katattā pāyāso. Pātabbassa, asitabbassa cāti dvinnaṃ byuppattinimittānaṃ sambhavato vā pāyāsoti vuccati. Uddhanatoti cullito. Sā hi upari dhīyanti ṭhapiyanti thālyādayo etthāti uddhananti vuccati. Āvajjitvāti pariṇāmetvā. Ghanabhāvanti kathinabhāvaṃ. Etthāpi vākye “yo so”ti padāni yojetabbāni. Pubbeti abbhuṇhakāle. Nimantaneti nimantanaṭṭhāne. Bhatte ākiritvā dentīti sambandho. Yāpanaṃ gacchati imāyāti yāgu. Kiñcāpi tanukā hoti, tathāpīti yojanā. Udakādīsūtiādisaddena kiñjikakhīrādayo saṅgayhanti. Yāgusaṅgahameva gacchati, kasmā? Udakādīnaṃ pakkuthitattāti adhippāyo. Tasmiṃ vāti sabhatte, pakkuthitaudakādike vā. Aññasmiṃ vāti pakkuthitaudakādito aññasmiṃ udakādike vā. Yattha yasmiṃ udakādike pakkhipanti, taṃ pavāraṇaṃ janetīti yojanā.

Whatever milk-rice or sour gruel does not show the bottom, that does not occasion the pavāraṇā—this is the connection. Because it is made with milk (payas/khīra), it is called pāyāso (milk-rice). Or it is called pāyāso from the possibility of two etymological derivations: being drinkable and being edible. Uddhana means a hearth. For vessels like cooking pots are placed or set upon it, hence it is called uddhana. Āvajjitvā means having transformed. Ghanabhāva means a solid state. Here too, in the sentence, the words “yo so” should be connected. Pubbe means in the early morning. Nimantane means at the place of invitation. The connection is that they give it after having sprinkled it on the food. Gruel (yāgu) is so called because one is sustained (yāpanaṃ gacchati) by it. Even though it is thin, still—this is the connection. In “water, etc.”—by the word “etc.,” things like fermented rice-gruel and milk are included. It is included only as gruel. Why? The meaning is: because the water, etc., have been cooked. “In that” means in the meal with its food, or in the cooked water, etc. “Or in another” means in other water, etc., apart from the cooked water, etc. In whatever water, etc., they place it, that occasions the pavāraṇā—this is the connection.

Suddharasakoti macchamaṃsakhaṇḍanhārūhi amisso suddho macchādirasako. Rasakayāgūti rasakabhūtā dravabhūtā yāgu. Ghanayāgūti kathinayāgu. Etthāti ghanayāguyaṃ. Pupphiatthāyāti pupphaṃ phullaṃ imassa khajjakassāti pupphī, pupphino attho payojanaṃ pupphiattho, tadatthāya katanti sambandho. Te taṇḍuleti te seditataṇḍule. Acuṇṇattā neva sattusaṅkhyaṃ, apakkattā na bhattasaṅkhyaṃ gacchanti. Tehīti seditataṇḍulehi. Te taṇḍule pacanti, karontīti sambandho.

Pure essence means the pure essence of fish, etc., unmixed with pieces of fish, meat, or sinews. Rasakayāgu means gruel that has become essence, that has become liquid. Ghanayāgu means thick gruel. Ettha means in thick gruel. For the purpose of a flower-shape (pupphiatthāya): a food that has a flower or bloom is pupphī. The purpose (attho) of the pupphī is pupphiattho. The connection is: made for that purpose. Te taṇḍule means those steamed rice grains. Because they are not ground, they do not count as flour; because they are not cooked, they do not count as cooked rice. Tehi means with those steamed rice grains. The connection is: they cook or prepare those rice grains.

“Yavehī”ti bahuvacanena satta dhaññānipi gahitāni. Esa nayo sālivīhiyavehīti etthāpi. Thuseti dhaññatace. Palāpetvāti paṭikkamāpetvā[M 0.0072]. Tanti cuṇṇaṃ gacchatīti sambandho. Kharapākabhajjitānanti kharo pāko kharapāko, kharapākena bhajjitā kharapākabhajjitā, tesaṃ. Na pavārenti asattusaṅgahattāti adhippāyo. Kuṇḍakampīti kaṇampi. Pavāreti sattusaṅgahattāti adhippāyo. Tehīti lājehi. Suddhakhajjakanti piṭṭhehi amissitaṃ suddhaṃ phalāphalādikhajjakaṃ. Yāguṃ pivantassa dentīti yojanā. Tānīti dve macchamaṃsakhaṇḍāni. Na pavāreti dvinnaṃ macchamaṃsakhaṇḍānaṃ akhāditattāti adhippāyo. Tatoti dvemacchamaṃsakhaṇḍato nīharitvā ekanti sambandho, tesu vā. Soti khādako bhikkhu. Aññanti dvīhi macchamaṃsakhaṇḍehi aññaṃ pavāraṇapahonakaṃ bhojanaṃ.

By “yavehī” (with barley) in the plural, the seven types of grains are also included. This same method applies also in “sālivīhiyavehī” (with fine rice, common rice, and barley). Thuseti means on the husk of the grain. Palāpetvā means having removed. The connection is: it becomes flour. Of those harshly fried (kharapākabhajjitānaṃ): harsh cooking is kharapāko; fried with harsh cooking is kharapākabhajjitā; “of those” refers to them. The meaning is: they do not occasion the pavāraṇā because they are not included as flour. Kuṇḍakampi means even bran. The meaning is: it occasions the pavāraṇā because it is included as flour. Tehīti means with parched grains. Suddhakhajjakaṃ means pure hard food, such as various fruits, unmixed with flour. The construction is: they give it to one who is drinking gruel. Tāni means the two pieces of fish and meat. The meaning is: it does not occasion the pavāraṇā because the two pieces of fish and meat have not been eaten. Tato means having taken one from the two pieces of fish and meat, or from among them; this is the connection. So means the monk who is eating. Aññaṃ means other food sufficient for the pavāraṇā, apart from the two pieces of fish and meat.

Avatthutāyāti pavāraṇāya avatthubhāvato. Taṃ vitthārento āha “yaṃ hī”ti. Hisaddo vitthārajotako. Yanti maṃsaṃ. Idaṃ panāti idaṃ maṃsaṃ pana. Paṭikkhittamaṃsaṃ kappiyabhāvato apaṭikkhipitabbaṭṭhāne [V 1.0060] ṭhitattā paṭikkhittampi maṃsabhāvaṃ na jahāti. Nanu khāditamaṃsaṃ pana akappiyabhāvato paṭikkhipitabbaṭṭhāne ṭhitattā khādiyamānampi maṃsabhāvaṃ jahātīti āha “yaṃ panā”tiādi. Kuladūsakakammañca vejjakammañca uttarimanussadhammārocanañca sāditarūpiyañca kula…pe… rūpiyāni, tāni ādīni yesaṃ kuhanādīnanti kula…pe… rūpiyādayo, tehi. Sabbatthāti sabbesu vāresu.

Avatthutāya means because of being without a basis for the pavāraṇā. Explaining this in detail, he says, “yaṃ hī.” The word “hi” illuminates the expansion. Yaṃ means meat. Idaṃ pana means but this meat. Rejected meat, even though rejected, does not lose its nature as meat, because it is permissible and stands in a position where it should not be rejected. He says “yaṃ panā,” etc., to show that eaten meat, on the other hand, being impermissible and standing in a position where it should be rejected, does lose its nature as meat even while being eaten. By means of those things beginning with family-corrupting actions… etc… and silver, which have deceit, etc., as their beginning, namely: the act of corrupting families, the act of being a physician, the announcement of a superior human state, and accepted silver. Sabbatthāti means on all occasions.

Evantiādi nigamananidassanaṃ. Tanti bhojanaṃ. Yathāti yenākārena. Yena ajjhohaṭaṃ hoti, so paṭikkhipati pavāretīti yojanā. Katthacīti kismiñci pattādike. Tasmiṃ ce antareti tasmiṃ khaṇe ce. Aññatrāti aññasmiṃ ṭhāne. Patte vijjamānabhojanaṃ anajjhoharitukāmo hoti yathā, evanti yojanā. Hīti saccaṃ. Sabbatthāti sabbesu padesu. Tatthāti kurundīyaṃ. Ānisadassāti āgamma nisīdati etenāti ānisado, tassa pacchimantatoti sambandho. Paṇhiantatoti pasati ṭhitakāle vā gamanakāle [M 0.0073] vā bhūmiṃ phusatīti paṇhī, tassa antato. “Dāyakassā”tipadaṃ “pasāritahattha”nti padena ca “aṅga”nti padena ca avayavīsambandho. Hatthapāsoti hatthassa pāso samīpo hatthapāso, hattho pasati phusati asmiṃ ṭhāneti vā hatthapāso, aḍḍhateyyahattho padeso. Tasminti hatthapāse.

Evaṃ, etc., is the concluding illustration. Taṃ means that food. Yathā means in whatever manner. The construction is: the one by whom it has been consumed is the one who rejects or makes the pavāraṇā. Katthaci means in some receptacle, such as a bowl. Tasmiṃ ce antare means if at that moment. Aññatra means in another place. The connection is: just as one is unwilling to consume the food present in the bowl, so it is. Hīti means truly. Sabbatthāti means in all places. Tatthāti means in the Kurundī commentary. Of the seat (ānisadassa): one comes and sits (āgamma nisīdati) with this, thus it is a seat (ānisado); the connection is to its latter end. From the end of the heel (paṇhiantato): the heel (paṇhī) is so called because it touches the ground while standing or walking; from its end. The word “dāyakassa” has a genitive relationship (of the whole to its parts) with the words “pasāritahattha” and “aṅga.” Hatthapāso means the proximity (pāso) of the hand is hatthapāso; or, the hand touches (pasati) in this place, thus it is hatthapāso, a space of two and a half cubits. Tasmiṃ means in that hatthapāso.

Upanāmetīti samīpaṃ nāmeti. Anantaranisinnopīti hatthapāsaṃ avijahitvā anantare ṭhāne nisinnopi bhikkhu vadatīti yojanā. Bhattapacchinti bhattena pakkhittaṃ pacchiṃ. Īsakanti bhāvanapuṃsakaṃ. Uddharitvā vā apanāmetvā vāti sambandhitabbaṃ. Dūreti navāsane. Itoti pattato. Gato dūtoti sambandho.

Upanāmeti means he brings it near. Anantaranisinnopi: the construction is: even a monk seated in an adjacent place, without leaving arm’s reach, speaks. Bhattapacchi means a basket into which food has been placed. Īsakaṃ is an adverbial neuter. It should be connected as: having lifted it or having removed it. Dūre means on a new seat. Ito means from the bowl. The connection is: gone far away.

Parivesanāyāti parivesanatthāya, bhattagge vā. Tatrāti asmiṃ parivesane. Tanti bhattapacchiṃ. Phuṭṭhamattāvāti phusiyamattāva. Kaṭacchunā uddhaṭabhatte pana pavāraṇā hotīti yojanā. Hīti saccaṃ, yasmā vā. Tassāti parivesakassa. Abhihaṭe paṭikkhittattāti abhihaṭassa bhattassa paṭikkhittabhāvato.

'For serving' means for the purpose of serving, or in the dining hall. 'There' means in this serving. 'That' refers to the food basket. 'Just touched' means just having been touched. The explanation is that an invitation occurs when food is lifted out with a ladle. 'Hi' means truly, or because. 'His' means of the server. 'Because of being refused when offered' means because of the state of the offered food having been refused.

“Kāyena vācāya vā paṭikkhipantassa pavāraṇā hotī”ti saṅkhepena vuttamatthaṃ vitthārena dassento āha “tatthā”tiādi. Tatthāti tesu kāyavācāpaṭikkhepesu. Macchikabījaninti makkhikānaṃ uttāsaniṃ bījaniṃ. Khakārassa hi chakāraṃ katvā “macchikā”ti vuccati “sacchikatvā”tiādīsu [V 1.0061] viya (a. ni. 3.103). Ettha hi “sakkhikatvā”ti vattabbe khakārassa chakāro hoti.

To explain in detail the meaning stated briefly as, 'For one who rejects with body or speech, an invitation occurs,' he said, 'there,' and so on. 'There' means among these rejections by body and speech. 'A fly-whisk' means a fan for scaring away flies. For by making the letter 'kha' into 'cha', it is called 'macchikā', just as in instances like 'sacchikatvā' (AN 3.103). Here, indeed, where 'sakkhikatvā' should be said, the 'kha' becomes 'cha'.

Eko vadatīti sambandho. Apanetvāti pattato apanetvā. Etthāti vacane. Kathanti kenākārena hotīti yojanā. Vadantassa nāmāti ettha nāmasaddo garahattho “atthī”tipadena yojetabbo. Atthi nāmāti attho. Itopīti pattatopi. Tatrāpīti tasmiṃ vacanepi.

One speaks—this is the connection. 'Having removed' means having removed from the bowl. 'Here' refers to the statement. 'How' means in what manner it happens—this is the explanation. 'For one who speaks, nāma'—here the word 'nāma' has a pejorative sense and should be connected with the word 'atthi'. The meaning is 'there is indeed'. 'From this too' means even from the bowl. 'There too' means in that statement too.

Samaṃsakanti maṃsena saha pavattaṃ. Rasanti dravaṃ. Tanti vacanaṃ. Paṭikkhipato hoti. Kasmā? Maccho ca raso ca macchena misso raso [M 0.0074] cāti atthassa sambhavato. Idanti vatthuṃ. Maṃsaṃ visuṃ katvāti “maṃsassa rasaṃ maṃsarasa”nti maṃsapadatthassa padhānabhāvaṃ akatvā, rasapadatthasseva padhānabhāvaṃ katvāti attho.

'With meat' means occurring with meat. 'Juice' means liquid. 'That' means the statement. It is a rejection. Why? Because of the possibility of the meaning being fish and juice, or juice mixed with fish. 'This' means the object. 'Having separated the meat' means that in the compound 'meat-juice', one does not make the meaning of the word 'meat' primary, but makes the meaning of the word 'juice' primary—this is the meaning.

Āpucchantanti “maṃsarasaṃ gaṇhathā”ti āpucchantaṃ. Tanti maṃsaṃ. Karambakoti missakādhivacanametaṃ. Yañhi aññena aññena missetvā karonti, so “karambako”ti vuccati. Ayaṃ panettha vacanattho – karoti samūhaṃ avayavinti karo, karīyati vā samūhena avayavināti karo, avayavo, taṃ vakati ādadātīti karambako, samūho. “Kadambako”tipi pāṭho, sopi yuttoyeva anumatattā paṇḍitehi. Abhidhānepi evameva atthī. Attho pana aññathā cintetabbo. Imasmiṃ vā atthe rakārassa dakāro kātabbo. Maṃsena misso, lakkhito vā karambako maṃsakarambako. Na pavāretīti yesaṃ kesañci missakattā na pavāreti. Pavāretīti maṃsena missitattā pavāreti.

'Asking' means asking, 'Will you take meat broth?'. 'That' means meat. 'Karambaka' is a term for a mixture. For whatever is made by mixing one thing with another is called 'karambaka'. Herein, this is the word-meaning: because it makes a collection of parts, it is 'kara'; or, because a whole is made by a collection, it is 'kara', a part; because it takes that, it is 'karambaka', a collection. 'Kadambaka' is also a variant reading, and it is proper, being approved by the wise. It is also thus in the lexicon. The meaning, however, should be considered otherwise. Or, in this meaning, the letter 'ra' should be made into 'da'. A 'meat-karambaka' is a karambaka mixed with, or designated by, meat. 'He does not invite' means: because it is a mixture of just anything, he does not invite. 'He invites' means: because it is mixed with meat, he invites.

Yo pana paṭikkhipati, so pavāritova hotīti yojanā. Nimantaneti nimantanaṭṭhāne. Hīti saccaṃ. Tatthāti kurundiyaṃ. Yenāti yena bhattena. Etthāti “yāguṃ gaṇhathā”tiādivacane. Adhippāyoti aṭṭhakathācariyānaṃ adhippāyo. Etthāti “yāgumissakaṃ gaṇhathā”tiādivacane. Duddasanti dukkaraṃ dassanaṃ. Idañcāti “missakaṃ gaṇhathā”tivacanañca. Na samānetabbanti samaṃ na ānetabbaṃ, samānaṃ vā na kātabbaṃ. Hīti saccaṃ, yasmā vā. Idaṃ panāti missakaṃ pana. Etthāti missake. Visuṃ katvāti rasakhīrasappīni āveṇiṃ katvā. Tanti rasādiṃ.

The explanation is: whoever refuses, he is indeed considered to have been invited. 'At an invitation' means at the place of invitation. 'Hi' means truly. 'There' means in the Kurundī commentary. 'By which' means by which food. 'Here' means in a statement such as, 'Take the rice-gruel'. 'Intention' means the intention of the commentary teachers. 'Here' means in a statement such as, 'Take the mixed rice-gruel'. 'Difficult to see' means difficult of seeing. 'And this' means the statement, 'Take the mixture'. 'Should not be made equal' means should not be brought as equal, or should not be made equal. 'Hi' means truly, or because. 'But this' means but the mixture. 'Here' means in the mixture. 'Having separated' means having made the juice, milk, and ghee distinct. 'That' means the juice, etc.

Kaddīyati maddīyatīti kaddamo. Undati pasavati vaḍḍhatīti udakaṃ. Undati vā kledanaṃ karotīti [V 1.0062] udakaṃ, nilīne satte gupati rakkhatīti gumbo, guhati saṃvaratīti vā gumbo. Anupariyāyantenāti anukkamena parivattitvā [M 0.0075] āyantena. Tanti nāvaṃ vā setuṃ vā. Majjhanhikanti ahassa majjhaṃ majjhanhaṃ, ahasaddassa nhādeso, majjhanhaṃ eva majjhanhikaṃ. Potthakesu pana majjhantikanti pāṭho atthi, so apāṭhoyeva. Yo ṭhito pavāreti, tena ṭhiteneva bhuñjitabbanti yojanā. Ānisadanti pīṭhe phuṭṭhaānisadamaṃsaṃ. Acāletvāti acāvetvā. Ayameva vā pāṭho. Upari ca passesu ca amocetvāti vuttaṃ hoti. Adinnādāne viya ṭhānācāvanaṃ na veditabbaṃ. Saṃsaritunti saṃsabbituṃ. Nanti bhikkhuṃ.

Because it is dragged and trampled, it is 'mud'. Because it flows, produces, and grows, it is 'water'. Or, because it flows and moistens, it is 'water'. Because it protects and guards beings that hide therein, it is a 'thicket'; or because it conceals and covers, it is a 'thicket'. 'By going around in order' means by turning around sequentially and arriving. 'That' means either a boat or a bridge. 'Midday' means: the middle of the day is 'majjhanha'; 'nha' is a substitute for the word 'aha'; 'majjhanha' itself is 'majjhanhika'. In books, however, there is the reading 'majjhantika', but that is a wrong reading. The explanation is: one who invites while standing, by him, while standing, it should be eaten. 'Buttocks' means the flesh of the buttocks touching the seat. 'Without moving' means without dislodging. Or this is the reading itself. It means 'without releasing above and on the sides'. Dislodging from a place should not be understood as in the case of taking what is not given. 'To rub' means to rub together. 'Him' means the monk.

Atirekaṃ ricati gacchatīti atirittaṃ, na atirittaṃ anatirittanti atthaṃ dassento āha “na atiritta”nti. “Adhika”ntiiminā atirittasaddassa atisuññatthaṃ nivatteti. Adhi hutvā eti pavattatīti adhikaṃ. Taṃ panāti anatirittaṃ pana hotīti sambandho. Tatthāti “akappiyakata”ntiādivacane. Vitthāro evaṃ veditabboti yojanā. Tatthāti atirittaṃ kātabbesu vatthūsu. Yaṃ phalaṃ vā yaṃ kandamūlādi vā akatanti yojanā. Akappiyabhojanaṃ vāti kuladūsakakammādīhi nibbattaṃ akappiyabhojanaṃ vā atthīti sambandho. Yoti vinayadharo bhikkhu. Tena katanti yojanā. “Bhuttāvinā pavāritena āsanā vuṭṭhitena kata”ntivacanato bhuttāvinā apavāritena āsanā vuṭṭhitena kattabbanti siddhaṃ. Tasmā pāto addhānaṃ gacchantesu dvīsu eko pavārito, tassa itaro piṇḍāya caritvā laddhaṃ bhikkhaṃ attanā abhutvāpi “alametaṃ sabba”nti kātuṃ labhati eva. Yanti khādanīyabhojanīyaṃ. “Tadubhayampī”tiiminā atirittañca atirittañca atirittaṃ, na atirittaṃ anatirittanti atthaṃ dasseti.

Because it goes beyond and surpasses, it is 'excessive'; showing the meaning of 'not excessive' as 'non-excessive', he says, 'not excessive'. By the word 'additional', he negates the meaning of 'completely empty' for the word 'excessive'. Because it exists as superior and proceeds, it is 'additional'. The connection is: 'but that' means 'but it is non-excessive'. 'There' means in the statement beginning with 'made unallowable'. The explanation is: the detailed explanation should be understood thus. 'There' means among the things to be made excessive. The explanation is: whatever fruit or whatever root, etc., is not made so. The connection is: 'or unallowable food' means there is unallowable food produced by actions such as corrupting families. 'Who' means the Vinaya-holding monk. The explanation is: 'done by him'. From the statement, 'done by one who has eaten, has been invited, and has risen from his seat', it is established that it should be done by one who has eaten, has not been invited, and has risen from his seat. Therefore, in the morning, when two are traveling, if one has been invited, the other, having gone for alms and obtained food, even without eating it himself, is indeed able to make it so by saying, 'This is enough for all'. 'What' means edible or consumable food. By 'both of these', it shows the meaning that what is excessive is excessive, and what is not excessive is non-excessive.

Tassevāti anatirittasseva. Etthāti anatiritte, “kappiyakata”nti ādīsu sattasu vinayakammākāresu vā. Anantareti vinayadharassa anantare āsane. Pattato nīharitvāti sambandho. Tatthevāti bhuñjanaṭṭhāneyeva. Tassāti nisinnassa. Tenāti bhattaṃ ānentena bhikkhunā bhuñjitabbanti yojanā. “Nisinnena bhikkhunā”ti kāritakammaṃ [M 0.0076] ānetabbaṃ. Kasmā “hatthaṃ dhovitvā”ti vuttanti pucchanto āha “kasmā”ti. Hīti kāraṇaṃ. Yasmā akappiyaṃ hoti, tasmā hatthaṃ dhovitvāti mayā vuttanti adhippāyo. Tassāti bhattaṃ ānentassa. Yenāti vinayadharena. Puna yenāti evameva. Yañcāti khādanīyabhojanīyañca. Yena vinayadharena paṭhamaṃ akataṃ, teneva kattabbaṃ. Yañca khādanīyabhojanīyaṃ paṭhamaṃ akataṃ, taññeva kattabbanti vuttaṃ hoti[V 1.0063]. Tatthāti paṭhamabhājane. Hīti saccaṃ. Paṭhamabhājanaṃ suddhaṃ dhovitvā katampi niddosameva. Tena bhikkhunāti pavāritena bhikkhunā.

'Of that very one' means of the non-excessive itself. 'Here' means in the non-excessive, or in the seven types of Vinaya procedures such as 'made allowable'. 'Immediately next' means in the seat immediately next to the Vinaya expert. The connection is 'having removed from the bowl'. 'Right there' means in the eating place itself. 'Of him' means of the one seated. The explanation is: 'by him' means it should be eaten by the monk who brings the food. The causative action 'by the seated monk' must be supplied. Asking, 'Why is it said, "having washed the hands"?', he says, 'Why?'. 'Hi' means the reason. The intention is: 'Because it is unallowable, therefore it was said by me, "having washed the hands"'. 'Of him' means of the one bringing the food. 'By whom' means by the Vinaya expert. 'Again by whom' means in just the same way. 'And what' means edible and consumable food. By whichever Vinaya expert it was not done at first, by that very one it should be done. And whichever edible or consumable was not done at first, that very thing should be done—this is what is said. 'There' means in the first container. 'Hi' means truly. The first container, even if it is made so after being purely washed, is indeed faultless. 'By that monk' means by the monk who has been invited.

Kuṇḍepīti ukkhaliyampi. Sā hi kuḍati odanādiṃ dāhaṃ karotīti kuṇḍoti vuccati. Tanti atirittakataṃ khādanīyabhojanīyaṃ. Yena panāti vinayadharena pana. Bhikkhuṃ nisīdāpentīti sambandho. Maṅgalanimantaneti maṅgalatthāya nimantanaṭṭhāne. Tatthāti maṅgalanimantane. Karontenāti karontena vinayadharena.

“In a pot” (kuṇḍe pi) means also in a cooking pot (ukkhali). For it burns rice and so forth, causing heat; hence it is called 'kuṇḍa'. “That” (taṃ) refers to the edible and consumable food that has been made 'excessive'. “But by whom” (yena pana) means but by the Vinaya expert. The connection is “making a monk sit.” “At an auspicious invitation” (maṅgalanimantane) means at the place of invitation for an auspicious purpose. “There” (tattha) means at the auspicious invitation. “By doing” (karontena) means by the Vinaya expert doing so.

Gilānena bhuñjitāvasesameva na kevalaṃ gilānātirittaṃ nāma, gilānaṃ pana uddissa ābhataṃ gilānātirittameva nāmāti dassento āha “na kevala”ntiādi. Yaṃkiñci gilānanti upasampannaṃ vā anupasampannaṃ vā yaṃkiñci gilānaṃ. Yaṃ dukkaṭaṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ asaṃsaṭṭhavasena vuttanti yojanā. Anāhāratthāyāti pipāsacchedanaābādhavūpasamatthāya.

Not only are the leftovers from a sick person's meal called 'gilānātiritta', but also what is brought specifically for the sick is called 'gilānātiritta'—showing this, he says, “not only,” etc. “Whatever sick person” (yaṃ kiñci gilānaṃ) refers to any sick person, whether ordained or not ordained. The connection is: “What was said to be an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) was stated on the basis of its not being mixed.” “For the purpose of no food” (anāhāratthāya) means for the sake of quenching thirst and alleviating illness.

241. Sati paccayeti ettha paccayassa sarūpaṃ dassetuṃ “pipāsāya satī”ti ca “ābādhe satī”ti ca vuttaṃ. Tena tenāti sattāhakālikena ca yāvajīvikena ca. Tassāti ābādhassa. Idaṃ padaṃ “upasamanattha”nti ettha samudhātuyā sambandhe sambandho, yupaccayena sambandhe kammanti daṭṭhabbanti. Pañcamaṃ.

241. Here, to show the nature of the condition in “when there is a condition” (sati paccaye), it is said: “when there is thirst” (pipāsāya sati) and “when there is illness” (ābādhe sati). “By this and that” (tena tena) means by the seven-day and by the lifelong medicines. “Of that” (tassa) means of the illness. This word “for the purpose of pacification” (upasamanatthaṃ) here should be seen as a connection in relation to the root 'sam', or as the object in relation to the suffix 'yu'. The fifth.

6. Dutiyapavāraṇasikkhāpadaṃ

6. The Second Training Rule on Invitation

242. Chaṭṭhe na ācaritabboti anācāroti vutte paṇṇattivītikkamoti āha “paṇṇattivītikkama”nti. “Karotī”tiiminā “attānamācaratī”tiādīsu [M 0.0077] viya carasaddo karasaddatthoti dasseti. Upanandhīti ettha upasaddo upanāhattho, nahadhātu bandhanatthoti dassento āha “upanāha”ntiādi. Janito upanāho yenāti janitaupanāho. Iminā “upanandho”ti padassa upanahatīti upanandhoti katthutthaṃ dasseti.

242. In the sixth, when 'not to be practiced', meaning 'improper conduct', is said, he says it is a 'transgression of the rule'. By 'does' (karoti), he shows that the word 'cara', as in 'he conducts himself' (attānam ācarati) and so forth, has the meaning of the word 'kara'. In 'upanandhī', showing that the prefix 'upa' has the meaning of 'tying on' and the root 'nah' has the meaning of 'binding', he says 'upanāha' and so on. 'He by whom malice is generated' is 'janitaupanāho'. By this, he shows that the word 'upanandho' has the agentive meaning 'one who binds on malice' (upanahatīti upanandho).

243. Abhihaṭṭhunti ettha tuṃpaccayo tvāpaccayatthoti āha “abhiharitvā”ti. Padabhājane pana vuttanti sambandho. Sādhāraṇameva atthanti yojanā. Assāti bhikkhussa. Tīhākārehīti sāmaṃ jānanena ca aññesamārocanena ca tassārocanena cāti tīhi kāraṇehi. Āsādīyate [V 1.0064] maṅkuṃ karīyate āsādanaṃ, taṃ apekkho āsādanāpekkhoti dassento āha “āsādana”ntiādi.

243. Regarding 'abhihaṭṭhuṃ', he says that here the affix 'tuṃ' has the meaning of the affix 'tvā', thus 'having brought' (abhiharitvā). The connection is that it is stated in the word analysis. The interpretation is that the meaning is common. 'Of him' (assa) refers to the monk. 'By three means' (tīhākārehi) means by three reasons: by knowing oneself, by others informing, and by his informing. 'Āsādīyate' means to be humiliated or made ashamed; 'āsādana' is the act of humiliating. Showing that 'āsādanāpekkho' is one who expects that, he says 'āsādana' and so on.

Yassa atthāya abhihaṭanti sambandho. Itarassāti abhihārakato aññassa bhuttassāti. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

The connection is: 'for whose sake they bring'. 'For another' (itarassa) means for someone other than the one who brought it, for one who has eaten. The sixth.

7. Vikālabhojanasikkhāpadaṃ

7. The Training Rule on Eating at the Wrong Time

247. Sattame girimhīti pabbatamhi. So hi himavamanādivasena jalaṃ, sārabhūtāni ca bhesajjādivatthūni girati niggiratīti girīti vuccati. Aggasamajjoti uttamasamajjo. Imehi padehi aggo samajjo aggasamajjo, girimhi pavatto aggasamajjo giraggasamajjoti atthaṃ dasseti. Samajjoti ca sabhā. Sā hi samāgamaṃ ajanti gacchanti janā etthāti samajjoti vuccati. “Girissa vā”tiādinā girissa aggo koṭi giraggo, tasmiṃ pavatto samajjo giraggasamajjoti attho dassito. Soti giraggasamajjo. Bhavissati kirāti yojanā. Bhūmibhāgeti avayaviādhāro, sannipatatīti sambandho. Naṭañca nāṭakañca naṭanāṭakāni. “Naccaṃ gītaṃ vāditañcā”ti idaṃ tayaṃ “nāṭaka”nti vuccati. Tesanti naṭanāṭakānaṃ. Dassanatthanti dassanāya ca savanāya ca. Savanampi hi dassaneneva saṅgahitaṃ. Apaññatte [M 0.0078] sikkhāpadeti ūnavīsativassasikkhāpadassa tāva apaññattattā. Teti sattarasavaggiyā. Tatthāti giraggasamajjaṃ. Athāti tasmiṃ kāle. Nesanti sattarasavaggiyānaṃ adaṃsūti sambandho. Vilimpetvāti vilepanehi vividhākārena limpetvā.

247. In the seventh, 'girimhi' means 'on the mountain'. For it is called 'giri' (mountain) because it swallows (girati) water, as in the Himavā and other mountains, and essential substances such as medicines. 'Aggasamajjo' means 'supreme assembly'. By these words, he shows the meaning: a supreme assembly is an 'aggasamajjo'; a supreme assembly held on a mountain is a 'giraggasamajjo'. 'Samajjo' also means 'assembly' (sabhā). For it is called 'samajjo' because people (janā) come (ajanti, gacchanti) together (samāgamaṃ) there. By the phrase 'or of the mountain' (girissa vā) and so on, the meaning is shown that 'giragga' is the peak or summit of the mountain, and 'giraggasamajjo' is the assembly held there. 'So' refers to the 'giraggasamajjo'. The interpretation is 'it will be, indeed'. 'In a part of the ground' (bhūmibhāge) is a locative of the whole; the connection is 'they gather' (sannipatatīti). 'Dancer' (naṭa) and 'dramatic performance' (nāṭaka) are 'naṭanāṭakāni'. This triad of 'dancing' (naccaṃ), 'singing' (gītaṃ), and 'playing instruments' (vāditaṃ) is called 'nāṭaka'. 'Of them' (tesaṃ) refers to the dancers and dramatic performances. 'For the purpose of seeing' (dassanatthaṃ) means for seeing and for hearing, for hearing is indeed included under seeing. 'When the training rule was not yet established' (apaññatte sikkhāpade) refers to the fact that the training rule for those under twenty years of age had not yet been established. 'They' (te) refers to the group of seventeen. 'There' (tattha) means at that 'giraggasamajja'. 'Then' (atha) means at that time. The connection is that 'to them' (nesaṃ) refers to the group of seventeen, and 'they gave' (adaṃsu). 'Having anointed' (vilimpetvā) means having anointed in various ways with unguents.

249. “Vikāle”ti sāmaññena vuttepi visesakālova gahetabboti āha “kālo”tiādi. So cāti bhojanakālo ca. Majjhanhiko hotīti yojanā. Tenevāti bhojanakālassa adhippetattā eva. Assāti “vikāle”tipadassa. “Vikālo nāma…pe… aruṇuggamanā”ti padabhājanena aruṇuggamanato yāva majjhanhikā kālo nāmāti attho nayena dassito hoti. Tatoti ṭhitamajjhanhikato. Sūriyassa atisīghattā vegena ṭhitamajjhanhikaṃ vītivatteyyāti āha “kukkuccakena pana na kattabba”nti. Kālatthambhoti kālassa jānanatthāya thūṇo. Kālantareti kālassa abbhantare.

249. Even though 'at the wrong time' (vikāle) is stated generally, a specific time should be understood; hence he says 'time' (kālo) and so on. And that is the mealtime. The interpretation is that it is midday. Therefore, it is precisely because the mealtime is intended. 'Of it' (assa) refers to the word 'vikāle'. By the word analysis 'the wrong time means... until the rising of the dawn' (vikālo nāma…pe… aruṇuggamanā), the meaning is shown by implication that the time from the rising of the dawn until midday is called 'time'. 'From that' (tato) means from the fixed midday. Because the sun is very swift, it might quickly pass the fixed midday; hence he says 'but one should not act with scruples'. 'Time-pillar' (kālatthambho) means a pillar for knowing the time. 'Within the time' (kālantare) means within the time.

Avasesaṃ khādanīyaṃ nāmāti ettha vinicchayo evaṃ veditabboti yojanā. Yanti khādanīyaṃ [V 1.0065] atthīti sambandho. Vanamūlādipabhedaṃ yampi khādanīyaṃ atthi, tampi āmisagatikaṃ hotīti yojanā. Seyyathidanti pucchāvācakanipātasamudāyo. Idaṃ khādanīyaṃ seyyathā katamanti attho. Idampīti idaṃ dvādasavidhampi. Pisaddena na pūvādiyevāti dasseti.

The interpretation is that the determination regarding 'the rest is called edible food' should be understood thus. The connection is that 'whatever' (yaṃ) means 'there is edible food'. The interpretation is that whatever edible food there is, of various kinds such as forest roots, that too is categorized as material food. 'Namely' (seyyathidaṃ) is a collection of interrogative particles. The meaning is 'what kind of edible food is this?'. 'Even this' (idampi) means even these twelve kinds. By the word 'pi', he shows that it is not only cakes and so on.

Tatthāti dvādasasu khādanīyesu, ādhāre bhummaṃ. Mūlati patiṭṭhāti ettha, etenāti vā mūlaṃ. Khāditabbanti khādanīyaṃ. Mūlameva khādanīyaṃ mūlakhādanīyaṃ, tasmiṃ vinicchayo evaṃ veditabboti yojanā. Mūlakamūlādīni lokasaṅketo padesatoyeva veditabbāni. Taṃ tañhi nāmaṃ ajānantānaṃ atisammūḷhakāraṇattā saha pariyāyantarena vacanatthaṃ vakkhāma. Sūpassa hitaṃ sūpeyyaṃ, sūpeyyaṃ paṇṇaṃ etesanti sūpeyyapaṇṇā, tesaṃ mūlāni sūpeyyapaṇṇamūlāni. Āmīyati anto pavesīyatīti āmiso, ākāro antokaraṇattho, āmisassa gati viya gati etesanti āmisagatikāni [M 0.0079] . Etthāti mūlesu. Jaraḍḍhanti jarabhūtaṃ upaḍḍhaṃ. Aññampīti vajakalimūlato aññampi.

'Therein' (tattha) refers to the twelve kinds of edible foods; this is a locative in the sense of support. A root (mūlaṃ) is so called because one is established (mūlati = patiṭṭhāti) on it, or by it. 'To be eaten' (khāditabbaṃ) is 'edible' (khādanīyaṃ). A root that is edible is 'root-edible' (mūlakhādanīyaṃ); the interpretation is that the determination regarding it should be understood thus. Radish roots and so on are to be understood only according to local convention and region. For those who do not know those particular names, which can cause extreme confusion, we will explain the word meanings along with alternative terms. 'Sūpeyya' is what is suitable for soup; 'sūpeyyapaṇṇā' are those that have 'sūpeyya' leaves; their roots are 'sūpeyyapaṇṇamūlāni'. Material food (āmiso) is so called because it is made to enter inside (āmīyati = anto pavesīyati); the 'ā' has the sense of 'making inside'. 'Āmisagatikāni' are those that have a nature like the nature of material food. 'Here' (ettha) refers to in the roots. 'Jaraḍḍha' means become old and half-rotten. 'Also other' (aññampi) means also other than the vajakalī root.

Yāni pana mūlāni vuttāni, tāni yāvajīvikānīti yojanā. Pāḷiyaṃ vuttānīti sambandho. Khādanīyatthanti khādanīyassa, khādanīye vā vijjamānaṃ, khādanīyena vā kātabbaṃ kiccaṃ, payojanaṃ vāti khādanīyatthaṃ. “Khādanīye”tiiminā “tattha vuttābhidhammatthā”tiādīsu viya khādanīyatthapadassa uttarapadatthapadhānabhāvaṃ dasseti. Tattha khādanīyassa, khādanīye vā vijjamānaṃ, khādanīyena vā kātabbaṃ kiccaṃ nāma jighacchāharaṇameva. Yañhi pūvādikhādanīyaṃ khāditvā jighacchāharaṇaṃ hoti, tassa kiccaṃ kiccaṃ nāmāti vuttaṃ hoti. Taṃ kiccaṃ, payojanaṃ vā neva pharanti, neva nipphādenti. Eseva nayo “na bhojanīye bhojanīyatthaṃ pharantī”tietthāpi.

The interpretation is that the roots that have been mentioned are permissible for a lifetime. The connection is that they are stated in the Pāḷi. 'The purpose of edible food' (khādanīyattha) means the purpose of edible food, or what exists in edible food, or a function to be performed by edible food, or a purpose. By 'in edible food' (khādanīye), he shows that the meaning of the latter part of the word 'khādanīyattha' is primary, as in cases like 'therein, the meaning of the Abhidhamma stated' and so on. Therein, the function of edible food, or what exists in edible food, or a function to be performed by edible food, is simply the alleviation of hunger. For when hunger is alleviated by eating edible food such as cakes, that is said to be its function. That function or purpose they neither fulfill nor accomplish. The same principle applies also in 'nor do they fulfill the purpose of staple food in staple food'.

Tesanti mūlānaṃ anto, lakkhaṇanti vā sambandho. Ekasmiṃ janapade khādanīyatthabhojanīyatthesu pharamānesu aññesupi janapadesu pharantiyevāti dassanatthaṃ “tesu tesu janapadesū”ti vicchāpadaṃ vuttaṃ. Kiñcāpi hi bahūsu janapadesu pathavīrasaāporasasampattivasena khādanīyatthabhojanīyatthaṃ pharamānampi ekasmiṃ janapade pathavīrasaāporasavipattivasena apharamānaṃ bhaveyya, vikāravasena pana tattha pavattattā taṃ janapadaṃ pamāṇaṃ na kātabbaṃ, gahetabbamevāti vuttaṃ hoti. Pakatiāhāravasenāti aññehi yāvakālika, sattāhakālikehi amissitaṃ attano pakatiyāva āhārakiccakaraṇavasena. “Manussāna”ntiiminā aññesaṃ tiracchānādīnaṃ khādanīyatthabhojanīyatthaṃ [V 1.0066] pharamānampi na pamāṇanti dasseti. Tanti mūlaṃ. Hīti saccaṃ. Nāmasaññāsūti nāmasaṅkhātāsu saññāsu.

'Tesaṃ' means the end of the roots; or, the connection is 'lakkhaṇaṃ'. To show that when things for the purpose of edibles and staple foods are pervasive in one region, they are also pervasive in other regions, the explanatory phrase 'tesu tesu janapadesu' is stated. For although in many regions, due to an abundance of earth-essence and water-essence, things for the purpose of edibles and staple foods may be pervasive, yet in one region, due to a deficiency of earth-essence and water-essence, they might not be pervasive; but because of an alteration prevailing there, that region should not be taken as the standard, but it should still be included, it is said. 'By the nature of sustenance' means by performing the function of nourishment by its own nature, unmixed with other items allowed for a limited time or for a week.
