By 'manussānaṃ', he shows that even if things for the purpose of edibles and staple foods are pervasive for animals and others, that is not the standard. 'Taṃ' means the root. 'Hi' means 'truly'. 'Nāmasaññāsu' means in perceptions designated as names.

Yathā mūle lakkhaṇaṃ dassitaṃ, evaṃ kandādīsupi yaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ dassitanti yojanā. Na kevalaṃ pāḷiyaṃ āgatānaṃ haliddādīnaṃ mūlaṃyeva yāvajīvikaṃ hoti, atha kho tacādayopīti āha “yañceta”ntiādi. Yaṃ etaṃ aṭṭhavidhanti sambandho.

The interpretation is that just as the characteristic is shown in the root, so too the characteristic shown applies to the tubers and so on. He says 'yañcetaṃ' and so on to show that not only the roots of turmeric and the like, which are mentioned in the Pāḷi text, are permissible for a lifetime, but also the bark and so on. The connection is 'whatever is eightfold'.

Evaṃ [M 0.0080] mūlakhādanīye vinicchayaṃ dassetvā idāni kandakhādanīye taṃ dassento āha “kandakhādanīye”tiādi. Tattha kandakhādanīyeti kaṃ sukhaṃ dadātīti kando, padumādikando, sukhassa adāyakā pana kandā ruḷhīvasena kandāti vuccanti, kando eva khādanīyaṃ kandakhādanīyaṃ, tasmiṃ vinicchayo evaṃ veditabboti yojanā. Eseva nayo uparipi. Yanti kandaṃ. Iminā taṃsaddānapekkho yaṃsaddopi atthīti ñāpeti. Tatthāti kandakhādanīye. Taruṇo, sukhakhādanīyoti visesanapadāni yathāvacanaṃ uparipi yojetabbāni. Evamādayo pharaṇakakandā yāvakālikāti sambandho.

Having thus shown the determination regarding root edibles, now, showing that regarding tuber edibles, he says 'kandakhādanīye' and so on. Therein, regarding 'kandakhādanīya': 'kanda' is what gives pleasure, such as a lotus tuber; but tubers that do not give pleasure are called 'kanda' by convention. The tuber itself is edible, hence 'kandakhādanīya'; the interpretation is that the determination regarding it should be understood thus. The same principle applies further on as well. 'Yaṃ' refers to the tuber. By this, he makes known that the word 'yaṃ' also exists, not depending on the word 'taṃ'. 'Tattha' refers to tuber edibles. 'Taruṇo' and 'sukhakhādanīyo' are qualifying terms that should be connected further on according to the text. The connection is that such spreading tubers are permissible for a limited time.

Adhototi visaraso udakena adhūnito. Teti kandā saṅgahitāti sambandho.

'Adhoto' means having a strong taste and not being stirred with water. The connection is that 'te' means the included tubers.

Mūle alati pavattatīti muḷālo, udakato vā uddhaṭamatte milati nimilatīti muḷālaṃ. Evamādi pharaṇakamuḷālaṃ yāvakālikanti yojanā. Taṃ sabbampīti sabbampi taṃ muḷālaṃ saṅgahitanti sambandho.

'Muḷāla' is what moves at the root, or it closes or withers as soon as it is pulled from the water. The interpretation is that such spreading lotus stalks are permissible for a limited time. The connection is that 'taṃ sabbampi' means all of that lotus stalk is included.

Masati vijjhatīti matthako. Evamādi matthako yāvakālikoti yojanā. Jaraḍḍhabundoti jarabhūtaaḍḍhasaṅkhāto pādo.

'Matthaka' is what is crushed or pierced. The interpretation is that such a 'matthaka' is permissible for a limited time. 'Jaraḍḍhabundo' means a stalk or base that is old and half-decayed.

Khanīyati avadārīyatīti khandho, khāyatīti vā khandho. “Antopathavīgato”tipadaṃ “sālakalyāṇikhandho”tipadeneva yojetabbaṃ, na aññehi. Evamādi khandho yāvakālikoti yojanā. Avasesāti tīhi daṇḍakādīhi avasesā.

'Khandho' is so called because it is dug or split, or because it decays. The phrase 'antopathavīgato' should be connected only with the phrase 'sālakalyāṇikhandho', not with others. The interpretation is that such a trunk is permissible for a limited time. 'Avasesā' means what remains from the three, daṇḍaka, etc.

Tacati saṃvarati paṭicchādetīti taco. Sarasoti ettha evakāro yojetabbo, saraso evāti attho. Tesaṃ saṅgahoti sambandho. Hīti saccaṃ. Etanti kasāvabhesajjaṃ, “anujānāmi [V 1.0067] …pe… bhojanīyattha”nti vacanaṃ vā. Etthāti kasāvabhesajje. Etesampīti matthakakhandhattacānampi.

'Taco' is so called because it covers, restrains, or conceals. Regarding 'saraso', here the particle 'eva' should be connected, meaning 'juicy indeed'. The connection is 'their inclusion'. 'Hi' means truly. 'Etaṃ' refers to the astringent medicine, or the statement 'I allow... for the purpose of nourishment.' 'Ettha' means in reference to the astringent medicine. 'Etesampi' means of the top, trunk, and bark as well.

Patatīti pattaṃ. Etesanti mūlakādīnaṃ. Evarūpāni pattāni ca ekaṃsena yāvakālikānīti yojanā. Yā loṇī ārohati, tassā loṇiyā pattaṃ yāvajīvikanti yojanā. Dīpavāsinoti tambapaṇṇidīpavāsino[M 0.0081], jambudīpavāsino vā. Yāni vā pharantīti vuttānīti sambandho. Tesanti nimbādīnaṃ. Idaṃ padaṃ pubbaparāpekkhakaṃ, tasmā dvinnaṃ majjhe vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Paṇṇānaṃ anto natthīti sambandho.

'Pattaṃ' is so called because it falls. 'Etesaṃ' refers to roots, etc. The interpretation is that such leaves are, without exception, permissible for a limited time. The interpretation is that the leaf of the salt creeper which climbs is permissible for life. 'Dīpavāsino' means inhabitants of Tambapaṇṇi Island or Jambudīpa. The connection is: 'or what spreads' refers to what has been mentioned. 'Tesaṃ' refers to the neem tree, etc. This phrase depends on what precedes and follows; therefore, it should be understood as stated in the middle of the two. The connection is: 'there is no limit to leaves'.

Pupphati vikasatīti pupphaṃ. Evamādi pupphaṃ yāvakālikanti yojanā. Tassāti pupphassa. Assāti evameva.

'Pupphaṃ' is so called because it blossoms or blooms. The interpretation is that such a flower is permissible for a limited time. 'Tassa' means of the flower. 'Assa' means likewise.

Phalatīti phalaṃ. Yānīti phalāni. Pharantīti sambandho. Nesanti phalānaṃ pariyantanti sambandho. Yāni vuttāni, tāni yāvajīvikānīti yojanā. Tesampīti phalānampi pariyantanti sambandho.

'Phalaṃ' is so called because it bears fruit. 'Yāni' means fruits. 'Pharanti' is the connection. The connection is: 'nesaṃ' means the limit of fruits. The interpretation is that those which are mentioned are permissible for life. The connection is: 'tesampi' also means the limit of fruits.

Asīyati khipīyati, chaḍḍīyatīti vā aṭṭhi. Evamādīni pharaṇakāni aṭṭhīni yāvakālikānīti yojanā. Tesanti aṭṭhīnaṃ.

'Aṭṭhi' is so called because it is eaten, thrown away, or discarded. The interpretation is that such spreading stones or seeds are permissible for a limited time. 'Tesaṃ' means of the stones or seeds.

Pisīyati cuṇṇaṃ karīyatīti piṭṭhaṃ. Evamādīni pharaṇakāni piṭṭhāni yāvakālikānīti yojanā. Adhotakanti udakena adhūnitaṃ. Tesanti piṭṭhānaṃ.

'Piṭṭhaṃ' is so called because it is ground or made into powder. The interpretation is that such spreading flours are permissible for a limited time. 'Adhotakaṃ' means not rinsed with water. 'Tesaṃ' means of the flours.

Nirantaraṃ asati sambajjhatīti niyyāso. Sesāti ucchuniyyāsato sesā. Pāḷiyaṃ vuttaniyyāsāti sambandho. Tatthāti niyyāsakhādanīye. Saṅgahitānaṃ niyyāsānaṃ pariyantanti yojanā. Evantiādi nigamanaṃ.

'Niyyāso' is so called because it adheres or is connected continuously. 'Sesā' means the rest from sugarcane resin. The connection is 'the resins mentioned in the Pāḷi text'. 'Tattha' means in edible resin. The interpretation is 'the limit of the included resins'. 'Evaṃ' and so forth is the conclusion.

Vuttamevāti heṭṭhā paṭhamapavāraṇasikkhāpade vuttamevāti. Sattamaṃ.

'Vuttameva' means what was stated below in the first training rule on invitation. The seventh.

8. Sannidhikārakasikkhāpadaṃ

8. The Training Rule on Storing Up

252. Aṭṭhame [V 1.0068] abbhantare jāto abbhantaro. Mahātheroti mahantehi thiraguṇehi yutto. Iminā “belaṭṭho”ti saññānāmassa saññināmiṃ dasseti. Padhānaghareti samathavipassanānaṃ padahanaṭṭhānagharasaṅkhāte ekasmiṃ āvāse. Sukkhakuranti ettha sosanakurattā na sukkhakuraṃ hoti, kevalaṃ pana asūpabyañjanattāti āha “asūpabyañjanaṃ [M 0.0082] odana”nti. Sosanakurampi yuttameva. Vakkhati hi “taṃ piṇḍapātaṃ udakena temetvā”ti. “Odana”ntiiminā kurasaddassa odanapariyāyataṃ dasseti. Odanañhi karoti āyuvaṇṇādayoti “kura”nti vuccati. Soti belaṭṭhasīso. Tañca khoti tañca sukkhakuraṃ āharatīti sambandho. Paccayagiddhatāyāti piṇḍapātapaccaye luddhatāya. Thero bhuñjatīti sambandho. Manussānaṃ ekāhārassa sattāhamattaṭṭhitattā “sattāha”nti vuttaṃ. Tatoti bhuñjanato paranti sambandho. Cattāripīti ettha pisaddena adhikānipi sattāhāni gahetabbāni.

252. In the eighth, 'abbhantaro' means 'born within'. 'Mahāthera' means endowed with great and steadfast virtues. By this, he shows the person for the name 'Belaṭṭha'. 'Padhānaghara' refers to a dwelling designated as a place for striving in serenity and insight. Regarding 'sukkhakuraṃ', here, because it is 'sosanakuraṃ', it is not 'sukkhakuraṃ'; however, since it is merely without soup or relish, he says, 'rice without soup or relish'. 'Sosanakuraṃ' is also fitting. For he will say, 'Having moistened that alms food with water.' By 'odanaṃ', he shows that the word 'kura' is a synonym for rice. For rice creates life, complexion, etc., thus it is called 'kura'. 'So' is Belaṭṭhasīsa. 'Tañca kho' is connected to 'and he brings that dried rice'. 'Paccayagiddhatāya' means through greed for the alms food requisite. 'The Thera eats' is the connection. Because a single meal for humans lasts for about seven days, 'sattāhaṃ' is stated. 'Tato' means after eating—this is the connection. Regarding 'cattāripi', here, with the particle 'pi', even more than seven days should be understood.

253. Itīti idaṃ tayaṃ. “Sannidhi kāro assā”ti samāso visesanaparanipātavasena gahetabbo. “Sannidhikiriyanti attho”ti iminā karīyatīti kāroti kammatthaṃ dasseti. Ekarattanti antimaparicchedavasena vuttaṃ tadadhikānampi adhippetattā. Assāti “sannidhikāraka”nti padassa.

253. 'Iti' refers to this triad. The compound 'sannidhi kāro assā' should be understood in the sense of the post-position of the adjective. By 'the meaning is the act of storing', he shows that 'kāro', from 'karīyati', has the sense of the object. 'Ekarattaṃ' is stated as a final limit, because even more than that is intended. 'Assa' refers to the word 'sannidhikāraka'.

Sannidhikārakassa sattāhakālikassa nissaggiyapācittiyāpattiyā paccayattā sannidhikārakaṃ yāmakālikaṃ khādanīyabhojanīyaṃ asamānampi suddhapācittiyāpattiyā paccayo hotīti āha “yāmakālikaṃ vā”ti. Paṭiggahaṇeti paṭiggahaṇe ca gahaṇe ca. Ajjhoharitukāmatāya hi paṭiggahaṇe ca paṭiggahetvā gahaṇe cāti vuttaṃ hoti. Yaṃ pattaṃ aṅguliyā ghaṃsantassa lekhā paññāyati, so patto duddhoto hoti saceti yojanā uttaravākye yaṃsaddaṃ disvā pubbavākye taṃsaddassa gamanīyattā. Gaṇṭhikapattassāti bandhanapattassa. Soti sneho. Paggharati sandissatīti sambandho. Tādiseti duddhote, gaṇṭhike vā. Tatthāti dhovitapatte āsiñcitvāti sambandho. Hīti saccaṃ. Abbohārikāti na voharitabbā, voharituṃ na yuttāti attho. Yanti khādanīyabhojanīyaṃ pariccajantīti sambandho. Hīti saccaṃ, yasmā vā. Tatoti apariccattakhādanīyabhojanīyato nīharitvāti sambandho.

Because the storing of a seven-day allowable is a condition for an offense of relinquishment and confession, even if the stored item is not what is permissible for a watch or an edible and staple food, it becomes a condition for a pure offense of confession. Therefore, he says, 'or what is permissible for a watch.' 'At receiving' means both at receiving and at taking. For with the intention to consume, it is said that there is both receiving and taking after having received. The construction is that 'a bowl that shows a mark when rubbed with a finger is poorly washed,' because seeing the word 'yaṃ' in the subsequent sentence, the word 'taṃ' is to be understood in the preceding sentence. 'Of a knotted bowl' means of a bound bowl. 'So' means grease. 'It oozes' is connected with 'it appears.' 'Such' refers to either a poorly washed bowl or a knotted one. 'There' is connected to 'having poured into the washed bowl.' 'Hi' means truly. 'Abbohārika' means 'should not be used' or 'is not proper to use'—this is the meaning. 'Yaṃ' is connected to 'they relinquish the edible and staple food.' 'Hi' means truly, or because. 'Tato' is connected to 'having taken out from the unrelinquished edible and staple food'.

Akappiyamaṃsesūti [M 0.0083] niddhāraṇasamudāyo. Sati paccayeti pipāsasaṅkhāte paccaye sati. Anatirittakatanti [V 1.0069] atirittena akataṃ sannidhikārakaṃ khādanīyabhojanīyanti yojanā. Ekameva pācittiyanti sambandho. Vikappadvayeti sāmisanirāmisasaṅkhāte vikappadvaye. Sabbavikappesūti vikālasannidhiakappiyamaṃsayāmakālikapaccayasaṅkhātesu sabbesu vikappesu.

'Among impermissible meats' is a collective specification. 'When there is a condition' means when there is the condition known as thirst. The construction of 'not made surplus' is: stored edible and staple food not made surplus. 'Only one pācittiya' is the connection. 'In two options' means in the two options known as with meat and without meat. 'In all options' means in all the options, namely: unseasonable time, storing, impermissible meat, and the condition related to what is permissible for a watch.

255. Āmisasaṃsaṭṭhanti āmisena saṃsaṭṭhaṃ sattāhakālikaṃ yāvajīvikaṃ.

255. 'Mixed with food items' means a seven-day allowable or a lifetime allowable mixed with food items.

256. Catubbidhakālikassa sarūpañca vacanatthañca dassento āha “vikālabhojanasikkhāpade”tiādi. Tattha niddiṭṭhaṃ khādanīyabhojanīya”ntiiminā yāvakālikassa sarūpaṃ dasseti. “Yāva…pe… kālika”ntiiminā vacanatthaṃ dasseti. “Saddhiṃ…pe… pāna”ntiiminā yāmakālikassa sarūpaṃ dasseti. “Yāva…pe… kālika”ntiiminā vacanatthaṃ dasseti. “Sabbiādi pañcavidhaṃ bhesajja”ntiiminā sattāhakālikassa sarūpaṃ dasseti. “Sattāhaṃ…pe… kālika”ntiiminā vacanatthaṃ dasseti. “Ṭhapetvā…pe… sabbampī”tiiminā yāvajīvikassa sarūpaṃ dasseti. “Yāva…pe… jīvika”ntiiminā vacanatthaṃ dasseti. Sabbavacanattho lahukamattameva, garuko panevaṃ veditabbo – yāva yattako majjhanhiko kālo yāvakālo, so assatthī, taṃ vā kālaṃ bhuñjitabbanti yāvakālikaṃ. Yāmo kālo yāmakālo, so assatthi, taṃ vā kālaṃ paribhuñjītabbanti yāmakālikaṃ. Sattāho kālo sattāhakālo, so assatthi, taṃ vā kālaṃ nidahitvā paribhuñjitabbanti sattāhakālikaṃ. Yāva yattako jīvo yāvajīvo, so assatthi, yāvajīvaṃ vā pariharitvā paribhuñjitabbanti yāvajīvikanti.

256. To show the nature (sarūpa) and the meaning of the word (vacanattha) of the four kinds of time-limited allowables (kālika), he says, 'in the training rule on eating at the wrong time,' etc. There, by 'the edible and staple food (khādanīyabhojanīya)' that is specified, he shows the nature of what is permissible for a limited time (yāvakālika). By 'yāva…pe… kālika,' he shows the meaning of the word. By 'saddhiṃ…pe… pāna,' he shows the nature of what is permissible for a watch (yāmakālika). By 'yāva…pe… kālika,' he shows the meaning of the word. By 'the five kinds of medicine beginning with ghee (sappi-ādi pañcavidhaṃ bhesajja),' he shows the nature of what is permissible for seven days (sattāhakālika). By 'sattāhaṃ…pe… kālika,' he shows the meaning of the word. By 'ṭhapetvā…pe… sabbampī,' he shows the nature of what is permissible for life (yāvajīvika). By 'yāva…pe… jīvika,' he shows the meaning of the word. The meaning of all these words is only brief, but the detailed meaning should be understood thus: As long as the midday time lasts, that is the 'yāvakāla'; it is 'yāvakālika' because it should be eaten within that time. A watch is a period of time, that is the 'yāmakāla'; it is 'yāmakālika' because it should be consumed within that time. Seven days is a period of time, that is the 'sattāhakāla'; it is 'sattāhakālika' because it should be stored and consumed within that time. As long as life lasts, that is the 'yāvajīva'; it is 'yāvajīvika' because it should be kept and consumed for as long as one lives.

Tatthāti catubbidhesu kālikesu. Satakkhattunti anekavāraṃ. Yāva kālo nātikkamati, tāva bhuñjantassāti yojanā. Ahorattaṃ bhuñjantassāti sambandhoti. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

'Tattha' means among the four kinds of time-limited allowables. 'Satakkhattuṃ' means many times. The construction is, 'As long as the time has not passed, so long may one eat.' 'Eating day and night' is the connection. The eighth.

9. Paṇītabhojanasikkhāpadaṃ

9. The Training Rule on Superior Food.

257. Navame [M 0.0084] pakaṭṭhabhāvaṃ nītanti paṇītanti vutte paṇītasaddo uttamatthoti āha “uttamabhojanānī”ti. Sampanno nāma na madhuraguṇo, atha kho madhuraguṇayuttaṃ bhojanamevāti āha “sampattiyutta”nti. Kassāti karaṇatthe cetaṃ sāmivacanaṃ, kenāti hi attho. “Surasa”ntiiminā sādīyati assādīyatīti sādūti vacanatthassa sarūpaṃ dasseti.

257. In the ninth, regarding the statement 'brought to a prominent state, thus excellent (paṇīta),' the word 'paṇīta' means 'best'; thus he said, 'best foods.' 'Endowed' does not mean the quality of sweetness, but rather food endowed with the quality of sweetness; thus it is said, 'endowed with excellence.' 'Of whom'—this is a genitive word in the instrumental sense, for the meaning is 'by whom.' By 'delicious,' he shows the nature of the meaning of the word 'tasty,' which is 'tasted and relished'.

259. “Yo [V 1.0070] pana…pe… bhuñjeyyā”ti ettha vinicchayo evaṃ veditabboti yojanā. Suddhānīti odanena asaṃsaṭṭhāni. Odanasaṃsaṭṭhāni sabbiādīnīti sambandho. Etthāti imasmiṃ sikkhāpade. Hīti saccaṃ. “Paṇītasaṃsaṭṭhānī”tiiminā paṇītehi sabbiādīhi saṃsaṭṭhāni bhojanāni paṇītabhojanānīti atthaṃ dasseti. “Sattadhaññanibbattānī”ti iminā bhojanānaṃ sarūpaṃ dasseti.

259. Regarding the phrase 'Yo pana…pe… bhuñjeyya,' the construction is that the judgment here should be understood thus. 'Pure' means unmixed with rice. 'Ghee, etc., mixed with rice' is the connection. 'Here' means in this training rule. 'Hi' means truly. With 'mixed with choice food,' he shows the meaning that foods mixed with choice items, such as ghee, etc., are called choice foods. With 'produced from seven kinds of grain,' he shows the nature of the foods.

“Sabbinā bhatta”ntiādīnaṃ pañcannaṃ vikappānaṃ majjhe tīsupi vikappesu “bhatta”nti yojetabbaṃ. Evaṃ vākyaṃ katvā viññāpane āpattiṃ dassetvā samāsaṃ katvā viññāpane taṃ dassento āha “sabbibhattaṃ dehī”tiādi.

Among the five alternatives beginning with 'food with ghee,' the word 'food' should be connected in the three middle alternatives as well. Having constructed the sentence thus and shown the offense in the request, he then shows it in the request made with a compound, saying, 'Give ghee-food,' etc.

Itoti gāvito laddhenāti sambandho. Visaṅketanti saṅketato ñāpitato vigataṃ virahitanti attho. Hīti saccaṃ. Iminā visaṅketassa guṇadosaṃ dasseti.

'From this' is connected with 'obtained from a cow.' 'Without agreement' means devoid of, free from an agreement or indication—this is the meaning. 'Hi' means truly. By this, he shows the advantage and disadvantage of being without agreement.

Kappiyasabbinā dehīti kappiyasabbinā saṃsaṭṭhaṃ bhattaṃ dehīti yojanā. Eseva nayo sesesupi. Yena yenāti yena yena sabbiādinā. Tasmiṃ tassāti etthāpi vicchāvasena attho daṭṭhabbo. Pāḷiyaṃ āgatasabbi nāma gosabbi, ajikāsabbi, mahiṃsasabbi, yesaṃ maṃsaṃ kappati, tesaṃ sabbi ca. Navanītaṃ nāma evameva. Telaṃ nāma tilatelaṃ, sāsapatelaṃ, madhukatelaṃ, eraṇḍatelaṃ, vasātelañca. Madhu nāma makkhikāmadhu. Phāṇitaṃ nāma ucchumhā nibbattaṃ. Maccho nāma udakacaro. Pāḷianāgato maccho nāma natthi. Maṃsaṃ nāma [M 0.0085] yesaṃ maṃsaṃ kappati, tesaṃ maṃsaṃ. Khīradadhīni sabbisadisāneva. Vuttaṃ yathā evaṃ “navanītabhattaṃ dehī”tiādīsupi sūpodanaviññattidukkaṭameva hotīti yojanā. Hīti saccaṃ. So cāti so cattho. Tatthāti tasmiṃ atthe. Kiṃ payojanaṃ. Nattheva payojananti adhippāyo.

'Give with allowable ghee'—the construction is 'give food mixed with allowable ghee.' This same principle applies to the rest. 'By whatever' means by whatever, such as ghee, etc. 'In that'—here too, the meaning should be understood by way of distinction. In the Pāḷi, 'ghee' refers to cow's ghee, goat's ghee, buffalo's ghee, and the ghee of those whose flesh is allowable. 'Fresh butter' is likewise. 'Oil' means sesame oil, mustard oil, madhuka oil, castor oil, and fat oil. 'Honey' means bee's honey. 'Molasses' means what is produced from sugarcane. 'Fish' means an aquatic creature. There is no such thing as a fish not mentioned in the Pāḷi. 'Flesh' means the flesh of those whose flesh is allowable. Milk and curd are just like ghee. The construction is: just as it is said, so also in cases like 'give fresh butter food,' there is only a dukkaṭa offense for requesting soup and rice. 'Hi' means truly. 'So ca' means 'that meaning.' 'Tattha' means in that meaning. What is the purpose? The intention is: there is no purpose at all.

Paṭiladdhaṃ bhojananti sambandho. Ekarasanti ekakiccaṃ. Tatoti navapaṇītabhojanato nīharitvāti sambandho.

'Obtained food' is the connection. 'One taste' means one purpose. 'From that' is connected with 'having taken it out from the nine choice foods'.

Sabbānīti nava pācittiyāni sandhāya vuttaṃ.

'All' is said in reference to the nine pācittiya offenses.

261. Ubhayesampīti bhikkhubhikkhunīnampi. Sabbīti cettha yo naṃ paribhuñjati, tassa balāyuvaḍḍhanatthaṃ sabbati gacchati pavattatīti sabbi, ghataṃ. Tatiyakkhareneva sajjhāyitabbaṃ likhitabbañca[V 1.0071]. Kasmā? Tatiyakkharaṭṭhāneyeva sabba gatiyanti gatiatthassa sabbadhātussa dhātupāṭhesu āgatattāti. Navamaṃ.

261. 'For both' means for both monks and nuns. Here, 'sabbi' (ghee) is so called because for one who partakes of it, it 'goes' (sabbati), 'moves' (gacchati), 'proceeds' (pavattati) for the purpose of increasing strength and life. It should be recited and written with the third letter. Why? Because in the lists of roots, the root 'sab' with the meaning of 'going' is found in the position of the third letter. The ninth.

10. Dantaponasikkhāpadaṃ

10. The Training Rule on Tooth-cleaners.

263. Dasame dantakaṭṭhanti dantaponaṃ. Tañhi danto kasīyati vilekhīyati anenāti “dantakaṭṭha”nti vuccati. “Sabba”nti ādinā sabbameva paṃsukūlaṃ sabbapaṃsukūlaṃ, tamassatthīti “sabbapaṃsukūliko”ti atthaṃ dasseti. Soti bhikkhu paribhuñjati kirāti sambandho. Susāneti āḷahane. Tañhi chavānaṃ sayanaṭṭhānattā “susāna”nti vuccati niruttinayena. Tatthāti susāne. Puna tatthāti evameva. Ayyasarūpañca vosāṭitakasarūpañca dassetuṃ vuttaṃ “ayyavosāṭitakānīti etthā”ti. Tattha “ayyā…pe… pitāmahā”tiiminā ayyasarūpaṃ dasseti. “Vo…pe… bhojanīyānī”tiiminā vosāṭitakasarūpaṃ. Ayyasaṅkhātānaṃ pitipitāmahānaṃ atthāya, te vā uddissa chaḍḍitāni vosāṭitakasaṅkhatāni [M 0.0086] khādanīyabhojanīyāni ayyavosāṭitakānīti viggaho kātabbo. Manussā ṭhapenti kirāti sambandho. Yanti khādanīyabhojanīyaṃ. Tesanti ñātakānaṃ. Piṇḍaṃ piṇḍaṃ katvāti saṅghāṭaṃ saṅghāṭaṃ katvā. Aññanti vuttakhādanīyabhojanīyato aññaṃ. Ummārepīti susānassa indakhīlepi. So hi uddhaṭo kilesamāro etthāti “ummāro”ti vuccati. Bodhisatto hi abhinikkhamanakāle puttaṃ cumbissāmīti ovarakassa indakhīle ṭhatvā passanto mātaraṃ puttassa nalāṭe hatthaṃ ṭhapetvā sayantiṃ disvā “sace me puttaṃ gaṇheyyaṃ, mātā tassa pabujjheyya, pabujjhamānāya antarāyo bhaveyyā”ti abhinikkhamanantarāyabhayena puttadāre pariccajitvā indakhīlato nivattitvā mahābhinikkhamanaṃ nikkhami. Tasmā bodhisattassa ṭhatvā puttadāresu apekkhāsaṅkhātassa mārassa uddhaṭaṭṭhānattā so indakhīlo nippariyāyena “ummāro”ti vuccati, aññe pana rūḷhīvasena. Thiroti thaddho. Ghanabaddhoti ghanena baddho. Kathinena maṃsena ābaddhoti attho. Vaṭhati thūlo bhavatīti vaṭho, muddhajadutiyoyaṃ, so assatthīti vaṭharoti dassento āha “vaṭharoti thūlo”ti. “Sallakkhemā”tiiminā “maññe”ti ettha manadhātu sallakkhaṇattho, makārassekāroti dasseti. Hīti saccaṃ. Tesanti manussānaṃ.

263. In the tenth, 'dantakaṭṭha' means a tooth-cleaner. For it is called 'dantakaṭṭha' because the teeth are scraped and cleaned with it. By 'sabba,' and so on, he shows that 'sabbapaṃsukūla' means every kind of rag-robe, and that one who possesses this is a 'sabbapaṃsukūlika.' The connection is: 'He' (so), a bhikkhu, uses it (paribhuñjati), so it is said (kirā). 'Susāne' means in a charnel ground. For it is called 'susāna' by etymological analysis because it is a place where corpses lie. 'Tattha' means in the charnel ground. 'Puna tattha' means likewise. To show the form of 'ayya' and the form of 'vosāṭitaka,' it is said, 'in ayyavosāṭitakāni.' There, with 'ayyā…pe… pitāmahā,' he shows the form of 'ayya.' With 'vo…pe… bhojanīyānī,' he shows the form of 'vosāṭitaka.' The analysis of 'ayyavosāṭitakāni' should be made thus: edible and soft foods, designated as 'vosāṭitaka,' which are discarded for the sake of those called 'ayya'—fathers and grandfathers—or which are discarded having been intended for them. The connection is: people place them, so it is said. 'Yaṃ' means edible and soft food. 'Tesaṃ' means of the relatives. 'Piṇḍaṃ piṇḍaṃ katvā' means having made it into lump after lump. 'Aññaṃ' means other than the aforementioned edible and soft food. 'Ummārepi' means even at the threshold post of the charnel ground. For it is called 'ummāro' because Māra, the defilement, is uprooted here. When the Bodhisatta was making his renunciation, he stood at the threshold post of the inner chamber, thinking, 'I will kiss my son.' Seeing the mother sleeping with her hand placed on her son's forehead, he thought, 'If I were to take my son, his mother would awaken, and her awakening would be an obstacle.' Fearing this obstacle to his renunciation, he forsook his son and wife, turned back from the threshold post, and went forth in the great renunciation. Therefore, because that threshold post was the place where the Māra known as attachment to his son and wife was uprooted for the Bodhisatta, it is called 'ummāro' in a direct sense; for others, however, it is by convention. 'Thiro' means stiff. 'Ghanabaddho' means bound by what is dense; the meaning is bound with hard flesh. 'Vaṭhati' means 'it becomes thick,' hence 'vaṭha'; this is the second [letter] of the retroflex class. Showing that one possesses this, he says, 'vaṭharo means thick.' With 'sallakkhemā,' he shows that here in 'maññe,' the root 'man' has the meaning of 'to discern,' and that the 'a' [of the root] becomes 'e'. 'Hi' means truly. 'Tesaṃ' means of the people.

264. Sammāti aviparītaṃ. Asallakkhetvāti āhārasaddassa khādanīyabhojanīyādīsu nirūḷhabhāvaṃ amaññitvā. Bhagavā pana ṭhapesīti sambandho. Yathāuppannassāti yenākārena uppannassa[V 1.0072]. Pitā puttasaṅkhāte dārake saññāpento viya bhagavā te bhikkhū saññāpentoti yojanā.

264. 'Sammā' means not wrongly. 'Asallakkhetvā' means not having discerned the established meaning of the word 'āhāra' in relation to edible and soft foods, and so on. The connection is: 'But the Blessed One established it.' 'Yathāuppannassa' means of that which has arisen in whatever manner. The construction is: just as a father instructs a child considered his son, so the Blessed One instructs those bhikkhus.

265. Etadevāti tiṇṇamākārānamaññataravasena adinnameva sandhāyāti sambandho. Hīti saccaṃ. Mātikāyaṃ “dinna”nti vuttaṭṭhānaṃ natthi, atha kasmā padabhājaneyeva vuttanti āha “dinnanti ida”ntiādi. “Dinna”nti idaṃ uddhaṭanti sambandho. Assāti “dinna”nti padassa. Niddese ca “kāyena…pe… dente”ti uddhaṭanti yojanā. Evanti imehi tīhākārehi dadamāneti sambandho. Evanti imehi dvīhākārehi[M 0.0087]. Ādīyamānanti sambandho. Rathareṇumpīti rathikavīthiyaṃ uṭṭhitapaṃsumpi. Pubbeti paṭhamapavāraṇasikkhāpade. Evaṃ paṭiggahitaṃ etaṃ āhāraṃ dinnaṃ nāma vuccatīti yojanā. “Etamevā”ti evassa sambhavato tassa phalaṃ dassetuṃ vuttaṃ “na ida”ntiādi. Nissaṭṭhaṃ na vuccatīti yojanā.

265. The connection is: 'Etadeva' refers to what is not given, in one of the three ways. 'Hi' means truly. In the Mātikā, there is no place where 'dinna' is said; why then is it said only in the analysis of the terms? He says, 'this 'dinna',' and so on. The connection is: this 'dinna' is extracted. 'Assa' means of the word 'dinna.' And the construction is: in the explanation, 'by body...pe...while giving' is extracted. The connection is: 'Evaṃ' means while giving in these three ways. 'Evaṃ' means in these two ways. The connection is with 'ādīyamānaṃ' (while taking). 'Rathareṇumpi' means even the dust raised in a chariot-street. 'Pubbe' means in the first training rule on Pavāraṇā. The construction is: this food, thus received, is called 'given.' To show the result of this possibility, 'etameva' is said, as in 'not this,' and so on. The construction is: it is not called 'relinquished'.

Tatthāti “kāyenā”tiādivacane. Hīti saccaṃ. Natthu karīyati imāyāti natthukaraṇī, tāya. Nāsāpuṭena paṭiggaṇhātīti sambandho. Akallakoti gilāno. Hīti saccaṃ. Kāyena paṭibaddho kāyapaṭibaddho kaṭacchuādīti āha “kaṭacchuādīsū”tiādi. Hīti saccaṃ. Pātiyamānanti pātāpiyamānaṃ.

'Tattha' means in the phrase 'by body,' and so on. 'Hi' means truly. 'Snuff is made by this,' thus 'natthukaraṇī' (snuff-inhaler); by that. The connection is: one receives it with the nostril. 'Akallako' means sick. 'Hi' means truly. 'Attached to the body' is 'kāyapaṭibaddho,' such as a ladle; thus he says 'in ladles, etc.' 'Hi' means truly. 'Pātiyamānaṃ' means being caused to drink.

Etthāti imasmiṃ sikkhāpade. “Pañcahaṅgehī”ti padassa vitthāraṃ dassento āha “thāmamajjhimassā”tiādi. Tanti dātabbavatthuṃ.

'Ettha' means in this training rule. Showing the detailed explanation of the word 'pañcahaṅgehi' (with five factors), he says, 'thāmamajjhimassa' (of one of middle strength), and so on. 'Taṃ' means the object to be given.

Tatthāti “hatthapāso paññāyatī”tivacane. Gacchantopi ṭhiteneva saṅgahito. Bhūmaṭṭhassāti bhūmiyaṃ ṭhitassa. Ākāsaṭṭhassāti ākāse ṭhitassa. “Hatthaṃ aṅga”nti padehi avayavisambandho kātabbo. Vuttanayenevāti “bhūmaṭṭhassa ca sīsenā”tiādinā vuttanayeneva. Pakkhīti sakuṇo. So hi pakkhayuttattā pakkhīti vuccati. Hatthīti kuñjaro. So hi soṇḍasaṅkhātahatthayuttattā hatthīti vuccati. Addhena aṭṭhamaṃ ratanamassāti addhaṭṭhamaratano, hatthī, tassa. Tenāti hatthinā.

'Tattha' means in the statement 'the hand's reach is known.' Even one who is going is included as one who is standing. 'Bhūmaṭṭhassa' means of one standing on the ground. 'Ākāsaṭṭhassa' means of one standing in the air. With the words 'hand' and 'limb,' the relationship of part and whole should be made. 'Vuttanayeneva' means in the very way that has been stated, beginning with 'and by the head of one on the ground.' 'Pakkhī' means a bird. For because it is endowed with wings (pakkha), it is called 'pakkhī.' 'Hatthī' means an elephant. For because it is endowed with a 'hand' (hattha) known as a trunk, it is called 'hatthī.' 'Addhaṭṭhamaratano' is analyzed as 'having seven and a half cubits'; this refers to an elephant; of that. 'Tena' means by that elephant.

Eko dāyako vadatīti sambandho. Oṇamatīti heṭṭhā namati. Ettāvatāti ekadesasampaṭicchanamattena. Tatoti sampaṭicchanato. Ugghāṭetvāti vivaritvā. Kājenāti byābhaṅgiyā. Sā hi kacati bandhati vividhaṃ bhāraṃ asminti kācoti vuccati, cakārassa jakāre kate kājopi yuttoyeva. Tiṃsa hatthā ratanāni imassāti tiṃsahattho, veṇu. Guḷakumbhoti [V 1.0073] phāṇitena pūrito ghaṭo. Paṭiggahitamevāti kumbhesu hatthapāsato bahi ṭhitesupi abhihārakassa [M 0.0088] hatthapāse ṭhitattā paṭiggahitamevāti vuttaṃ hoti. Ucchuyantadoṇitoti ucchuṃ pīḷanayantassa ambaṇato.

The connection is: 'A single donor speaks.' 'Oṇamati' means it bends low. 'Ettāvatā' means by the mere acceptance of a part. 'Tato' means from that acceptance. 'Ugghāṭetvā' means having uncovered. 'Kājena' means by a carrying pole. For it is called 'kāca' because various loads are bound (kacati) on it; when 'c' is made 'j', 'kāja' is also correct. 'Tiṃsahattho' (thirty-cubit) refers to a bamboo pole, analyzed as 'thirty cubits are its precious measures.' 'Guḷakumbho' means a pot filled with treacle. 'It is indeed accepted' is said because, although the pots are outside the hand's reach, they are within the hand's reach of the one offering. 'Ucchuyantadoṇito' means from the trough of the machine that presses sugarcane.

Bahū pattā ṭhapitā hontīti sambandho. Yatthāti yasmiṃ ṭhāne. Ṭhitassa bhikkhuno hatthapāseti yojanā. Ṭhatvā phusitvā “nisinnassa bhikkhuno”ti pāṭhasesena yojetabbaṃ. Ṭhitena vā nisinnena vā nipannena vā dāyakena diyyatīti sambandho.

The connection is: 'Many bowls are placed.' 'Yattha' means in which place. The construction is: 'in the hand's reach of a standing bhikkhu.' 'Having stood and touched' should be connected with the remainder of the text: 'of a seated bhikkhu.' The connection is: it is given by a donor who is standing, sitting, or lying down.

Pathaviyaṃ ṭhitā hontīti sambandho. Yaṃ yanti yaṃ yaṃ pattaṃ. Yattha katthacīti yesu kesucīti sambandho. Tanti taṃ vacanaṃ.

The connection is: 'They are placed on the ground.' 'Yaṃ yaṃ' means whichever bowl. The connection is: 'Yattha katthaci' means in whichever ones. 'Taṃ' means that statement.

Tattha tasmiṃ ṭhāne jāto tatthajāto, aluttasamāsoyaṃ, soyeva tatthajātako, tasmiṃ. Hīti saccaṃ, yasmā vā. Tatthajātake na ruhati yathā, evaṃ na ruhatiyevāti yojanā. Thāmamajjhimena purisena suṭṭhu haritabbanti saṃhāriyaṃ, taṃyeva saṃhārimaṃ yakārassa makāraṃ katvā, na saṃhārimaṃ asaṃhārimaṃ, tasmiṃ. Tepīti te asaṃhārimāpi. Hīti saccaṃ, yasmā vā. Tatthajātakasaṅkhepūpagāti tatthajātake samodhānetvā khepaṃ pakkhepaṃ upagatā. Hīti saccaṃ, yasmā vā. Idañhi vākyantarattā punappunaṃ vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tānīti tintiṇikādipaṇṇāni. Sandhāretunti sammā dhāretuṃ. Ṭhito dāyakoti sambandho.

‘Born there’ (tatthajāto) means born in that place; this is an unelided compound. That very one is ‘tatthajātaka,’ in that. ‘Hi’ means truly, or because. The construction is: ‘just as it does not grow in one born there, so it does not grow indeed.’ ‘To be gathered’ (saṃhāriyaṃ) means what should be well carried by a man of middling strength; that very ‘saṃhāriyaṃ’ becomes ‘saṃhārimaṃ’ by changing the ‘y’ to ‘m’; ‘not to be gathered’ (asaṃhārimaṃ) means not ‘saṃhārimaṃ,’ in that. ‘They too’ means those not to be gathered also. ‘Hi’ means truly, or because. ‘Having come to be included with what is born there’ means having been combined with what is born there, they have come to be rejected, cast aside. ‘Hi’ means truly, or because. For this, being another statement, should be seen as spoken repeatedly. ‘Those’ means leaves such as tamarind leaves, etc. ‘To bear’ means to rightly bear. The connection is: ‘the donor standing.’

Laddhassa laddhassa vatthussa sannidhiṭṭhānattā, pakkhittaṭṭhānattā vā thavīyati pasaṃsīyatīti thavikā, tato. Puñchitvā paṭiggahetvāti “puñchitvā vā paṭiggahetvā vā”ti aniyamavikappattho vāsaddo ajjhāharitabbo. Tesu tesu vatthūsu rañjati laggatīti rajo, taṃ. Vinaye paññattaṃ dukkaṭaṃ vinayadukkaṭaṃ. Taṃ panāti bhikkhaṃ pana. Paṭiggahetvā dethāti maṃ paṭiggahāpetvā mama dethāti adhippāyo.

‘Thavikā’ (a bag) is so called because it is praised and esteemed for being a place for the accumulation or placement of acquired objects; from that (thavikā). ‘Having wiped or received’ means that the word ‘vā’ (or) should be supplied as having the sense of an indefinite alternative, as in ‘either having wiped or having received.’ ‘Dust’ (rajo) is what clings or adheres to those various objects; that (dust). A wrong-doing prescribed in the Vinaya is a ‘vinayadukkaṭa.’ ‘But as for that’ means but as for the alms. ‘Having received, give’ implies the intention: ‘Having caused me to receive it, then give it to me.’

Tato tatoti tasmā tasmā ṭhānā uṭṭhāpetvāti sambandho. Tanti bhikkhaṃ. Tassāti anupasampannassa.

The connection is: ‘From that, from that’ means having raised up from each and every place. ‘That’ refers to the alms. ‘Of that’ refers to one who is not fully ordained.

So vattabboti so diyyamāno bhikkhu dāyakena bhikkhunā vattabboti yojanā. Imanti sarajapattaṃ. Tenāti diyyamānabhikkhunā. Tathā [M 0.0089] kātabbanti yathā dāyakena bhikkhunā vuttaṃ, tathā [V 1.0074] kātabbanti attho. Uplavatīti upari gacchati, plu gatiyanti hi dhātupāṭhesu (saddanītidhātumālāyaṃ 16 ḷakārantadhātu) vuttaṃ. Ettha uiti upasaggassa atthadassanatthaṃ “uparī”ti vuttaṃ, pakāralakārasaṃyogo daṭṭhabbo. Potthakesu pana “uppilavatī”ti likhanti, so apāṭho. Kañjikanti bilaṅgaṃ. Tañhi kena jalena añjiyaṃ abhibyattaṃ assāti “kañjiya”nti vuccati, tameva kañjikaṃ yakārassa kakāraṃ katvā. Taṃ pavāhetvā, apanetvāti attho. Yatthāti yasmiṃ ṭhāne. Sukkhameva bhattaṃ bhajitabbaṭṭhena sevitabbaṭṭhenāti sukkhabhattaṃ, tasmiṃ. Puratoti bhikkhussa purato, pubbe vā. Phusitānīti bindūni. Tāni hi sambādhaṭṭhānesupi phusantīti phusitānīti vuccanti.

The construction is: ‘He should be spoken to’ means that the monk who is being given to should be spoken to by the donor monk. ‘This’ refers to the bowl with residue. ‘By him’ means by the monk who is being given to. ‘It should be done thus’ means it should be done as the donor monk instructed. ‘Uplavati’ means it goes above; for in the Dhātupāṭha (Saddanīti Dhātumālā, 16, ḷ-ending roots), ‘plu’ is said to mean ‘to go.’ Here, to show the meaning of the prefix ‘u,’ ‘upari’ (above) is stated; the combination of ‘p’ and ‘l’ should be noted. In some books, however, they write ‘uppilavati,’ but that is an incorrect reading. ‘Kañjika’ means bilaṅga (sour gruel). For it is called ‘kañjiya’ because it is mixed with some water and becomes apparent; that same word becomes ‘kañjika’ by changing the ‘y’ to ‘k.’ ‘Having poured it out’ means having removed it. ‘Where’ means in whichever place. ‘Dry food’ (sukkhabhattaṃ) means food that is to be eaten dry, in the sense of being consumed or served; in that. ‘In front’ means in front of the monk, or before. ‘Drops’ (phusitāni) means droplets. For they are called ‘phusitāni’ because they touch or sprinkle even in confined places.

Uḷuṅkoti kosiyasakuṇanāmo dīghadaṇḍako eko bhājanaviseso, tena. Thevāti phusitāni. Tāni hi sambādhaṭṭhānesupi phusitattā thavīyanti pasaṃsīyantīti “thevā”ti vuccanti. Carukenāti carīyati bhakkhīyatīti caru, habyapāko, taṃ karoti anenāti carukaṃ, thālyādikaṃ khuddakabhājanaṃ, tena ākiriyamāneti sambandho. Kāḷavaṇṇakāmehi mānīyatīti masi. Khādatīti chāro khakārassa chakāraṃ, dakārassa ca rakāraṃ katvā, khāraraso, so imissatthīti chārikā. Uppatitvāti uddhaṃ gantvā. Hīti saccaṃ, yasmā vā.

‘Uḷuṅka’ (a ladle) is a specific type of vessel with a long handle, named after the Kosiyasakuṇa bird (owl); by that. ‘Thevā’ means drops. For they are called ‘thevā’ because, being sprinkled even in confined places, they are praised (thavīyanti) and esteemed. ‘By the caruka’ means by a small vessel like a pot; it is called ‘caruka’ because ‘caru’ (an oblation of cooked grain), which is eaten (carīyati) or consumed, is made with it; the connection is: ‘when being scattered by that.’ ‘Masi’ (soot) is so called because it is esteemed (mānīyati) by those who desire the black color. It corrodes (khādati), thus it is `chāro` (alkaline substance), the word being formed by changing the letter ‘kh’ to ‘ch’ and the letter ‘d’ to ‘r’; `khāraraso` is the alkaline taste; `chārikā` (ash) is so called because it has this. ‘Having gone up’ means having ascended. ‘Hi’ means truly, or because.

Phāletvāti chinditvā. Dentānaṃ anupasampannānanti sambandho. Pāyāsassāti pāyāsena. Tathāpīti tena mukhavaṭṭiyā gahaṇākārenapi.

‘Having split’ means having cut. The connection is: ‘of those not yet fully ordained who are giving.’ ‘Of rice porridge’ means with rice porridge. ‘Even so’ means even by that manner of taking it at the rim of the mouth.

Ābhogaṃ katvāti “paṭiggahessāmī”ti manasikāraṃ katvā. Soti niddaṃ okkanto bhikkhu. Vaṭṭatiyevāti ābhogassa katattā vaṭṭatiyeva. Anādaranti anādarena, karaṇatthe cetaṃ upayogavacanaṃ, anādaraṃ hutvāti vā yojetabbaṃ. Kecīti abhayagirivāsino. Kāyena paṭibaddho kāyapaṭibaddho, tena paṭibaddho kāyapaṭibaddhapaṭibaddho[M 0.0090], tena. Vacanamattamevāti “paṭibaddhapaṭibaddha”nti ekaṃ atirekaṃ paṭibaddhavacanamattameva nānaṃ, atthato pana kāyapaṭibaddhamevāti adhippāyo. Yampīti yampi vatthu. Tatrāti tasmiṃ vaṭṭane. Tanti anujānanaṃ.

‘Having made an intention’ means having formed the thought, ‘I will receive it.’ ‘He’ refers to a monk who has fallen asleep. ‘It is indeed permissible’ means it is indeed permissible because the intention was made. ‘Disregard’ means through disregard; this is a locative expression in the instrumental sense, or it should be construed as ‘being disregardful.’ ‘Some’ refers to the Abhayagirivāsins. ‘Bound to the body’ (kāyapaṭibaddho); ‘bound to that which is bound to the body’ (kāyapaṭibaddhapaṭibaddho) means bound by that. ‘Merely a word’ means that the difference is only the single extra word ‘bound’ in ‘bound to what is bound,’ but the intention is that in meaning it is just what is bound to the body. ‘Whatever’ means whatever thing. ‘There’ means in that permissibility. ‘That’ refers to the allowance.

Neyyo adhippāyaṃ netvā ñāto attho imassāti neyyatthaṃ. Etthāti sutte, suttassa vā. Yanti vatthu patatīti sambandho. Parigaḷitvāti bhassitvā. Suddhāyāti nirajāya. Sāmanti sayaṃ. Puñchitvā vātiādīsu tayo vāsaddā aniyamavikappatthā. Puñchitādīsu hi ekasmiṃ kicce [V 1.0075] kate itarakiccaṃ kātabbaṃ natthīti adhippāyo. Tenāti tena bhikkhunā, “āharāpetumpī”tipade kāritakammaṃ. “Kasmā na vaṭṭatī”ti pucchā. Hīti vitthāro. Vadantena bhagavatāti sambandho. Etthāti suttavacanesu. “Pariccattaṃ taṃ bhikkhave dāyakehī”ti vacanenāti yojanā. Adhippāyoti nītattho adhippāyo, nippariyāyena itattho ñātattho adhippāyoti vuttaṃ hoti.

‘Neyyattha’ (of implicit meaning) is so called because its meaning is known by drawing out the intention. ‘Here’ means in the sutta, or of the sutta. The connection is: ‘Whatever’ means the object that falls. ‘Having slipped down’ means having fallen. ‘Pure’ means free from dust. ‘By oneself’ means by oneself. In ‘having wiped or,’ etc., the three instances of the word ‘vā’ (or) have the sense of an indefinite alternative. For the intention is that when one action, such as wiping, is done, there is no need to do the other actions. ‘By him’ means by that monk; in the phrase ‘even to cause to bring,’ it is a causative action. ‘Why is it not permissible?’ is a question. ‘Hi’ is an elaboration. The connection is: ‘by the Blessed One who is speaking.’ ‘Here’ means in the words of the sutta. The construction is: by the statement, “That, bhikkhus, has been relinquished by the donors.” ‘Intention’ means an explicit intention (nītattho adhippāyo); it is said to be an intention whose meaning is explicit, whose meaning is known directly, without circumlocution.

Evaṃ nītatthamadhippāyaṃ dassetvā neyyattha, madhippāyaṃ dassento āha “yasmā cā”ti ādi. Tanti paribhuñjanaṃ anuññātanti sambandho. Dutiyadivasepīti pisaddo sampiṇḍanattho, aparadivasepīti attho. Adhippāyoti neyyattho adhippāyo netvā iyyattho ñātattho adhippāyoti vuttaṃ hoti.

Having thus shown the explicit intention, showing the implicit intention, he said, ‘And since…’ and so on. The connection is: ‘That’ means the use is allowed. ‘Even on the second day’: the particle ‘pi’ has the sense of inclusion, meaning ‘even on a subsequent day.’ ‘Intention’ means an implicit intention (neyyattho adhippāyo); it is said to be an intention whose meaning is to be drawn out, whose meaning is to be understood.

Bhuñjantānaṃ bhikkhūnanti sambandho. Hīti vitthāro. Dantāti dasanā. Te hi daṃsīyanti bhakkhīyanti etehīti “dantā”ti vuccanti. Satthaṃyeva satthakaṃ khuddakaṭṭhena, tena paṭiggahitena satthakena. Etanti malaṃ. Tanti lohagandhamattaṃ. Pariharantīti paṭiggahetvā haranti. Hīti saccaṃ, yasmā vā. Taṃ satthakaṃ paribhogatthāya yasmā na pariharanti, tasmā eseva nayoti attho. Uggahitapaccayā, sannidhipaccayā vā doso natthīti vuttaṃ hoti. Tatthāti tesu takkakhīresu. Nīlikāti nīlavaṇṇā snehā. Āmakatakkādīsūti apakkesu takkakhīresu.

The connection is: ‘of the monks who are eating.’ ‘Hi’ is an elaboration. ‘Dantā’ means teeth (dasanā). For they are called ‘dantā’ because one bites (daṃsīyati) and eats with them. ‘A small knife’ (satthakaṃ) is just a knife (satthaṃ), in the sense of being small; by that small knife which has been received. ‘This’ refers to the impurity. ‘That’ is merely the smell of metal. ‘They carry’ means they take up and carry. ‘Hi’ means truly, or because. The meaning is: because they do not carry that small knife for the purpose of personal use, therefore this is the method. It is said that there is no fault on account of taking it up or on account of storing. ‘There’ means in that buttermilk and milk. ‘Nīlikā’ refers to blue-colored oily substances. ‘In unripe buttermilk and the like’ means in uncooked buttermilk and milk.

Kiliṭṭhaudakanti [M 0.0091] samalaṃ udakaṃ. Tassāti sāmaṇerassa. Pattagataṃ odananti sambandho. Assāti sāmaṇerassa. Uggahitakoti avagahitako. “Uññāto”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 1.112) viya ukāro okāraviparīto hoti, apaṭiggahetvā gahitattā duggahitakoti vuttaṃ hoti.

‘Soiled water’ means impure water. ‘His’ refers to the novice. The connection is: ‘the rice in the bowl.’ ‘His’ refers to the novice. ‘Uggahitaka’ means `avagahitaka`. As in ‘uññāto’ etc. (Saṃ. Ni. 1.112), the ‘u’ is the opposite of ‘o’; it is said to be ‘duggahita’ (improperly taken) because it was taken without having been formally received.

Etenāti odanena. Paṭiggahitameva hoti hatthato amuttattāti adhippāyo.

‘By this’ means by the rice. The intention is: it is indeed considered received because it has not been released from the hand.

Puna paṭiggahetabbaṃ sāpekkhe satīti adhippāyo. Ettoti ito pattato. Sāmaṇero pakkhipatīti sambandho. Tatoti pattato. Kecīti abhayagirivāsino. Tanti “puna paṭiggahetabba”nti vadantānaṃ kesañci ācariyānaṃ vacanaṃ veditabbanti sambandho. Yanti pūvabhattādi.

The intention is: ‘It should be received again’ if there is expectation. ‘From this’ means from this bowl. The connection is: ‘the novice places it.’ ‘From that’ means from the bowl. ‘Some’ refers to the residents of Abhayagiri. The connection is: ‘That’ should be understood as the statement of some teachers who say, ‘It should be received again.’ ‘Yanti’ refers to cakes, cooked rice, and so on.

Attano [V 1.0076] vāti sāmaṇerassa vā. Sāmaṇerāti āmantanaṃ. Tassāti sāmaṇerassa. Bhājaneti yāgupacanakabhājane. Yāgukuṭanti yāguyā pūritaṃ kuṭaṃ. Tanti yāgukuṭaṃ. “Bhikkhunā paṭiggaṇhāpetu”nti kāritakammaṃ upanetabbaṃ. Gīvaṃ ṭhapetvā āvajjetīti sambandho. Āvajjetīti pariṇāmeti.

‘Attano vā’ means ‘or one's own’, or ‘of the novice’. ‘Sāmaṇerā’ is a vocative. ‘Tassa’ refers to ‘of the novice’. ‘Bhājane’ means ‘in the vessel for cooking gruel’. ‘Yāgukuṭaṃ’ means ‘a pot filled with gruel’. ‘Taṃ’ refers to ‘that gruel pot’. The causative action ‘should be caused to be received by a bhikkhu’ is to be supplied. The connection is: ‘having placed the neck, he inclines it’. ‘Āvajjeti’ means ‘he inclines’.

Paṭiggahaṇūpagaṃ bhāranti thāmamajjhimena purisena saṃhārimaṃ bhāraṃ. Balavatā sāmaṇerenāti sambandho. Telaghaṭaṃ vāti telena pakkhittaṃ ghaṭaṃ vā. Laggentīti lambenti. Ayameva vā pāṭho.

‘Paṭiggahaṇūpagaṃ bhāraṃ’ means ‘a load that can be carried by a man of average strength’. The connection is: ‘by a strong novice’. ‘Telaghaṭaṃ vā’ means ‘or a pot filled with oil’. ‘Laggenti’ means ‘they hang’. Or this is the very reading.

Nāgassa danto viyāti nāgadantako, sadisatthe ko. Aṅkīyate lakkhīyate anenāti aṅkuso, gajamatthakamhi vijjhanakaṇḍako. Aṅkuso viyāti aṅkusako, tasmiṃ aṅkusake vā laggitā hontīti sambandho. Gaṇhatoti gaṇhantassa. Mañcassa heṭṭhā heṭṭhāmañco, tasmiṃ. Tanti telathālakaṃ.

‘Nāgassa danto viya’ means ‘like an elephant's tusk’, hence ‘nāgadantako’; the suffix ‘-ka’ is in the sense of similarity. ‘Aṅkīyate lakkhīyate anena’ means ‘that by which one is marked or distinguished’, thus ‘aṅkusa’, which is ‘the piercing spike on an elephant's head’. ‘Aṅkuso viya’ means ‘like a goad’, hence ‘aṅkusako’; the connection is ‘or they are hung on that goad-like peg’. ‘Gaṇhato’ means ‘of one who takes’. ‘Mañcassa heṭṭhā’ means ‘beneath the bed’, hence ‘heṭṭhāmañco’, ‘a lower bed’; ‘tasmiṃ’ means ‘on that’. ‘Taṃ’ refers to ‘the oil dish’.

Ārohantehi [M 0.0092] ca orohantehi ca niccaṃ sevīyatīti nisseṇī, tassā majjhaṃ nisseṇimajjhaṃ, tasmiṃ. Kaṇṇe uṭṭhitaṃ kaṇṇikaṃ, kaṇṇamalaṃ, kaṇṇikaṃ viya kaṇṇikaṃ, yathā hi kaṇṇamalaṃ kaṇṇato uṭṭhahitvā sayaṃ pavattati, evaṃ telādito uṭṭhahitvā sayaṃ pavattatīti vuttaṃ hoti. Ghanacuṇṇanti kathinacuṇṇaṃ. Taṃsamuṭṭhānameva nāmāti tato telādito samuṭṭhānameva nāma hotīti attho. Etanti kaṇṇikādi. Idaṃ padaṃ pubbāparāpekkhaṃ.

‘Ārohantehi ca orohantehi ca niccaṃ sevīyati’ means ‘that which is constantly used by those ascending and descending’, thus a ‘ladder’ (nisseṇī); ‘nisseṇimajjhaṃ’ is the middle of that ladder, and ‘tasmiṃ’ means ‘on that’. ‘Kaṇṇe uṭṭhitaṃ kaṇṇikaṃ’ means ‘that which arises in the ear, kaṇṇikaṃ’, which is ‘earwax’; ‘kaṇṇikaṃ viya kaṇṇikaṃ’ means ‘like earwax’, for just as earwax arises from the ear and moves on its own, so too it is said that oil and so on arises and moves on its own. ‘Ghanacuṇṇaṃ’ means ‘hard powder’. ‘Taṃsamuṭṭhānameva nāma’ means ‘it is simply called that which arises from that’, meaning that it is simply called that which arises from oil, etc. ‘Etaṃ’ refers to ‘kaṇṇika’ and so on. This word is dependent on what precedes and follows.

Yottenāti rajjunā. Añño detīti sambandho.

‘Yottena’ means ‘with a rope’. The connection is: ‘another gives’.

Pavisante ca nikkhamante ca varati āvarati imāyāti vati, taṃ. Ucchūti rasālo. So hi usati visaṃ dāhetīti ucchūti vuccati, taṃ. Timbarusakanti tindukaṃ. Tañhi temeti bhuñjantaṃ puggalaṃ addeti rasenāti timbo, rusati khudditaṃ nāsetīti rusako, timbo ca so rusako cāti “timbarusako”ti vuccati, taṃ. Vatidaṇḍakesūti vatiyā atthāya nikkhaṇitesu daṇḍakesu. Mayaṃ panāti saṅgahakārācariyabhūtā buddhaghosanāmakā mayaṃ pana, attānaṃ sandhāya bahuvacanavasena vuttaṃ. Na puthulo pākāroti aḍḍhateyyahatthapāsānatikkamaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Hatthasatampīti ratanasatampi.

That by which one obstructs and prevents those entering and exiting is called a fence (vati); ‘taṃ’ refers to that. ‘Ucchū’ is sugarcane (rasālo). It is called ‘ucchū’ because it burns (usati) and consumes (dāheti) poison; ‘taṃ’ refers to that. ‘Timbarusaka’ is the tinduka tree. It is called ‘timbo’ because it moistens (temeti) and afflicts (addeti) the person eating it with its juice (rasena); it is called ‘rusako’ because it destroys (nāseti) hunger (khudditaṃ); since it is both ‘timbo’ and ‘rusako’, it is called ‘timbarusako’; ‘taṃ’ refers to that. ‘Vatidaṇḍakesu’ means ‘on the stakes dug in for the purpose of a fence’. ‘Mayaṃ pana’ means ‘but we’, referring to us, Buddhaghosa by name, who are the teachers who compiled the collection; this is said using the plural to refer to oneself. ‘The wall is not thick’ is said with reference to exceeding two and a half cubits of stone. ‘Hatthasataṃpi’ means ‘even a hundred ratanas’.

Soti [V 1.0077] sāmaṇero. Bhikkhussa detīti yojanā. Aparoti sāmaṇero.

‘So’ refers to ‘the novice’. The construction is: ‘he gives to the bhikkhu’. ‘Aparo’ refers to ‘the other novice’.

Phalaṃ imissatthīti phalinī, inapaccayo itthiliṅgajotako ī, taṃ sākhanti yojanā. Phalinisākhanti samāsatopi pāṭho atthi. Macchikavāraṇatthanti madhuphāṇitādīhi makkhanaṭṭhāne nilīyantīti makkhikā, tāyeva macchikā khakārassa chakāraṃ katvā, tāsaṃ nivāraṇāya. Mūlapaṭiggahamevāti mūle paṭiggahaṇameva, paṭhamapaṭiggahamevāti vuttaṃ hoti.

‘Phalaṃ imissatthīti phalinī’ means ‘fruit is in this, thus fruit-bearing’; the suffix ‘-ina’ has ‘ī’ indicating the feminine gender. The construction is: ‘that branch’. ‘Phalinisākhā’ (fruit-bearing branch) is also a reading in compound form. ‘Macchikavāraṇatthaṃ’ (for warding off flies) means that ‘makkhikā’ (flies) hide in places smeared with honey, molasses, etc.; these same ‘makkhikā’ are called ‘macchikā’ by changing the ‘kha’ sound to ‘cha’, and it is ‘for warding them off’. ‘Mūlapaṭiggahameva’ means ‘only the reception at the root’; that is, the first reception is meant.

Bhikkhu gacchatīti sambandho. Arittenāti kenipātena. Tañhi arati nāvā gacchati anenāti arittaṃ, tena. Tanti paṭiggahaṇārahaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ[M 0.0093]. Anupasampannenāti kāritakammaṃ. Tasmimpīti cāṭikuṇḍakepi. Tanti anupasampannaṃ.

The connection is: ‘the bhikkhu goes’. ‘Arittena’ means ‘by an oar’ (kenipātena). For by that (anena) a boat goes (gacchati) without stopping (a-rati), thus it is an ‘oar’ (arittaṃ); ‘by that’ (tena). ‘Taṃ’ refers to ‘an item suitable for receiving’. Regarding ‘by one not fully ordained’, this implies a causative action. ‘Tasmiṃpi’ means ‘even in that’, that is, ‘even in a pot or vessel’. ‘Taṃ’ refers to ‘the unordained one’.

Pātheyyataṇḍuleti pathassa hite taṇḍule. Tesanti sāmaṇerānaṃ. Itarehīti bhikkhūhi gahitataṇḍulehi. Sabbehi bhikkhūhi bhuttanti sambandho. Etthāti bhikkhūhi gahitehi sāmaṇerassa taṇḍulehi yāgupacane na dissatīti sambandho. Kāraṇanti parivattetvā bhuttassa ca aparivattetvā bhuttassa ca kāraṇaṃ.

‘Pātheyyataṇḍule’ means ‘on the rice beneficial for the journey’. ‘Tesaṃ’ refers to ‘of the novices’. ‘Itarehi’ means ‘by the others’, that is, ‘with the rice taken by the bhikkhus’. The connection is: ‘eaten by all the bhikkhus’. The connection for ‘Ettha’ is: ‘here, in the cooking of the gruel, the novice's rice taken by the bhikkhus is not apparent’. ‘Kāraṇaṃ’ refers to ‘the reason for both having eaten after exchanging and having eaten without exchanging’.

Bhattaṃ pacitukāmo sāmaṇeroti yojanā. Bhikkhunā āropetabbaṃ, aggi na kātabboti sambandho. Puna paṭiggahaṇakiccaṃ natthi mūle paṭiggahitattāti adhippāyo.

The construction is: ‘the novice desiring to cook rice’. The connection is: ‘it should be placed on by the bhikkhu, a fire should not be made’. The intention is: ‘there is no need for receiving again, because it was already received at the beginning’.

Assāti sāmaṇerassa. Tatoti aggijālanato.

‘Assa’ refers to ‘of the novice’. ‘Tato’ means ‘from that’, that is, ‘from the kindling of the fire’.

Tatte udaketi udake tāpe. Tatoti taṇḍulapakkhipanato.

‘Tatte udake’ means ‘in hot water’, that is, ‘when the water is heated’. ‘Tato’ means ‘from that’, that is, ‘from the act of putting in rice’.

Pidhānanti ukkhalipidhānaṃ. Tassevāti hatthakukkuccakassa bhikkhuno eva. Dabbiṃ vāti kaṭacchuṃ vā. So hi darīyati viloḷīyati imāyāti dabbīti vuccati.

‘Pidhānaṃ’ means ‘a pot lid’. ‘Tasseva’ refers to ‘of that very monk who is scrupulous about his hands’. ‘Dabbiṃ vā’ means ‘or a ladle’ or ‘a spoon’. For by this one stirs and mixes, thus it is called ‘dabbī’.

Tatrāti tasmiṃ ṭhapane. Tassevāti lolabhikkhusseva. Tatoti pattato. Puna tatoti sākhādito. Tatthāti phalarukkhe.

‘Tatra’ means ‘in that placing’. ‘Tasseva’ refers to ‘of that very greedy monk’. ‘Tato’ means ‘from that’, that is, ‘from the bowl’. ‘Puna tato’ means ‘again from that’, that is, ‘from the branch, etc.’. ‘Tattha’ means ‘in the fruit tree’.

Vitakkaṃ sodhetunti “mayhampi dassatī”ti vitakkaṃ sodhetuṃ. Tatoti ambaphalādito.

‘Vitakkaṃ sodhetuṃ’ means ‘to purify the thought’, specifically ‘to purify the thought, “he will give to me also”’. ‘Tato’ means ‘from that’, that is, ‘from mangoes, fruits, etc.’.

Puna [V 1.0078] tatoti mātāpitūnamatthāya gahitatelādito. Teti mātāpitaro. Tatoyevāti tehiyeva taṇḍulehi sampādetvāti sambandho.

‘Puna tato’ means ‘again from that’, that is, ‘from the oil, etc., taken for the sake of his parents’. ‘Te’ refers to ‘the parents’. ‘Tatoyeva’ means ‘from that very’, and the connection is ‘having prepared it with that very rice’.

Etthāti tāpitaudake. Amuñcanteneva hatthenāti yojanā. Aṅganti vināsaṃ gacchantīti aṅgārā. Darīyanti phalīyantīti dārūni.

‘Ettha’ means ‘in heated water’. The construction is: ‘with a hand that does not let go’. ‘Aṅgārā’ (embers) are so called because they go (gacchanti) to destruction (aṅgaṃ). ‘Dārūni’ (wood) are so called because they are split (darīyanti) and broken (phalīyanti).

Vutto sāmaṇeroti yojanā.

The construction is: ‘the novice who was spoken to’.

Gavati [M 0.0094] paribhuñjantānaṃ vissaṭṭhaṃ saddaṃ karotīti guḷo, guḷati visato jīvitaṃ rakkhatīti vā guḷo, taṃ bhājento bhikkhūti sambandho. Tassāti lolasāmaṇerassa.

That which makes a distinct sound (vissaṭṭhaṃ saddaṃ) for those partaking of it is called ‘guḷa’ (molasses); or, ‘guḷa’ is that which protects (rakkhati) life from poison (visato). The connection is: ‘the bhikkhu distributing it’. ‘Tassa’ refers to ‘of the greedy novice’.

Dhūmassatthāya vaṭṭīyati vaṭṭitvā karīyatīti dhūmavaṭṭi, taṃ. Mukhīyati viparīyatīti mukhaṃ. Kaṃ vuccati sīsaṃ, taṃ tiṭṭhati etthāti kaṇṭho.

That which is rolled and made for the purpose of smoke is called a ‘dhūmavaṭṭi’ (smoke-wick); ‘taṃ’ refers to that. ‘Mukhaṃ’ (mouth) is so called because it is turned or changed (mukhīyati, viparīyati). ‘Kaṃ’ is said to be the head (sīsaṃ); that stands (tiṭṭhati) here (ettha), thus it is the ‘throat’ (kaṇṭho).

Bhattuggāroti uddhaṃ girati niggiratīti uggāro, bhattameva uggāro bhattuggāro, uggārabhattanti attho. Dantantareti dantavivare.

Regarding ‘bhattuggāro’: ‘uggāra’ is that which one emits upwards. Food itself is the ‘uggāra’, thus ‘bhattuggāro’; the meaning is ‘regurgitated food’. ‘Dantantare’ means ‘in the gaps between the teeth’.

Upakaṭṭhe kāleti āsanne majjhanhike kāle. Kakkhāretvāti sañcitvā. Tassa atthaṃ dassetuṃ vuttaṃ “dve tayo kheḷapiṇḍe pātetvā”ti. Phaḷusaṅkhātaṃ siṅgaṃ visāṇaṃ asmiṃ atthīti siṅgī, soyeva kaṭukabhayehi viramitabbattā siṅgīveroti vuccati. Aṅkīyati rukkho navaṃ uggatoti lakkhīyati etehīti aṅkurā, samaṃ loṇena udakaṃ, samaṃ vā udakena loṇaṃ asminti samuddo, tassa udakaṃ avayavīavayavabhāvenāti samuddodakaṃ, tena apaṭiggahitenāti sambandho. Phāṇati guḷato thaddhabhāvaṃ gacchatīti phāṇitaṃ. Karena hatthena gahitabbāti karakā, vassopalaṃ, karena gaṇhitumarahāti attho. Katakaṭṭhināti katakanāmakassa ekassa rukkhavisesassa aṭṭhinā. Tanti udakaṃ. Kapitthoti ekassa ambilaphalassa rukkhavisesassa nāmaṃ.

‘Upakaṭṭhe kāle’ means ‘at the approaching midday time’. ‘Kakkhāretvā’ means ‘having accumulated’. To explain its meaning, it is said, ‘having let fall two or three lumps of phlegm’. ‘Siṅgī’ is so called because a horn (siṅgaṃ) known as ‘phaḷusa’ is present in it; it is called ‘siṅgīvera’ because one should refrain (viramitabba) from its bitter (kaṭuka) and fearsome (bhaya) nature. ‘Aṅkurā’ (sprouts) are so called because by them a tree is marked (aṅkīyati) or distinguished (lakkhīyati) as newly sprouted. ‘Samudda’ (ocean) is so called because in it water is equal with salt, or salt is equal with water; ‘samuddodakaṃ’ (ocean water) refers to its water in terms of whole and part, and the connection is ‘by that unreceived ocean water’. ‘Phāṇitaṃ’ (molasses) is that which attains (gacchati) a hard state (thaddhabhāvaṃ) from jaggery (guḷato). ‘Karakā’ (hailstone) is so called because it should be taken by the hand (karena gahitabbā); the meaning is it is worthy to be taken by the hand. ‘Katakaṭṭhinā’ means ‘with the kernel of a particular tree called kataka’. ‘Taṃ’ refers to ‘water’. ‘Kapittha’ is the name of a particular sour-fruit tree.

Bahalanti āvilaṃ. Sanditvāti visanditvā. Kakudhasobbhādayoti kakudharukkhasamīpe ṭhitā sobbhādayo. Rukkhatoti kakudharukkhato. Parittanti appakaṃ.

'Bahalaṃ' means 'turbid'. 'Sanditvā' means 'having flowed forth'. 'Kakudhasobbhādayo' refers to 'ponds, etc., standing near the kakudha tree'. 'Rukkhato' means 'from the kakudha tree'. 'Parittaṃ' means 'a small amount'.

Pānīyaghaṭe pakkhittāni hontīti sambandho. Tanti vāsamattaṃ udakaṃ. Tatthevāti ṭhapitapupphavāsitapānīyeyeva[V 1.0079]. Ṭhapitaṃ dantakaṭṭhanti sambandho. Ajānantassa bhikkhussāti yojanā. Anādare cetaṃ sāmivacanaṃ. Hīti saccaṃ, yasmā vā.

'Pānīyaghaṭe pakkhittāni honti' is the connection. 'Taṃ' refers to 'just enough water for scenting'. 'Tattheva' means 'right there', referring to 'in the placed, flower-scented water itself'. 'Ṭhapitaṃ dantakaṭṭhaṃ' is the connection. 'Ajānantassa bhikkhussa' is the construction. 'Anādare cetaṃ sāmivacanaṃ' means 'and this is a genitive case used in the sense of disregard'. 'Hi' means 'truly', or 'because'.

Kiṃ [M 0.0095] mahābhūtaṃ vaṭṭati, kiṃ na vaṭṭatīti yojanā. Yaṃ panāti mahābhūtaṃ pana. Aṅgalagganti aṅgesu laggaṃ, mahābhūtanti sambandho. Etthāti sede. Sujhāpitanti aṅgārasadisaṃ katvā suṭṭhu jhāpitaṃ.

'Kiṃ mahābhūtaṃ vaṭṭati, kiṃ na vaṭṭati' is the construction. As for 'Yaṃ pana', it refers to 'but the great element'. 'Aṅgalaggaṃ' means 'stuck to the limbs'; the connection is with 'the great element'. 'Ettha' means 'in sweat'. 'Sujjhāpitaṃ' means 'thoroughly burnt', having been made like a burning coal.

Cattārīti pathavī chārikā gūthaṃ muttanti cattāri. Mahāvikaṭānīti mahantāni sappadaṭṭhakkhaṇasaṅkhāte vikārakāle kattabbāni osadhāni. Etthāti “asati kappiyakārake”ti vacane. Kālodissaṃ nāmāti byādhodissa, puggalodissa, kālodissa, samayodissa, desodissa, vasodissa, bhesajjodissasaṅkhātesu sattasu odissesu kālodissaṃ nāmāti attho. Dasamaṃ.

'Cattāri' refers to the four: 'earth, ashes, dung, and urine'. 'Mahāvikaṭāni' means 'great medicines to be used at the time of a disorder, designated as the moment of being bitten by a snake'. 'Ettha' refers to the statement, 'when there is no one to render it allowable'. 'Kālodissaṃ nāma' means that among the seven designations—namely, designation with respect to illness, person, time, occasion, place, dwelling, and medicine—it is the designation with respect to time that is meant. The tenth.

Bhojanavaggo catuttho.

The Food Chapter is the fourth.

5. Acelakavaggo

5. The Chapter on Naked Ascetics

1. Acelakasikkhāpada-atthayojanā

1. An Explanation of the Meaning of the Training Rule on Naked Ascetics

269. Acelakavaggassa paṭhame parivisati etthāti parivesananti dassento āha “parivesanaṭṭhāna”nti. Paribbājakapabbajasaddā samānāti āha “paribbājakasamāpannoti pabbajjaṃ samāpanno”ti. Titthena samaṃ pūratīti samatitthīkaṃ, nadīādīsu udakaṃ, samatitthikaṃ viyāti samatitthikaṃ, pattabhājanesu yāgubhattaṃ. Tesanti mātāpitūnaṃ dentassāti sambandho. “Dāpetī”ti ettha dādhātuyā sampadānassa suvijānitattā taṃ adassetvā kāritakammameva dassento āha “anupasampannenā”ti.

269. In the first section of the Chapter on Naked Ascetics, showing that 'parivesanaṃ' means 'one serves here', he said 'parivesanaṭṭhānaṃ' (the place of serving). Stating that the words 'paribbājaka' and 'pabbajja' are synonymous, he said, 'paribbājakasamāpanno' means 'one who has undertaken the going forth (pabbajjaṃ samāpanno)'. 'Samatitthikaṃ' is so called because 'it fills level with the ford' (titthena samaṃ pūrati), like water in rivers and so on; and like that which is level with the ford (samatitthikaṃ viya), so is gruel or rice in bowls and vessels called 'samatitthikaṃ'. The connection of 'tesaṃ' is with 'dentassa', meaning 'of one who gives to his parents'. Regarding 'dāpeti', because the recipient (sampadāna) of the root 'dā' is easily understood, he does not show it, but showing only the causative agent, he said, 'by one who is not fully ordained' (anupasampannenā).

273. “Santike”tiiminā “upanikkhipitvā”ti ettha upasaddassa samīpatthaṃ dasseti. Tesanti [V 1.0080] titthiyānaṃ. Tatthāti bhājane. Itoti pattato. Idhāti mayhaṃ bhājane. Nanti khādanīyabhojanīyaṃ. Tassāti titthiyassāti. Paṭhamaṃ.

273. By 'santike' (near), he shows that the prefix 'upa' in 'upanikkhipitvā' (having placed near) has the meaning of nearness. 'Tesaṃ' refers to 'of the sectarians'. 'Tattha' means 'in the container'. 'Ito' means 'from the bowl'. 'Idha' means 'in my container'. 'Naṃ' refers to 'hard and soft food'. 'Tassa' means 'of the sectarian'. The first.

2. Uyyojanasikkhāpadaṃ

2. The Training Rule on Dismissal

274. Dutiye [M 0.0096] paṭikkamanaasanasālasaddānaṃ pariyāyattā vuttaṃ “asanasālāyapī”ti. Bhattassa vissajjanaṃ bhattavissaggoti kate bhattakiccanti āha “bhattakicca”nti. Sambhūdhātussa papubbaapadhātvatthattā vuttaṃ “na pāpuṇī”ti.

274. In the second, because the words 'paṭikkamana' (retreat), 'āsana' (sitting-place), and 'sālā' (hall) are synonyms, it is said, 'asanasālāyapi' (even in the sitting-hall). 'Bhattavissaggo' is the dismissal of the meal; when this is done, it is the 'meal-duty' (bhattakiccaṃ), thus he said 'bhattakiccaṃ'. Because the root 'sambhū' has the meaning of the root 'āp' preceded by 'pa', it was said, 'na pāpuṇi' (did not reach).

276. Vuttāvasesanti vuttehi mātugāmena saddhiṃ hasitukāmatādīhi avasesaṃ. Tasminti uyyojitabhikkhumhi. Atthatoti vijahantavijahitabhikkhūnaṃ avinābhāvasaṅkhātaatthato. Itarenāti uyyojakabhikkhunā. Tatthāti “dassanūpacāraṃ vā savanūpacāraṃ vā”tivacane. Etthāti niddhāraṇasamudāyo, dassanūpacārasavanūpacāresūti attho. “Tathātiiminā dvādasahatthapamāṇaṃ atidisati. Tehīti kuṭṭādīhi. Tassāti dassanūpacārātikkamassa. “Vuttapakāramanācāra”nti iminā “na añño koci paccayo”ti ettha aññasaddassa apādānaṃ dasseti, “kāraṇa”ntiiminā paccayasaddassatthaṃ.

276. 'Vuttāvasesaṃ' refers to what remains from what has been said, such as the desire to laugh with a woman, and so on. 'Tasmiṃ' refers to 'in that dismissed monk'. 'Atthato' means 'from the meaning', that is, from the meaning designated as the inseparability of the monks who are abandoning or have been abandoned. 'Itarena' means 'by the other', referring to the dismissing monk. 'Tattha' refers to the expression 'either the range of sight or the range of hearing'. 'Ettha' indicates a specification from a group, meaning 'in the range of sight or the range of hearing'. By 'tathā', he applies by extension the measure of twelve cubits. 'Tehi' refers to 'by walls, etc.'. 'Tassa' refers to 'of the transgression of the range of sight'. By 'vuttapakāramanācāraṃ' (improper conduct of the kind stated), he shows the ablative sense of the word 'añño' (other) in 'na añño koci paccayo' (no other reason); and by 'kāraṇaṃ' (reason), he shows the meaning of the word 'paccayo'.

277. Kalisaddassa pāpaparājayasaṅkhātesu dvīsu atthesu pāpasaṅkhāto kodhoti āha “kalīti kodho”ti. “Āṇa”ntiiminā sāsanasaddassatthaṃ dasseti. Vuttañhi “āṇā ca sāsanaṃ ñeyya”nti. Kodhavasena vadatīti sambandho. Dassetvā vadatīti yojanā. Imassa ṭhānaṃ nisajjaṃ ālokitaṃ vilokitaṃ passatha bhoti yojanā. Imināpīti amanāpavacanaṃ vacanenāpīti. Dutiyaṃ.

277. Among the two meanings of the word 'kali', namely 'evil' (pāpa) and 'defeat' (parājaya), the one designated as 'evil' is anger (kodha); thus he said, 'kali is anger'. By 'āṇā' (command), he shows the meaning of the word 'sāsana' (instruction). For it is said, 'Command and instruction should be known'. The connection is: 'he speaks out of anger'. The construction is: 'he speaks having pointed out'. The construction is: 'Good lady, see the standing, sitting, looking at, and looking around of this person'. 'Imināpi' means 'even by this, that is, by unpleasant speech'. The second.

3. Sabhojanasikkhāpadaṃ

3. The Training Rule on a Meal

279. Tatiye “sayaniyaghare”ti vattabbe yakāralopaṃ katvā “sayanighare”ti vuttanti āha “sayanighare”ti. Yatoti ettha tosaddo paṭhamādīsu atthesu dissati. “Yatonidāna”ntiādīsu (su. ni. 275) paṭhamatthe. “Antarāye asesato”tiādīsu (dha. sa. aṭṭha. ganthārambhakathā 7) dutiyatthe[M 0.0097]. “Aniccato”tiādīsu (paṭṭhā. 1.1.409) tatiyatthe. “Mātito pitito”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.311) pañcamyatthe. “Yaṃ [V 1.0081] parato dānapaccayā”tiādīsu (jā. 2.22.585) chaṭṭhyatthe. “Purato pacchato”tiādīsu (pāci. 576) sattamyatthe. “Padamato”tiādīsu kāraṇatthe dissati. Idhāpi kāraṇattheyevāti āha “yasmā”ti. Yasmā kāraṇā ayyassa bhikkhā dinnā, tasmā gacchatha bhante tumheti attho. Yanti bhikkhaṃ. Voti tumhehi. Adhippāyoti purisassa ajjhāsayo. “Pariyuṭṭhito”ti sāmaññato vuttepi atthapakaraṇādito rāgapariyuṭṭhitovādhippetoti āha “rāgapariyuṭṭhito”ti, rāgena paribhavitvā uṭṭhitoti attho.

279. In the third, concerning 'sayanighare', he states that this is said with the elision of the letter 'ya', when 'sayaniyaghare' ought to be said. Here, in 'yato', the suffix 'to' is seen in the sense of the first case and so on. In 'yatonidānaṃ', etc., it is in the sense of the first case. In 'antarāye asesato', etc., it is in the sense of the second. In 'aniccato', etc., it is in the sense of the third. In 'mātito pitito', etc., it is in the sense of the fifth. In 'yaṃ parato dānapaccayā', etc., it is in the sense of the sixth. In 'purato pacchato', etc., it is in the sense of the seventh. In 'padamato', etc., it is seen in the sense of cause. Here too, it is in the sense of cause; hence he says 'yasmā' (because). The meaning is: 'Because the alms were given to the venerable one for a reason, therefore, venerable sirs, you may go'. 'Yaṃ' means 'the alms'. 'Vo' means 'by you'. 'Adhippāyo' (intention) is the person's disposition. Although 'pariyuṭṭhito' (assailed) is spoken generally, from the meaning and the context it is intended as 'rāgapariyuṭṭhito' (assailed by lust); the meaning is 'arisen after being overwhelmed by lust'.

280. Sabhojananti ettha sakāro sahasaddakāriyo ca akārukārānaṃ asarūpattā akārato ukārassa lopo ca tīsu padesu pacchimānaṃ dvinnaṃ padānaṃ tulyatthanissitasamāso ca pubbapadena saha bhedanissitabāhiratthasamāso ca hoti, iti imamatthaṃ dassento āha “saha ubhohi janehī”ti. Atha vā bhuñjitabbanti bhojanaṃ, saṃ vijjati bhojanaṃ asmiṃ kuleti sabhojananti dassento āha “atha vā”tiādi. Hīti saccaṃ. Tenevāti teneva aññamaññaṃ bhuñjitabbattā. Assāti “sabhojane”tipadassa. Ghareti ettha pubbo sayanisaddo lopoti āha “sayanighare”ti. Iminā “datto”tiādīsu viya pubbapadalopasamāsaṃ dasseti. Piṭṭhasaṅghāṭassāti ettha piṭṭhasaṅghāṭo nāma na aññassa yassa kassaci, atha kho sayanigharagabbhassevāti āha “tassa sayanigharagabbhassā”ti. Yathā vā tathā vāti yena vā te na vā ākārena. Katassāti piṭṭhivaṃsaṃ āropetvā vā anāropetvā vā katassāti. Tatiyaṃ.

280. Here, in 'sabhojanaṃ', the syllable 'sa' functions as the word 'saha' (together); and due to the dissimilarity of the vowels 'a' and 'u', there is an elision of 'u' after 'a'; and among the three terms, there is a compound of the latter two based on equivalent meaning, and a compound with the preceding term based on an external meaning related to difference. Showing this meaning, he said, 'saha ubhohi janehi' (together with both people). Alternatively, 'bhojanaṃ' is what is to be eaten, and showing that 'sabhojanaṃ' means 'a family wherein a meal is found', he said, 'Alternatively…', and so on. 'Hi' means 'truly'. 'Teneva' means 'for that very reason', that is, 'due to eating with one another'. 'Assa' refers to the word 'sabhojane'. Regarding 'ghare', he says that here the preceding word 'sayani' is elided, thus forming 'sayanighare'. By this, he shows a compound with the elision of the preceding word, as in 'datto', etc. Here, 'piṭṭhasaṅghāṭassa' (of the gable) does not refer to anything else, but specifically to the inner chamber of the sleeping house; hence he said, 'tassa sayanigharagabbhassa' (of that inner chamber of the sleeping house). 'Yathā vā tathā vā' means 'in whatever way or in that way'. 'Katassa' means 'of that which is made', whether placed on the ridge-pole or not. The third.

284. Catutthapañcamesu yathā ca sabhojanasikkhāpadaṃ paṭhamapārājikasamuṭṭhānaṃ, evameva tānipīti yojanāti. Catutthapañcamāni.

284. In the fourth and fifth, the connection is that just as the training rule on a meal has the same origin as the first pārājika offense, so too do these. The fourth and fifth.

6. Cārittasikkhāpadaṃ

6. The Training Rule on Conduct

294. Chaṭṭhe [M 0.0098] kasmā tehi “dethāvuso bhatta”nti vuttaṃ, nanu bhikkhūnaṃ evaṃ vattuṃ na vaṭṭatīti āha “ettha taṃ kirā”tiādi. Tasmāti yasmā abhihaṭaṃ ahosi, tasmā.

294. In the sixth, as to why they said, 'Give us food, friends'—for surely it is not allowable for monks to speak thus—he said, 'Here, it is said…', and so on. 'Tasmā' (therefore) means: because it was brought, therefore.

295. Idaṃ pana vacanaṃ āhāti sambandho. Pasādaññathattanti pasādassa aññenākārena bhāvo. Nanti khādanīyaṃ. “Gahetvā āgamaṃsū”tiiminā “ussāriyitthā”ti ettha ukārassa uggahatthatañca [V 1.0082] saradhātussa gatyatthatañca ajjataniñuṃvibhattiyā tthattañca dasseti, uggahetvā sāriṃsu agamaṃsūti attho.

295. The connection is: 'this statement is said.' 'Pasādaññathatta' means the state of faith being otherwise. 'Nanti' refers to something edible. By 'gahetvā āgamaṃsū,' it shows that in the word 'ussāriyitthā,' the vowel 'u' has the sense of taking up, the root 'sar' has the meaning of going, and 'ttha' is the aorist (`ajjatanī`) ending that is a substitute for `uṃ`. The meaning is: having taken, they went away.

298. Yatthāti yasmiṃ ṭhāne. Ṭhitassa bhikkhuno cittaṃ uppannanti yojanā. Tatoti cittuppannato. Yanti bhikkhuṃ. Pakativacanenāti uccāsaddamakatvā pavattena sabhāvavacanena. Antovihāreti vacanassa atisambādhattā ayuttabhāvaṃ maññamāno āha “api ca antoupacārasīmāyā”ti.

298. 'Yattha' means in which place. The connection is: 'the mind of the standing bhikkhu arises.' 'Tato' means from the arising of the mind. 'Yanti' refers to the bhikkhu. 'Pakativacanena' means with natural speech, by speaking in a natural tone without making a loud noise. Considering the unsuitability due to the excessive confinement implied in the phrase 'antovihāreti,' he says, 'but also within the boundary of the vicinity.'

302. Gāmassa antare ārāmo tiṭṭhatīti antarārāmo vihāro, taṃ gacchatīti dassento āha “antogāme”tiādīti. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

302. A monastery is an `antarārāma` because 'a park stands within a village.' To show that one goes there, it is said: 'within the village,' and so forth. The Sixth.

7. Mahānāmasikkhāpadaṃ

7. The Mahānāma Training Rule

303. Sattame “bhagavato”tipadaṃ “cūḷapituputto”tipade sambandho, “mahallakataro”tipade apādānaṃ. Cūḷapituputtoti suddhodano, sakkodano, sukkodano, dhotodano, amitodanoti pañca janā bhātaro, amitā, pālitāti dve bhaginiyo. Tesu bhagavā ca nando ca jeṭṭhabhātubhūtassa suddhodanassa puttā, ānando kaniṭṭhabhātubhūtassa amitodanassa putto, mahānāmo ca anuruddho ca tatiyassa sukkodanassa puttā. Sakkodanadhotodanānaṃ puttā apākaṭā. Tissatthero amitāya nāma bhaginiyā putto, pālitāya puttadhītarā apākaṭā. Tasmā cūḷapituno sukkodanassa [M 0.0099] putto cūḷapituputtoti attho daṭṭhabbo. Dvīsu phalesūti heṭṭhimesu dvīsu phalesu. Ussannasaddo bahupariyāyoti āha “bahū”ti. Vajatoti goṭṭhato. Tañhi gāvo gocaraṭṭhānato paṭikkamitvā nivāsatthāya vajanti gacchanti asminti vajoti vuccati.

303. In the Seventh, the word 'bhagavato' is connected to the word 'cūḷapituputto,' and it is in the ablative sense with respect to the word 'mahallakataro.' 'Cūḷapituputto' means son of a paternal uncle. Suddhodana, Sakkodana, Sukkodana, Dhotodana, and Amitodana were five brothers, and Amitā and Pālitā were two sisters. Among them, the Blessed One and Nanda were the sons of the eldest brother, Suddhodana; Ānanda was the son of the youngest brother, Amitodana; Mahānāma and Anuruddha were the sons of the third brother, Sukkodana. The sons of Sakkodana and Dhotodana are not well-known. The Elder Tissa was the son of the sister named Amitā; the sons and daughters of Pālitā are not well-known. Therefore, 'cūḷapituputto' should be understood as the son of the paternal uncle, Sukkodana. 'Dvīsu phalesu' means in the two lower fruits. The word 'ussanna' has many synonyms, so he says 'bahū.' 'Vajato' means from the cattle pen (`goṭṭhato`). For cows, having returned from the grazing ground, go (`vajanti`) to it for their dwelling; therefore, it is called a 'vaja' (cattle pen).

306. Tasmiṃ samayeti tasmiṃ pavāraṇasamaye. “Ettakehī”tipadassa nāmavasena vā parimāṇavasena vā duvidhassa atthassa adhippetattā vuttaṃ “nāmavasena parimāṇavasenā”ti. Tesu nāmaṃ sandhāya etaṃ nāmaṃ etesaṃ bhesajjānanti ettakānīti vacanattho kātabbo, parimāṇaṃ sandhāya etaṃ parimāṇaṃ etesanti ettakānīti vacanattho kātabbo. “Aññaṃ bhesajja”nti ettha aññasaddassa apādānaṃ nāmaṃ vā parimāṇaṃ vā bhaveyyāti āha “sabbinā pavārito”tiādi.

306. 'Tasmiṃ samaye' means at that time of Pavāraṇā. Because the word 'ettakehi' is intended to have a twofold meaning, either by way of name or by way of quantity, it is said 'by way of name or by way of quantity.' Among these, with reference to name, the meaning of the word 'ettakāni' should be taken as 'this is the name of these medicines.' With reference to quantity, the meaning of the word 'ettakāni' should be taken as 'this is the quantity of these.' Regarding 'aññaṃ bhesajjaṃ,' thinking that the point of departure (`apādāna`) for the word 'añña' could be either name or quantity, he said 'sabbinā pavārito,' and so forth.

310. Yeti [V 1.0083] dāyakā, pavāritā hontīti sambandhoti. Sattamaṃ.

310. 'Ye' means the donors. The connection is 'pavāritā honti.' The Seventh.

8. Uyyuttasenāsikkhāpadaṃ

8. The Training Rule on an Engaged Army

311. Aṭṭhame “abhimukha”ntiiminā abhisaddassatthaṃ dasseti. “Uyyāto”tipadassa uṭṭhahitvā yātoti dassento āha “nagarato niggato”ti. “Katauyyoga”nti iminā uṭṭhahitvā yuñjati gacchatīti uyyuttāti dasseti. Dhātūna, manekatthattā vuttaṃ “gāmato nikkhanta”nti.

311. In the Eighth, by 'abhimukha,' he shows the meaning of the prefix 'abhi.' To show that the word 'uyyāto' means 'having risen up, he went,' he says 'nagarato niggato.' By 'katauyyoga,' he shows that 'uyyutta' means 'one who, having risen up, engages or goes.' Because roots have many meanings, it is said 'gāmato nikkhanta.'

314. Dvādasa purisā imassa hatthinoti dvādasapuriso, āvudho hatthesu etesanti āvudhahatthā. Ninnanti ninnaṭṭhānaṃ, passato bhikkhunoti sambandhoti. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

314. 'Dvādasapuriso' is from 'dvādasa purisā imassa hatthino' (twelve men of this elephant). 'Āvudhahatthā' is from 'āvudho hatthesu etesaṃ' (weapons are in their hands). 'Ninnaṃ' means a low-lying place. The connection is 'passato bhikkhuno.' The Eighth.

9. Senāvāsasikkhāpadaṃ

9. The Training Rule on Army Lodgings

319. Navame “tiṭṭhatu vā”tiādinā vasanākāraṃ dasseti. Vāsaddo “caṅkamatu vā”tiatthaṃ sampiṇḍeti. Kiñci iriyāpathanti catūsu [M 0.0100] iriyāpathesu kiñci iriyāpathaṃ. Yathā ruddhamāne sañcāro chijjati, evaṃ ruddhā saṃvutā hotīti yojanā. “Ruddho”ti iminā “palibuddho”ti ettha paripubbassa budhidhātussa adhippāyatthaṃ dassetīti. Navamaṃ.

319. In the Ninth, by 'tiṭṭhatu vā,' and so forth, he shows the manner of dwelling. The word 'vā' also includes the meaning 'or let him walk.' 'Kiñci iriyāpathaṃ' means any posture among the four postures. The connection is: just as movement is cut off when one is obstructed, so she is obstructed and restrained. By 'ruddho,' he shows the intended meaning of the root 'budh' with the prefix 'pari' in the word 'palibuddho.' The Ninth.

10. Uyyodhikasikkhāpadaṃ

10. The Training Rule on Military Displays

322. Dasame yujjhantīti saṃpaharanti. “Balassa aggaṃ etthā”tiiminā bhinnādhikaraṇabāhiratthasamāsaṃ dasseti. “Jānantī”tipadaṃ atthasampuṇṇatthāya pakkhittaṃ. Agganti koṭṭhāsaṃ. Balaṃ gaṇīyati etthāti balagganti vacanatthopi yujjati. Tenāha “balagaṇanaṭṭhāna”nti. Idañhi vacanaṃ ambasecanagarusinanayena vuttaṃ. Kathaṃ? “Balagaṇanaṭṭhāna”nti vadantena aṭṭhakathācariyena “balassa aggaṃ jānanti etthāti balagga”nti vacanatthassa piṇḍattho ca ñāpīyati, “balaṃ gaṇīyati etthāti balagga”nti vacanattho ca dassīyati. Viyūhīyate sampiṇḍīyate byūho, senāya byūho senābyūhoti atthaṃ dasseti “senāya viyūha”ntiādinā. Aṇati bheravasaddaṃ karotīti aṇīkaṃ, muddhajaṇakāro, hatthīyeva aṇīkaṃ [V 1.0084] hatthāṇīkaṃ. Eseva nayo sesesupi. Yo hatthī pubbe vutto, tena hatthināti yojanāti. Dasamaṃ.

322. In the Tenth, 'yujjhanti' means they clash. By 'balassa aggaṃ ettha' (the best of the force is here), he shows a `bahubbīhi` compound with an external referent. The word 'jānantī' is inserted to complete the meaning. 'Aggaṃ' means a part. The etymology 'balaṃ gaṇīyati etthāti balaggaṃ' (the force is counted here, therefore it is a `balagga`) also fits. Hence, he says 'balagaṇanaṭṭhānaṃ' (a place for counting the force). This statement is made according to the method of the Ambasecana and Garusina. How? By saying 'balagaṇanaṭṭhānaṃ,' the commentator indicates the condensed meaning of the etymology 'balassa aggaṃ jānanti etthāti balaggaṃ' (they know the best of the force here, therefore it is a `balagga`), and also shows the etymology 'balaṃ gaṇīyati etthāti balaggaṃ.'
