474. In the ninth, `we` refers to us who are called the group of six. `Because done` means because the acts have been done. `Dhamma` means the true nature. `In these` means in these four acts of the Sangha. The ninth.

10. Chandaṃ adatvāgamanasikkhāpadaṃ

10. The Training Rule on Going Away Without Giving Consent.

481. Dasame codeti parassa dosaṃ āropetīti codako. Tena ca codakena codetabbo dosaṃ āropetabboti cudito, soyeva cuditako, tena ca. “Anuvijjakoti ca vinayadharo. So hi codakacuditakānaṃ mataṃ anuminetvā vidati jānātīti anuvijjako. Ettāvatāpīti ettakenapi pamāṇenāti. Dasamaṃ.

481. In the tenth, `he accuses`: one who imputes a fault to another is an accuser (`codako`). And one who is to be accused by that accuser, to whom a fault is to be imputed, is the accused (`cudito`); that very one is the `cuditako`. `And the investigator` (`anuvijjako`) is a Vinaya expert. For he, having inferred the opinion of the accuser and the accused, finds out and knows; thus he is the investigator (`anuvijjako`). `Even to this extent` means even by this much measure. The tenth.

11. Dubbalasikkhāpadaṃ

11. The Training Rule Concerning the Weak.

484. Ekādasame “alajjītā”tiādīsu (pari. 295) viya yakāralopena niddesoti āha “yathāmittatāyā”ti. “Yo yo”ti iminā yathāsaddassa vicchatthaṃ dasseti. Yathāvuḍḍhantiādīsu [V 1.0103] (cūḷava. 311 ādayo) viya yo yo [M 0.0122] mitto “yathāmitta”nti vacanattho kātabbo. Sabbapadesūti “yathāsandiṭṭhatā”tiādīsu sabbesu padesūti. Ekādasamaṃ.

484. In the eleventh, he says that the indication is by the elision of the letter `y`, as in `alajjītā` and so on (Parivāra 295), and as in `yathāmittatāyā`. By `yo yo` (whoever), he shows the distributive meaning of the word `yathā`. The meaning of the word `yathāmitta` should be construed as `yo yo mitto` (whoever is a friend), as in `yathāvuḍḍha` and so on (Cūḷavagga 311 and others). `In all instances` means in all instances, such as in `yathāsandiṭṭhatā` and so on. The eleventh.

12. Pariṇāmanasikkhāpadaṃ

12. The Training Rule on Diversion.

489. Dvādasame yanti padatthavinicchayatthasaṅkhātaṃ yaṃ vacanaṃ. Tatthāti tiṃsakakaṇḍe. Idhāti dvenavutikaṇḍe, sikkhāpade vā. Puggalassāti parapuggalassāti. Dvādasamaṃ.

489. In the twelfth, `yanti` refers to that statement which is designated for the purpose of determining the meaning of a word. `Tattha` (there) refers to the section of thirty. `Idha` (here) refers to the section of ninety-two, or to this training rule. `Of a person` means of another person. The twelfth.

Sahadhammikavaggo aṭṭhamo.

The Sahadhammika Chapter, the Eighth.

9. Ratanavaggo

9. The Jewel Chapter.

1. Antepurasikkhāpada-atthayojanā

1. The Explanation of the Meaning of the Training Rule Concerning the Inner Palace.

494. Rājavaggassa paṭhame parittakoti guṇena khuddako. Pāsādavarasaddassa uparisaddena sambandhitabbabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ vuttaṃ “pāsādavarassa upari gato”ti. Iminā pāsādavarassa upari uparipāsādavaraṃ, taṃ gato upagatoti uparipāsādavaragatoti vacanatthaṃ dasseti. Ayyānanti bhikkhūnaṃ. “Kāraṇā”ti iminā “vāhasā”ti padassatthaṃ dasseti. Tehīti ayyehi.

494. In the first of the Royal Chapter, `parittako` means small in virtue. To show that the word `pāsādavara` should be connected with the word `upari`, it is stated as `pāsādavarassa upari gato` (gone above the excellent palace). By this, he shows the meaning of the word `uparipāsādavaragato` as: an upper excellent palace above the excellent palace; one who has gone (`gato`), gone up to (`upagato`), to that. `Ayyānaṃ` means of the monks. By `kāraṇā` (by reason of), he shows the meaning of the word `vāhasā`. `Tehi` (by them) means by the venerable ones.

497. Antaranti khaṇaṃ, okāsaṃ vā vivaraṃ vā. Ghātetunti hanituṃ. Icchatīti iminā patthadhātuyā yācanatthaṃ dasseti. “Rājantepuraṃ hatthisammadda”ntiādīsu vacanattho evaṃ veditabboti yojanā. Hatthisammaddanti hatthisambādhaṭṭhānaṃ. Assehi sammaddo etthāti assasammaddo. Rathehi sammaddo etthāti rathasammaddoti vacanatthaṃ atidisanto āha “eseva nayo”ti. “Sammatta”nti paṭhamakkharena pāṭhassa sambādhassa avācakattā vuttaṃ “taṃ na gahetabba”nti. Tatthāti pāṭhe. “Hatthīnaṃ sammadda”nti iminā uttarapadassa sammaddanaṃ sammaddanti bhāvatthaṃ dasseti, purimapadena chaṭṭhīsamāsañca. Purimapāṭhe pana uttarapadassa adhikaraṇatthañca pubbapadena tatiyāsamāsañca dasseti. Bāhiratthasamāsotipi vuccati. Pacchimapāṭhe “hatthisammadda”ntiādipadassa [V 1.0104] liṅgavipallāsañca [M 0.0123] “atthī”ti pāṭhasesena yojetabbatañca dassetuṃ vuttaṃ “hatthisammaddo atthī”ti. Rajitabbānīti rajanīyāni, rajituṃ arahānīti attho. Iminā sambandhakāle purimapāṭhe rañño antepureti vibhattivipallāso kātabboti. Pacchimapāṭhe pana mukhyatova yujjati. Tena vuttaṃ “tasmiṃ antepure”ti.

497. `Antara` means a moment, an opportunity, or an opening. `Ghātetuṃ` means to kill. By `icchati` (he desires), he shows that the root `patth` has the meaning of requesting. The construction is that the meaning of phrases like `Rājantepuraṃ hatthisammadda` should be understood in this way. `Hatthisammadda` means a place crowded with elephants. Extending this explanation, he says, `the same method applies`: `assasammaddo` is a place where there is a crowding by horses; `rathasammaddo` is a place where there is a crowding by chariots. Because the reading `sammatta`, with its first syllable, does not express the meaning of `sambādha` (crowding), it is said, `that should not be taken`. `There` refers to that reading. By `hatthīnaṃ sammadda` (a crowding of elephants), he shows that the latter word `sammadda` has the sense of a verbal noun, `sammaddanaṃ` (crowding), and that it is a genitive compound with the prior word. In the prior explanation, however, he shows that the latter word has a locative sense and that it is an instrumental compound with the prior word. It is also called an external-referent compound. In the latter reading, to show the gender inversion of the word `hatthisammadda` and that it should be connected with the remainder of the reading, `atthī` (exists), it is said, `hatthisammaddo atthī` (there is a crowd of elephants). `Rajitabbāni` means `rajanīyāni` (things to be enjoyed); the meaning is ‘worthy of being enjoyed.’ By this, at the time of connection in the earlier reading, a change of case ending to `rañño antepure` (in the king’s inner palace) should be made. But in the latter reading, it fits directly. Hence, it is said, `in that inner palace`.

498. Avasittassāti khattiyābhisekena abhisittassa. Itoti sayanigharato. Iminā pañcamībāhirasamāsaṃ dasseti. Rañño ratijananaṭṭhena ratanaṃ vuccati mahesī. Mahesīti ca sābhisekā devī. Nipubba gamudhātussa nipubbakamudhātuyā pariyāyabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ vuttaṃ “niggatanti nikkhanta”nti. Paṭhamaṃ.

498. ‘Avasittassa’ means one anointed with the consecration of a warrior. ‘Ito’ means from the sleeping chamber. By this, he shows an external compound in the ablative case. The chief queen is called ‘ratana’ (jewel) because she causes delight to the king. ‘Mahesī’ means the consecrated queen. To show the synonymous nature of the root gam with the prefix ni- and the root kam with the prefix ni-, it is said, ‘niggata’ means ‘nikkhanta’ (gone forth). The first.

2. Ratanasikkhāpadaṃ

2. The Training Rule on Jewels

502. Dutiye pamussitvāti sativippavāsena pamussitvā. Puṇṇapattanti tuṭṭhidāyaṃ. Tañhi manorathapuṇṇena pattabbabhāgattā “puṇṇapatta”nti vuccati. Tassa sarūpaṃ dassetuṃ vuttaṃ “satato pañca kahāpaṇā”ti. Idha pana kahāpaṇānaṃ pañcasatattā pañcavīsakahāpaṇā adhippetā. Ābharaṇasaddassa alaṅkārasaddena pariyāyabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ vuttaṃ “alaṅkāra”nti. “Mahālataṃ nāmā”ti iminā na yo vā so vā alaṅkāro, atha kho visesālaṅkāroti dasseti. Mahantāni mālākammalatākammāni etthāti mahālatā. Latāgahaṇena hi mālāpi gahitā. Navahi koṭīhi agghaṃ imassāti navakoṭiagghanakaṃ, navakoṭisaṅkhātaṃ agghaṃ arahatīti vā navakoṭiagghanakaṃ.

502. In the second, ‘pamussitvā’ means having forgotten due to loss of mindfulness. ‘Puṇṇapatta’ means a gift of satisfaction. For it is called ‘puṇṇapatta’ because it is a portion to be attained with one’s desires fulfilled. To show its form, it is said, ‘five kahāpaṇas from a hundred.’ Here, however, since there are five hundred kahāpaṇas, twenty-five kahāpaṇas are intended. To show that the word ‘ābharaṇa’ is a synonym for the word ‘alaṅkāra’, it is said, ‘alaṅkāra’ (ornament). By ‘named Mahālataṃ’, he shows that it is not just any ornament, but a special ornament. ‘Mahālatā’ means: great garland-work and creeper-work are in it. Indeed, by the mention of ‘latā’ (creeper), garlands are also included. ‘Navakoṭiagghanakaṃ’ means its worth is nine crores; or, it is called ‘navakoṭiagghanakaṃ’ because it is worthy of a value reckoned at nine crores.

504. Ante samīpe vasanasīlattā paricāriko “antevāsī”ti vuccatīti āha “paricāriko”ti.

504. Because of the characteristic of living (vasanasīlattā) near (ante samīpe), an attendant is called an ‘antevāsī’; thus, it is said, ‘an attendant’ (paricāriko).

506. Dve leḍḍupātāti thāmamajjhimassa purisassa dve leḍḍupātā. Saṅgha…pe… navakammānaṃ atthāya uggaṇhantassa vā uggaṇhāpentassa vā dukkaṭanti [M 0.0124] yojanā. Avasesanti jātarūparajatato avasesaṃ. Mātukaṇṇapiḷandhanatālapaṇṇampīti mātuyā kaṇṇe piḷandhitatālapaṇṇampi, paṭisāmentassāti sambandho.

506. ‘Dve leḍḍupātā’ means two clod-throws by a man of average strength. For the Sangha… for the purpose of new construction, for one who collects or has another collect, there is an offense of wrong doing (dukkaṭa)—this is the construction. ‘Avasesa’ means the remainder apart from gold and silver. ‘Mātukaṇṇapiḷandhanatālapaṇṇampi’ means even a palm leaf worn as an ornament in a mother’s ear; the connection is with ‘paṭisāmentassa’ (for one who is putting it away).

“Kappiyabhaṇḍaṃ hotī”ti iminā akappiyabhaṇḍaṃ na vaṭṭatīti dasseti. Idanti bhaṇḍaṃ. Palibodho [V 1.0105] nāmāti attano palibodho nāma. Chandenapīti vaḍḍhakīādīnaṃ chandahetunāpi. Bhayenapīti rājavallabhānaṃ bhayahetunāpi. Balakkārenāti karaṇaṃ kāro, balena kāro balakkāro, tena, balakkāro hutvā pātetvāti attho.

By ‘it is allowable property’ (kappiyabhaṇḍaṃ hoti), he indicates that unallowable property is not suitable. ‘Idaṃ’ refers to the property. ‘Palibodho nāma’ means one’s own hindrance. ‘Chandena’ means even due to the desire of carpenters and the like. ‘Bhayena’ means even due to the fear of royal favorites and the like. ‘Balakkārena’: ‘kāro’ is action; action by force is ‘balakkāro’; by that. The meaning is: having become forceful, having overthrown.

Tatthāti mahārāme. Yatthāti yasmiṃ ṭhāne, saṅkā uppajjatīti sambandho. Mahājanasañcaraṇaṭṭhānesūti bahūnaṃ janānaṃ sañcaraṇasaṅkhātesu ṭhānesu. Nagahetabbassa hetuṃ dassetuṃ vuttaṃ “palibodho na hotī”ti. Yasmā palibodho na hoti, tasmā na gahetabbanti adhippāyo. Ekoti eko bhikkhu passatīti sambandho. Okkammāti okkamitvā.

‘Tattha’ means in the Great Monastery. ‘Yattha’ means in which place; the connection is with ‘doubt arises’. ‘Mahājanasañcaraṇaṭṭhānesu’ means in places known as frequented by many people. To show the reason for not taking it, it was said, ‘there is no impediment’ (palibodho na hoti). Because there is no impediment, therefore it should not be taken—this is the intended meaning. ‘Eko’ means one monk sees; this is the connection. ‘Okkamma’ means having descended.

Rūpasaddo bhaṇḍapariyāyoti āha “bhaṇḍa”nti. Bhaṇḍaṃ rūpaṃ nāmāti yojanā. Bhaṇḍikanti bhaṇḍena niyuttaṃ puṭakaṃ. Gaṇetvāti gaṇanaṃ katvā. Nimittantīti ettha itisaddo nāmapariyāyo. Lañchanādi nimittaṃ nāmāti hi yojanā. Lañchanādīti ādisaddena nīlapilotikādayo saṅgaṇhāti. Lākhāyāti jatunā.

The word ‘rūpa’ is a synonym for property—thus, he says ‘bhaṇḍa’. ‘Property is form’—this is the construction. ‘Bhaṇḍika’ means a container connected with property. ‘Gaṇetvā’ means having made a count. In ‘nimittaṃ’, here the word ‘iti’ is a synonym for name. Indeed, ‘a mark and so on is called a sign’—this is the construction. By ‘lañchanādi’ (marks and so on), with the word ‘ādi’ he includes blue cloths and the like. ‘Lākhāya’ means with resin.

Patirūpā nāma idha lajjikukkuccakāti āha “lajjino kukkuccakā”ti. Thāvaranti jaṅgamā aññaṃ thāvaraṃ. Addhunoti kālassa. Samādapetvāti aññe samādapetvā. Uddissa ariyā tiṭṭhanti, esā ariyāna yācanā”ti (jā. 1.7.59) vuttanayena yācitvāti attho.

‘Patirūpā nāma’ here means those with shame and scruples—thus, it is said, ‘lajjino kukkuccakā’. ‘Thāvaraṃ’ means stationary, which is other than moving. ‘Addhuno’ means of time. ‘Samādapetvā’ means having encouraged others. The meaning is having requested, in the manner spoken of: ‘The noble ones stand for a purpose, this is the request of the noble ones’ (Jā. 1.7.59).

507. Ratanasammatanti manussānaṃ upabhogaparibhoganti. Dutiyaṃ.

507. ‘Ratanasammataṃ’ (considered a treasure) means for the enjoyment and use of humans. The second.

3. Vikālagāmappavisanasikkhāpadaṃ

3. The Training Rule on Entering a Village at an Unseemly Time

508. Tatiye [M 0.0125] “tiracchānabhūtaṃ katha”nti iminā “tiracchānakatha”nti padassa tulyanissitasamāsaṃ dasseti. Rājapaṭisaṃyuttanti rājūhi paṭisaṃyuttaṃ.

508. In the third, by means of ‘talk that has become animal-like,’ he shows that the word ‘tiracchānakathā’ is an appositional compound. ‘Rājapaṭisaṃyuttaṃ’ means connected with kings.

512. Sambahulā bhikkhūti sambandho. Tasmiṃ gāmeti tasmiṃ paṭhamapavisanagāme. Taṃ kammanti taṃ icchitakammaṃ. Antarāti gāmavihārānamantare. Bhummatthe cetaṃ nissakkavacanaṃ.

512. ‘Several bhikkhus’—this is the connection. ‘In that village’ means in that village first entered. ‘That action’ means that desired action. ‘Antarā’ means between the village and the monastery. And this is an ablative expression in the sense of the locative.

Kulaghare vāti ñātikulaupaṭṭhākakulaghare vā. Telabhikkhāya vāti telayācanatthāya vā. Passeti [V 1.0106] attano passe samīpeti vuttaṃ hoti. Tenāti gāmamajjhamaggena. Anokkammāti anokkamitvā, apakkamitvāti atthoti. Tatiyaṃ.

‘Or in a family house’ means or in the house of a family of relatives or a family of supporters. ‘Or for oil-alms’ means or for the purpose of asking for oil. ‘Passeti’ means it is said that he brings it near to himself. ‘Tena’ means by the middle path of the village. ‘Anokkamma’ means not having stepped aside, not having turned away—this is the meaning. The third.

4. Sūcigharasikkhāpadaṃ

4. The Training Rule on the Needle-case

517. Catutthe kakārassa padapūraṇabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ vuttaṃ “bhedanameva bhedanaka”nti. Assatthiatthe apaccayoti āha “taṃ assa atthī”ti. Assāti pācittiyassa. Paṭhamaṃ sūcigharaṃ bhinditvā pacchā pācittiyaṃ desetabbanti attho. Araṇidhanuketi araṇiyā dhanuke. Vedhaketi kāyabandhanavedhaketi. Catutthaṃ.

517. In the fourth, to show that the syllable ‘ka’ is a pleonasm, it is said, ‘“bhedana” itself is “bhedanaka”.’ He says, ‘that exists for him,’ to show that the suffix ‘a’ is in the sense of possession. ‘For him’ means for the one who has a pācittiya offense. The meaning is: first having broken the needle-case, afterwards the pācittiya should be confessed. ‘Araṇidhanuke’ means in a bow made of araṇi-wood. ‘Vedhake’ means in a piercer for a waistband. The fourth.

5. Mañcasikkhāpadaṃ

5. The Training Rule on the Bed

522. Pañcame chedanameva chedanakaṃ, tamassatthīti chedanakanti atthaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “vuttanayamevā”ti.

522. In the fifth, it is said, ‘it is in the same way as has been explained,’ referring to the meaning of ‘chedanaka’: ‘“chedana” itself is “chedanaka”, and that exists for him.’

Nikhaṇitvāti pamāṇātirekaṃ nikhaṇitvā. Uttānaṃ vā katvāti heṭṭhupari parivattanaṃ vā katvā. Ṭhapetvāti lambaṇavasena ṭhapetvāti. Pañcamaṃ.

‘Nikhaṇitvā’ means having dug beyond the measure. ‘Or having made it upturned’ means or having turned it upside down. ‘Ṭhapetvā’ means having placed it by way of hanging. The fifth.

6. Tūlonaddhasikkhāpadaṃ

6. The Training Rule on Cotton Padding

526. Chaṭṭhe [M 0.0126] etthāti mañcapīṭhe. Avanahitabbanti onaddhaṃ, tūlena onaddhaṃ tūlonaddhanti atthopi yujjati. Tūlaṃ pakkhipitvāti mañcapīṭhe cimilikaṃ pattharitvā tassupari tūlaṃ pakkhipitvāti atthoti. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

526. In the sixth, ‘ettha’ means on a bed or bench. ‘Avanahitaṃ’ means covered; the meaning ‘covered with cotton’ (tūlena onaddhaṃ) becomes ‘tūlonaddhaṃ’ (padded with cotton) is also fitting. ‘Having placed cotton’ means having spread a mattress-cover on the bed or bench and having placed cotton on top of it—this is the meaning. The sixth.

7. Nisīdanasikkhāpadaṃ

7. The Training Rule on the Sitting Cloth

531. Sattame katthāti kismiṃ khandhake, kismiṃ vatthusmiṃ vā. Hīti saccaṃ. Tatthāti cīvarakkhandhake, paṇītabhojanavatthusmiṃ vā. “Yathā nāmā”ti iminā “seyyathāpī”ti padassa atthaṃ dasseti, “purāṇo cammakāro”ti iminā “purāṇāsikoṭṭho”ti padassa. Cammakāro hi asinā cammaṃ kuṭati chindatīti “asikoṭṭho”ti vuccati. Vatthuppannakālamupanidhāya vuttaṃ “purāṇo”ti[V 1.0107]. Tamevūpamaṃ pākaṭaṃ karonto āha “yathā hī”ti. Hīti tappākaṭīkaraṇaṃ, taṃ pākaṭaṃ karissāmīti hi attho. Cammakāro kaḍḍhatīti sambandho. Vitthatanti visālaṃ. Sopīti udāyīpi. Taṃ nisīdanaṃ kaḍḍhatīti yojanā. Tenāti kaḍḍhanahetunā. Tanti udāyiṃ. Santhatasadisanti santhatena sadisaṃ. Ekasmiṃ anteti ekasmiṃ koṭṭhāse, phāletvāti sambandhoti. Sattamaṃ.

531. In the seventh, ‘kattha’ means ‘in which section, or in which matter.’ ‘Hi’ means ‘truly.’ ‘Tattha’ means ‘in the Robes Section, or in the matter of fine food.’ By ‘yathā nāma’ he shows the meaning of the word ‘seyyathāpi’; by ‘an old leatherworker’ he shows the meaning of the word ‘purāṇāsikoṭṭha’. For a leatherworker pounds or cuts leather with a knife, thus he is called an ‘asikoṭṭha’. ‘Old’ is said with reference to the time the story arose. Making that very simile clear, he says, ‘yathā hi.’ ‘Hi’ is for making that clear; for the meaning is, ‘I will make that clear.’ ‘The leatherworker pulls’ is the connection. ‘Vitthataṃ’ means ‘extensive.’ ‘So’pi’ means ‘Udāyī too.’ ‘He pulls that sitting cloth’ is the construction. ‘Tena’ means ‘for the reason of pulling.’ ‘Taṃ’ refers to Udāyī. ‘Santhatasadisaṃ’ means ‘similar to a felt rug.’ ‘Ekasmiṃ ante’ means ‘in one portion’; the connection is with ‘phāletvā’ (having split). The seventh.

8. Kaṇḍupaṭicchādisikkhāpadaṃ

8. The Training Rule on the Itch-covering Cloth

537. Aṭṭhame “katthā”tiādīni vuttanayāneva.

537. In the eighth, ‘kattha’ and so forth are as explained before.

539. “Yassā”ti padassa visayaṃ dassetuṃ vuttaṃ “bhikkhuno”ti. “Nābhiyā heṭṭhā”ti iminā nābhiyā adho adhonābhīti vacanatthaṃ dasseti, “jāṇumaṇḍalānaṃ uparī”ti iminā jāṇumaṇḍalānaṃ ubbha ubbhajāṇumaṇḍalanti. Ubbhasaddo hi uparipariyāyo sattamyantanipāto. Kaṇḍukhajjusaddānaṃ vevacanattā vuttaṃ “kaṇḍūti khajjū”ti. Kaṇḍati bhedanaṃ karotīti kaṇḍu. Khajjati byadhanaṃ karotīti khajju. Kesuci potthakesu “kacchū”ti pāṭho atthi, so ayutto.

539. To explain the scope of the word ‘yassā,’ it is said, ‘of a bhikkhu.’ By ‘below the navel,’ it shows the verbal meaning of adhonābhi to be ‘below the navel’; by ‘above the knee-circles,’ it shows the meaning of ubbhajāṇumaṇḍala to be ‘above the knee-circles.’ Indeed, the word ‘ubbha’ is a synonym for ‘upari’ and is an indeclinable with a locative sense. Since the words ‘kaṇḍu’ and ‘khajju’ are synonyms, it is said, ‘kaṇḍu is khajju.’ It cuts, thus it is kaṇḍu. It afflicts, thus it is khajju. In some texts, the reading ‘kacchū’ is found, but that is incorrect.

Lohitaṃ [M 0.0127] tuṇḍaṃ etissāti lohitatuṇḍikā. Piḷayati vibādhayatīti piḷakā. Ā bhuso asuciṃ savati paggharāpetīti assāvoti vacanatthaṃ dassento āha “asucipaggharaṇa”nti. Arisañca bhagandarā ca madhumeho ca. Ādisaddena dunnāmakādayo saṅgaṇhāti. Tattha ari viya īsati abhibhavatīti arisaṃ. Bhagaṃ vuccati vaccamaggaṃ, taṃ darati phāletīti bhagandarā, gūthasamīpe jāto vaṇaviseso. Madhu viya muttādiṃ mihati secatīti madhumeho, so ābādho muttameho sukkameho rattamehoti anekavidho. Thullasaddo mahantapariyāyoti āha “mahā”ti. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

Its beak is red, thus it is lohitatuṇḍikā (red-beaked). It torments, it oppresses, thus it is a piḷakā. Explaining the verbal meaning of assāva as ‘it greatly emits and causes impurities to flow,’ he says, ‘the flowing of impurities.’ And hemorrhoids, fistulas, and diabetes. By the word ‘ādi’ (etc.), it includes diseases with bad names and so on. Among them, it strives to overcome like an enemy, thus it is arisaṃ. `Bhaga` is said to be the excretory passage; it tears, it splits it, thus it is bhagandarā, a specific type of sore that arises near the feces. It secretes urine and so on like honey, thus it is madhumeho; that disease is of many kinds: urinary diabetes, semen diabetes, blood diabetes, and so on. The word ‘thulla’ is a synonym for ‘mahanta,’ thus he says, ‘great.’ The eighth.

9. Vassikasāṭikasikkhāpadaṃ

9. The Training Rule concerning the Rains-Cloth.

542. Navame vasse vassakāle adhiṭṭhātabbāti vassikā, vassikā ca sā sāṭikā ceti vassikasāṭikāti. Navamaṃ.

542. In the ninth: it is to be determined at the time of the rains, thus it is a vassikā. And that vassikā is a cloth, a sāṭikā, thus it is a vassikasāṭikā. The ninth.

10. Nandattherasikkhāpadaṃ

10. The Training Rule concerning the Elder Nanda.

547. Dasame [V 1.0108] “catūhi aṅgulehī”ti iminā caturo aṅgulā caturaṅgulāti asamāhāradiguṃ dasseti. Ūnakappamāṇoti bhagavato lāmakapamāṇo. Iminā omakasaddassa lāmakatthaṃ dassetīti daṭṭhabbanti. Dasamaṃ.

547. In the tenth: by ‘with four fingers,’ it shows that caturo aṅgulā (four fingers) is a non-collective dvigu compound for caturaṅgula. Ūnakappamāṇa (less than the proper measure) means the Blessed One's inferior measure. By this, it should be understood that the word omaka has the meaning of ‘inferior.’ The tenth.

Ratanavaggo navamo.

The Ratanavagga, the ninth chapter.

Iti samantapāsādikāya vinayasaṃvaṇṇanāya

Thus in the Samantapāsādikā, the Commentary on the Vinaya.

Khuddakavaṇṇanāya yojanā samattā.

The elucidation of the Commentary on the Khuddaka is completed.

6. Pāṭidesanīyakaṇḍaṃ

6. The Section on Pāṭidesanīya Offenses.

1. Paṭhamapāṭidesanīyasikkhāpada-atthayojanā

1. Elucidation of the Meaning of the First Pāṭidesanīya Training Rule.

Khuddakānaṃ anantarā pāṭidesanīyā ye dhammā saṅgītikārehi ṭhapitā, idāni tesaṃ dhammānaṃ ayaṃ vaṇṇanā bhavatīti yojanā.

This is the elucidation: now comes the commentary on those Pāṭidesanīya rules which were established by the compilers immediately after the minor rules.

552. Paṭhamapāṭidesanīye [M 0.0128] tāva attho evaṃ veditabboti yojanā. Paṭiāgamanakāleti piṇḍāya caraṇaṭṭhānato pakkamitvā, paṭinivattitvā vā āgamanakāle. Sabbevāti ettha niggahītalopavasena sandhi hotīti āha “sabbamevā”ti. “Kampamānā”ti iminā papubbavidhadhātuyā kampanatthaṃ dasseti. Apehīti ettha apapubbaidhātu gatyatthoti āha “apagacchā”ti.

552. This is the elucidation: first, in the first Pāṭidesanīya, the meaning should be understood thus. Paṭiāgamanakāle (at the time of returning) means at the time of coming, having departed from the place of the alms-round, or having returned. In sabbeva, he says it is sabbameva, because here a euphonic combination occurs by way of eliding the niggahīta. By kampamānā (trembling), it shows the meaning of trembling for the root kamp preceded by pa. In apehi (go away), he says, ‘apagaccha,’ because here the root i preceded by apa has the meaning of going.

553. Paṭidesetabbākāraṃ dasseti anenāti paṭidesetabbākāradassanaṃ. Dvinnaṃ saddānaṃ pariyāyabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ vuttaṃ “rathikāti racchā”ti. Rathassa hitā rathikā. Ṇyapaccaye kate “racchā”ti (moggallāne 4.72 sutte) vuccati. Racchantarena anibbiddhā racchā byūho nāmāti āha “anibbijjhitvā”tiādi. Byūheti sampiṇḍeti jane aññattha gantumapadānavasenāti [V 1.0109] byūho. Siṅghāṭakaṃ nāma maggasandhīti āha “maggasamodhānaṭṭhāna”nti. Siṅghati maggasamodhānaṃ karoti etthāti siṅghāṭakaṃ. Etesūti rathikādīsu. Eseva nayoti dukkaṭapāṭidesanīye atidisati. Hīti saccaṃ. “Vacanato”ti padaṃ “veditabbo”ti pade ñāpakahetu. Dadamānāya bhikkhuniyā vasenāti yojanā. Etthāti sikkhāpade. Tasmāti yasmā apamāṇaṃ, tasmā.

553. By this, it shows the manner of what is to be confessed, thus it is the showing of the manner of what is to be confessed. To show that the two words are synonyms, it is said, ‘Rathikā is racchā.’ Rathikā is what is suitable for a chariot. When the suffix ṇya is applied, it is called racchā (in Moggallāna’s grammar, 4.72). A street (racchā) not pierced by another street is called a byūha; thus he says, ‘without being pierced,’ and so on. It gathers people together by way of not giving an opportunity to go elsewhere, thus it is a byūha. A siṅghāṭaka is a meeting of paths; thus he says, ‘a place where paths converge.’ Here one makes a convergence of paths, thus it is a siṅghāṭaka. Etesu means in these, i.e., streets and so on. This is the same method; it is extended to the dukkaṭa and pāṭidesanīya. Hī means truly. The word vacanato is the indicative cause for the word veditabbo. The elucidation is with reference to a bhikkhunī who is giving. Ettha means in this training rule. Tasmā means: because it is without measure, therefore.

Idanti vacanaṃ vuttanti sambandho. Sambhinne ekarase kālikattayeti yojanā.

The word idaṃ is what was said; this is the connection. The elucidation is: when mixed, of a single flavor, for the three time-periods.

556. “Dāpetī”ti hetutthakiriyāya kāritakattukāritakammāni dassetuṃ vuttaṃ “aññātikāya aññena kenacī”ti. Aññenāti attanā aññena. “Tāya eva vā bhikkhuniyā aññena vā kenacī”ti padāni “paṭiggahāpetvā”tipade kāritakammānīti. Paṭhamaṃ.

556. To show the agent and object of the causative action of the causative verb dāpeti (causes to give), it is said, ‘by a non-relative, by some other.’ Aññena (by another) means by someone other than oneself. The phrases ‘by that same bhikkhunī or by some other’ are the objects of the causative action in relation to the word paṭiggahāpetvā (having caused to receive). The first.

2. Dutiyapāṭidesanīyasikkhāpadaṃ

2. The Second Pāṭidesanīya Training Rule.

558. Dutiye purimasikkhāpadena āpatti antaragharattāti adhippāyo. Iminā sikkhāpadena āpatti bhaveyya vosāsamānattāti [M 0.0129] adhippāyo. Dentiyā pana neva iminā, na purimena āpatti aññassa bhattattāti adhippāyoti. Dutiyaṃ.

558. In the second, the intention is that an offense occurs according to the previous training rule because of being inside the house. The intention is that an offense would occur by this training rule because of giving instructions. But for the one giving, there is no offense either by this rule or by the previous one, because it is food belonging to another; this is the intention. The second.

3. Tatiyapāṭidesanīyasikkhāpadaṃ

3. The Third Pāṭidesanīya Training Rule.

562. Tatiye “ubhato”ti ettha karaṇatthe toti āha “dvīhī”ti. “Ubhatopasanna”nti byāsopi samāsopi yuttoyeva, samāse topaccayassa alopo hoti. “Ubhato”tipadassa sarūpaṃ dassetuṃ vuttaṃ “upāsakenapi upāsikāyapī”ti. Kasmā ubhato pasannaṃ hotīti āha “tasmiṃ kirā”tiādi. Yasmā tasmiṃ kule…pe… sotāpannāyeva honti kira, tasmā “ubhatopasanna”nti vuttaṃ hoti. “Sacepī”ti ettha pisaddena asītikoṭidhanato adhikampi sampiṇḍeti. Hāyanassa kāraṇaṃ dasseti “yasmā”tiādinā.

562. In the third, here in ubhato, he says ‘dvīhi’ (by two) because the suffix -to is in the instrumental sense. Ubhatopasanna (devoted on both sides) is correct both as an analysis and as a compound; in the compound, there is non-elision of the suffix -to. To show the form of the word ubhato, it is said, ‘by a male lay follower and by a female lay follower.’ Why is it devoted on both sides? He says, ‘in that family, it is said…’ and so on. Because in that family… they are, it is said, only stream-enterers, therefore it is said to be ubhatopasanna. Here in sacepi (even if), by the word pi, it also includes more than eighty koṭis of wealth. It shows the reason for the decline with ‘because…’ and so on.

569. “Gharato nīharitvā”ti ettha “nīharitvā”ti padassa kammaṃ dassetuṃ vuttaṃ “āsanasālaṃ [V 1.0110] vā vihāraṃ vā”ti. “Ānetvā”tiiminā nīpubbaharadhātuyā atthaṃ dasseti. Dvāreti attano gehadvāreti. Tatiyaṃ.

569. Here in ‘having brought out from the house,’ to show the object of the word nīharitvā, it is said, ‘to a sitting hall or to a monastery.’ By this, ‘ānetvā’ (having brought), it shows the meaning of the root hara preceded by nī. Dvāre (at the door) means at the door of one's own house. The third.

4. Catutthapāṭidesanīyasikkhāpadaṃ

4. The Fourth Pāṭidesanīya Training Rule.

570. Catutthe avaruddhasaddo pariruddhasaddassa pariyāyoti āha “pariruddhā hontī”ti. Āraññakassa senāsanassa parisamantato ruddhā āvutā hontīti attho.

570. In the fourth, he says, ‘they are enclosed (pariruddhā honti)’ because the word avaruddha is a synonym for the word pariruddha. The meaning is: the forest resting place is blocked and surrounded on all sides.

573. “Pañcanna”nti niddhāraṇe sāmivacanabhāvañca “yaṃkiñcī”ti niddhāraṇīyena sambandhitabbabhāvañca dassetuṃ vuttaṃ “pañcasu sahadhammikesu yaṃ kiñcī”ti. “Pesetvā khādanīyaṃ bhojanīyaṃ āharissāmī”tiiminā paṭisaṃviditākāradassanaṃ. “Ārāma”nti sāmaññato vuttepi āraññakasenāsanassa [M 0.0130] ārāmo eva adhippetoti āha “āraññakasenāsanārāmañcā”ti. Tassāti āraññakasenāsanārāmassa. “Kasmā”ti pucchāya “paṭimocanattha”nti visajjanāya sametuṃ sampadānatthe nissakkavacanaṃ kātabbaṃ. Kimatthanti hi attho. Paṭimocanatthanti tadatthe paccattavacanaṃ. Paṭimocanasaṅkhātāya atthāyāti hi attho. Atthasaddo ca payojanavācako. Payojanāyāti hi attho. Atha vā “paṭimocanattha”nti visajjanāyaṃ. “Kasmā”ti pucchāya sametuṃ nissakkatthe paccattavacanaṃ kātabbaṃ. Paṭimocanasaṅkhātā atthāti hi attho. Atthasaddo ca kāraṇavācako. Kāraṇāti hi attho. Evañhi pucchāvisajjanānaṃ pubbāparasamasaṅkhāto vicayo hāro paripuṇṇo hotīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Amhākanti khādanīyabhojanīyapaṭiharantānaṃ amhākaṃ. Amheti corasaṅkhāte amhe.

573. To show that 'pañcannaṃ' (of five) is in the determinative sense and is a genitive expression, and that 'yaṃ kiñci' (whatever) should be connected with what is to be determined, it is said, 'whatever among five co-religionists'. By 'Having sent, I will bring hard and soft food,' the manner of the arrangement is shown. Although 'ārāma' (monastery) is stated generally, a monastery that is a forest dwelling is intended; thus, it is said, 'and the monastery that is a forest dwelling'. 'Tassa' (of that) refers to the monastery that is a forest dwelling. To reconcile the question 'Kasmā' (Why?) with the answer 'paṭimocanatthaṃ' (for the purpose of release), the ablative case should be used in the sense of the dative. For the meaning is, 'For what purpose?'. 'Paṭimocanatthaṃ' is an accusative word in that sense. For the meaning is, 'for the purpose called release.' And the word 'attha' denotes utility. For the meaning is, 'for the sake of utility.' Alternatively, in the answer 'paṭimocanatthaṃ,' to reconcile it with the question 'Kasmā,' the accusative case should be used in the sense of the ablative. For the meaning is, 'the purpose called release.' And the word 'attha' denotes cause. For the meaning is, 'because of the cause.' In this way, it should be understood that the method of exegesis known as 'vicaya,' which is the balance of the preceding and succeeding of question and answer, is complete. 'Amhākaṃ' means 'of us who are bringing back hard and soft food.' 'Amhe' means 'us who are designated as thieves.'

“Tassā”ti padassatthaṃ dassetuṃ vuttaṃ “etissā yāguyā”ti. Aññānipīti paṭisaṃviditakulato aññānipi kulāni. Tenāti paṭisaṃviditakulena. Kurundivāde yāguyā paṭisaṃviditaṃ katvā yāguṃ aggahetvā pūvādīni āharanti, vaṭṭatīti adhippāyo.

To show the meaning of the word 'tassā' (of that), it is said 'of this porridge' (etissā yāguyā). 'Aññānipi' (others too) refers to families other than the family with which an arrangement has been made. 'Tena' (by that) means by the family with which an arrangement has been made. According to the Kurundī commentary, having made an arrangement for porridge, but not taking the porridge, they bring cakes and other items; the intended meaning is that this is permissible.

575. Ekassāti bhikkhussa. Tassāti paṭisaṃviditabhikkhussa, catunnaṃ vā pañcannaṃ vā bhikkhūnaṃ atthāyāti yojanā. Aññesampīti catupañcabhikkhuto aññesampi. Adhikamevāti paribhuttato atirekameva. Yaṃ panāti khādanīyabhojanīyaṃ pana, yampi khādanīyabhojanīyaṃ vanato āharitvā dentīti yojanā. “Tatthajātaka”nti ettha tasaddassa visayaṃ [V 1.0111] dassetuṃ vuttaṃ “ārāme”ti. Aññena dinnanti sambandho. Nanti mūlakhādanīyādiṃ. Paṭisaṃviditanti paṭikacceva suṭṭhu jānāpitanti atthoti. Catutthaṃ.

575. 'Ekassa' (of one) refers to a monk. 'Tassa' (of that) refers to the monk with whom an arrangement was made, or the connection is 'for the benefit of four or five monks'. 'Aññesampi' (for others too) means for others besides the four or five monks. 'Adhikameva' (even more) means just what is in excess of what has been consumed. 'Yaṃ pana' (now, whatever) refers to hard and soft food, and the connection is 'whatever hard and soft food they bring from the forest and give'. In 'tatthajātaka' (produced there), to show the scope of the word 'ta', it is said 'in the monastery'. The connection is 'given by another'. 'Naṃ' (it) refers to root foods, etc. 'Paṭisaṃvidita' (made known) means having been well-informed in advance—this is the meaning. The fourth.

Iti samantapāsādikāya vinayasaṃvaṇṇanāya

Thus in the Samantapāsādikā, the Commentary on the Vinaya,

Pāṭidesanīyavaṇṇanāya

the Commentary on the Pāṭidesanīya Rules:

Yojanā samattā.

The Elucidation is completed.

7. Sekhiyakaṇḍaṃ

7. The Section on the Trainings

1. Parimaṇḍalavagga-atthayojanā

1. The Elucidation of the Meaning of the Chapter on Wearing the Robe Evenly

Sikkhitasikkhena [M 0.0131] tīsu sikkhāsu catūhi maggehi sikkhitasikkhena tādinā aṭṭhahi lokadhammehi akampiyaṭṭhena tādinā, iṭṭhāniṭṭhesu vā avikāraṭṭhena tādinā bhagavatā yāni sikkhāpadāni “sekhiyānī”ti bhāsitāni, dāni tesampi sikkhāpadānaṃ ayampi vaṇṇanākkamo bhavatīti yojanā.

By the Tādin, who is trained in the training through the three trainings and trained in the training through the four paths; by the Tādin, who is such because of being unshaken by the eight worldly conditions; or by the Tādin, who is such because of being unperturbed by the desirable and undesirable—by the Blessed One, those training rules called 'sekhiyāni' were spoken. Now, this is also the sequence of the commentary for those training rules—this is the connection.

576. Tatthāti sekhiyasikkhāpadesu, attho evaṃ veditabboti yojanā. “Samantato”tiiminā parityūpasaggassatthaṃ dasseti. “Nābhimaṇḍalaṃ jāṇumaṇḍala”nti ettha uddhaṃsaddo ca adhosaddo ca ajjhāharitabboti āha “uddha”ntiādi. Aṭṭhaṅgulamattanti bhāvanapuṃsakaṃ, nivāsetabbanti sambandho. Tatoti aṭṭhaṅgulamattato. Yathā paṭicchannaṃ hoti, evaṃ nivāsentassāti yojanā. Tatridaṃ pamāṇanti tassa nivāsanassa idaṃ pamāṇaṃ. Tādisassāti dīghato muṭṭhipañcakassa tiriyaṃ aḍḍhateyyahatthassa nivāsanassa. Jāṇumaṇḍalaṃ paṭicchādanatthaṃ vaṭṭatīti yojanā. Tatthāti cīvaresu. Na tiṭṭhatīti viraḷattā na tiṭṭhati. Tiṭṭhatīti ghanattā tiṭṭhati.

576. Herein, in the sekhiyā training rules, the meaning should be understood thus—this is the connection. By 'all around' (samantato), he shows the meaning of the prefix 'pari-'. In 'the navel circle, the knee circle,' he says that the words 'above' and 'below' should be supplied—thus, 'above,' etc. 'A measure of eight fingerbreadths' is a neuter noun of state; 'should be worn' is the connection. 'From that' (tato) means from the measure of eight fingerbreadths. The connection is 'for one who wears it so that it is properly covered'. 'This is the measure here' refers to 'this is the measurement of that lower robe'. 'Of such a one' refers to a lower robe that is five fists in length and two and a half cubits in width. The connection is 'it is suitable for covering the knee circle'. 'Therein' refers to the robes. 'Does not remain' means it does not stay due to its sparseness. 'Remains' means it stays due to its density.

Nivāsentassa cātiettha casaddo avadhāraṇattho, nivāsentassevāti attho. Kevalaṃ evaṃ nivāsentasseva dukkaṭaṃ na hoti, atha kho tathā nivāsentassāpi dukkaṭamevāti yojanā. Ye pana nivāsanadosāti sambandho. Aññeti purato ca pacchato ca olambetvā nivasanato aññe[V 1.0112]. Te sabbeti sabbe te nivāsanadosā. Etthāti imasmiṃ vibhaṅge. Tatthevāti khandhakeyeva.

Here, in 'nivāsentassa ca' (for the wearer, and), the word 'ca' has an emphatic meaning; it means 'only for the wearer.' The connection is: it is not that there is no offense of wrong-doing only for one who wears it thus, but rather for one who wears it otherwise, there is indeed an offense of wrong-doing. 'But those faults of wearing' is the connection. 'Others' means other faults than that of wearing it hanging down in front and behind. 'All those' means all those faults of wearing. 'Here' means in this Analysis. 'Just there' means in the Khandhaka itself.

Asañcicca nivāsentassa anāpattīti sambandho. Eseva nayo “asatiyā”ti etthāpi. Ajānantassāti ettha ajānanaṃ duvidhaṃ nivāsanavattassa ajānanaṃ, ārūḷhorūḷhabhāvassa ajānananti. Tattha ārūḷhorūḷhabhāvassa ajānanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “ajānantassā”ti dassento [M 0.0132] āha “ajānantassāti etthā”tiādi. Hīti saccaṃ. Tassāti nivāsanavattassa. Assāti bhikkhuno. Taṃ panāti āpattito amokkhanaṃ pana. Tasmāti yasmā yujjati, tasmā. Yoti bhikkhu. Kurundiyaṃ vuttanti sambandho. Sukkhā jaṅghā imassāti sukkhajaṅgho. Mahantaṃ piṇḍikamaṃsaṃ imassāti mahāpiṇḍikamaṃso. Tassāti bhikkhussa.

The connection is: for one who wears it unintentionally, there is no offense. This same principle applies also to 'when unmindful' (asatiyā). In 'for one who does not know' (ajānantassa), not knowing is of two kinds: not knowing the duty of wearing the robe properly, and not knowing whether it has become displaced. Here, showing that 'for one who does not know' is stated with reference to not knowing whether it has become displaced, he says, 'in “for one who does not know,”' etc. 'Hi' (indeed) means truly. 'Tassa' (his) refers to the duty of wearing the robe properly. 'Assa' (his) refers to the monk. 'Taṃ pana' (but that) refers to non-exemption from the offense. 'Tasmā' (therefore) means 'because it is fitting, therefore'. 'Yo' (who) refers to the monk. 'As stated in the Kurundī' is the connection. 'Sukkhajaṅgho' means one who has thin shanks. 'Mahāpiṇḍikamaṃso' means one who has large calf muscles. 'Tassa' (his) refers to the monk.

Vaṇoti aru. Tañhi vaṇati gattavicuṇṇanaṃ karotīti vaṇoti vuccati. Vāḷamigā vā corā vāti ettha vāsaddo avuttasampiṇḍanattho, tena aññāpi udakacikkhallādayo āpadā saṅgayhanti.

'Vaṇa' (wound) means a sore. It is called a 'vaṇa' because it injures and causes the disintegration of the body. In 'wild animals or thieves,' the word 'or' (vā) is used for the purpose of including what is unstated; hence other dangers such as water and mud are also included.

577. Idhāti imasmiṃ vibhaṅge, sikkhāpade vā. Ubho kaṇṇeti purato ca pacchato ca niggate dve kaṇṇe. Avisesenāti “antaraghare”ti ca “ārāme”ti ca visesaṃ akatvā sāmaññena. Vihārepīti saṅghasannipātabuddhupaṭṭhānatherupaṭṭhānādikālaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ.

577. 'Here' (idha) means in this Analysis, or in the training rule. 'Both corners' refers to the two corners that have come out in front and behind. 'Without distinction' means generally, without making a distinction between 'inside a house' and 'in a monastery'. 'Even in a monastery' (vihārepi) is stated with reference to times such as a gathering of the Sangha, attendance on the Buddha, or attendance on elders.

578. Kāyekadese kāyasaddo vattatīti āha “jāṇumpi urampī”ti. “Na sīsaṃ pārutenā”tiiminā “suppaṭicchannenā”tipadassa atibyāpitadosaṃ paṭikkhipati. Gaṇṭhikanti pāso. So hi gantheti bandhatīti vā, gantheti bandhati etthāti vā katvā ganthikoti vuccati. Nthakārassa vāṇṭhakāre kate gaṇṭhiko, taṃ gaṇṭhikaṃ paṭimuñcitvā. Ubho kaṇṇeti cīvarassa dve koṇe. Galavāṭakatoti ettha galoti kaṇṭho. So hi khajjabhojjaleyyapeyyasaṅkhātaṃ catubbidhaṃ asanaṃ galati panno hutvā kucchiyaṃ patati itoti galoti vuccati. Āvāṭoyeva khuddakaṭṭhena āvāṭako, khuddakatthe ko. Gale ṭhito āvāṭako galavāṭako. Akārato hi ākārassa lopo “papa”ntiādīsu (jā. 1.1.2) viya. Ettha hi paāpanti padacchedo, akārato ākārassa ca lopo. Pavaddhaṃ āpaṃ papaṃ, mahantaṃ udakanti attho. Sīsaṃ vivaritvāti sambandho.

578. He says that the word 'body' (kāya) applies to a part of the body, as in 'the knee or the chest.' By 'not with head covered,' he refutes the fault of over-application of the word 'well-covered.' 'Gaṇṭhika' (knot) means a noose. It is called a 'gaṇṭhika' because it ties or binds, or because one ties or binds there. Or, when the letters 'nth' are made into 'ṇṭh,' it becomes 'gaṇṭhiko'; having loosened that knot. 'Both corners' means the two corners of the robe. In 'galavāṭakato' (from the neck-opening), 'gala' means the throat. It is called 'gala' because the four kinds of food—hard, soft, to be licked, and to be drunk—having been swallowed, fall from there into the stomach. An 'āvāṭa' is a hole; with 'ko' in the sense of 'small', it becomes 'āvāṭako'. An 'āvāṭako' situated at the 'gala' is a 'galavāṭako'. For the elision of 'ā' after 'a' occurs, as in 'papa' (Jā. 1.1.2), etc. Here the word division is 'pa-āpa,' and there is elision of 'ā' after 'a'. 'Papaṃ' is 'pavaddhaṃ āpaṃ', meaning 'abundant water,' 'a large amount of water.' The connection is 'having uncovered the head.'

579. Vāsaṃ [V 1.0113][M 0.0133] upagatoti vā vāsena upagatoti vā atthaṃ paṭikkhipanto āha “vāsatthāya upagatassā”ti.

579. Rejecting the meaning 'having gone to a dwelling' or 'having approached by means of a dwelling,' he says, 'of one who has approached for the purpose of dwelling.'

580. Hatthapāde akīḷanto susaṃvuto nāmāti dassento āha “hatthaṃ vā pādaṃ vā akīḷāpento”ti.

580. Showing that one who does not fidget with their hands and feet is called 'well-restrained,' he says, 'not causing the hand or foot to play.'

582. Okkhittacakkhūti ettha osaddo heṭṭhāpariyāyoti āha “heṭṭhā khittacakkhū”ti. “Hutvā”tiiminā kiriyāvisesanabhāvaṃ dasseti. Yugayuttakoti yuge yuttako. Damiyitthāti danto. Ābhuso jānāti kāraṇākāraṇanti ājāneyyo. Ettakanti catuhatthapamāṇaṃ. Yo gacchati, assa bhikkhuno dukkaṭā āpatti hotīti yojanā. “Parissayabhāva”nti ca “parissayābhāva”nti ca dve pāṭhā yujjantiyeva.

582. In 'okkhittacakkhu' (eyes cast down), the particle 'o' has the meaning of 'downward'; thus he says, 'eyes cast downward.' By 'hutvā' (having been), he indicates the adverbial sense. 'Yugayuttaka' (yoked to a yoke) means 'joined to a yoke.' 'Damiyittha' (should be tamed) means 'tamed' (danto). An 'ājāneyyo' (thoroughbred) is one who repeatedly knows cause and non-cause. 'Ettaka' (this much) means a measure of four cubits. The connection is: 'For the bhikkhu who goes, there is an offense of wrong-doing.' Both readings, 'parissayabhāva' (the state of danger) and 'parissayābhāva' (the absence of danger), are indeed suitable.

584. Itthambhūtalakkhaṇeti imaṃ pakāraṃ itthaṃ cīvarukkhipanaṃ, bhavati gacchatīti bhūto, bhikkhu. Lakkhīyati anenāti lakkhaṇaṃ, cīvaraṃ. Itthaṃ bhūto itthambhūto, tassa lakkhaṇaṃ itthambhūtalakkhaṇaṃ, tasmiṃ. Karaṇavacanaṃ daṭṭhabbanti yojanā. Itthambhūtalakkhaṇaṃ nāma kiriyāvisesanassa sabhāvoti āha “ekato vā…pe… hutvāti attho”ti. Antoindakhīlatoti gāmassa antoindakhīlatoti. Paṭhamo vaggo.

584. In 'itthambhūtalakkhaṇe' (in the characteristic of being in such a state): 'itthaṃ' means 'in this manner,' referring to the lifting of the robe; 'bhūta' means 'one who is' or 'one who goes,' i.e., a bhikkhu. A 'lakkhaṇa' is that by which something is characterized; here, the robe. 'Itthambhūta' is 'one who is in such a state'; its characteristic is 'itthambhūtalakkhaṇa'; 'tasmiṃ' means 'in that.' The connection is: it should be understood as an instrumental expression. 'The characteristic of being in such a state' is the nature of an adverbial modifier; thus he says, 'the meaning is "from one side... (etc.)... having been."' 'Antoindakhīlato' means 'within the village boundary post.' The First Section.

2. Ujjagghikavagga-atthayojanā

2. Elucidation of the Ujjagghika Chapter

586. Uccāsaddaṃ katvā jagghanaṃ hasanaṃ ujjaggho, soyeva ujjagghikā, tāya. Iti imamatthaṃ dassento āha “mahāhasitaṃ hasanto”ti. Etthāti “ujjagghikāyā”tipade.

586. Laughing while making a loud sound is 'ujjaggha'; that itself is 'ujjagghikā'; 'tāya' is the instrumental. Showing this meaning, he said, 'laughing a great laugh.' 'Ettha' (here) refers to the word 'ujjagghikāya'.

588. Kittāvatāti kittakena pamāṇena, evaṃ nisinnesu theresūti sambandho, niddhāraṇe cetaṃ bhummavacanaṃ. Vavatthapetīti idañcīdañca kathetīti vavatthapeti. Ettāvatāti ettakena pamāṇena.

588. 'Kittāvatā' means 'by what measure?' The connection is with 'when the elders are thus seated'; and this is a locative of specification. 'Vavatthapeti' means he speaks of this and that. 'Ettāvatā' means 'by this measure.'

590. Niccalaṃ katvā kāyassa ujuṭṭhapanaṃ kāyapaggaho nāmāti āha “niccalaṃ katvā”tiādi. Eseva nayo bāhupaggahasīsapaggahesupīti. Dutiyo vaggo.

590. Making the body motionless and holding it erect is called 'kāyapaggaha' (stiffening the body); thus he says, 'making motionless,' and so on. This same principle applies also to 'bāhupaggaha' (stiffening the arms) and 'sīsapaggaha' (stiffening the head). The Second Section.

3. Khambhakatavagga-atthayojanā

3. Elucidation of the Khambhakata Chapter

596. Khambho [V 1.0114][M 0.0134] kato yenāti khambhakato. Khambhoti ca paṭibaddho. Kattha paṭibaddhoti āha “kaṭiyaṃ hatthaṃ ṭhapetvā”ti. Sasīsaṃ avaguṇṭhayati pariveṭhatīti oguṇṭhitoti āha “sasīsaṃ pāruto”ti.

596. 'Khambhakato' is one who has made himself like a post. And 'khambha' means supported. Where is it supported? He says, 'having placed the hand on the hip.' One who covers or wraps himself including the head is 'oguṇṭhito'; thus he says, 'covered including the head.'

600. Uddhaṃ ekā koṭi imissā gamanāyāti ukkuṭikāti dassento āha “ukkuṭikā vuccatī”tiādi. Etthāti “ukkuṭikāyā”tipade.

600. Showing that 'ukkuṭikā' is so-called because one end is raised for this one's going, he said, 'it is called ukkuṭikā,' and so on. 'Ettha' (here) refers to the word 'ukkuṭikāya'.

601. Hatthapallatthīkadussapallatthīkesu dvīsu dussapallatthike āyogapallatthīkāpi saṅgahaṃ gacchatīti āha “āyogapallatthikāpi dussapallatthikā evā”ti.

601. Among the two, 'hatthapallatthikā' (sitting cross-legged with hands clasped) and 'dussapallatthikā' (sitting cross-legged supported by a cloth), 'āyogapallatthikā' (sitting cross-legged supported by a strap) is also included under 'dussapallatthikā'; thus he says, 'sitting cross-legged supported by a strap is also a form of sitting cross-legged supported by a cloth.'

602. Satiyā upaṭṭhānaṃ sakkaccanti āha “satiṃupaṭṭhapetvā”ti.

602. 'Sakkaccaṃ' (respectfully) means the presence of mindfulness; thus he says, 'having established mindfulness.'

603. Piṇḍapātaṃ dentepīti piṇḍapātaṃ patte pakkhipantepi. Patte saññā pattasaññā, sā assatthīti pattasaññī. “Katvā” tiiminā kiriyāvisesanabhāvaṃ dasseti.

603. 'Piṇḍapātaṃ dente'pi' (even when giving almsfood) means 'even when placing almsfood in the bowl.' 'Pattasaññā' is perception of the bowl; one who has this is 'pattasaññī.' By 'katvā,' he indicates the adverbial sense.

604. Samasūpakaṃ piṇḍapātanti ettha sūpapiṇḍapātānaṃ samaupaḍḍhabhāvaṃ āsaṅkā bhaveyyāti āha “samasūpako nāmā”tiādi. Yatthāti piṇḍapāte. Bhattassa catutthabhāgapamāṇo sūpo hoti, so piṇḍapāto samasūpako nāmāti yojanā. Oloṇī ca sākasūpeyyañca maccharaso ca maṃsaraso cāti dvando. Tattha oloṇīti ekā byañjanavikati. Sākasūpeyyanti sūpassa hitaṃ sūpeyyaṃ, sākameva sūpeyyaṃ sākasūpeyyaṃ. Iminā sabbāpi sākasūpeyyabyañjanavikati gahitā. Maccharasamaṃsarasādīnīti ettha ādisaddena avasesā sabbāpi byañjanavikati saṅgahitā. Taṃ sabbaṃ rasānaṃ raso rasarasoti katvā “rasaraso”ti vuccati.

604. Regarding 'a meal with equal curry' (samasūpakaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ), lest there be a suspicion that the curry and the almsfood are of equal halves, he says, 'What is called a meal with equal curry?' and so on. 'Yattha' (wherein) refers to the almsfood. The connection is: when the curry is the measure of a fourth part of the rice, that almsfood is called 'a meal with equal curry.' 'Oloṇī, sākasūpeyya, maccharasa, and maṃsarasa' is a dvandva compound. Therein, 'oloṇī' is one kind of condiment. 'Sākasūpeyya': 'sūpeyya' is what is suitable for soup; a vegetable itself that is suitable for soup is 'sākasūpeyya.' By this, all kinds of vegetable-soup condiments are included. In 'fish-broth, meat-broth, and so on,' by the word 'and so on,' all remaining kinds of condiments are included. All that, being the taste of tastes, is called 'rasaraso' (the finest taste).

605. Samapuṇṇaṃ samabharitanti vevacanameva. Thūpaṃ kato thūpīkatoti atthaṃ dassento āha “thūpīkato nāmā”tiādi.

605. 'Samapuṇṇaṃ' and 'samabharitaṃ' are simply synonyms. Showing that the meaning of 'thūpīkato' is 'made into a heap' (thūpaṃ kato), he says, 'What is called thūpīkato?' and so on.

Tatthāti [M 0.0135] “thūpīkata”ntiādivacane. Tesanti abhayattheratipiṭakacūḷanāgattherānaṃ. Iti pucchiṃsu, tesañca therānaṃ vādaṃ ārocesunti yojanā. Theroti cūḷasumanatthero. Etassāti tipiṭakacūḷanāgattherassa[V 1.0115]. Sattakkhattunti satta vāre. Kutoti kassācariyassa santikā. Tasmāti yasmā yāvakālikena paricchinno, tasmā. Āmisajātikaṃ yāgubhattaṃ vā phalāphalaṃ vāti yojanā. Tañca khoti tañca samatitthikaṃ. Itarena panāti nādhiṭṭhānupagena pattena pana. Yaṃ pūvaucchukhaṇḍaphalāphalādi heṭṭhā orohati, taṃ pūvaucchukhaṇḍaphalāphalādīti yojanā. Pūvavaṭaṃsakoti ettha vaṭaṃsakoti uttaṃso. So hi uddhaṃ tasīyate alaṅkarīyateti vaṭaṃsoti vuccati ukārassa vakāraṃ, takārassa ca ṭakāraṃ katvā, soyeva vaṭaṃsako, muddhani pilandhito eko alaṅkāraviseso. Pūvameva taṃsadisattā pūvavaṭaṃsako, taṃ. Pupphavaṭaṃsako ca takkolakaṭukaphalādivaṭaṃsako cāti dvando, te.

'Tattha' refers to the phrase 'thūpīkata,' and so on. 'Tesaṃ' refers to the elders Abhayatthera and Tipiṭakacūḷanāgatthera. The connection is: 'Thus they asked, and they reported the view of those elders.' 'Thero' refers to the elder Cūḷasumana. 'Etassa' refers to the elder Tipiṭakacūḷanāga. 'Sattakkhattuṃ' means seven times. 'Kuto' means from which teacher. 'Tasmā' means: because it is limited by what is allowable for a time, therefore... The connection is: 'material things such as rice gruel, cooked rice, or various fruits.' 'Tañca kho' means 'and that which is level.' 'Itarena pana' means 'but by the other bowl,' that is, one that has not been determined. The connection is: 'whatever, such as cakes, pieces of sugarcane, or various fruits, falls down, that...' In 'pūvavaṭaṃsako,' 'vaṭaṃsako' means an 'uttaṃso' (crest). It is called 'vaṭaṃso' because it is raised up and adorned; this is formed by changing 'u' to 'va' and 'ta' to 'ṭa'. 'Vaṭaṃsako' itself is a particular kind of ornament worn on the head. A 'pūvavaṭaṃsako' is a cake that resembles that. 'Pupphavaṭaṃsako ca takkolakaṭukaphalādivaṭaṃsako ca' is a dvandva compound; 'te' refers to them.

Idhāti imasmiṃ sikkhāpade. Nanu sabbathūpīkatesu paṭiggahaṇassa akappiyattā paribhuñjanampi na vaṭṭatīti āha “sabbattha panā”tiādi. Tattha sabbatthāti sabbesu thūpīkatesūti. Tatiyo vaggo.

'Idha' means in this training rule. Is it not so that since accepting is improper in the case of all heaped-up almsfood, consuming it is also not allowable? Thus he says, 'But in all cases,' and so on. Therein, 'sabbattha' (in all cases) means in the case of all heaped-up almsfood. The Third Section.

4. Sakkaccavagga-atthayojanā

4. Elucidation of the Sakkacca Chapter

608. Tattha tatthāti tasmiṃ tasmiṃ ṭhāne. Odhinti avadhiṃ mariyādaṃ.

608. 'Tattha tattha' means 'in that and that place.' 'Odhiṃ' means a limit, a boundary.

610. Thūpakatoti thūpameva thūpakaṃ, tato thūpakatoti dassento āha “matthakato”ti.

610. Regarding 'thūpakato': 'thūpaka' is simply 'thūpa' (a heap). Showing that 'thūpakato' means 'from the heap,' he says, 'from the top.'

611. Māghātasamayādīsūti “pāṇe mā ghātethā”ti rājāno bheriṃ carāpenti etthāti māghāto, soyeva samayo māghātasamayo. Ādisaddena aññaṃ paṭicchannakāraṇaṃ gahetabbaṃ.

611. Regarding 'māghātasamayādīsu': a 'māghāta' is when kings have a drum beaten, proclaiming, 'Do not kill living beings'; that very time is a 'māghātasamayo.' By the word 'ādi' (and so on), another concealed reason should be understood.

615. Tesanti mayūraṇḍakukkuṭaṇḍānanti. Catuttho vaggo.

615. 'Tesaṃ' refers to peacock eggs and chicken eggs. The Fourth Section.

5. Kabaḷavagga-atthayojanā

5. Elucidation of the Chapter on Morsels

617. “Mukhadvāra”nti [M 0.0136] kammassa “anāhaṭe”ti ca “vivarissāmī”ti ca dvīsu kiriyāsu sambandhabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ vuttaṃ “anāharite mukhadvāra”nti.

617. The phrase 'anāharite mukhadvāra' is stated in order to show that 'mukhadvāra' (the mouth-opening) is the object connected with the two actions 'anāhaṭe' (when... has not been brought) and 'vivarissāmī' (I will open).

618. Sakalaṃ hatthanti pañcaṅguliṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ.

618. 'Sakalaṃ hatthaṃ' (the whole hand) is said in reference to the five fingers.

619. Sakabaḷenāti [V 1.0116] ettha kabaḷasaddena vacanassa aparipuṇṇakāraṇaṃ sabbampi gahetabbaṃ.

619. In 'sakabaḷena', by the word 'kabaḷa' should be understood every cause for the incompleteness of speech.

620. Piṇḍukkhepakantiādīsu vicchatthe kapaccayoti āha “piṇḍaṃ ukkhipitvā ukkhipitvā”ti. Tvāsaddena kiriyāvisesanabhāvaṃ dasseti.

620. In words such as 'piṇḍukkhepaka,' the suffix '-ka' has a repetitive sense; thus he says, 'piṇḍaṃ ukkhipitvā ukkhipitvā' (having lifted up the morsel again and again). By the word 'tvā,' he indicates the adverbial sense.

624. “Avakiritvā”ti iminā sitthāvakārakanti ettha avapubbo kiradhātuyeva, na karadhātūti dasseti.

624. By means of 'avakiritvā' (having scattered down), he shows that in the word 'sitthāvakāraka', the root is 'kir' with the prefix 'ava', not the root 'kar'.

626. “Capucapū”ti evaṃ saddanti “capucapū”ti evaṃ anukaraṇaravanti. Pañcamo vaggo.

626. 'Capucapū'ti evaṃ saddanti' means 'they make an imitative sound like "capucapū".' The Fifth Section.

6. Surusuruvagga-atthayojanā

6. Elucidation of the Surusuru Chapter

627. “Surusurū”ti evaṃ saddanti “surusurū”ti evaṃ anukaraṇaravaṃ. Davanaṃ kīḷananti iminā vacanatthena parihāso davo nāmāti āha “davoti parihāsavacana”nti. Tanti so davo. Liṅgavipallāso hesa. Na kātabbaṃ na kātabboti sambandho. Silakabuddhoti silāya kato, silena niyutto vā buddho. Apaṭibuddhoti apaṭividdho buddho, parihāsavacanametaṃ. Godhammoti gunnaṃ dhammo. Ajadhammoti ajānaṃ dhammo. Migasaṅghoti migānaṃ saṅgho. Pasusaṅghoti pasūnaṃ saṅgho.

627. “‘Surusurū’ti evaṃ saddanti”: They make a sound like ‘surusuru’; this is an onomatopoeic sound. Because of the meaning of the expression “davanaṃ kīḷanaṃ” (‘sport is play’), `dava` is a word for jesting; thus he says, “davoti parihāsavacanaṃ” (‘`dava` is a word for jesting’). “Tanti so davo”: That `tanti` is `dava`. This is a change of gender. The connection is “na kātabbaṃ na kātabbaṃ” (‘it should not be done, it should not be done’). “Silakabuddho” means a Buddha made of stone or one connected with stone. “Apaṭibuddho” means an unawakened Buddha; this is a term of derision. “Godhammo” is the way of cattle. “Ajadhammo” is the way of goats. “Migasaṅgho” is a herd of deer. “Pasusaṅgho” is a herd of beasts.

628. “Bhuñjantenā”ti padaṃ “nillehitu”nti pade bhāvakattā.

628. The word “bhuñjantenā” (“by one who is eating”) functions as the agent for the word “nillehituṃ” (“to lick”).

631. Evaṃnāmaketi [M 0.0137] “kokanuda”nti evaṃ nāmaṃ assa pāsādassāti evaṃnāmako, pāsādo, tasmiṃ. “Padumasaṇṭhāno”ti iminā pāsādassa sadisūpacārena “kokanudo”ti nāmalabhanaṃ dasseti. Tenāti padumasaṇṭhānattā. Assāti pāsādassa. Puggalikampīti parapuggalasantakaṃ gahetabbaṃ “attano santakampī”ti attapuggalasantakassa visuṃ gayhamānattā. Saṅkhampīti pānīyasaṅkhampi. Sarāvampīti pānīyasarāvampi. Thālakampīti pānīyathālakampi.

631. “Evaṃnāmake”: A palace of such a name, that is, one named ‘Kokanada’; “tasmiṃ” means ‘in that palace.’ By “padumasaṇṭhāno” (‘having the shape of a lotus’), he shows that the palace obtained the name ‘Kokanada’ through a metaphor based on its similarity to a lotus. “Tenā” means: because of its lotus-like form. “Assā” means: of the palace. “Puggalikampi”: This should be taken as ‘belonging to another person,’ since ‘what belongs to oneself’ is mentioned separately. “Saṅkhampi” means: also a conch for water. “Sarāvampi” means: also a saucer for water. “Thālakampi” means: also a bowl for water.

632. “Uddharitvā”ti sāmaññato vuttavacanassa kammāpādānāni dassetuṃ vuttaṃ “sitthāni udakato”ti. Bhinditvāti cuṇṇavicuṇṇāni katvā. Bahīti antaragharato bahi.

632. The phrase “sitthāni udakato” (‘grains of rice from the water’) is stated in order to show the object and the ablative source for the general term “uddharitvā” (‘having lifted out’). “Bhinditvā” means: having made them into fine powder. “Bahī” means: outside the inner house.

634. Setacchattanti [V 1.0117] ettha setasaddo paṇḍarapariyāyoti āha “paṇḍaracchatta”nti. Vatthapaliguṇṭhitanti vatthehi samantato veṭhitaṃ. Setaṃ chattaṃ setacchattaṃ. Kiḷañjehi kataṃ chattaṃ kiḷañjacchattaṃ. Paṇṇehi kataṃ chattaṃ paṇṇacchattaṃ. Maṇḍalena baddhaṃ maṇḍalabaddhaṃ. Salākāhi baddhaṃ salākabaddhaṃ. Tānīti tīṇi chattāni. Hīti saccaṃ. Yampi ekapaṇṇacchattanti yojanā. Etesūti tīsu chattesu. Assāti yassa kassaci gahaṭṭhassa vā pabbajitassa vā. Soti yo koci gahaṭṭho vā pabbajito vā. Chattapādukāya vāti chattadaṇḍanikkhepanāya pādukāya vā. Etthāti imasmiṃ sikkhāpade.

634. “Setacchattaṃ”: Here the word `seta` (white) is a synonym for `paṇḍara` (pale); thus he says “paṇḍaracchattaṃ”. “Vatthapaliguṇṭhitaṃ” means wrapped all around with cloths. “Setaṃ chattaṃ” is “setacchattaṃ” (a white umbrella). An umbrella made from rushes is a “kiḷañjacchattaṃ”. An umbrella made from leaves is a “paṇṇacchattaṃ”. Bound with a hoop is “maṇḍalabaddhaṃ”. Bound with ribs is “salākabaddhaṃ”. “Tāni” means: the three umbrellas. “Hī” means: truly. The connection is also “yampi ekapaṇṇacchattaṃ” (‘also a single-leaf umbrella’). “Etesū” means: among these three umbrellas. “Assā” means: for anyone, whether a householder or one who has gone forth. “So” means: anyone, whether a householder or one who has gone forth. “Chattapādukāya vā” means: or with a stand for the umbrella. “Etthā” means: in this training rule.

635. Majjhimassāti pamāṇamajjhimassa. “Catuhatthappamāṇo”tiiminā catuhatthato ūnātireko daṇḍo na daṇḍo nāmāti dasseti. Daṇḍo pāṇimhi assāti vacanatthaṃ atidisanto āha “vuttanayenevā”ti.

635. “Majjhimassā” means: of middling measure. By “catuhatthappamāṇo” (“of four cubits' measure”), he shows that a staff shorter or longer than four cubits is not called a staff. Extending the meaning of the expression “a staff in his hand,” he says, “in the way already stated.”

636. “Satthapāṇimhī”ti ettha asi eva adhippetoti āha “asi”nti. Asinti khaggaṃ.

636. In “satthapāṇimhi” (‘with a weapon in hand’), a sword (`asi`) is intended; thus he says, “asi”. “Asin” means a sword (`khaggaṃ`).

637. “Āvudhaṃ nāma cāpo kodaṇḍo”ti pāḷiyaṃ vuttavacanaṃ upalakkhaṇamevāti dassento āha “āvudhapāṇissāti etthā”tiādi. Sabbāpi dhanuvikati āvudhanti veditabbāti yojanā. Yathā asiṃ [M 0.0138] sannahitvā ṭhito satthapāṇīti saṅkhyaṃ na gacchati, evaṃ dhanuṃ kaṇṭhe paṭimukko āvudhapāṇīti āha “sace panā”tiādi, iminā āvudho pāṇinā gahitoyeva āvudhapāṇi nāmāti dassetīti. Chaṭṭho vaggo.

637. Showing that the statement in the Pāli, ‘A weapon is a bow, a longbow,’ is merely an exemplification, he says, ‘Here in “āvudhapāṇissā”ti…’ and so on. The connection is that all varieties of bows are to be understood as weapons. Just as one standing with a sword girded on is not reckoned as “satthapāṇī” (‘with weapon in hand’), so too, regarding one with a bow slung on his neck not being “āvudhapāṇī”, he says, ‘But if…’ etc. By this he shows that one is called “āvudhapāṇi” only when a weapon is actually held in the hand. The Sixth Chapter.

7. Pādukavagga-atthayojanā

7. Elucidation of the Chapter on Footwear

638. Aṅgulantaranti pādaṅgulavivaraṃ. Pādukanti upāhanaviseso. So hi pajjate imāyāti pādukāti vuccati, sā bahupaṭalā cammamayā vā hoti kaṭṭhamayā vā. Paṭimuñcitvāti pādukaṃ paṭimuñcītvā.

638. “Aṅgulantaran” means the space between the toes. “Pādukan” is a type of footwear. It is called “pādukā” because one goes (`pajjate`) by means of it; it is multi-layered and can be made of leather or of wood. “Paṭimuñcitvā” means having put on the footwear.

640. Dvīhi janehi gahitoti sambandho. Vaṃsenāti veṇunā, yāne nisinnoti sambandho. Visaṅkharitvāti vipattiṃ karitvā. Dvepīti dhammakathikadhammapaṭiggāhakasaṅkhātā ubhopi janā. Vaṭṭatīti desetuṃ vaṭṭati.

640. The connection is: ‘held by two people.’ “Vaṃsenā” means: with a bamboo; the connection is ‘sitting in a vehicle.’ “Visaṅkharitvā” means: having brought about ruin. “Dvepī” means: both people, that is, the one designated as the speaker of the Dhamma and the one designated as the recipient of the Dhamma. “Vaṭṭatī” means: it is proper to teach.

641. Sayanagatassāti [V 1.0118] sayanaṃ gatassa, sayane nipannassāti attho. Nipannassa desetuṃ na vaṭṭatīti sambandho.

641. “Sayanagatassā” means for one who has gone to a bed, that is, one who is lying on a bed. The connection is that it is not proper to teach one who is lying down.

642. Tīsu pallatthikāsu yāya kāyaci pallatthikāya nisinnassa dhammaṃ desetuṃ na vaṭṭatīti dassento āha “pallatthikāyā”tiādi.

642. Showing that it is not proper to teach the Dhamma to one sitting in any of the three cross-legged postures, he says, “pallatthikāyā”ti, and so on.

643. Yathā veṭhiyamāne kesanto na dissati, evaṃ veṭhitasīsassāti yojanā.

643. The connection for “veṭhitasīsassā” (‘for one with a wrapped head’) is: just as the end of the hair is not seen when it is being wrapped.

647. Chapakasaddassa ca caṇḍālasaddassa ca vevacanattā vuttaṃ “caṇḍālassā”ti. Caṇḍālo hi saṃ sunakhaṃ pacatīti chapakoti vuccati sakārassa chakāraṃ katvā. Chapakassa esā chapakī, caṇḍālabhariyā. Yatrāti ettha trapaccayo paccatte hotīti āha “yo hi nāmā”ti. Yo rājā ucce āsane nisīditvā mantaṃ pariyāpuṇissati nāma, ayaṃ rājā yāva ativiya adhammikoti vuttaṃ hoti. “Sabbamida”nti ayaṃ saddo liṅgavipallāsoti āha “sabbo aya”nti[M 0.0139]. “Loko”ti iminā idhasaddassa visayaṃ dasseti. Carimasaddo antimapariyāyo. Antimoti ca lāmako. Lāmakoti ca nāma idha vipattīti āha “saṅkara”nti. Saṅkaranti vipattiṃ. “Nimmariyādo”ti iminā “saṅkaraṃ gato”ti padānaṃ adhippāyatthaṃ dasseti. Carimaṃ gataṃ carimagataṃ, sabbo ayaṃ loko carimagatoti attho. Idha ca jātake (jā. 1.4.33) ca kesuci potthakesu “camarikata”nti pāṭho atthi, so ayuttoyeva. Tatthevāti ambarukkhamūleyeva. Tesanti rājabrāhmaṇānaṃ.

647. “Caṇḍālassā” is said because the word `chapaka` and the word `caṇḍāla` are synonyms. A `caṇḍāla` is called a `chapaka` because he cooks a dog (`saṃ` = `sunakhaṃ`), changing the `sa` to `cha`. The wife of a `chapaka` is a `chapakī`, a `caṇḍāla`'s wife. In “yatrā”, the suffix `-tra` is in the dative sense; thus he says, “yo hi nāmā”. It means: a king who would learn a mantra while sitting on a high seat is said to be extremely unrighteous. The word “sabbamidaṃ” is a change of gender; thus he says, “sabbo ayaṃ”. By “loko” (‘world’), he indicates the domain of the word `idha` (‘here’). The word `carima` is a synonym for `antima` (‘last’). And `antima` means `lāmaka` (‘base’). And `lāmaka` here means ruin (`vipatti`); thus he says, “saṅkaraṃ”. “Saṅkaran” means ruin. By “nimmariyādo” (‘without boundaries’), he shows the intended meaning of the phrase “saṅkaraṃ gato” (‘gone to ruin’). “Carimaṃ gataṃ” is “carimagataṃ”; the meaning is that this whole world has gone to the final stage. Here and in the Jātaka (Jā 1.4.33), in some books the reading is “camarikata”, but this is incorrect. “Tatthevā” means: at the foot of that very amba tree. “Tesan” means: of the king and the brahmins.

Tatthāti tissaṃ gāthāyaṃ. Pāḷiyāti attano ācārapakāsakaganthasaṅkhātāya pāḷiyā. Na passareti ettha resaddo antissa kāriyoti āha “na passantī”ti. Yo cāyanti yo ca ayaṃ. Ayaṃsaddo padālaṅkāramatto, brāhmaṇoti attho. Adhīyatīti ajjhāyati, sikkhatīti attho.

“Tatthā” means: in the third verse. “Pāḷiyā” means: by the Pāli text, designated as the book that proclaims one's own conduct. In “na passareti”, the sound `re` is a corruption of `nti`; thus he says, “na passanti”. “Yo cāyan” means: `yo ca ayaṃ`. The word `ayaṃ` is merely a metrical filler; the meaning is ‘the brahmin.’ “Adhīyatī” means `ajjhāyati`; the meaning is, ‘he learns.’

Tatoti bodhisattena vuttagāthāto paranti sambandho. Tassāti gāthāya. Bhoti bodhisattaṃ āmanteti. “Bhutto”ti padassa kammavācakabhāvamāvikātuṃ vuttaṃ “mayā”ti. Assāti odanassa. Iminā suci parisuddhaṃ maṃsaṃ sucimaṃsaṃ, tena upasecanamassāti sucimaṃsūpasecanoti bāhiratthasamāsaṃ dasseti. Dhammeti ācāradhamme. Baddho hutvāti thaddho hutvā, ayameva vā pāṭho[V 1.0119]. Vaṇṇasaddassa saṇṭhānādike aññe atthe paṭikkhipituṃ vuttaṃ “pasattho”ti. Thomitoti tasseva vevacanaṃ.

The connection is “tato… paran” (‘after that’), that is, after the verse spoken by the Bodhisatta. “Tassā” means: of the verse. “Bho” is an address to the Bodhisatta. “Mayā” (‘by me’) is stated in order to reveal the passive sense of the word “bhutto” (‘eaten’). “Assā” means: of the rice. By this he shows the exocentric compound in “sucimaṃsūpasecano”: `suci parisuddhaṃ maṃsaṃ` is `sucimaṃsaṃ` (‘clean, pure meat’), and that is its relish (`upasecana`). “Dhamme” means: in the customary conduct. “Baddho hutvā” means: having become stiff (`thaddho hutvā`), or this itself is the reading. In order to reject other meanings of the word `vaṇṇa`, such as shape, “pasattho” (‘praised’) is said. “Thomito” is a synonym for that.

Athāti anantare. Nanti brāhmaṇaṃ. Tassāti gāthādvayassa. Brāhmaṇāti purohitaṃ ālapati. Sampatīti sandīṭṭhike. “Yā vutti vinipātena, adhammacaraṇena vā”ti padānaṃ sambandhaṃ dassetuṃ vuttaṃ “nippajjatī”ti.

“Athā” means: immediately after. “Nan” refers to the brahmin. “Tassā” means: of the pair of verses. “Brāhmaṇā” is an address to the royal priest. “Sampatī” means: in the present. “Nippajjatī” (‘arises’) is said in order to show the connection with the words, ‘Whatever livelihood is by means of downfall or by unrighteous conduct…’

Mahābrahmeti ettha brahmasaddo brāhmaṇavācakoti āha “mahābrāhmaṇā”ti. Aññepīti rājabrāhmaṇehi aparepi. “Pacantī”ti vutte [M 0.0140] avinābhāvato “bhuñjantī”ti atthopi gahetabboti āha “pacanti ceva bhuñjanti cā”ti. “Na kevala”ntiādinā aññepīti ettha pisaddassa sampiṇḍanatthaṃ dasseti, tvaṃ ācarissasīti sambandho. Puna tvanti taṃ, upayogatthe cetaṃ paccattavacanaṃ, “mā bhidā”tiiminā sambandhitabbaṃ. “Pāsāṇo”tiiminā asmasaddo pāsāṇapariyāyoti dasseti. Tenāti bhindanahetunā.

Here in `mahābrahme`, the word `brahma` denotes a brahmin; thus he says, `mahābrāhmaṇā`. `Aññe pi` means: others apart from the king and the brahmin. When `pacanti` ('they cook') is said, the meaning `bhuñjanti` ('they eat') should also be understood due to the invariable connection; thus he says, 'they both cook and eat.' By 'Not only…' and so on, he shows the collective sense of the word `pi` in `aññe pi`; the connection is, 'you will behave thus.' `Puna tvaṃ` means `taṃ` ('you'); this is a personal pronoun in the sense of application and should be connected with `mā bhidā` ('do not break'). By `pāsāṇo`, he shows that the word `asma` is a synonym for `pāsāṇa` ('stone'). `Tena` means: by that cause of breaking.

648. Attano kaṅkhāṭhānassa pucchanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “na kathetabba”nti.

648. With reference to asking about one's own point of doubt, it is said: 'It should not be told.'

649. Samadhurenāti samaṃ dhurena, samaṃ mukhenāti attho.

649. `Samadhurena` means: level with the yoke, that is, level with the front.

652. Yaṃ mūlaṃ vā yā sākhā vā gacchatīti yojanā. Khandheti rukkhassa khandhe. Nikkhamatīti uccārapassāvo nikkhamati. Tiṇaṇḍupakanti tiṇena kataṃ, tiṇamayaṃ vā aṇḍupakaṃ. Etthāti uccārapassāvakheḷesu.

652. The connection is: whatever root or branch it goes to. `Khandhe`: on the trunk of the tree. `Nikkhamati` means excrement and urine come out. `Tiṇaṇḍupakaṃ` means a support made of grass or consisting of grass. `Ettha` means in excrement, urine, and saliva.

653. Adhippetaudakaṃ dassetuṃ vuttaṃ “paribhogaudakamevā”ti. Sattamo vaggo.

653. To show the intended water, it was said: 'It is just water for use.' The Seventh Chapter.

Etthāti sekhiyesu. Sūpabyañjanapaṭicchādaneti sūpabyañjane odanena paṭicchādeti. Samattā sekhiyā.

`Ettha` means in the Sekhiyas. `Sūpabyañjanapaṭicchādane` means one covers the curry and side dishes with rice. The Sekhiyas are completed.

8. Sattādhikaraṇasamatha-atthayojanā

8. An Exposition of the Meaning of the Seven Settlements of Legal Issues

655. Saṅkhyaṃ [V 1.0120] paricchijjatīti saṅkhyāparicchedo. Tesanti catubbidhānamadhikaraṇānaṃ. Tassāti tesaṃ khandhakaparivārānaṃ. Tatthevāti tesu eva khandhakaparivāresu. Sabbatthāti sabbesu sikkhāpadesūti.

655. A determination of number (`saṅkhyāparicchedo`) is so called because number is determined (`saṅkhyaṃ paricchijjati`). `Tesaṃ` means: of the four kinds of legal issues. `Tassa` means: of those Khandhakas and Parivāras. `Tattheva` means: right in those Khandhakas and Parivāras. `Sabbattha` means: in all the training rules.

Iti samantapāsādikāya vinayasaṃvaṇṇanāya

Thus in the Samantapāsādikā, the Commentary on the Vinaya,

Bhikkhuvibhaṅgavaṇṇanāya yojanā samattā.

The Exposition of the Commentary on the Bhikkhuvibhaṅga is completed.

Jādilañchitanāmena nekānaṃ vācito mayā.

I have been addressed by many with the name Jādilañchita.

Sādhuṃ mahāvibhaṅgassa, samatto yojanānayoti.

The methodical exposition of the Mahāvibhaṅga is well completed.

Bhikkhunīvibhaṅgo

The Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga

1. Pārājikakaṇḍaatthayojanā

1. An Exposition of the Meaning of the Pārājika Section

Evaṃ [M 0.0141][V 1.0121] bhikkhuvibhaṅgassa, katvāna yojanānayaṃ;

Bhikkhunīnaṃ vibhaṅgassa, karissaṃ yojanānayaṃ.

Having thus made the methodical exposition of the Bhikkhuvibhaṅga, I shall now make the methodical exposition of the Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga.

Yoti vibhaṅgo. Vibhaṅgassāti vibhaṅgo assa. Assāti hoti. Tassāti bhikkhunīnaṃ vibhaṅgassa. Yatoti yasmā. Ayaṃ panettha yojanā – bhikkhūnaṃ vibhaṅgassa anantaraṃ bhikkhunīnaṃ yo vibhaṅgo saṅgahito assa, tassa bhikkhunīnaṃ vibhaṅgassa saṃvaṇṇanākkamo patto yato, tato tassa bhikkhunīnaṃ vibhaṅgassa apubbapadavaṇṇanaṃ kātuṃ tāva pārājike ayaṃ saṃvaṇṇanā hotīti. Apubbānaṃ padānaṃ vaṇṇanā apubbapadavaṇṇanā, taṃ.

`Yo` means the Vibhaṅga. `Vibhaṅgassa` means `vibhaṅgo assa` ('of its analysis'). `Assa` means `hoti` ('is'). `Tassa` means of the Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga. `Yato` means `yasmā` ('because'). This is the connection here: since the turn for the commentary on the Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga—that analysis for the bhikkhunīs which is included immediately after the Bhikkhuvibhaṅga—has arrived, therefore, in order to comment on the new words of that Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga, this commentary on the Pārājika section occurs first. A commentary on new words (`apubbānaṃ padānaṃ vaṇṇanā`) is an `apubbapadavaṇṇanā`; it is this that is to be done.

1. Paṭhamapārājikasikkhāpadaṃ

1. The First Pārājika Training Rule

656. “Tena…pe… sāḷho”ti ettha “etthā”ti pāṭhaseso yojetabbo. Dabbaguṇakiriyājātināmasaṅkhātesu pañcasu saddesu sāḷhasaddassa nāmasaddabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ vuttaṃ “sāḷhoti tassa nāma”nti. Migāramātuyāti visākhāya. Sā hi migāraseṭṭhinā mātuṭṭhāne ṭhapitattā migāramātā nāma. Navakammaṃ adhiṭṭhātīti navakammikanti dassento āha “navakammādhiṭṭhāyika”nti. “Paṇḍiccena samannāgatā”tiiminā paṇḍā vuccati paññā, sā sañjātā imissāti paṇḍitāti vacanatthaṃ dasseti. Veyyattikenāti visesena añjati pākaṭaṃ gacchatīti viyatto, puggalo, tassa idaṃ veyyattikaṃ, ñāṇaṃ, tena. “Paṇḍā”ti vuttapaññāya “medhā”ti vuttapaññāya visesabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ vuttaṃ “pāḷigahaṇe”tiādi. “Medhā”ti hi vuttapaññā “paṇḍā”ti vuttapaññāya viseso hoti satisahāyattā. Tatrupāyāyāti aluttasamāso [V 1.0122] “tatramajjhattatā”tiādīsu (dha. sa. aṭṭha. yevāpanakavaṇṇanā) viya. “Kammesū”ti iminā tasaddassa visayaṃ dasseti[M 0.0142]. Kattabbakammupaparikkhāyāti kattabbakammesu vicāraṇāya. Casaddena “katākata”nti padassa dvandavākyaṃ dasseti. Parivesanaṭṭhāneti paribhuñjituṃ visanti pavisanti etthāti parivesanaṃ, tameva ṭhānaṃ parivesanaṭṭhānaṃ, tasmiṃ. Nikūṭeti ettha kūṭasaṅkhātasikharavirahite okāseti dassento āha “koṇasadisaṃ katvā dassite gambhīre”ti. Vityūpasaggo vikāravācako, sarasaddo saddavācakoti āha “vippakārasaddo”ti. Carati anenāti caraṇaṃ pādo, tasmiṃ uṭṭhito gilāno etissāti caraṇagilānāti dassento āha “pādarogena samannāgatā”ti.

656. In the passage 'Tena...pe... sāḷho,' the remainder of the text, 'etthā,' should be connected. To show that among the five kinds of words—substance, quality, action, class, and name—the word 'Sāḷha' is a name-word, it is said: 'Sāḷho is his name.' `Migāramātuyā` means of Visākhā. For she was named Migāramātā because she was established in the position of a mother by the treasurer Migāra. Showing that `navakammikā` means 'one who supervises new work,' he says `navakammādhiṭṭhāyikā`. By the phrase 'possessed of sagacity,' he shows the meaning of the word `paṇḍitā`: wisdom is called `paṇḍā`, and because it has arisen in her, she is `paṇḍitā`. `Veyyattikena`: a person is `viyatta` because he is especially manifest, becomes evident; `veyyattikaṃ` is what pertains to him, that is, knowledge; `tena` means by that. To show that the wisdom called `medhā` is a special aspect of the wisdom called `paṇḍā`, it is said 'in grasping the Pāli text,' etc. For the wisdom called `medhā` is a special aspect of the wisdom called `paṇḍā` because it is accompanied by mindfulness. `Tatrupāyāyā` is a compound with an unelided vowel, like in `tatramajjhattatā`, etc. By `kammesu`, he shows the referent of the word `tassa`. `Kattabbakammupaparikkhāya` means by investigation into the duties to be done. By the word `ca`, he indicates that the word `katākata` is a dvandva phrase. `Parivesanaṭṭhāne`: a `parivesana` is a place one enters to partake of food; that very place is a `parivesanaṭṭhāna`; `tasmiṃ` means in that. `Nikūṭe`: here, showing a place devoid of a so-called peak (`kūṭa`), he says: 'in a deep place shown made like a corner.' The prefix `vi-` indicates alteration, and `sara` indicates sound; thus he says: 'a distorted sound.' `Caraṇa` is the foot, because one walks (`carati`) with it; she for whom a sickness has arisen in it is `caraṇagilānā`; showing this, he says: 'afflicted with a disease of the foot.'

657. “Tintā”ti iminā avassutasaddo idha kilinnatthe eva vattati, na aññattheti dasseti. Assāti “avassutā”tipadassa. Padabhājane vuttanti sambandho. Tatthāti padabhājane. Vatthaṃ raṅgajātena rattaṃ viya, tathā kāyasaṃsaggarāgena suṭṭhu rattāti yojanā. “Apekkhāya samannāgatā”ti iminā apekkhā etissamatthīti apekkhavatīti atthaṃ dasseti. Paṭibaddhaṃ cittaṃ imissanti paṭibaddhacittāti dassento āha “paṭibandhitvā ṭhapitacittā viyā”ti. Dutiyapadavibhaṅgepīti “avassuto”ti dutiyapadabhājanepi. Puggalasaddassa sattasāmaññavācakattā purisasaddena viseseti. Adhoubbhaiti nipātānaṃ chaṭṭhiyā samasitabbabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ vuttaṃ “akkhakānaṃ adho”tiādi. Nanu yathā idha “akkhakānaṃ adho”ti vuttaṃ, evaṃ padabhājanepi vattabbaṃ, kasmā na vuttanti āha “padabhājane”tiādi. Padapaṭipāṭiyāti “adho”ti ca “akkhaka”nti ca padānaṃ anukkamena. Etthāti adhakkhakaubbhajāṇumaṇḍalesu. Sādhāraṇapārājikehīti bhikkhubhikkhunīnaṃ sādhāraṇehi pārājikehi. Nāmamattanti nāmameva.

657. By `tintā`, he shows that the word `avassuta` is used here only in the sense of 'stained,' not in any other sense. `Assa` means of the word `avassutā`. The connection is: 'as stated in the Padabhājana.' `Tattha` means in the Padabhājana. The connection is: just as a cloth is dyed with a coloring substance, so she is thoroughly dyed with the lust for bodily contact. By 'possessed of expectation,' he shows the meaning: `apekkhavatī` means 'one for whom there is expectation.' Showing that `paṭibaddhacittā` means 'she whose mind is attached,' he says: 'as if her mind were bound and fixed.' Even in the analysis of the second word (`dutiyapadavibhaṅgepi`), that is, in the Padabhājana on `avassuto`. Because the word `puggala` is a general term for a being, he specifies with the word `purisa`. To show that the particles `adho` and `ubbhaṃ` should be compounded in the genitive case, it is said 'below the collarbones,' etc. But just as it is said here 'below the collarbones,' so it should have been said in the Padabhājana. Why was it not said? To answer this, he says: 'in the Padabhājana,' etc. `Padapaṭipāṭiyā` means in the sequence of the words `adho` and `akkhaka`. `Ettha` means in the regions below the collarbones and above the knees. `Sādhāraṇapārājikehi` means by the pārājikas that are common to bhikkhus and bhikkhunīs. `Nāmamattaṃ` means just the name.

659. Evanti imāya pāḷiyā vibhajitvāti sambandho. Tatthāti “ubhatoavassute”tiādivacane. “Ubhatoavassute”ti pāṭho mūlapāṭhoyeva, nāññoti dassentena visesamakatvā “ubhatoavassuteti ubhato avassute”ti vuttaṃ. Ubhatoti ettha [M 0.0143] ubhasarūpañca tosaddassa chaṭṭhyatthe pavattiñca dassetuṃ vuttaṃ “bhikkhuniyā ceva purisassa cā”ti. Tattha bhikkhunīpurisasaddehi ubhasarūpaṃ dasseti. “Yā”ti ca “sa”iti ca dvīhi saddehi topaccayassa chaṭṭhyatthaṃ, ubhinnaṃ avassutabhāve satīti attho. Bhāvapaccayena vinā bhāvattho ñātabboti āha “avassutabhāve”ti. Yathāparicchinnenāti “adhakkhakaṃ, ubbhajāṇumaṇḍala”nti [V 1.0123] yena yena paricchinnena. Attanoti bhikkhuniyā. Tassa vāti purisassa vā. Idhāpīti kāyapaṭibaddhena kāyāmasanepi.

659. The connection is: `evaṃ` means 'having analyzed by means of this Pāli passage.' `Tattha` means in the statement beginning `ubhatoavassute`. Showing that the reading `ubhatoavassute` is the root text itself and not another, without making a distinction, it is said: '`ubhatoavassute` means `ubhato avassute` (lustful on both sides).' `Ubhato`: here, to show both the form of `ubha` and the use of the suffix `-to` in the sense of the genitive, it is said: 'of both the bhikkhunī and the man.' There, by the words `bhikkhunī` and `purisa`, he shows the form of `ubha`. By the two words `yā` and `sa`, he shows the genitive sense of the suffix `-to`; the meaning is: 'when there is a state of lust in both.' He says `avassutabhāve` to show that the abstract sense is to be understood even without an abstract suffix. `Yathāparicchinnena` means by whatever has been demarcated, as in 'below the collarbones, above the knees.' `Attano` means of the bhikkhunī. `Tassa vā` means or of the man. `Idhāpi` means also here, in the case of touching a body-part connected to the body.

Tatrāti tesu bhikkhubhikkhunīsu. Na kāretabbo “kāyasaṃsaggaṃ sādiyeyyā”ti avuttattāti adhippāyo. Acopayamānāpīti acālayamānāpi, pisaddo sambhāvanattho, tena copayamānā pagevāti dasseti. Evaṃ pana satīti citteneva adhivāsayamānāya sati pana. Kiriyasamuṭṭhānatāti imassa sikkhāpadassa kiriyasamuṭṭhānabhāvo. Tabbahulanayenāti “vanacarako (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 2.201; 3.133), saṅgāmāvacaro”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 2.108) viya tassaṃ kiriyāyaṃ bahulato samuṭṭhānanayena. Sāti kiriyasamuṭṭhānatā.

`Tatra` means among those bhikkhus and bhikkhunīs. The intention is that it should not be done, because it is not said 'she should consent to bodily contact.' `Acopayamānāpi` means even if not moving it. The word `pi` has the sense of possibility; by this he shows that if she does move it, it is so all the more. `Evaṃ pana sati` means but when she consents only with the mind. `Kiriyasamuṭṭhānatā` means the state of arising from action of this training rule. `Tabbahulanayena` means by way of arising predominantly from that action, as in 'forest-dweller,' 'one who frequents battlefields,' etc. `Sā` refers to the state of arising from action.

660. Etthāti ubbhakkhakaadhojāṇumaṇḍalesu.
