'Saṇṭhāpetuṃ' means to place well; the meaning is to restore to its natural state. 'Nakhasesaṃ' means: a nail is the only remainder of a severed finger, thus 'nakhaseso'; it refers to that. 'Aṅguṭṭho' (thumb) is what arises at the front, at the tip. By the phrase 'in the same way as explained,' he refers to the statement 'without showing the remaining nail.' 'Kaṇḍaranāmakā' means the great sinews. For since they support the body, they are called 'kaṇḍarā,' with 'dh' becoming 'ḍ.' 'Yesu' means 'in which tendons,' a locative of specification.

Yassa vaggulipakkhakā viya aṅguliyo sambandho honti, ayaṃ phaṇahatthako nāmāti yojanā. Etanti phaṇahatthakaṃ. Chaḷaṅgulādayopi phaṇahatthakeyeva saṅgahetabbāti āha “yassapi cha aṅguliyo”tiādi. Yassapi cha aṅguliyo honti, ayampi phaṇahatthako nāma upacārena.

The construction is: 'One whose fingers are connected together like the wings of a bat is called a `phaṇahatthaka`.' He says that those with six fingers and so on should also be included under `phaṇahatthaka`, with the words: 'Even one who has six fingers,' etc. One who has six fingers is also called a `phaṇahatthaka` by extension.

Khujjoti ettha khujjo sarīro yassatthīti khujjoti vacanatthaṃ dassento āha “khujjasarīro”ti. Kasmā khujjoti āha “urassa vā”tiādi. Yassa pana vaṅkaṃ, ayampi khujjo nāmāti yojanā. Vaṅkanti ca kuṭilaṃ. Hīti saccaṃ, yasmā vā. Brahmujugattoti ujuṃ gattaṃ ujugattaṃ, brahmuno ujugattaṃ viya ujugattaṃ imassa mahāpurisassāti brahmujugatto, mahāpuriso.

Here, regarding `khujjo`, showing the meaning of the word `khujjo` as 'one who has a hunched body,' he says 'a hunchbacked body.' Why is one a `khujjo`? He says, 'of the chest or...' etc. The construction is: 'But one who is bent is also called a `khujjo`.' And `vaṅkaṃ` means crooked. `Hi` means 'truly' or 'because.' 'Straight-limbed like Brahmā' means: a straight body is `ujugattaṃ`; like the straight body of Brahmā is the straight body of this Great Being, thus he is `brahmujugatto`, the Great Being.

Saṃkhepena vuttamatthaṃ vitthārena dassento āha “jaṅghavāmanassa hī”tiādi. Yesanti ubhinnaṃ kāyānaṃ. Bhūtānanti amanussānaṃ pisācakapetānaṃ. Attabhāvo hoti viyāti yojanā. Parivaṭumoti parisamantato vaṭṭulasarīro.

Showing in detail the meaning stated in brief, he says, 'For of the shin-dwarf...' and so on. 'Yesaṃ' refers to both bodies. 'Bhūtānaṃ' means of non-human beings, such as pisācas and petas. The construction is 'attabhāvo hoti viya.' 'Parivaṭumo' means one with a body that is round all over.

Galagaṇḍīti [V 1.0232][M 0.0270] ettha gale gaṇḍo yassatthīti galagaṇḍīti vacanatthaṃ dassento āha “yassā”tiādi. Etanti “galagaṇḍī”ti etaṃ vacanaṃ. Tatthāti galagaṇḍipabbājane. Yanti vacanaṃ.

Here, regarding `galagaṇḍī`, showing the meaning of the word `galagaṇḍī` as 'one who has a goiter on the neck,' he says 'one who has,' etc. 'Etaṃ' refers to this word, 'galagaṇḍī.' 'Tattha' means in the case of the banishment of one with a goiter. 'Yaṃ' refers to the word.

Sipadīti ettha sithilaṃ padaṃ imassāti sipadīti vutte bhārapādoyeva gahetabboti āha “bhārapādo vuccatī”ti. Bhāraṃ pādaṃ yassāti bhārapādo. Ete dve thūlapādarogīsu vattantīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Sañjātapiḷakoti sañjātaphoṭo. Upanāhanti bhusaṃ bandhanaṃ. Udakaāvāṭeti udakena puṇṇāyaṃ kāsuyaṃ. Udakavālikāyāti udakatintena marunā. Yathā sirā paññāyanti, evaṃ milāpetunti yojanā. Īdisanti sirāpaññāyanajaṅghatelanāḷikasabhāvaṃ. Tathāti yathā pabbajjākāle karoti, tathā katvāti attho.

Here, regarding `sipadī`, when it is said 'one with a loose foot,' it should be taken as `bhārapādo` (one with a heavy foot); thus he says, '`bhārapādo` is said.' `Bhārapādo` is one who has a heavy foot. It should be understood that these two terms apply to those with the disease of swollen feet. `Sañjātapiḷako` means a blister has arisen. `Upanāha` means a tight binding. `Udakaāvāṭe` means in a pit filled with water. `Udakavālikāya` means with sand wet with water. The construction is: 'They should make it wither so that the veins become visible.' `Īdisaṃ` means having such a nature, that of the shin-oil-tube for making veins appear. `Tathā` means 'having done so'; the meaning is, as one does at the time of ordination.

Pāparogīti ettha pāparogassa sarūpaṃ dassento āha “arisa”itiādi. Tattha ariso ca bhagandaro ca pittañca semho ca kāso ca soso cāti dvando, te ādayo yesaṃ teti arisa…pe… sosādayo. Ādisaddena heṭṭhā vutte ābādhe saṅgaṇhāti. Tattha pittasemhasaddehi taṃsamuṭṭhāno rogo gahetabbo. “Niccāturo”ti iminā pāparogīti ettha mantutthe pavattassa īpaccayassa niccayogatthaṃ dasseti.

Here, regarding `pāparogī`, showing the nature of a 'bad disease,' he says 'hemorrhoids,' and so on. Therein, 'hemorrhoids and fistula and bile and phlegm and cough and consumption' is a dvanda compound; those of which these are the beginning are 'hemorrhoids... consumption, etc.' By the word `ādi` (etc.), he includes the afflictions mentioned below. Therein, by the words `pitta` (bile) and `semha` (phlegm), the disease arising from them should be understood. With 'constantly ill,' he shows that in `pāparogī`, the suffix `-ī`, which occurs in the sense of 'possessing that,' indicates the meaning of constant connection.

Parisadūsanoti ettha itisaddo nāmapariyāyo, parisadūsano nāmāti hi attho. Yo attano virūpatāya parisaṃ dūseti, ayaṃ parisadūsano nāmāti yojanā. Chasarīradosaṃ ādiṃ katvā parisadūsanabhāvaṃ vitthārento āha “atidīgho vā”tiādi. Atidīgho vāti ettha na kevalaṃ paresaṃ dvaṅgulādimattadīgho, atha kho diguṇādidīghovādhippetoti āha “aññesa”ntiādi. Nābhipadesoti attano nābhipadeso. Yathā hi atidīghe paravacanena atidīghassa sarūpaṃ veditabbaṃ, tathā atirassādīsupi atirassasarūpanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Mahodaroti mahāudaro. Kappasīso vāti hatthisīso [M 0.0271] viya yugasīso vā. Kappasaddo hettha yugatthavācako. Kaṇṇikakeso vāti kaṇṇikasadisehi kesehi samannāgato. “Jātipalitehī”ti iminā jarāvātena pahataṃ palitaṃ nivatteti. Pakatitambakesoti ettha pakatisaddena kenaci payogena tambakesaṃ nivatteti. Āvaṭṭasīsoti punappunaṃ vaṭṭatīti āvaṭṭo, kesāvaṭṭo, so etassa sīse atthīti āvaṭṭasīso. Uddhaggehīti uddhaṃ koṭīhi. Jālabaddhena viyāti jālena baddhena iva.

Regarding `parisadūsano`, here the word `iti` is a synonym for 'name'; for the meaning is 'is called a defiler of an assembly.' The construction is: 'Whoever defiles an assembly by his own deformity is called a defiler of an assembly.' Beginning with the six bodily defects, elaborating on the state of being a defiler of an assembly, he says 'excessively tall or...' and so on. Here, 'excessively tall' is not intended to mean merely taller than others by two finger-breadths and the like, but rather twice as tall and the like; thus he says 'than others,' and so on. `Nābhipadeso` means one's own navel region. For just as in the case of 'excessively tall' the nature of excessive height should be known from the statement about others, so too in the cases of 'excessively short,' etc., the nature of excessive shortness should be understood. `Mahodaro` means one with a large belly. `Kappasīso` means like an elephant's head or like a yoke's head. Here the word `kappa` signifies 'yoke.' `Kaṇṇikakeso` means endowed with hair like a `kaṇṇikā` flower. 'With gray hair from birth' excludes gray hair struck by the wind of old age. Regarding 'with naturally copper-colored hair,' here the word 'naturally' excludes hair that has become copper-colored by some application. `Āvaṭṭasīso` means: a swirl (`āvaṭṭo`) is what turns (`vaṭṭati`) again and again, a swirl of hair; this exists on his head, thus he is `āvaṭṭasīso`. 'With upturned ends' means with ends pointing upward. 'Like bound with a net' means as if bound with a net.

Sambaddhabhamuko vāti aññamaññasambaddhabhamuko vā. Makkaṭabhamukoti makkaṭassa bhamu viya [V 1.0233] bhamu etassāti makkaṭabhamuko. Vāsikoṇenāti tacchanīkoṭiyā. Visamacakkaloti ettha cakkākārena lāti pavattati, cakkākāraṃ vā lāti gaṇhātīti cakkalo. Kekaroti valiro. So hi kucchitaṃ karotīti kekaroti vuccati. Kakkaṭassevāti kakkaṭassa iva. Mūsikakaṇṇoti ākhukaṇṇo. Jaṭukakaṇṇoti vaggulikaṇṇo. Aviddhakaṇṇoti acchiddakaṇṇo. Hīti saccaṃ, yasmā vā. Soti aviddhakaṇṇo. Kaṇṇe bhagandaro etassāti kaṇṇabhagandaro, soyeva kaṇṇabhagandariko. Gaṇḍo kaṇṇe etassāti gaṇḍakaṇṇo. Paggharitapubbenāti paggharitapūyena. Ṭaṅkito kaṇṇo yassāti ṭaṅkitakaṇṇo. Gobhattanāḷikāyāti gunnaṃ bhattapānatthaṃ katāya nāḷikāya. Biḷārakkhi viya atipiṅgalaṃ akkhi etassāti atipiṅgalakkhi. Madhuvaṇṇo viya piṅgalaṃ akkhi etassāti madhupiṅgalakkhi. Nippakhumakkhīti ettha pakhumaṃ vuccati akkhamhi jātaṃ lomaṃ. Tañhi akkhino pakkhadvaye jātattā pakhumanti vuccati. Natthi pakhumaṃ akkhimhi etassāti nippakhumakkhi. Assupaggharaṇaṃ akkhimhā etassāti assupaggharaṇakkhi. Pupphaṃ sañjātaṃ yassa akkhinoti pupphitaṃ. Pupphitaṃ akkhi yassāti pupphitakkhi. Akkhipākenāti akkhino dalapariyantesu paccanakena rogena.

‘One with connected eyebrows’ means one whose eyebrows are connected to each other. ‘Monkey-browed’ means one who has eyebrows like a monkey's. ‘With a carpenter's adze-corner’ means with the edge of a carpenter's adze. Regarding ‘one with uneven eyes’ (`visamacakkalo`), herein `cakkalo` means one who moves in a circle or takes on a circular shape. ‘Squint-eyed’ (`kekaro`) means `valiro`. For since one does a contemptible thing, one is called `kekaro`. ‘Like a crab’s’ means like a crab's. ‘Mouse-eared’ means having the ears of a mouse. ‘Bat-eared’ means having the ears of a bat. ‘Unpierced ear’ means an ear without a hole. `Hi` means ‘truly’ or ‘because.’ ‘He’ refers to the one with an unpierced ear. `Kaṇṇabhagandaro`, ‘one with a fistula in the ear,’ is the same as `kaṇṇabhagandariko`. `Gaṇḍakaṇṇo` means one who has a tumor in the ear. ‘With oozed pus’ means with pus that has oozed. `Ṭaṅkitakaṇṇo` means one whose ear is chiseled. ‘With a cow's feeding trough’ means with a trough made for the food and drink of cattle. `Atipiṅgalakkhi` means one whose eye is extremely tawny like a cat's eye. `Madhupiṅgalakkhi` means one whose eye is tawny like the color of honey. Regarding `nippakhumakkhi`, ‘one with eyelashless eyes,’ herein `pakhuma` is said to be the hair growing on the eye. Since it grows on the two sides of the eye, it is called `pakhuma`. `Nippakhumakkhi` is one who has no eyelashes on the eye. `Assupaggharaṇakkhi` means one from whose eye tears drip. ‘Flowered’ (`pupphitaṃ`) means a film has grown in one's eye. `Pupphitakkhi`, ‘one with a flowered eye,’ is one whose eye has a film. ‘With suppuration of the eye’ means with the disease of suppuration at the edges of the eyelids.

Cipiṭanāsikoti anunnatanāsiko. Sukatuṇḍasadisāyāti suvānaṃ mukhena sadisāya.

`Cipiṭanāsiko` (flat-nosed) means one with a nose that is not prominent. 'Like a parrot's beak' means resembling a parrot's beak.

Paṭaṅgamaṇḍūkassevāti [M 0.0272] paṭaṅganāmakassa maṇḍūkassa mukhanimittaṃ iva mukhanimittaṃyevāti yojanā. Ukkhalimukhavaṭṭisadisehīti ukkhaliyā mukhavaṭṭinā sadisehi. Bhericammasadisehīti bheriyā mukhe nahitacammena sadisehi. Eḷamukhoti eḷāya niccapaggharitaṃ mukhametasseti eḷamukho. Uppakkamukhoti uppakkaṃ kuthikaṃ mukhametassāti uppakkamukho. Saṅkhatuṇḍakoti saṅkhassa tuṇḍena sadiso oṭṭho etassāti saṅkhatuṇḍako.

The construction is: 'Like the appearance of the mouth of a frog named Paṭaṅga.' 'Like the rim of a pot's mouth' means similar to the rim of a pot's mouth. 'Like the skin of a drum' means similar to the skin stretched over the face of a drum. 'Ram-mouthed' is one whose mouth constantly drips like a ram's. 'Festering-mouthed' is one whose mouth is festering and putrid. 'Conch-lipped' is one whose lip is like the spout of a conch shell.

Aṭṭhakadantasadisehīti aṭṭhakanāmakassa naṅgalassa dantehi sadisehi. Dante pidahitunti sambandho. Dantantareti dantavivare, dantamajjhe vā. Kalandakadanto viyāti kāḷakānaṃ danto viya.

'Like the teeth of an Aṭṭhaka plow' means resembling the teeth of a plow named Aṭṭhaka. The connection is with 'to cover the teeth.' 'Between the teeth' means in the gaps between the teeth, or in the middle of the teeth. 'Like the tooth of a squirrel' means like the teeth of crows.

Mahāhanukoti mahanto hanu etassāti mahāhanuko. Cipiṭahanukoti anunnatahanuko. Nimmassudāṭhikoti natthi massu ca dāṭhi ca etassāti nimmassudāṭhiko. Bhaṭṭhaaṃsakūṭoti bhaṭṭho patito aṃsakūṭo imassāti bhaṭṭhaaṃsakūṭo. Godhāgattoti godhāya gattaṃ viya gattaṃ imassāti godhāgatto[V 1.0234]. Sabbaṃpetanti sabbampi etaṃ “kacchugatto”tiādivacanaṃ. Etthāti “kacchugatto”tiādivacane. Vinicchayo veditabboti yojanā.

`Mahāhanuko` means one who has a great jaw. `Cipiṭahanuko` means one with an unprominent jaw. `Nimmassudāṭhiko` means one who has no beard and no tusks. `Bhaṭṭhaaṃsakūṭo` means one whose shoulder-blade has fallen. `Godhāgatto` means one whose body is like that of a lizard. All this refers to the statement beginning with ‘one with a scabby body,’ and the determination should be understood in connection with it.

Bhaṭṭhakaṭikoti bhaṭṭhā pannā kaṭi etassāti bhaṭṭhakaṭiko. Accuggatehi ānisadamaṃsehīti sambandho. Vātaṇḍikoti vātena pūrito aṇḍakoso etassāti vātaṇḍiko. Saṅghaṭṭanajāṇukoti anto natattā aññamaññaṃ saṅghaṭṭanaṃ jāṇu etassāti saṅghaṭṭanajāṇuko. Vikaṭoti tiriyagamanapādo. Upaḍḍhapiṇḍikassa atthaṃ saha bhedena dassento āha “so duvidho”tiādi. Tattha duvidho so upaḍḍhapiṇḍiko samannāgatoti yojanā. Atha vā so upaḍḍhapiṇḍiko heṭṭhā orūḷhāhi mahantīhi jaṅghapiṇḍikāhi samannāgato vā upari ārūḷhāhi mahantīhi jaṅghapiṇḍikāhi samannāgato vāti duvidhoti yojanā. Piṭṭhikapādoti piṭṭhiyaṃ uṭṭhito pādo etassāti piṭṭhikapādo. Gaṇḍikaṅguli vāti gaṇḍena uṭṭhito aṅguli [M 0.0273] etassāti gaṇḍikaṅguli. Sabbopesāti esa sabbopi jano. Parisaṃ dūsetīti parisadūsano.

`Bhaṭṭhakaṭiko`: one whose hips have fallen. The connection is with having excessively high buttock-flesh. `Vātaṇḍiko`: one whose scrotum is filled with wind. `Saṅghaṭṭanajāṇuko`: one whose knees knock together because they are bent inwards. `Vikaṭo`: one whose foot moves sideways. Explaining the meaning of `upaḍḍhapiṇḍika` together with its divisions, it is said: 'It is of two kinds,' etc. Here the construction is that the `upaḍḍhapiṇḍika` is endowed in two ways. Or, the construction is that the `upaḍḍhapiṇḍika` is of two kinds: one endowed with large calf-muscles that have descended below, or one endowed with large calf-muscles that have ascended above. `Piṭṭhikapādo`: one whose foot is raised on the back. `Gaṇḍikaṅguli`: one whose finger is raised with a lump. All these people defile the assembly, thus they are defilers of the assembly.

Pubbādīhītiādisaddena cakkhupasādassa antarāyakarāni aññānipi vatthūni gahetabbāni. Dvīhi vā akkhīhi, ekena vā akkhināti yojanā. Ubhayampīti dvinnaṃ aṭṭhakathācariyānaṃ ubhayampi vacanaṃ. Pāḷiyaṃ “andhaṃ pabbājentī”ti avatvā “kāṇaṃ pabbājentī”ti vuttattā “pariyāyenā”ti vuttaṃ. Mahāaṭṭhakathāyañhi “jaccandho”ti iminā dveakkhikāṇaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Kuṇīti kuṇanaṃ saṃkocanaṃ kuṇaṃ, tametassatthīti kuṇī. Khañjoti khañjati gativekallabhāvena pavattatīti khañjo. Kuṇḍapādakoti ettha kuṇḍoti khañjasseva nāmaṃ. Khañjo hi kuḍati gamanaṃ paṭihanatīti kuṇḍoti vuccati. Kasmā kuṇḍapādako? Kasmā piṭṭhipādamajjhena caṅkamantoti āha “majjhe saṃkuṭitapādattā”ti. Iminā hi kuṇḍapādassa ca piṭṭhipādamajjhena caṅkamanassa ca hetuṃ dasseti. Eseva nayo anantaravākyepi. Sabbopesāti esa sabbopi jano.

By the word 'etc.' in 'by pus, etc.,' other things that obstruct the eye-sensitivity should also be understood. The construction is: 'with two eyes or with one eye.' 'Both' refers to the statements of both commentators. In the Pāḷi text, because it says 'they ordain a one-eyed person' instead of 'they ordain a blind person,' the term 'by implication' is used. In the Great Commentary, 'one blind from birth' is said with reference to one who is blind in both eyes. Kuṇī: kuṇa is contraction; one who has this is a kuṇī. Khañjo: one who limps, proceeding with an impaired gait. Kuṇḍapādako: here 'kuṇḍa' is another name for 'khañja' (lame), for a lame person obstructs his gait and is thus called 'kuṇḍa.' Why is he a kuṇḍapādaka? Why does he walk on the middle of the back of his foot? It is said: 'Because his foot is contracted in the middle.' This explains the reason for being a kuṇḍapādaka and for walking on the middle of the back of his foot. This same principle applies to the subsequent sentence. Sabbopesā: this means all these people.

Pakkhahatoti ettha eko pakkho hato vināso etassāti pakkhahatoti atthaṃ dassento āha “eko hattho vā”tiādi. “Pakkhapāto”tipi pāṭho, so apāṭhoyeva. Pakkhasaddo hi koṭṭhāsavācako, na paṅgulapariyāyo, pīṭhasabbī vuccatīti pīṭhena sabbati gacchati sīlenāti pīṭhasabbī vuccati. “Jiṇṇabhāvena dubbalo”ti iminā jīraṇaṃ jarā, tāya dubbalo jarādubbaloti vacanatthaṃ dasseti. Balavā hotīti āgantukarogānamabhāvena balavā hoti, “vacībhedo nappavattatī”ti iminā mukhamattameva gacchati pavattati, na vacībhedo ettha janeti [V 1.0235] mūgoti dasseti. Yassa vacībhedo na pavattati, ayaṃ mūgo nāmāti yojanā. Mammananti khalitavacanaṃ. Yo ekameva akkharaṃ catupañcakkhattuṃ vadati, tassetamadhivacanaṃ.

Pakkhahato: here, to show the meaning of pakkhahata as 'one whose side is struck or destroyed,' the text says: 'one hand or,' etc. There is also the reading 'pakkhapāta,' but that is not the correct reading. For the word 'pakkha' denotes a part; it is not a synonym for 'lame.' One is called a pīṭhasabbī because one goes by means of a chair by nature. By 'weak due to being worn out,' the meaning of the word jarādubbalo is shown: aging is old age, and one is weak because of that. 'He is strong' means he is strong due to the absence of adventitious diseases. By 'articulation of speech does not occur,' it is shown that only the mouth moves and functions but does not produce articulated speech; thus he is mute. The construction is: one whose articulation of speech does not occur is called mute. Mammana is stammering speech. This is the designation for one who repeats a single syllable four or five times.

Badhīroti sutihīno. So hi hananaṃ sotapasādassa nāsanaṃ vadho, taṃ īrati gacchatīti badhīroti vuccati. Yo sabbena sabbaṃ na suṇāti, ayaṃ badhīro nāmāti yojanā. Iminā naṭṭhapasādataṃ dasseti[M 0.0274]. Ubhayadosavasenāti upalakkhaṇavasena vuttaṃ andhamūgabadhirapabbājane tidosavasenapi vuttattā. Teti hatthacchinnādayo dvattiṃsajane. Osāraṇaṃ apatto puggalo atthi, taṃ puggalaṃ saṅgho osāreti ceti yojanā. Osāretīti saṅghe paveseti.

Badhiro: one who is devoid of hearing. He is called badhira because he goes (īrati) to vadha, that is, the striking and destruction of the ear-sensitivity. The construction is: whoever does not hear at all is called deaf. This shows the destruction of the faculty. 'By reason of both faults' is said by way of indication, for in the matter of ordaining the blind, mute, and deaf, it is also stated to be 'by reason of three faults.' 'They' refers to the thirty-two kinds of persons, such as those with severed hands. The construction is: there is a person who has not attained rehabilitation, and the Saṅgha rehabilitates that person. 'Rehabilitates' means it allows him to enter the Saṅgha.

58. Alajjīnissayavatthukathā

58. The Discussion on the Matter of Dependence on a Shameless Person

120. “Alajjīnaṃ ovāda”nti pāṭhasesena yojite sāmyatthe sāmivacanampi yujjateva. Taṃ nayaṃ adassetvā “upayogatthe sāmivacana”nti vuttaṃ. “Bhikkhūhi sabhāgata”nti iminā bhikkhūhi samāno sīlādiguṇasaṅkhāto bhāgo imassāti bhikkhusabhāgo, tassa bhāvo bhikkhusabhāgatanti vacanatthaṃ dasseti. “Lajjibhāva”nti iminā bhāvapaccayassa sarūpaṃ dasseti. Navaṭṭhānanti abhinavaṭṭhānaṃ. Gatena bhikkhunāti sambandho.

120. When the phrase 'advice to the shameless' is connected with the remainder of the text, in the sense of ownership the genitive case is indeed appropriate. Without showing that method, it was said: 'The genitive case is in the sense of relation.' By 'association with bhikkhus,' it shows the meaning of the word thus: `bhikkhusabhāgo` is one who has a share, consisting of such qualities as virtue, in common with the bhikkhus; the state of that is `bhikkhusabhāgatā`. By 'the state of being scrupulous,' it shows the nature of the abstract suffix `-bhāva`. `Navaṭṭhāna` means a new situation. The connection is with 'by the bhikkhu who has gone.'

Theroti nissayadāyako thero. Gahetukāmoti nissayaṃ gahetukāmo. Ācāranti nissayapaṭipannassa ācāraṃ. Tadahevāti tasmiṃ gataahani eva. Ābhogassa katattā, aruṇuggamanassa ca ajānanattā vuttaṃ “anāpattī”ti. Aruṇuggamanaṃ ajānantopi ābhogassa akatattā vuttaṃ “aruṇuggamane dukkaṭa”nti. “Dve tīṇi divasānī”ti padena catu pañca cha divasānipi gahetabbāni lakkhaṇahāranayena anissitena vasitabbabhāvena samānaphalattā. Tenāha “sattāhaṃ vasissāmī”ti. Laddhaparihāroti laddho parihāro āpattiapanayanaṃ yenāti laddhaparihāro.

`Thera` means the elder who gives dependence. `Desiring to take` means desiring to take dependence. `Conduct` means the conduct of one who has undertaken dependence. `On that very day` means on that very day that he went. Because attention was made and because of not knowing the sunrise, it is said, 'no offense.' Although not knowing the sunrise, because attention was not made, it is said, 'an offense of wrong-doing at sunrise.' By the phrase 'two or three days,' four, five, and six days should also be understood by the method of inference from a characteristic, because the result—the state of having to dwell without dependence—is the same. Therefore it is said, 'I will dwell for seven days.' `One who has obtained exemption` means: he by whom the exemption, the removal of an offense, has been obtained is one who has obtained exemption.

59. Gamikādinissayavatthukathā

59. The Discussion on the Matter of Dependence for Travelers, etc.

121. “Karaṇīyanissayo”ti iminā nissayagahaṇaṃ nissayo uttarapadalopavasena, so karaṇīyo imassāti nissayakaraṇīyoti [M 0.0275] visesanaparanipātabhāvaṃ dasseti. Nissayaṃ alabhamānenāti ettha kiṃ nissayassa alabhanaṃ nāmāti āha “attanā”tiādi. Vutthapubbanti [V 1.0236] vasitapubbaṃ. Ekarattaṃ vasantenāpīti pisaddo dvirattādike kā nāma kathāti dasseti. Vissamanto vā satthaṃ pariyesanto vā hutvāti yojanā. Nāvāya gacchantassāti nāvāya addhānamaggaṃ paṭipannassa.

121. By `karaṇīyanissayo`, it is shown that `nissayo` stands for 'the taking of dependence' by way of elision of the final member of the compound, and that there is post-position of the adjective, as in `nissayakaraṇīyo`, meaning 'one for whom dependence is to be taken.' Regarding 'by one not obtaining dependence,' what is this 'not obtaining dependence'? It is said, 'by oneself,' etc. `Having dwelt before` means having resided before. Regarding 'even by one dwelling for one night,' the particle `pi` shows: 'what need is there to speak of two nights or more?' The connection is: 'being one who is resting or one who is searching for a teacher.' `Of one going by boat` means of one who has set out on a long journey by boat.

Yāciyamānenāti ettha bahukattupasaṅgattā vuttaṃ “tena gilānenā”ti. “Mānenā”ti iminā yācitumasakkuṇeyyatādīni nivatteti.

Regarding 'by one being requested,' because many agents are implied, it is specified 'by that sick person.' By 'through pride,' this excludes such things as the inability to ask.

Phāsu hotīti ettha āvāsasappāyādivasena phāsu hotīti āsaṅkā bhaveyyāti āha “samathavipassanānaṃ paṭilābhavasenā”ti. Hīti saccaṃ. Imaṃ parihāranti imaṃ phāsuvihāraparihāraṃ. Thāmagatāya vipassanāyāti yojanā. Samatho vā taruṇo hotīti yojanā. Etassevāti taruṇasamathavipassanikasseva bhikkhuno. Tassa nissāyāti ettha tassa ovādaṃ nissāyāti yojanā. Atha vā upayogatthe sāmivacanaṃ. Taṃ nissayadāyakaṃ nissāyāti hi attho. Yattako kālo āsaḷhīpuṇṇamā atthi, tattakaṃ kālanti yojanā. “Āsaḷhīpuṇṇamā”ti ettha “yāvā”ti nipātapayogattā abhividhiavajhatthe nissakkavacanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yatthāti yasmiṃ ṭhāne.

Regarding 'it is comfortable,' lest the doubt should arise that it is comfortable by way of suitable lodgings and so on, it is said, 'by way of attaining serenity and insight.' `Hi` means indeed. `This exemption` means this exemption for a comfortable abiding. The connection is with 'with insight that has gained strength.' The connection is with 'or serenity is tender.' `Of this very one` means of that very bhikkhu with tender serenity and insight. Regarding 'depending on him,' the connection is 'depending on his instruction.' Or, the genitive is in the sense of relation, for the meaning is 'depending on that giver of dependence.' The construction is: 'for as long a time as there is until the Āsaḷhī full moon, for that long a time.' Here, in 'the Āsaḷhī full moon,' because of the use of the particle `yāva`, the accusative case should be understood in the sense of an inclusive limit. `Where` means in which place.

122. Pāḷiyaṃ gottenapīti ettha pisaddena na kevalaṃ nāmeneva, atha kho gottenapi sāvetunti dasseti. Tasmā “āyasmato pippalissā”ti nāmaṃ sāvetvātipi “āyasmato mahākassapassā”ti gottaṃ sāvetvāpi anusāvetabbaṃ. Tena vuttaṃ “mahākassapassā”tiādi. Iminā “konāmo te upajjhāyo? Upajjhāyo me bhante āyasmā mahākassapo nāmā”tiādīsu gottampi nāmeneva saṅgahitanti siddhaṃ hoti.

122. In the Pāḷi, regarding `gottenapi`, the particle `pi` shows that one should announce not only the name but also the clan name. Therefore, having announced the name, for instance, 'of the Venerable Pippali,' one should also make the formal announcement by announcing the clan name, for instance, 'of the Venerable Mahākassapa.' For this reason it is said, 'of Mahākassapa,' etc. By this it is established that in such phrases as, 'What is your preceptor's name? Venerable sir, my preceptor is the Venerable Mahākassapa by name,' the clan name is also included under the term 'name'.

123. Ekānusāvaneti [M 0.0276] padassa samānādhikaraṇabāhiratthasamāsabhāvaṃ nivattento āha “ekato anusāvane”ti. Tattha ekatoti ekakkhaṇe, ekapahārena vā. Vakkhati hi “ekakkhaṇe”ti ca “ekapahārenevā”ti ca. Iminā ekato anusāvanametesanti ekānusāvanāti asamānādhikaraṇabāhiratthasamāsaṃ dasseti. Ekenāti ekena anusāvanācariyena. Ekassāti ekassa upasampadāpekkhassa. “Ekakkhaṇe”ti iminā “ekato”ti padassa atthaṃ dasseti. “Upasampādetu”nti dvinnaṃ upasampadāpekkhānaṃ upasampādetuṃ.

123. Regarding the word `ekānusāvane`, rejecting the analysis of it as a `bahubbīhi` compound with members in apposition, it is said to mean 'in a single announcement.' Therein, `ekato` means at one moment, or with one stroke. For it will be said both 'at one moment' and 'with one stroke indeed.' By this, it is shown to be a `bahubbīhi` compound with members not in apposition, dissolved as `ekato anusāvanam etesan'ti ekānusāvanā` (those for whom the announcement is single). `Ekena` means by one announcing teacher. `Ekassa` means of one candidate for higher ordination. By 'at one moment,' the meaning of the word `ekato` is shown. `To ordain` means to ordain two candidates.

Purimanayenevāti “ekena ekassa, aññena itarassā”tiādinā pubbe vuttanayeneva. Ekato [V 1.0237] anusāvane kātunti “ekena ekassa, aññena aññassa, itarena itarassā”ti evaṃ tīhi ācariyehi tiṇṇaṃ upasampadāpekkhānaṃ ekakkhaṇe anusāvane kātuṃ. Tañca khoti ettha tasaddassa “anusāvane kātu”nti padasseva atthavisayataṃ dassetuṃ vuttaṃ “anusāvanakiriya”nti. Dve vā tayo vāti ettha vāsaddo aniyamavikappattho. Sace ekenācariyena dve anusāveti, “ayaṃ buddharakkhito ca ayaṃ dhammarakkhito cā”ti anusāvetabbā. Sace tayo anusāveti, “ayaṃ buddharakkhito ca ayaṃ dhammarakkhito ca ayaṃ saṅgharakkhito cā”ti anusāvetabbā. Yathā ekenācariyena dve vā tayo vā ekato anusāvetabbā, evaṃ dvīhi vā tīhi vā ācariyehi eko anusāvetabbotipi vadanti. Ekena upajjhāyena karaṇabhūtena, eko upajjhāyo hutvāti vā attho. “Ekapahārenevā”ti iminā “ekato”ti padassa atthaṃ dasseti. Dve tisso kammavācāti dvīhi ācariyehi dve, tīhi ācariyehi tisso kammavācā. Ekena upajjhāyena anusāvane eko vā dve vā tayo vā ācariyā vaṭṭanti, nānupajjhāyena anusāvane pana nānācariyā eva vaṭṭantīti dassento āha “sace panā”tiādi. Tissattheroti kammavācācariyabhūto tissatthero[M 0.0277]. Sumanattherassāti upajjhāyabhūtassa sumanattherassa. Idanti nānupajjhāyena ekassācariyassānusāvanaṃ. Esa paṭikkhepoti “na tveva nānupajjhāyenā”ti eso paṭikkhepo.

`In the same way as before` means in the same way as stated before with 'by one for one, by another for the other,' etc. `To make the announcement together` means for three teachers to make the announcement at one moment for three candidates for higher ordination, thus: 'by one for one, by another for another, by the other for the other.' And regarding `tañca kho`, the word `ta` is stated to show that the phrase `anusāvane kātuṃ` is its object of meaning, that is, 'the act of announcing.' Regarding `dve vā tayo vā`, the word `vā` has the sense of an unrestricted alternative. If one teacher announces for two, they should be announced as, 'This is Buddharakkhita and this is Dhammarakkhita.' If he announces for three, they should be announced as, 'This is Buddharakkhita and this is Dhammarakkhita and this is Saṅgharakkhita.' Just as two or three may be announced for together by one teacher, so too, they say, one may be announced for by two or three teachers. `By one preceptor` means by one acting as preceptor, or the meaning is 'being one preceptor.' By `ekapahāreneva`, he shows the meaning of the word `ekato`. `Two or three formal acts` means two formal acts by two teachers, three formal acts by three teachers. He says 'but if...' etc., to show that when the announcement is by one preceptor, one, two, or three teachers are allowable, but when the announcement is by different preceptors, then only different teachers are allowable. `The elder Tissa` means the elder Tissa who is the teacher for the formal act. `Of the elder Sumana` means of the elder Sumana who is the preceptor. `This` means the announcement by one teacher when there are different preceptors. `This is the rejection` means the rejection 'but not with different preceptors.'

63. Upasampadāvidhikathā

63. The Discourse on the Procedure for Higher Ordination

126. Taṃ upajjhanti taṃ upajjhāyaṃ. “Upajjhā”ti ca “upajjhāyo”ti ca hi atthato ekaṃ, byañjanameva nānaṃ yathā “sabhā sabhāya”nti. Ettha upajjhāsaddo rājādigaṇo (rupasiddhi 599 sutte; saddanīti 1140 sutte), upajjhāyasaddo purisādigaṇo. Sabhāsaddo itthiliṅgo, sabhāyasaddo pulliṅgo vā napuṃsakaliṅgo vā. “Vitthāyantī”ti saddo nāmadhātūti āha “vitthaddhagattā hontī”ti. Vitthasaddo hi dabbavācakattā nāmasaddo, vikārena thaddho gatto etesanti vitthā, ddhakārassa lopaṃ katvā, tato āyapaccayo hoti. Yanti yaṃ antarāyajātaṃ. Tava sarīreti tuyhaṃ kāye. “Nibbatta”nti iminā “jāta”nti ettha janadhātuyā jananatthaṃ dasseti, “vijjamāna”nti iminā janīdhātuyā pātubhāvatthaṃ dasseti. Santanti saṃvijjamānaṃ. Itiādi kathetabbanti yojanā.

126. They take him as preceptor; that is, the preceptor. For 'upajjhā' and 'upajjhāyo' are one in meaning, differing only in form, just like 'sabhā' and 'sabhāya.' Here, the word 'upajjhā' belongs to the rājādi group, while 'upajjhāya' belongs to the purisādi group. The word 'sabhā' is feminine, and 'sabhāya' is either masculine or neuter. The word 'vitthāyanti,' he says, is a denominative verb meaning 'they become stiff-bodied.' For the word 'vittha' is a noun because it denotes a substance; by modification, 'those whose bodies are stiff' becomes 'vitthā' by eliding the 'ddha' and then adding the suffix '-āya.' 'Yanti' means whatever obstacle arises. 'Tava sarīre' means 'in your body.' By 'nibbattaṃ,' it indicates the meaning of generation from the root 'jan' in the sense of 'born'; by 'vijjamānaṃ,' it indicates the meaning of appearance from the root 'janī.' 'Santanti' means 'existing.' The connection is that it should be stated thus, etc.

64. Cattāronissayādikathā

64. The Discourse on the Four Requisites, etc.

128. Upasampannasamanantaramevāti [V 1.0238] upasampanno hutvā samanantarameva, na kālantareti attho. Ekaporisāti ettha porisasaddo upari vitthate bhujapamāṇe ca posapamāṇe ca vattati. Purisassa pamāṇā porisā, pamāṇatthe ṇapaccayo. Chāyāti ātapābhāvo. Metabbāti pametabbā. “Vassāno”tiādi “utupamāṇaṃ ācikkhitabba”nti ettha ācikkhaṇākāradassanaṃ. Utuno pamāṇanti atthaṃ nivārento āha “ettha cā”tiādi. Arati punappunaṃ gacchatīti utu[M 0.0278], pamiyati saṃvaccharo paricchijjiyati anenāti pamāṇaṃ. Yattakehi divasehi aparipuṇṇoti sambandho. Yassāti divasabhāgassa. Yo utu aparipuṇṇo, tassa utunoti pāṭhaseso yojetabbo. “Utupamāṇaṃ ācikkhitabbaṃ, divasabhāgo ācikkhitabbo”ti padānaṃ aparampi atthavikappaṃ dassento āha “atha vā”tiādi. Tattha ayaṃ nāma utūti ayaṃ utu vassāno nāmāti vā hemanto nāmāti vā gimho nāmāti vā. Pubbanhoti ahassa pubbo pubbanho. Tattha pacchimanayova pāsaṃsataro. Kasmā? Purimanaye utuparipuṇṇe divasabhāgācikkhaṇassa abhāvā, pacchimanaye pana paripuṇṇaṃ vā aparipuṇṇaṃ vā utupamāṇaṃ ācikkhitabbaṃ. Upasampannadivasabhāgova “pubbanho”ti vā “sāyanho”ti vā ācikkhitabbo. Saṃgītīti ettha saṃ ekato katvā gāyitabbā kathetabbāti saṃgītīti vacanatthaṃ dassento āha “idameva sabbaṃ ekato katvā”tiādi. Tattha kinti kiṃ utuṃ. Idaṃ nāmāti idaṃ nāma utuṃ. Vadeyyāsīti āgantukānaṃ vuḍḍhanavakabhāvādiñāpanatthaṃ katheyyāsi.

128. 'Immediately after higher ordination' means right after having been given higher ordination, without any interval. 'One porisa': here the word 'porisa' applies both to a man's height and to the height of a man with arms stretched upwards. A 'porisa' is the measure of a man; the suffix '-ṇa' is in the sense of measure. 'Shade' is the absence of the sun's heat. 'To be measured' means it should be measured. Regarding 'the rainy season,' etc., in the phrase 'the measure of the season should be declared,' the manner of declaration is shown. Refuting the meaning 'the measure of the season,' he says, 'here also,' etc. 'Utu' is so called because it goes and comes again and again; 'pamāṇa' is that by which the year is measured and divided. The connection is: 'by how many days is it incomplete?' 'Of which' refers to the portion of the day. The remainder of the text should be supplied as: 'of that season which is incomplete.' Showing another alternative meaning for the phrases 'the measure of the season should be declared' and 'the portion of the day should be declared,' he says: 'or else,' etc. Therein, 'this is the season named so-and-so' means this season is called the rainy season, or the cool season, or the hot season. 'Forenoon' is the first part of the day. Therein, the latter method is more commendable. Why? Because in the former method, when the season is complete, there is no declaration of the portion of the day, but in the latter method, the measure of the season should be declared whether it is complete or incomplete. The portion of the day of the higher ordination should be declared as 'forenoon' or 'afternoon.' 'Recitation' (saṃgīti): here, showing the etymological meaning that it should be chanted or spoken having been brought together, he says, 'all this together,' etc. Therein, 'what' means 'which season.' 'This is called' means 'this season is called.' 'You should speak' means you should speak in order to inform newcomers about the status of seniority and juniority, etc.

129. Dutiyanti sahāyaṃ bhikkhuṃ vā sāmaṇeraṃ vā purisaṃ vā. Akaraṇīyānīti upasampannehi akattabbāni. Paṇḍupalāsoti ettha paṇḍūti setapītamisso vaṇṇo, palāsasaddo paṇṇavācako, na haritavācako, nāpi kiṃsukadumavācakoti dassento āha “paṇḍuvaṇṇo paṇṇo”ti. Paṇḍupalāsoti samāsopi byāsopi yuttoyeva. Samāsakāle paṇḍu yassatthīti paṇḍu, soyeva palāso paṇḍupalāsoti kātabbo. Pupphaphalādiṃ bandhatīti bandhananti vacanatthena bandhanasaddo vaṇṭapariyāyoti āha “vaṇṭato”ti. Puthusilāti (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 3.60) ettha puthusaddo mahantapariyāyoti āha “mahāsilā”ti.

129. 'A second' means a companion, whether a bhikkhu, a novice, or a layman. 'Things not to be done' means things that should not be done by those who have received higher ordination. 'A pale leaf': here 'pale' (paṇḍu) is a color mixed with white and yellow. The word 'leaf' (palāsa) denotes a leaf, not a green one, nor the kiṃsuka tree—thus he says, 'a pale-colored leaf.' The term 'paṇḍupalāso' is suitable both as a compound and uncompounded. When compounded, it should be formed as: paṇḍu is that which has paleness; that very leaf is a paṇḍupalāso. Because it binds flowers, fruits, etc., it is a 'binding' (bandhana); by this verbal meaning, the word 'bandhana' is a synonym for 'stalk'—thus he says, 'from the stalk.' 'A broad stone': here the word 'broad' (puthu) is a synonym for 'great'—thus he says, 'a great stone'.

130. Tassāti [M 0.0279] ukkhepanīyakammārahassa bhikkhuno. Sāmaggīti saṅghasāmaggī. Tenāti ukkhepanīyakammārahena bhikkhunā. Sambhogeti āmisena ca dhammena ca sambhogahetu. Ettha sahaseyyāpi [V 1.0239] saṅgahitā āpattibhāvato. Anāpattīti anukkhittakabhāvato pācittiyāpattiyā anāpatti, alajjilakkhaṇābhāvato dukkaṭena anāpattīti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

130. 'Of him' means of a bhikkhu liable to an act of suspension (ukkhepanīyakamma). 'Concord' means the concord of the Saṅgha. 'By him' means by a bhikkhu liable to an act of suspension. 'Communion' means on account of communion in regard to both material things and the Dhamma. Here, lying down together is also included because it is an offense. 'No offense': it should be understood that there is no offense of expiation (pācittiya) because he has not been suspended, and no offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) because the characteristic of shamelessness is absent.

Iti samantapāsādikāya vinayasaṃvaṇṇanāya

Thus, in the Samantapāsādikā, the commentary on the Vinaya,

Dvāsattatiadhikavatthusatapaṭimaṇḍitassa mahākhandhakassa

of the Great Chapter, adorned with one hundred and seventy-two topics,

Atthavaṇṇanāya yojanā samattā.

the sub-commentary on the explanation of the meaning is completed.

2. Uposathakkhandhakaṃ

2. The Chapter on the Uposatha

68. Sannipātānujānanādikathā

68. Discussion on Gatherings, Approval, and so on

132. Uposathakkhandhake taranti otaranti etthāti titthaṃ, udakatitthaṃ, titthaṃ viyāti titthaṃ, laddhīti āha “titthaṃ vuccati laddhī”ti. Laddhi hi bahūnaṃ laddhikānaṃ otaraṇaṭṭhānattā titthaṃ nāma. Aññanti sāsanikaladdhito aññaṃ. Etesanti paribbājakānaṃ. Itoti imasmā sāsanikaladdhito. Yanti yaṃ dhammajātaṃ. Tesanti aññatitthiyānaṃ paribbājakānaṃ. Te labhantīti ettha tasaddo manussavisayoti āha “te manussā”ti. Mūgasūkarāti ettha thūlasarīrassa sūkarassa saddamattassāpi abhāvato mūgasūkaro nāmāti āha “thūlasarīrasūkarā”ti.

132. In the Chapter on the Uposatha, a `tittha` is a place where one crosses over or descends, a water-ford; like a ford is a `tittha`. He said 'a doctrine' with the words 'a `tittha` is called a doctrine.' For a doctrine is called a ford because it is a place of descent for many adherents of doctrines. `Aññaṃ` means other than the doctrine of the Dispensation. `Etesaṃ` means 'of these wanderers.' `Ito` means 'from this doctrine of the Dispensation.' `Yaṃ` means 'whatever kind of dhamma.' `Tesaṃ` means 'of those wanderers of other sects.' In 'they obtain' (`te labhanti`), the word `te` refers to human beings; thus he said, 'those humans.' Regarding `mūgasūkara`, since there is not even the sound of a large-bodied boar, it is called a 'dumb boar'; thus he said, 'large-bodied boars'.

135. Assāti bhikkhuno. Soti sampajānamusāvādo. Kinti kiṃ āpatti. Dukkaṭanti padassa dukkaṭaṃ kammanti āsaṅkā bhaveyyāti āha “dukkaṭāpattī”ti. Sā ca kho dukkaṭāpatti musāvādalakkhaṇena na hotīti yojanā. Kena hotīti āha “bhagavato pana vacanenā”ti. Vacanenāti ca “sampajānamusāvāde kiṃ hoti? Dukkaṭaṃ [M 0.0280] hotī”ti (mahāva. 135) vacanena. Akiriyasamuṭṭhānāti āvi kattabbāya āpattiyā akaraṇena akiriyasamuṭṭhānā.

135. `Assa` means 'of the bhikkhu.' `So` means 'a conscious lie.' `Kin ti` means 'what offense?' `Dukkaṭan ti`. Lest one should suspect that this word means 'a wrongly done deed,' he says 'an offense of wrong-doing.' And that offense of wrong-doing does not have the characteristic of a lie; this is the construction. By what does it come to be? He says: 'But by the Blessed One's word.' And 'by the word' means by the statement: 'What is there for a conscious lie? There is an offense of wrong-doing' (Mv I.135). `Akiriyasamuṭṭhānā` means arising from non-action, because it arises from the non-performance of an offense that should be confessed.

Manujenāti manussena. Vācāti vācāya. Yakārassa hi lopo. Giranti saddaṃ. Pareti aññe [V 1.0240] puggale. Vācasikanti vācāto samuṭṭhitaṃ. Ayaṃ panettha yojanā – bhikkhu kenaci āsanne ṭhitena manujena vācāya anālapanto hoti, pare dūre ṭhite puggale sandhāya giraṃ mahāsaddaṃ no ca bhaṇeyya, evampi vācasikameva āpajjeyyāti.

`Manujena` means 'by a human being.' `Vācā` means 'by speech,' for the letter 'y' is elided. `Giraṃ` means 'a sound.' `Pare` means 'other persons.' `Vācasikaṃ` means 'arisen from speech.' This is the construction here: if a bhikkhu, while not speaking with some human being standing nearby, should, with reference to other persons standing far away, utter a loud sound, in this way too he would incur a verbal offense.

Antarāyikoti ettha karotyatthe ṇikapaccayoti āha “antarāyakaro”ti. “Kimatthāyā”ti iminā kissāti ettha tadatthe catutthīti dasseti, hetvatthopi yujjateva. Sabbatthāti sabbesu “dutiyassa jhānassa adhigamāyā”tiādīsu. Itītiādi nigamanaṃ. Uddesato cāti “suṇātu me bhante saṅgho”tiādiuddesato ca. Niddesato cāti “pātimokkhanti ādimeta”ntiādiniddesato ca.

Here, regarding `antarāyiko`, he says 'one who creates an obstruction' (`antarāyakaro`) because the suffix `ṇika` has the sense of 'one who does.' By 'For what purpose?' (`kimatthāya`), he shows that here in `kissa` the dative is used in the sense of purpose, but the sense of cause is also suitable. `Sabbattha` means in all cases such as 'for the attainment of the second jhāna,' etc. `Iti`, etc., is the conclusion. `Uddesato ca` means 'and from the recitation,' such as the recitation 'Bhante, let the Saṅgha listen to me,' etc. `Niddesato ca` means 'and from the exposition,' such as the exposition 'The Pātimokkha is the beginning of this,' etc.

136. Devasikanti ettha ṇikapaccayo vicchatthe hotīti āha “divase divase”ti. Tatiye ca sattame ca pakkheti ekassa utuno aṭṭhasu pakkhesu tatiye ca sattame ca pakkhe. “Vacanato”ti padaṃ “vaṭṭatī”ti pade ñāpakahetu. Tathārūpe paccayeti tathārūpe vikaticārittasaṅkhāte paccaye. Anuvattitabbanti anumatiṃ vattitabbaṃ. Vacanatopīti pisaddo pubbe ñāpakahetuṃ sampiṇḍeti. Etanti “yasmiṃ tasmiṃ cātuddase vā pannarase vā uddisituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vacanaṃ.

136. Here, regarding `devasikaṃ`, he says 'day by day' (`divase divase`) because the suffix `ṇika` is in the sense of repetition. 'In the third and seventh fortnights' means in the third and seventh fortnights among the eight fortnights of one season. The word `vacanato` is an indicative cause for the word `vaṭṭati`. `Tathārūpe paccaye` means in such a condition reckoned as a deviation in conduct. `Anuvattitabbaṃ` means consent should be given. `Vacanatopīti`: the particle `pi` summarizes the preceding indicative cause. `Etaṃ` means the statement: 'it is allowable to recite on any fourteenth or fifteenth day'.

71. Sīmānujānanakathā

71. The Discussion on Authorizing a Boundary

138. Nimittā kittetabbāti nimittāni kittetabbāni. Nikārassa hi ākāro. Nimittaṃ katoti eso pabbato nimittaṃ katoti yojanā. Eseva nayo paratopi. “Eseva nayo”ti iminā “puratthimāya disāya kiṃ nimittaṃ? Pāsāṇo bhante, eso pāsāṇo nimitta”nti atthaṃ atidisati. Eseva nayo sesesupi. Kevalaṃ [M 0.0281] pana vanaudakesu “etaṃ vanaṃ, etaṃ udaka”nti vattabbaṃ. Nadiyaṃ “esā nadī”ti vattabbā. Ettha panāti etissaṃ uttarāyaṃ anudisāyaṃ pana. Hīti phalajotako. Tatthāti “nimittā kittetabbā”ti vacane. Sīmamaṇḍalanti sīmabimbaṃ. Sambandhantenāti purimanimittena pacchimanimittaṃ sambandhantena. Iminā ekantarikādivasena nimittakittanaṃ na vaṭṭati nimittenapi nimittānaṃ sambandhābhāvatoti dasseti. Purimanimittena pacchimanimittassa sambandhe sati ajja ekaṃ nimittaṃ kittetvā sve ekaṃ nimittaṃ kittetvāti evaṃ kālantarepi nimittaṃ kittetvā sammanituṃ vaṭṭatīti vadanti.

138. `Nimittā kittetabbā` means 'signs are to be announced'; for `ā` is the form instead of `ni`. `Nimittaṃ kato`: the construction is 'this mountain is made a sign.' The same method applies further on as well. By 'the same method,' he extends the meaning thus: 'What is the sign in the eastern direction?' 'A rock, bhante. This rock is the sign.' The same method applies to the remaining cases. But in the case of a forest or water, one should say, 'This is the forest,' 'This is the water.' For a river, one should say, 'This is the river.' `Ettha pana` means 'but here, in this northern intermediate direction.' `Hī` indicates the result. `Tattha` means in the statement 'signs are to be announced.' `Sīmamaṇḍalaṃ` means the boundary circle. `Sambandhantena` means connecting the subsequent sign with the preceding sign. By this he shows that announcing the signs intermittently, etc., is not allowable because there is no connection of the signs even by means of a sign. When there is a connection of the subsequent sign with the preceding sign, some say that it is allowable to agree upon it after having announced the signs at different times, for instance, announcing one sign today and one sign tomorrow.

Pabbatoti [V 1.0241] ettha pabbaṃ vuccati phaḷu, taṃ etasmiṃ atthīti pabbato. Vālikarāsissa suddhapaṃsupabbatapasaṅgattā vuttaṃ “vālikarāsi pana na vaṭṭatī”ti. Itaropīti vālikarāsito aññopi tividho pabbato. Hatthippamāṇatoti aḍḍhaṭṭhamaratanahatthipamāṇato. Catūsu disāsūti vihārassa catūsu disāsu. Catūhi vā tīhi vāti ettha vāsaddena tato adhikānipi gahetabbāni. Ekena vā nimittenāti yojanā. Itoti pabbatanimittato. Tasmāti yasmā ekena nimittena na vaṭṭati, tasmā. Tanti pabbataṃ. Tasmāti ekasseva nimittassa kittitattā. Yo pabbato atthi, taṃ pabbatanti yojanā. Antoti pabbatassa anto.

Here, regarding `pabbato`: a joint (`pabbaṃ`) is called a segment (`phaḷu`); because that exists in it, it is a `pabbato`. Because a heap of sand might be taken for a mountain of pure earth, it is said, 'But a heap of sand is not allowable.' `Itaro pi` means the other, threefold mountain apart from a heap of sand. `Hatthippamāṇato` means from the size of an elephant of seven and a half cubits. `Catūsu disāsu` means in the four directions of the monastery. Here in 'by four or by three,' by the word 'or' more than that should also be understood. 'Or by one landmark'; this is the construction. `Ito` means 'from this mountain landmark.' `Tasmā` means: because it is not allowable with one landmark, therefore... `Taṃ` means the mountain. `Tasmā` means because only one landmark was announced. 'Whatever mountain there is, that is the mountain'; this is the construction. `Anto` means the inside of the mountain.

Tatiyabhāgaṃ vāti ettha vāsaddena paṭhamabhāgopi ekadesopi gahetabbo. Tassāti tattakassa padesassa. Tatiyabhāgādito aparaṃ sabbapabbataṃ antokatvā sammataṃ dassento āha “sace”tiādi.

Here in 'or the third part,' by the word 'or' the first part or even a single part should be understood. `Tassa` means 'of that much of a region.' Showing that it is agreed upon by including the entire mountain apart from the third part and so on, he says, 'if,' etc.

Pāsāṇanimitte evaṃ vinicchayo veditabboti yojanā. Pasati ghanabhāvena bandhatīti pāsāṇo. Ayaguḷopi pāsāṇasaṅkhameva gacchati tena tassa sadisattā. Ayaguḷopīti ettha pisaddena tambakaṃsavaṭṭalohasuvaṇṇarajatādayopi saṅgaṇhāti. Yo kocīti silāpavāḷamaṇiādīsu yo koci. Dvattiṃsapalaguḷapiṇḍaparimāṇatā saṇṭhānato gahetabbā, na tulitvā gaṇanavasena. Khuddakataro pāsāṇoti [M 0.0282] yojanā. Yo piṭṭhipāsāṇo vā yo uṭṭhitapāsāṇo vāti yojanā kātabbā – uttaravākye tasaddassa aniyamaniddesavacanattā “pāsāṇasaṅkhaṃyevā”ti ettha evakārena “na pabbatasaṅkha”nti atthaṃ dasseti. Mahato piṭṭhipāsāṇassāti āyāmavitthārubbedhato mahantassa piṭṭhipāsāṇassa sakkassa paṇḍukambalapiṭṭhipāsāṇassa viya. Tanti piṭṭhipāsāṇaṃ. Na vaṭṭatīti kittetuṃ na vaṭṭati. Hīti laddhadosajotako. Tanti piṭṭhipāsāṇaṃ. Sīmāyāti sīmato. Vihāropīti na kevalaṃ nimittameva, vihāropi. Piṭṭhipāsāṇo na kittetabboti sambandho. Kittetvāti ettha “piṭṭhipāsāṇa”nti yojetabbaṃ.

Regarding a stone landmark, the decision should be known thus; this is the construction. It is a `pāsāṇo` because it binds by being solid. An iron ball also counts as a stone because of its similarity to it. Here in `ayaguḷo pi`, by the particle `pi` he also includes copper, bronze, sheet-metal, gold, silver, etc. `Yo koci` means any one among rock-crystal, coral, gems, etc. The size of a ball or lump of thirty-two `pala`s should be taken by its shape, not by way of weighing or counting. A smaller stone; this is the construction. The construction should be made as 'whether it is a flat stone or an upright stone.' Because in the following sentence the word `taṃ` is a word of indefinite reference, here in `pāsāṇasaṅkhaṃ yeva` the particle `eva` shows the meaning 'not counted as a mountain.' 'Of a large flat stone' means of a flat stone that is large in length, width, and height, like Sakka's Paṇḍukambala flat stone. `Taṃ` means the flat stone. `Na vaṭṭati` means it is not allowable to announce it. `Hī` indicates a fault that has been found. `Taṃ` means the flat stone. `Sīmāya` means from the boundary. `Vihāro pi` means not only the landmark, but the monastery too. A flat stone should not be announced; this is the connection. Here in `kittetvā`, 'flat stone' should be supplied.

Vananimitte evaṃ vinicchayo veditabboti yojanā. Vaniyati mayūrakokilādīhi sattehi sambhajiyatīti vanaṃ, vananti sambhajanti etthāti vā vanaṃ. Taco eva sāro etesanti tacasāro, tālanāḷikerādayo. Ādisaddena veṇuādayo saṅgaṇhāti. Anto sāro etesanti antosārā, sākasālādayo. Ādisaddena khadirādayo saṅgaṇhāti. Antosāramissakānanti antosārehi rukkhehi missakānaṃ. Rukkhānaṃ vananti ettha avayavaavayavibhāvena sambandho veditabbo. Iminā tiṇavanaṃ rukkhavananti ettha “tiṇānaṃ vana”nti vā “rukkhānaṃ vana”nti vā [V 1.0242] atthaṃ dasseti. Tiṇameva vanaṃ, rukkhoyeva vananti atthopi yujjateva. Cattāro vā pañca vā rukkhāti catupañcarukkhā, te mattaṃ pamāṇametthāti catupañcarukkhamattaṃ vanaṃ, tatoti catupañcarukkhamattato. Ekadesanti vanassa ekadesaṃ. Vanamajjheti vanassa vemajjhe, vanassūparīti attho. Rukkhantaresu eva hi vihāraṃ karonti. Ekadesanti vanassa ekadesaṃ. Tatthāti vane. “Ṭhitavana”nti padaṃ “kittetvā”ti pade avuttakammaṃ, “na kittetabba”nti pade vuttakammaṃ.

Regarding a forest landmark, the decision should be known thus; this is the construction. It is a `vanaṃ` because it is desired and frequented by creatures such as peacocks and cuckoos, or it is a `vanaṃ` because they desire and frequent it there. `Tacasārā` are those for which the bark itself is the heartwood, such as palm and coconut trees. By the word `ādi` he includes bamboo, etc. `Antosārā` are those for which the heartwood is inside, such as teak and sal trees. By the word `ādi` he includes acacia, etc. `Antosāramissakānaṃ` means of those mixed with trees that have heartwood inside. Here in 'a forest of trees,' the connection should be understood by way of the relation between the part and the whole. By this, here in 'a forest of grass' and 'a forest of trees,' he shows the meaning 'a forest of grass' or 'a forest of trees.' The meaning 'grass itself is the forest' or 'trees themselves are the forest' is also suitable. `Catupañcarukkhā` means four or five trees; a forest of that measure is one that has that as its measure; `tato` means from that which has the measure of four or five trees. `Ekadesaṃ` means a part of the forest. `Vanamajjhe` means in the very middle of the forest; the meaning is 'over the forest.' For they make their dwelling right among the trees. `Ekadesaṃ` means a part of the forest. `Tattha` means in the forest. The word `ṭhitavana` is the unexpressed object in the word `kittetvā`, and the expressed object in the word `na kittetabba`.

Rukkhanimitte evaṃ vinicchayo veditabboti yojanā. Rukkhiyati phalādikāmehi saṃvariyati rakkhiyatīti rukkho, mahiyaṃ ruhatīti vā rukkho. Jīvamānakoti lokavohāravasena mūlaṅkurādiharitasaṅkhātajīvamānako[M 0.0283]. Pariṇāhatoti visālabhāvato. Sūcidaṇḍakapamāṇoti sūciyā lekhaniyā daṇḍabhūtaveḷupamāṇo. So veḷu kaniṭṭhaṅgulipamāṇoti daṭṭhabbo. Tatoti aṭṭhaṅgulubbedhasūcidaṇḍakapamāṇapariṇāharukkhato. Vaṃsanaḷakasarāvādīsūti vaṃso ca naḷako ca sarāvo ca vaṃsanaḷakasarāvā, te ādayo yesaṃ kapālādīnanti vaṃsanaḷakasarāvādayo, tesu. Tatoti vaṃsādito. Taṃkhaṇampīti tasmiṃ nimittakkhaṇepi. Akāraṇanti apamāṇaṃ. Etanti navamūlasākhāniggamanaṃ. Vattuṃ vaṭṭatīti sāmaññanāmenapi visesanāmenapi vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Iminā pabbatādīsupi “pabbato”ti sāmaññanāmenapi “vaṅkapabbato vepullapabbato”ti visesanāmenapi vattuṃ vaṭṭatīti dasseti.

Regarding a tree landmark, the decision should be known thus; this is the construction. It is called a tree (rukkho) because it is sought after (rukkhiyati), enclosed (saṃvariyati), and protected (rakkhiyati) by those who desire its fruit and so on, or because it grows (ruhati) on the earth. ‘Living’ (jīvamānako) means what is conventionally called living, designated as roots, sprouts, green shoots, and so on. ‘Of mature girth’ (pariṇāhato) means because of its large size. ‘The size of a needle-stick’ (sūcidaṇḍakapamāṇo) means the size of a bamboo stick used as a needle or a stylus. That bamboo should be understood to be the size of the little finger. ‘From that’ (tato) means from a tree with a girth the size of a needle-stick eight finger-breadths thick. ‘In bamboo, reeds, clay dishes, etc.’ (vaṃsanaḷakasarāvādīsu): bamboo, reeds, and clay dishes are ‘bamboo, reeds, and clay dishes’; these and others such as potsherds are ‘bamboo, reeds, clay dishes, etc.’; ‘in these.’ ‘From that’ (tato) means from bamboo and so on. ‘Even at that moment’ (taṃkhaṇampi) means at the very moment of the boundary marker. ‘Without cause’ (akāraṇaṃ) means without a valid measure. ‘This’ (etaṃ) means the emergence of new roots and branches. ‘It is permissible to state’ (vattuṃ vaṭṭati) means it is permissible to state either its general name or its specific name. By this it is shown that in the case of mountains, etc., too, it is permissible to state a general name such as ‘mountain,’ or a specific name such as ‘Vaṅka Mountain’ or ‘Vepulla Mountain.’

Magganimitte evaṃ vinicchayo veditabboti yojanā. Maggiyati pathikehi, maggamūḷhehi vā anvesiyatīti maggo. Yo yādiso jaṅghamaggo vā sakaṭamaggo vā vinivijjhitvā dve tīṇi gāmantarāni gacchati, so tādiso jaṅghamaggo vā sakaṭamaggo vā vaṭṭatīti yojanā. Ukkamitvāti pakkamitvā. Yo jaṅghamaggo otarati, so na vaṭṭatīti yojanā. Avaḷañjāti aparibhogā. Gamanaṃ janetīti jaṅgho. Jaṇṇugopphakānaṃ majjhapadeso. Saha atthena paṇiyadhanenāti sattho, jaṅghena vicaranto sattho jaṅghasattho. Sakati samattheti bhāraṃ vahitunti sakaṭo, tena vicaranto sattho sakaṭasattho. Jaṅghasattho ca sakaṭasattho ca jaṅghasakaṭasatthā, tehi. Hīti saccaṃ, yasmā vā. Etanti nimittaṃ.

Regarding a path landmark, the decision should be known thus; this is the construction. It is called a path (maggo) because it is traveled upon (maggiyati) by way-farers, or because it is sought (anvesiyati) by those who have lost their way. The construction is: whatever kind of footpath or cart-track pierces through and goes between two or three villages, such a footpath or cart-track is permissible. ‘Having gone up’ (ukkamitvā) means having departed. The construction is: a footpath that descends is not permissible. ‘Disused’ (avaḷañja) means not in use. It generates (janeti) movement (gamanaṃ), thus it is a leg (jaṅgha); it is the middle part between the knee and the ankle. A caravan (sattho) is so called because it is together with (saha) its purpose (atthena), that is, with its merchandise; a caravan that travels on foot is a foot-caravan. It is able (sakati) or capable of carrying a load, thus it is a cart (sakaṭo); a caravan that travels by it is a cart-caravan. A foot-caravan and a cart-caravan are ‘foot-and-cart caravans’; ‘by them.’ ‘Hi’ means truly, or because. ‘This’ (etaṃ) means the boundary marker.

Koṇanti vihārakoṇaṃ. Gataṃ pana magganti yojanā. Parabhāgeti vihāraṃ parikkhipitvā gacchantehi catūhi maggehi parabhāge. Dasasu nāmesūti satipaṭṭhānaṭṭhakathādīsu āgatesu “maggo pantho patho pajjo”tiādīsu, abhidhānādīsu (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 2.373; ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.106) ca [V 1.0243] āgatesu “maggo pantho patho addhā”tiādīsu dasasu magganāmesu. Yena kenaci nāmenāti iminā [M 0.0284] pabbatādīsupi “pabbato giri selo addi nago acalo siluccayo sikharī bhūdharo”tiādīsu anekesu nāmesu yena kenaci nāmena kittetuṃ vaṭṭatīti dasseti.

‘At the corner’ (koṇaṃ) means at the corner of the monastery. The construction, however, is with the phrase ‘the path that has been taken’ (gataṃ maggaṃ). ‘In the outer area’ (parabhāge) means in the outer area of the four paths that go around enclosing the monastery. ‘Among the ten names’: among the ten names for a path found in the Commentary to the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta, etc., such as ‘maggo, pantho, patho, pajjo,’ and those found in the Abhidhāna, etc., such as ‘maggo, pantho, patho, addhā.’ ‘By any name whatsoever’: by this it is shown that in the case of mountains, etc., too, among the many names such as ‘pabbato, giri, selo, addi, nago, acalo, siluccayo, sikharī, bhūdharo,’ it is permissible to announce it by any name whatsoever.

Vammikanimitte evaṃ vinicchayo veditabboti yojanā. Upacikāhi vamiyati, sarabūgharagolikādayo satte vamatīti vā vammiko. Taṃdivasajātoti tasmiṃ nimittakittitadivase jāto. Tatoti aṭṭhaṅgulubbedhagovisāṇapamāṇavammīkato.

Regarding an anthill landmark, the decision should be known thus; this is the construction. It is called an anthill (vammiko) because it is spewed up (vamiyati) by termites, or because it spews out (vamati) creatures such as chameleons, house lizards, and iguanas. ‘Arisen on that day’ (taṃdivasajāto) means arisen on the day the boundary marker was announced. ‘From that’ (tato) means from an anthill the size of a cow’s horn, eight finger-breadths high.

Nadīnimitte evaṃ vinicchayo veditabboti yojanā. Nadati sandatīti nadī, nadanto eti gacchatīti vā nadī. Yassāti nadiyā, sotanti sambandho. “Anvaddhamāsa”ntiādinā ekapakkhe tikkhattuṃ ekamāse chakkhattuṃ vassantabhāvaṃ dīpeti. Vigatamatte satīti sambandho. “Īdise”ti iminā “anvaddhamāsa”ntiādiatthaṃ atidisati. Timaṇḍalanti heṭṭhā jāṇumaṇḍalaṃ, upari nābhimaṇḍalanti timaṇḍalaṃ. Yattha katthacīti titthe vā atitthe vā. Udakena temiyatīti yojanā, tintiyatīti attho. Na kevalaṃ nimitteyeva ayaṃ nadī hoti, atha kho nadīpāragamanādikepīti āha “bhikkhuniyā”tiādi. Idaṃ “nadīpāragamanepī”ti padeneva sambandhitabbaṃ.

Regarding a river landmark, the decision should be known thus; this is the construction. It sounds (nadati) and flows (sandati), thus it is a river (nadī); or it goes while sounding, thus it is a river. ‘Of which’ (yassā) means of the river; the connection is with ‘stream’ (sotaṃ). By ‘every half-month,’ etc., it indicates a state of raining three times in a fortnight and six times in a month. The connection is with ‘as soon as it has ceased.’ By ‘in such a case’ (īdise), it extends the meaning of ‘every half-month,’ etc. ‘Three circles’ (timaṇḍalaṃ) means the circle of the knees below and the circle of the navel above; thus ‘three circles.’ ‘Anywhere whatsoever’ (yattha katthaci) means either at a ford or not at a ford. The construction is ‘is wetted by the water’; the meaning is ‘it gets wet.’ It is not only in respect of a boundary marker that this is a river, but also in cases such as crossing a river; thus he said ‘for a bhikkhunī,’ etc. This should be connected only with the phrase ‘even in crossing a river.’

Yā panāti nadī pana, gatāti yojanā. Tanti nadiṃ. Vatinti pāḷiṃ. Rukkhapādeti rukkhassa mūle. Udakañca āvaraṇaṃ ajjhottharitvā pavattatiyevāti yojanā. Yathāti yenākārena. Apavattamānā hotīti sambandho.

‘But which’ (yā pana) means the river, however. The construction is with ‘gone’ (gatā). ‘That’ (taṃ) means the river. The Pāli text has `pavattati`. ‘At the foot of the tree’ (rukkhapāde) means at the root of the tree. The construction is: ‘The water, having completely submerged the banks, continues to flow.’ ‘As’ (yathā) means in which manner. The connection is with ‘it is not flowing.’

Dubbuṭṭhikāleti gimhasadise dubbuṭṭhikāle. “Nirudakabhāvenā”ti iminā “āvaraṇabhāvenā”ti visesanaṃ nivatteti. Sāti udakamātikā. Sampādentī hutvā niccaṃ pavattatīti yojanā. Nimittaṃ kātuṃ na vaṭṭatīti manussehi nīhaṭattā, sayañca agamanattā na vaṭṭati. Yā panāti udakamātikā pana. Mūleti paṭhamakāle. Kālantarena nadī hotīti sambandho. Tanti udakamātikaṃ.

‘In a time of poor rain’ (dubbuṭṭhikāle) means in a time of drought similar to the hot season. By ‘because of the absence of water,’ it negates the qualifier ‘because of being an enclosure.’ ‘That’ (sā) means the water channel. The construction is: ‘having been completed, it flows constantly.’ ‘It is not permissible to make it a boundary marker’: because it has been constructed by humans and because it does not flow by itself, it is not permissible. ‘But which’ (yā pana) means the water channel, however. ‘At the beginning’ (mūle) means at the initial time. The connection is: ‘after a time, it becomes a river.’ ‘That’ (taṃ) means the water channel.

Udakanimitte [M 0.0285] evaṃ vinicchayo veditabboti yojanā. Udati pasavatīti udakaṃ. Bhūmigatameva udakanti sambandho. Tañcāti bhūmigataudakañca. Āvāṭa…pe… samuddādīsu ṭhitaṃ [V 1.0244] apavattanakaudakanti yojanā. Ukkhepimanti ukkhipitvā gahitaṃ. Tanti vacanaṃ. Sūkarakhatāyapīti sūkarehi khatāya vāpiyāpi. Taṃkhaṇaññevāti tasmiṃ nimitte kittanakkhaṇeyeva. Āvāṭoyeva khuddakaṭṭhena āvāṭakaṃ. Tanti nimittasaññākaraṇaṃ. Kātuñcāti sayaṃ kātuñca. Kārāpetuñcāti parehi kārāpetuñca. Kasmā lābhasīmāyaṃ na vaṭṭati? Lābhasīmā hi aññesaṃ pīḷanaṃ karotīti. Iti imamatthaṃ nayato dassento āha “samānasaṃvāsakasīmā”tiādi. Etthāti samānasaṃvāsakasīmāyaṃ.

Regarding a water landmark, the decision should be known thus; this is the construction. It moistens (udati) or produces (pasavati), thus it is water (udakaṃ). The connection is with ‘water that is on the ground.’ ‘And that’ (tañca) means the water on the ground. The construction is: ‘water that does not flow, situated in a pit…(etc.)…up to the ocean.’ ‘Drawn up’ (ukkhepimaṃ) means taken after having been drawn up. ‘That’ (taṃ) means the statement. ‘Even in a pig-dug one’ (sūkarakhatāyapi) means even in a reservoir dug by pigs. ‘At that very moment’ (taṃkhaṇaññeva) means at the very moment of announcing the boundary marker. ‘A pit’ is a small pit made with a small piece of wood. ‘That’ (taṃ) means the act of marking the boundary marker. ‘And to make’ means to make it oneself. ‘And to have it made’ means to have it made by others. Why is it not permissible within a boundary for gains? Because a boundary for gains causes affliction to others. Thus, showing this meaning methodically, he said, ‘a boundary for common residence,’ etc. ‘Here’ (ettha) means within the boundary for common residence.

Aṭṭhadisaṃ sandhāya aṭṭha nimittāni vuttānīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Sāti sīmā. Ekena vā nimittenāti yojanā. Tiṇṇaṃ nimittānaṃ kittane nimittānaṃ ṭhitadisaṃ sallakkhetvā “puratthimāya disāyā”tiādinā kittetabbaṃ. Nimittānaṃ satakittane sīmāya aṭṭhadisaṃ sallakkhetvā ekissāyapi disāya bahunimittāni kittetabbāni. Siṅghāṭakasaṇṭhānāti tiṇṇaṃ maggānaṃ samāgamaṭṭhāne siṅghāṭakasaṇṭhānā, tikoṇā nāma hotīti adhippāyo. Caturassāti samacaturassā. Siṅghāṭakasaṇṭhānāti catunnaṃ maggānaṃ samodhānaṭṭhāne siṅghāṭakasaṇṭhānā. Aḍḍhacandamudiṅgādisaṇṭhānā pana nimittānaṃ ṭhitasaṇṭhānena hotīti daṭṭhabbā. Tanti sīmaṃ. Bandhitukāmehi nissañcārasamaye bandhitabbāti sambandho. Baddhasīmavihārānanti baddhā sīmā etesūti baddhasīmā, te eva vihārāti baddhasīmavihārā, tesaṃ. Disācārikabhikkhūnanti disāsu cārikabhikkhūnaṃ. Tatthāti tasmiṃ ekagāmakhette, bhikkhūnaṃ pesetabbanti sambandho. Ekajjhanti ekato. Aññānipīti sīmabandhagāmakhettato aññānipi. Mahāpadumatthero pana āhāti yojanā. Tatoti tehi nānāgāmakhettehi. Āgantabbanti sāmīcidassanavasena vuttaṃ. Tenāha “āgamanampi anāgamanampi vaṭṭatī”ti. Ekasīmabhāvato vuttaṃ “antonimittagatehi āgantabba”nti.

It should be understood that eight boundary markers have been mentioned with reference to the eight directions. ‘That’ (sā) means the boundary. The construction is with ‘by one boundary marker or….’ When announcing three boundary markers, having noted the direction in which the markers are situated, one should announce them with ‘in the eastern direction,’ etc. When announcing a hundred boundary markers, having noted the eight directions of the boundary, many markers may be announced even for a single direction. ‘Shaped like a crossroads’ (siṅghāṭakasaṇṭhānā): at the meeting place of three paths it is shaped like a crossroads; the intention is that it is triangular. ‘Square’ (caturassā) means an equilateral square. ‘Shaped like a crossroads’: at the meeting place of four paths it is shaped like a crossroads. But it should be understood that shapes such as a half-moon, a drum, etc., are determined by the shape in which the boundary markers are situated. ‘That’ (taṃ) means the boundary. The connection is: it should be established by those who wish to establish it at a time when there is no traffic. ‘Of monasteries with established boundaries’ (baddhasīmavihārānaṃ): those in which a boundary has been established are ‘with established boundaries’; they are themselves monasteries, thus ‘monasteries with established boundaries’; ‘of them.’ ‘Of bhikkhus wandering in the regions’ (disācārikabhikkhūnaṃ) means of bhikkhus wandering in the regions. ‘There’ (tattha) means in that single village-field. The connection is: ‘bhikkhus should be sent.’ ‘Together’ (ekajjhaṃ) means as one. ‘Others too’ (aññānipi) means others from village-fields other than the one where the boundary is being established. The construction is: ‘But the Elder Mahāpaduma said.’ ‘From there’ (tato) means from those various village-fields. ‘They should come’ is said from the perspective of showing propriety. Therefore he said, ‘Both coming and not coming are permissible.’ Because of its being a single boundary, it is said, ‘Those who have gone inside the boundary markers should come.’

Evaṃ sannipatitesu santesu sīmā bandhitabbāti sambandho. Pariyantaṃ katvāti heṭṭhimapariyantaṃ katvā.

The connection is: ‘When they have thus assembled, the boundary should be established.’ ‘Having made the limit’ (pariyantaṃ katvā) means having made the lower limit.

Pabbajjūpasampadādīnanti [M 0.0286] ettha bhaṇḍukammāpucchanaṃ (mahāva. aṭṭha. 98; vi. saṅga. aṭṭha. 144) sandhāya pabbajjāgahaṇaṃ vuttaṃ. Khaṇḍasīmāti vihārapaccantaṃ khaṇḍitaṃ viya chinditaṃ viya pavattā sīmā khaṇḍasīmā. Tanti khaṇḍasīmaṃ. Vattaṃ jānitabbanti ettha vattaṃ vitthārento āha “sace hī”tiādi. Sīmanti khaṇḍasīmaṃ. Yathāti yenākārena bandhiyamāneti sambandho. Tassā pamāṇaṃ dassento āha “sā”tiādi. Sāti khaṇḍasīmā. Abbhānakamme saddhiṃ [V 1.0245] kammārahena vīsati bhikkhū sandhāya vuttaṃ “ekavīsati bhikkhū”ti. Tatoti ekavīsatibhikkhuto. Gaṇhantīpīti ettha pisaddo sahassato oraṃ pana pagevāti dasseti. Sahassato adhikaṃ gaṇhantīpi vihārapaccante khaṇḍite khaṇḍasīmāyeva nāma. Tanti khaṇḍasīmaṃ.

Here, in ‘going forth, higher ordination, etc.’ (pabbajjūpasampadādīnaṃ), the taking of the going forth is mentioned with reference to asking permission for the act of shaving (bhaṇḍukamma). ‘A broken boundary’ (khaṇḍasīmā) is a boundary that exists at the edge of a monastery as if broken or cut off. ‘That’ (taṃ) means the broken boundary. Here, in ‘the duty should be known,’ elaborating on the duty, he said, ‘for if,’ etc. ‘The boundary’ (sīmaṃ) means the broken boundary. ‘As’ (yathā) means in which manner; the connection is with ‘being established.’ Showing its measure, he said, ‘that,’ etc. ‘That’ (sā) means the broken boundary. In the case of an act of rehabilitation (abbhānakamma), ‘twenty-one bhikkhus’ is said with reference to twenty bhikkhus along with the one fit for the formal act. ‘From that’ (tato) means from the twenty-one bhikkhus. Here in ‘they take’ (gaṇhantīpi), the word ‘pi’ (also/even) shows ‘how much more so if less than a thousand.’ Even if more than a thousand take it, when it is broken off at the edge of the monastery, it is still named a broken boundary. ‘That’ (taṃ) means the broken boundary.

Tatrāti khaṇḍasīmamahāsīmāsu ādhāre bhummaṃ. Athāti anantaraṃ. Evanti imāya avippavāsakammavācāya sammaniyamāne. Hīti phalajotako. Sīmanti samānasaṃvāsakasīmaṃ. Na sakkhissantīti paṭhamaṃ avippavāsaṃ asamūhanitvā sīmaṃ samūhanituṃ na sakkhissanti. Sīmantarikapāsāṇāti dvinnaṃ sīmānaṃ antare vemajjhe ṭhapitā pāsāṇā. Caturaṅgulapamāṇāpīti pisaddo ekaṅgulipamāṇāpi vaṭṭatīti dasseti.

Herein, tatra (there) refers to the location within chapter boundaries or great boundaries, in the locative sense. Atha (then) means immediately after. Evaṃ (thus) refers to being designated by this formal act of non-separation. Hi (indeed) is a particle indicating a result. Sīmaṃ (boundary) means a boundary for common residence. Na sakkhissanti (they will not be able) means they will not be able to dissolve the boundary without first having dissolved the state of non-separation. Sīmantarikapāsāṇā (stones in the boundary interval) refers to stones placed in the interval between two boundaries. Caturaṅgulapamāṇāpi (even four fingerbreadths in size)—the particle pi (even) indicates that a size of a single fingerbreadth is also permissible.

Samantāti khaṇḍasīmāya samantā. Anupariyāyantehīti anukkamena khaṇḍasīmapariyāyantehi bhikkhūhīti sambandho. Tatoti tehi sīmantarikapāsāṇehi, dvinnaṃ sīmānaṃ nimittāni paṭhamaṃ kittetvā pacchā tāsu yaṃ icchanti, taṃ bandhitabbabhāvaṃ dassento āha “sace panā”tiādi. Yathicchitaṃ bandhituṃ vaṭṭantopi porāṇāciṇṇaṃ dassetuṃ vuttaṃ “evaṃ santepī”tiādi. Ubhinnampīti dvīsu sīmāsu ṭhitānaṃ ubhinnampi kammanti sambandho. Hīti saccaṃ, yasmā vā.

Samantā means all around the chapter boundary. Anupariyāyantehi (by those going around) is connected with 'by the bhikkhus going around the periphery of the chapter boundary in sequence.' Tato means from those stones in the boundary interval. Showing that after first announcing the markers of the two boundaries, they may then bind whichever one they wish, he said: 'But if…' and so on. Although it is permissible to bind as they wish, in order to show the ancient practice, it is said: 'Even so…' and so on. Ubhinnampi (for both) is connected with 'the formal act for both of those standing in the two boundaries.' Hi means truly, or because.

Casaddo vākyārambhajotako. Esā sīmā nāmāti yojanā. Tatthāti piṭṭhipāsāṇādīsu pañcasu ṭhānesu. Nimittapāsāṇā yathāṭhāne na tiṭṭhantīti piṭṭhipāsāṇassupari nimittapāsāṇaṃ ṭhapitamattaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Piṭṭhipāsāṇaṃ pana vijjhitvā nimittapāsāṇaṃ tattha nikhaṇitvā yathā ṭhānā na cāventi, tathā ṭhapenti. Evaṃ sante yathāṭhāne tiṭṭhantiyevāti [M 0.0287] daṭṭhabbaṃ. Na sīmāti sīmāya pathavisandhārakaṃ udakaṃ pariyantaṃkatvā gatattā sīmā na jhāyati.

The particle ca indicates the commencement of a sentence. The construction is: 'This is called a boundary.' Tatra (therein) refers to the five locations, such as the back-stone and so on. 'The marker stones do not remain in their proper place' is said with reference to merely placing a marker stone on top of a back-stone. But they pierce the back-stone, fix the marker stone in it, and place it so that it does not move from its position. This being so, it should be understood that they do indeed remain in their proper place. Na sīmā (not a boundary) is said because the water that supports the earth of the boundary has receded past its limit, so the boundary is not established.

Kuṭigehepīti ettha kuṭīti ca gehanti ca agārasseva nāmaṃ. Agārañhi sītādidukkhassa kuṭanaṭṭhena chindanaṭṭhena ca nānādabbasambhārassa gahaṇaṭṭhena ca kuṭigehanti vuccati. Kuṭi eva gehaṃ kuṭigehaṃ, tasmimpi. Bhittiṃ akittetvāti idaṃ iṭṭhakadārumayaṃ bhittiṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Sace silāmayā bhitti nimittūpagā bhaveyya, bhittipi kittetabbā. Anto karitvāti kuṭigehassa bhittiyā vā anto katvā. Pamukheti kuṭigehassa ālinde. Nibbodakapatanaṭṭhāneti niggalitvā udakassa patanaṭṭhāne. Evaṃ sammatāya sīmāyāti yojanā.

Kuṭigehepi (even in a dwelling-hut): here, kuṭi (hut) and geha (house) are names for a dwelling. A dwelling is called a kuṭigeha because it obstructs (kuṭana) and cuts off (chindana) the suffering caused by cold, etc., and because it holds (gahaṇa) various materials. The hut itself is the house, a dwelling-hut; in that too. Bhittiṃ akittetvā (without announcing the wall): this is said with reference to a wall made of bricks and wood. If a stone wall were suitable as a marker, the wall too should be announced. Anto karitvā (having made it inside): that is, having made it inside the wall of the dwelling-hut. Pamukhe (at the front): on the porch of the dwelling-hut. Nibbodakapatanaṭṭhāne (at the place where water drips down): at the place where water falls after dripping off. The construction is: 'for a boundary thus agreed upon.'

“Kuṭṭaṃ [V 1.0246] akittetvā”ti idaṃ purimanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Antoti leṇassa, kuṭṭassa vā anto. Okāseti ekavīsatiyā bhikkhūnaṃ okāse. Evanti iminākārena sammaniyamāne. Antoti bhittiyā anto.

Kuṭṭaṃ akittetvā (without announcing the wall): this should be understood in the same way as before. Anto (inside) means inside the cave or the wall. Okāse (in the space) means in the space for twenty-one bhikkhus. Evaṃ (thus) means when being designated in this manner. Anto (inside) means inside the wall.

Heṭṭhā na otaratīti heṭṭhā ākāsatalattā na otarati. Nanu thambhe anusāritvā otaraṇo bhaveyya, kasmā na otaratīti? Thambhānamupari ekavīsatiyā bhikkhūnaṃ okāsābhāvatoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Heṭṭhā otaraṇākāraṃ dassento āha “sace panā”tiādi. Tulānanti thambhānamupari tiriyavasena ṭhitānaṃ rukkhavisesānaṃ. Uṭṭhahitvāti bhūmito uṭṭhahitvā. Tulārukkhehīti tulāsaṅkhātehi rukkhehi. “Ekasambandho”ti iminā na kevalaṃ tulārukkheheva ekasambandho, catūsu disāsu catunnaṃ bhittīnaṃ aññamaññampi sambandhoti dasseti. Heṭṭhāpi otaratīti bhittīnamupari ekavīsatiyā bhikkhūnaṃ okāsapahonakattā vuttaṃ. Sace thambhamatthake…pe… hotīti iminā bahūhi thambhehi katapāsādassa ekekasmiṃ thambhamatthake ekavīsatiyā bhikkhūnaṃ okāse sati heṭṭhā otaratīti dasseti. Niyyūhakādīsūti nāgadantakādīsu. Ādisaddena bhittikhilādayo saṅgaṇhāti. Bhitti cāti iṭṭhakadārumayā bhitti ca. Sace silāmayā bhitti [M 0.0288] ca thambhā ca honti, kittetabbā. Bhittilaggeti bhittīsu lagge, bhittīnaṃ vā laggaṭṭhāne. Heṭṭhāpāsādassāti heṭṭhāpāsāde “ṭhita”iti pade sambandho. Heṭṭhāpāsādassa vā thambhānanti yojanā. Heṭṭhā sammatāya sīmāya upari ārohanākāraṃ dassento āha “sace panā”tiādi. Nibbodakapatanaṭṭhāneti chadanakoṭiyaṃ.

Heṭṭhā na otarati (it does not descend below): it does not descend because below is open space. Surely, might it not descend by following along the pillars? Why does it not descend? It should be understood that this is because there is no space for twenty-one bhikkhus on top of the pillars. Showing the manner of descending below, he said: 'But if…' and so on. Tulānaṃ (of the beams) refers to the particular trees placed horizontally on top of the pillars. Uṭṭhahitvā (having arisen) means having arisen from the ground. Tulārukkhehi (by the beam-trees) means by the trees designated as beams. By 'ekasambandho' (one connection), it is shown that not only is there a single connection by means of the beam-trees, but the four walls in the four directions are also connected to one another. Heṭṭhāpi otarati (it also descends below) is said because there is sufficient space for twenty-one bhikkhus on top of the walls. By 'If on the top of a pillar… it is,' it is shown that in a mansion built with many pillars, if there is space for twenty-one bhikkhus on top of each pillar, it descends below. Niyyūhakādīsu (on turrets, etc.) means on projecting ornaments like 'elephant-tusks,' etc. The word ādi (etc.) includes wall-pegs and so on. Bhitti ca (and a wall) means a wall of brick and wood. If the wall and pillars are made of stone, they should be announced. Bhittilagge (attached to the wall) means attached on the walls, or at the place of attachment to the walls. Heṭṭhāpāsādassa (of the lower mansion): the connection is with the word ṭhita (standing) in 'in the lower mansion.' Or the construction is 'the pillars of the lower mansion.' Showing the manner of ascending above a boundary agreed upon below, he said: 'But if…' and so on. Nibbodakapatanaṭṭhāne (at the place where water drips down) means at the edge of the roof.

Tatthāti tasmiṃ tale. Piṭṭhipāsāṇe sīmaṃ bandhanti viya bandhantīti yojanā. Teneva paricchedenāti teneva talaparicchedena. Tālamūlapabbatepīti ettha tālamūlaṃ nāma heṭṭhā mahantaṃ hutvā anupubbena tanukaṃ hoti, tena sadise pabbatepi. Vitānasaṇṭhānoti ullocassa saṇṭhāno. Catūsu disāsu niggatasākharukkhasaṇṭhāno vā khujjarukkhasaṇṭhāno vā hoti. Yathā pabbato vitānasaṇṭhāno hoti, evaṃ mudiṅgasaṇṭhāno vā hoti paṇavasaṇṭhāno vāti yojanā. Tattha mudiṅgo majjhe thūlo hoti, mūle ca ante ca tanuko. Paṇavo majjhe tanuko hoti, mūle ca agge ca thūlo. Tesaṃ saṇṭhāno mudiṅgasaṇṭhāno vā paṇavasaṇṭhāno vā. Heṭṭhā vāti mudiṅgasaṇṭhānassa pabbatassa heṭṭhā vā. Majjhe vāti paṇavasaṇṭhānassa majjhe vā. Dve kūṭānīti dve sikharāni. Kūṭantaranti kūṭānaṃ majjhaṃ. Cinitvā vāti iṭṭhakasilāhi cinitvā vā. Pūretvā vāti paṃsuvālikāhi pūretvā vā.

Tatra (therein) means on that surface. The construction is: they bind the boundary as if binding it on a flat-topped rock. Teneva paricchedena (by that very delimitation) means by that very delimitation of the surface. Tālamūlapabbatepi (even on a palm-root mountain): here, a palm-root is large at the bottom and gradually becomes slender; so too on a mountain similar to that. Vitānasaṇṭhāno (having the shape of a canopy) means having the shape of a canopy. Or it has the shape of a tree with branches extending in the four directions, or the shape of a dwarf-palm. The construction is: just as a mountain has the shape of a canopy, so it may have the shape of a mudiṅga drum or a paṇava drum. Therein, a mudiṅga is thick in the middle and slender at the base and the end. A paṇava is slender in the middle and thick at the base and the tip. Their shape is the shape of a mudiṅga or a paṇava. Heṭṭhā vā (or below) means below the mudiṅga-shaped mountain. Majjhe vā (or in the middle) means in the middle of the paṇava-shaped mountain. Dve kūṭāni (two peaks) means two summits. Kūṭantaraṃ (between the peaks) means the middle of the peaks. Cinitvā vā (or having built) means having built with bricks and stones. Pūretvā vā (or having filled) means having filled with soil and sand.

Sappaphaṇasadisoti [V 1.0247] sappassa phaṇena sadiso, khujjo pabbatoti attho. Ākāsapabbhāranti bhittiyā aparikkhittaṃ ākāsasaṅkhātaṃ pabbhāraṃ. Sīmappamāṇoti saddhiṃ antosusirena sīmappamāṇo. Aggakoṭinti aggasaṅkhātaṃ koṭiṃ. Sace pana pabbatassa heṭṭhā antoleṇaṃ hotīti sambandho. Uparimassāti antoleṇassa upari ṭhitassa. Pāratoti bāhirato. Assāti pabbatassa bahīti sambandho. Oratoti antato. Leṇaṃ hotīti sambandho. Kittakaṃ mahantanti āha “sīmāparicchedamatikkamitvā ṭhita”nti. Kittakaṃ khuddakanti āha “sabbapacchimasīmāparimāṇa”nti. Tanti khuddakaṃ leṇaṃ[M 0.0289]. Atikhuddakanti sabbapacchimasīmāparimāṇābhāvato atikhuddakaṃ. Tatoti uparisīmato. Bahīti sīmato bahi. “Yadi sīmappamāṇaṃ, sīmā hotiyevā”ti iminā yadi na sīmappamāṇaṃ, na sīmā hotiyevāti dasseti.

Sappaphaṇasadiso (like a snake's hood) means similar to a snake's hood; the meaning is a humped mountain. Ākāsapabbhāraṃ (an open-air slope) means a slope designated as open-air, not enclosed by a wall. Sīmappamāṇo (of boundary-measure) means of boundary-measure including the inner hollow. Aggakoṭiṃ (the top-most point) means the point designated as the top. The connection is: 'But if there is an inner cave beneath the mountain.'
