This is the method: ‘Today is the Pavāraṇā on the fifteenth,’ thus it indicates the preliminary duty. ‘Assā’ti refers to the word. ‘Ñattin’ti refers to the motion: ‘Venerable sirs, may the Sangha hear me, today is the Pavāraṇā.’ ‘Pacchimehī’ti means by the monks who have undertaken the later rains-residence. ‘Uposathagge’ti means in the building, the place for observing the Uposatha. ‘Dve ñattiyo’ti means two motions: the Pavāraṇā motion and the Uposatha motion. ‘Idañcā’ti means this, however, which is about to be said. ‘Etthā’ti means in the place where the monks of the earlier and later groups associate. ‘Purimikāya upagatehī’ti is an ablative of separation, an ablative implying the scope of inference; the connection is with ‘thokatarā’ti, or it is a case of association; the connection is with ‘samasamā’ti. ‘Samasamā’ti means equal, or from being equal, they are equal; the meaning is exactly equal. The intention is that there is nothing less or more. ‘Itī’ti is this characteristic.

Soti [V 1.0279] pacchimiko bhikkhu. Itarenāti pacchimikena. Tesanti purimikānaṃ. Ekenāti purimikena. Ekassāti pacchimikassa. Puna ekenāti pacchimikena. “Ekassā”ti anuvattetabbo, purimikassāti attho. Purimavassūpagatehi adhikatarāti sambandho. Thokatarehīti pacchimavassūpagatehi thokatarehi purimavassūpagatehīti yojanā.

‘So’ti means the monk of the later group. ‘Itarenā’ti means by the one of the later group. ‘Tesan’ti means of the monks of the earlier group. ‘Ekenā’ti means by one of the earlier group. ‘Ekassā’ti means of one of the later group. ‘Puna ekenā’ti means again by one of the later group. ‘Ekassā’ti should be supplied, meaning of one of the earlier group. The connection is with ‘adhikatarā’ti: more numerous than those who undertook the earlier rains-residence. The construction for ‘Thokatarehī’ti is: by those who undertook the later rains-residence, being fewer than those who undertook the earlier rains-residence.

Kattikāyāti pacchimakattikāya. Cātumāsiniyā pavāraṇāyāti catunnaṃ māsānaṃ pūraṇiyā pavāraṇāya. Pavāraṇāñattiṃ ṭhapetvāti samasamā [M 0.0327] hutvāpi pavāraṇādivasattā pavāraṇāñattiṃ ṭhapetvā. Tehīti pacchimikehi. Itarehīti purimikehi. Tesanti pacchimikānaṃ. Thokatarā vāti ekādinā thokatarā vā. Tesanti purimikānaṃ. Tehīti pacchimikehi.

‘Kattikāyā’ti means the later Kattika. ‘Cātumāsiniyā pavāraṇāyā’ti means the Pavāraṇā that completes the four months. ‘Pavāraṇāñattiṃ ṭhapetvā’ti means setting aside the Pavāraṇā motion, even if they are equal in number, because it is the day of Pavāraṇā. ‘Tehī’ti means by those of the later group. ‘Itarehī’ti means by those of the earlier group. ‘Tesan’ti means of those of the later group. ‘Thokatarā vā’ti means fewer by one or more. ‘Tesan’ti means of those of the earlier group. ‘Tehī’ti means by those of the later group.

233. Saṅghasāmaggiyāti ettha kīdisī saṅghasāmaggī veditabbāti āha “kosambakasāmaggīsadisāva veditabbā”ti. Etthāti sāmaggīpavāraṇāyaṃ. Appamattaketi pattacīvarādiṃ paṭicca uppanne appamattake vivāde. Pavāraṇāyamevāti pavāraṇādivaseyeva. Kasmiṃ divase sāmaggīpavāraṇā kātabbāti āha “sāmaggīpavāraṇa”ntiādi. Paṭhamapavāraṇanti pubbakattikapuṇṇamiṃ. Yāva kattikacātumāsinī puṇṇamāti ayaṃ avadhi anabhividhiavadhi nāma. Kasmā? Kattikacātumāsinipuṇṇamiṃ ṭhapetvā antoyeva gahetabbattā. Etthantareti etasmiṃ dvinnaṃ puṇṇaminamantare aṭṭhavīsatipamāṇe divase kātabbā. Tatoti etthantarasaṅkhātā aṭṭhavīsadivasato.

233. Regarding ‘saṅghasāmaggiyā’ti: Here, what kind of Sangha harmony should be understood? He said: ‘It should be understood as similar to the harmony of Kosambī.’ ‘Etthā’ti means in the harmonious Pavāraṇā. ‘Appamattake’ti refers to a minor dispute that has arisen concerning bowls, robes, etc. ‘Pavāraṇāyamevā’ti means on the very day of Pavāraṇā. On which day should the harmonious Pavāraṇā be performed? He said: ‘The harmonious Pavāraṇā,’ etc. ‘Paṭhamapavāraṇan’ti means the first Pavāraṇā on the full moon of the earlier Kattika. ‘Yāva kattikacātumāsinī puṇṇamā’ti: this limit is called a non-inclusive limit. Why? Because it should be taken as only within, excluding the four-month Kattika full moon itself. ‘Etthantare’ti means it should be done within this interval between the two full moons, a period of twenty-eight days. ‘Tato’ti means from those twenty-eight days reckoned as the interval.

140. Dvevācikādipavāraṇākathā

140. The Discussion on the Two-Utterance Pavāraṇā and so forth

234. Ñattiṃ ṭhapentenāpīti pisaddo na kevalaṃ pavārentena eva dvevācikaṃ pavāretabbaṃ, atha kho ñattiṃ ṭhapentenāpi dvevācikañattiyeva ṭhapetabbāti dasseti. Ettha cāti “samānavassikaṃ pavāretu”nti pāṭhe ca. Samānavassikāti gaṇanavasena samānaṃ vassaṃ etesanti samānavassikā, samāne vasse upasampādentīti vā samānavassikā. Ekatoti ekasmiṃ khaṇe, ekapahārena vā.

234. Regarding ‘ñattiṃ ṭhapentenāpī’ti: the word ‘pi’ shows that not only should the one inviting perform a two-utterance Pavāraṇā, but also the one proposing the motion should propose a two-utterance motion itself. ‘Ettha cā’ti refers also to the reading ‘let him invite one of equal rains-residence.’ ‘Samānavassikā’ti means those whose rains-residence is equal by way of counting, or those who were ordained in the same rains-residence. ‘Ekato’ti means at a single moment, or with a single utterance.

141. Pavāraṇāṭṭhapanakathā

141. Discussion on the Postponement of the Pavāraṇā

236. Sabbaṃ saṅgaṇhātīti sabbasaṅgāhikaṃ. Puggalassa ṭhapanaṃ puggalikaṃ. Tatthāti dvīsu pavāraṇāṭṭhapanesu[V 1.0280]. Sabbasaṅgāhike ṭhapitā hotīti sambandho. Yāva rekāro atthi, tāvāti yojanā. Bhāsiyitthāti bhāsitā. Lapiyitthāti lapitā. Na pariyosiyitthāti apariyositā. Etthantareti etasmiṃ sukārarekārānaṃ antare. Ekapadepīti pisaddo ekakkharepīti atthaṃ sampiṇḍeti. Ṭhapitāti “suṇātu me bhante [M 0.0328] saṅgho, itthannāmo puggalo sāpattiko, tassa pavāraṇaṃ ṭhapemī”ti ñattiyā ṭhapitā. Yyakāreti “pavāreyyā”ti ettha yyakāre. Tatoti yyakārato. Puggalikaṭṭhapane pana aṭṭhapitā hotīti sambandho. Saṃkāratoti “saṅghaṃ bhante”ti ettha saṃkārato. Sabbapacchimoti tīsu vāresu tatiyavāre sabbesaṃ akkharānaṃ pacchimo ṭikāro atthīti yojanā. Etthantareti etasmiṃ saṃkāraṭikārānaṃ antare. Tasmāti yasmā pariyositā hoti, tasmā. “Eseva nayo”ti vuttavacanaṃ vitthārento āha “etāsupi hī”tiādi. Tattha etāsupīti dvevācikaekavācikasamānavassikāsupi. Pisaddo tevācikamapekkhati. Ṭhapanakhettanti ṭhapanassa bhūmi. Itisaddo parisamāpanattho.

236. Because it includes everything, it is all-inclusive (sabbasaṅgāhikaṃ). The postponement concerning an individual is an individual one (puggalikaṃ). ‘Tatthā’ti refers to the two postponements of the Pavāraṇā. The connection is: it is postponed in the all-inclusive postponement. The construction for ‘Yāva rekāro atthi, tāvā’ti is: as long as the letter ‘r’ exists. ‘Bhāsiyitthā’ti means spoken. ‘Lapiyitthā’ti means uttered. ‘Na pariyosiyitthā’ti means uncompleted. ‘Etthantare’ti refers to the interval between the letters ‘su’ and ‘ra’. Regarding ‘ekapadepī’ti: the word ‘pi’ consolidates the meaning into ‘even in a single letter (ekakkharepi).’ ‘Ṭhapitā’ti means postponed by the motion: ‘Venerable sirs, may the Sangha hear me. This person, named so-and-so, has committed an offense. I postpone his Pavāraṇā.’ ‘Yyakāre’ti refers to the syllable ‘yya’ in ‘pavāreyya’. ‘Tato’ti means from the syllable ‘yya’. However, in the individual postponement, the connection is: it is not postponed. ‘Saṃkārato’ti means from the syllable ‘saṃ’ in ‘saṅghaṃ bhante’. ‘Sabbapacchimo’ti: the construction is that in the third of the three utterances, the letter ‘ṭi’ is the very last of all the letters. ‘Etthantare’ti refers to the interval between the syllables ‘saṃ’ and ‘ṭi’. ‘Tasmā’ti means therefore, because it is completed. Expanding on the statement ‘Eseva nayo’, he says: ‘etāsupi hī’ti, etc. There, ‘etāsupī’ti means in the cases of the two-utterance, one-utterance, and same-rains-residence Pavāraṇās. The word ‘pi’ refers to the three-utterance one. ‘Ṭhapanakhettan’ti means the sphere of postponement. The word ‘iti’ has the sense of conclusion.

237. Anuyuñjiyamānoti ettha anuyuñjasaddo pucchanatthoti āha “pucchiyamāno”ti. Paratoti parasmiṃyeva khandhaketi (mahāva. 237) attho. Alaṃ bhikkhu mā bhaṇḍanantiādīnīti ettha ādisaddena “mā kalahaṃ, mā vivāda”ntivacanāni saṅgaṇhāti, vacanāni vatvā omadditvāti yojanā. Vacanomaddanāti vacaneneva omaddanā. Hīti saccaṃ. Idhāti imasmiṃ pavāraṇāṭṭhapanaṭṭhāne. Anuddhaṃsitaṃ paṭijānātīti ettha paṭijānanākāraṃ dassento āha “amūlakena pārājikena anuddhaṃsito ayaṃ mayā”ti. “Liṅganāsanāyā”ti iminā daṇḍakammanāsanasaṃvāsanāsanāni nivatteti.

237. Regarding ‘anuyuñjiyamāno’ti: here the word ‘anuyuñja’ has the meaning of questioning; hence he said ‘pucchiyamāno’ (being questioned). ‘Parato’ti means in another section itself (parasmiṃyeva khandhake), as in Mahāvagga 237. Regarding ‘alaṃ bhikkhu mā bhaṇḍanantiādīnī’ti: here, the word ‘ādi’ (etc.) includes statements like ‘mā kalahaṃ, mā vivādaṃ’ (do not quarrel, do not dispute). The construction is: having spoken the words and having suppressed. ‘Vacanomaddanā’ti means suppression by means of speech itself. ‘Hī’ti means truly. ‘Idhā’ti means on this occasion of postponing the Pavāraṇā. Regarding ‘anuddhaṃsitaṃ paṭijānātī’ti: here, showing the manner of confession, he says: ‘This one was accused by me of a groundless Pārājika offense.’ By this, ‘liṅganāsanāyā’ti, he precludes acts of punishment (daṇḍakamma), banishment (nāsana), and suspension of communion (saṃvāsanāsana).

238. Etanti “asukā āpattī”ti vacanaṃ. Kalahassa mukhanti kalahassa upāyo.

238. ‘Etan’ti refers to the statement ‘such and such an offense.’ ‘Kalahassa mukhan’ti means the cause of a quarrel.

143. Vatthuṭṭhapanādikathā

143. The Discussion on Setting Aside the Basis and so forth

239. Corā agamaṃsu kirāti sambandho. Pokkharaṇito nīharitvāti sambandho. Soti bhikkhu, evamāhāti sambandho. Vutthenāti vasantena, yena kenaci katanti sambandho. Taṃ puggalanti vatthukataṃ taṃ puggalaṃ. Etthāti “vatthuṃ ṭhapetvā saṅgho pavāreyyā”ti pāṭhe[M 0.0329]. Iminā vatthunā apadisāhīti sambandho. Nanti puggalaṃ. Anuvijjitvāti anuyuñjitvā, pucchitvāti attho.

239. The connection is with ‘corā agamaṃsu kirā’ti (the robbers came, it is said). The connection is with ‘pokkharaṇito nīharitvā’ti (having taken it out of the pond). ‘So’ti means the monk; the connection is with ‘evamāhā’ti (said thus). ‘Vutthenā’ti means by one who has resided; the connection is with ‘yena kenaci katan’ti (done by someone or other). ‘Taṃ puggalan’ti means that person who has been made the subject of the matter. ‘Etthā’ti refers to the reading ‘the Sangha should perform the Pavāraṇā after setting aside the matter.’ The connection is with ‘iminā vatthunā apadisāhī’ti (point him out by this matter). ‘Nan’ti means the person. ‘Anuvijjitvā’ti means having investigated, that is, having questioned.

Eko [V 1.0281] bhikkhu pūjesi, pivīti sambandho. Tassāti bhikkhussa. Tadanurūpoti tesaṃ pūjanapivanānaṃ anurūpo. Soti codako bhikkhu. Taṃ gandhanti taṃ sarīragandhaṃ. Yaṃ puggalanti yojanā. Ṭhapesīti pavāraṇāya ṭhapesi. Ayamassāti ayaṃ doso assa puggalassa.

The connection is with ‘eko bhikkhu pūjesi, pivī’ti (a certain monk paid respects and drank). ‘Tassā’ti means of the monk. ‘Tadanurūpo’ti means corresponding to that paying of respects and drinking. ‘So’ti means the accusing monk. ‘Taṃ gandhan’ti means that bodily odor. The construction is with ‘yaṃ puggalaṃ’. ‘Ṭhapesī’ti means he postponed the Pavāraṇā. ‘Ayamassā’ti means this is the fault of this person.

Idāneva nanti ettha “na”nti padaṃ “puggala”nti padena yojetabbaṃ. Naṃ puggalanti hi attho. Ubhayanti vatthuñca puggalañcāti ubhayaṃ. Kallaṃ vacanāyāti yuttaṃ kathetuṃ. Kasmā kallaṃ vacanāyāti yojanā. Pavāraṇato pubbe, pacchā cāti sambandho. Iti tasmā kallaṃ vacanāyāti yojanā. Idañhi ubhayanti vatthupuggalasaṅkhātaṃ idameva ubhayaṃ. Pavāraṇāya pubbeti yojanā. Ukkoṭentassāti cālentassa.

Regarding ‘idāneva nan’ti: here the word ‘naṃ’ should be connected with the word ‘puggala’. For the meaning is ‘naṃ puggalaṃ’ (that person). ‘Ubhayan’ti means both: the matter and the person. ‘Kallaṃ vacanāyā’ti means it is proper to speak. The construction is: Why is it proper to speak? The connection is with ‘pavāraṇato pubbe, pacchā cā’ti (before the Pavāraṇā and after). The construction is: Therefore, it is proper to speak. ‘Idañhi ubayan’ti means this very pair, reckoned as matter and person. The construction is with ‘pavāraṇāya pubbe’ti (before the Pavāraṇā). ‘Ukkoṭentassā’ti means of one who reopens a case.

144. Bhaṇḍanakārakavatthukathā

144. The Story of the Quarrel-Maker

240. Catutthapañcamāti chasu pakkhesu poṭṭhapādamāsassa juṇhapakkhakāḷapakkhasaṅkhātā catutthapañcamā. Tatiyoti sāvaṇamāsassa kāḷapakkho tatiyo. Tatiyacatutthapañcamā vāti ettha tatiyoti sāvaṇamāsassa kāḷapakkho. Catutthoti poṭṭhapādamāsassa juṇhapakkho. Pañcamoti tasseva kāḷapakkho. “Tatiya…pe… pañcamā vā”ti padāni “dve vā tayo vā”ti padehi yathākkamaṃ yojetabbāni. Catutthe vā kateti catutthapakkhe vā pannarasibhāvena kate. Dve cātuddasikāti tatiyapakkhe ca cātuddasiyā saddhiṃ dve cātuddasikā. Imeti bhaṇḍanakārakā. Teti bhaṇḍanakārakā.

240. "Fourth, fifth" means that among the six fortnights, the bright fortnight and the dark fortnight of the month of Poṭṭhapāda are designated the fourth and fifth. "Third" means the dark fortnight of the month of Sāvaṇa is the third. Regarding "third, fourth, or fifth," here "third" is the dark fortnight of the month of Sāvaṇa; "fourth" is the bright fortnight of the month of Poṭṭhapāda; "fifth" is its dark fortnight. The words "third... or fifth" should be connected respectively with the words "two or three." "Or done on the fourth" means or done in the fourth fortnight, having been made a fifteenth-day observance. "Two fourteenths" means two fourteenth-day observances, together with the fourteenth of the third fortnight. "These" refers to the quarrel-makers. "Those" refers to the quarrel-makers.

Asaṃvihitāti ettha akārassa virahatthaṃ dassento āha “saṃvidahanavirahitā”ti. Tattha saṃvidahanavirahitāti saṃvidahanarakkhavirahitā. Āgamanajānanatthāyāti bhaṇḍanakārakānaṃ āgamanassa jānanatthāya. Kilantatthāti tumhe kilantā bhavatha. “Sammohaṃ katvā”ti [M 0.0330] iminā vikkhitvāti padassa vikkhepaṃ katvāti atthaṃ dasseti. No ce labhethāti ettha kimatthāya na labhethāti āha “bahisīmaṃ gantu”nti. “Bhaṇḍanakārakānaṃ…pe… hontī”ti iminā alabhanassa kāraṇaṃ dasseti. Yanti āgamaṃ juṇhaṃ. Komudiyā cātumāsiniyāti pacchimakattikapuṇṇamāyaṃ. Sā hi kumudānamatthitāya komudī, catunnaṃ vassikānaṃ māsānaṃ pūraṇattā cātumāsinīti vuccati. Tadā hi kumudāni supupphitāni honti, tasmā kumudānaṃ samūhā, kumudāni eva vā komudā, te ettha atthīti komudīti vuccati, kumudavatīti vuttaṃ hoti[V 1.0282]. Avassaṃ pavāretabbanti dhuvaṃ pavāretabbaṃ. Hīti saccaṃ, yasmā vā. Tanti komudiṃ cātumāsiniṃ.

Regarding "unprepared" (asaṃvihitā): here, showing that the prefix "a-" implies absence, he says, "lacking preparation" (saṃvidahanavirahitā). In this context, "lacking preparation" means lacking preparation and protection. "For the purpose of knowing the arrival" means for the purpose of knowing the arrival of the quarrel-makers. "For the purpose of tiring" means "so that you will become tired." By "having caused confusion," he shows that the meaning of the word "having scattered" is "having caused scattering." Regarding "if one does not obtain," he asks for what reason one does not obtain, and says, "to go beyond the boundary." By "for the quarrel-makers... they are," he shows the reason for not obtaining it. "Yanti" means they go to the awaited bright fortnight. "Komudī Cātumāsinī" refers to the full moon of the later month of Kattika. It is called Komudī because of the presence of water lilies (kumuda), and Cātumāsinī because it marks the completion of the four rainy-season months. At that time, the water lilies are in full bloom; therefore, from the multitude of water lilies, or because the water lilies themselves are called komudā, and because they are present there, it is called Komudī; this is to say, it means "possessing water lilies." "The invitation must certainly be given" means the invitation must definitely be given. "Hi" means truly, or because. "Tanti" refers to the Komudī Cātumāsinī.

145. Pavāraṇāsaṅgahakathā

145. Discourse on the Acceptance of Pavāraṇā

241. Aññataro phāsuvihāroti ettha phāsuvihāro nāma koti āha “taruṇasamatho vā taruṇavipassanā vā”ti. Iminā taruṇasamathavipassanā phāsuṃ viharati anenāti phāsuvihāroti dasseti. Paribāhirā bhavissāmāti ettha kasmā imamhā phāsuvihārā paribāhirā bhavissantīti āha “anibaddharattiṭṭhānadivāṭṭhānādibhāvenā”tiādi. Tattha anibaddharattiṭṭhānadivāṭṭhānādibhāvenāti anibaddhadivāṭṭhānādibhāvena hetubhūtena, asakkontāti sambandho. Ādisaddena anibaddhacaṅkamādayo saṅgaṇhāti. “Chandadānaṃ paṭikkhipatī”ti iminā “sabbeheva ekajjhaṃ sannipatitabba”nti vākyassa aññatthāpohanaṃ dasseti. Hīti saccaṃ, yasmā vā. Imesu tīsu chandadānaṃ na vaṭṭati, tasmā paṭikkhipatīti yojanā. Ayaṃ pavāraṇāsaṅgaho nāma na dātabboti yojanā. Taruṇasamathavipassanālābhī ekapuggalo vā hotūti yojanā. “Ekassapi dātabboyevā”ti iminā ayaṃ pavāraṇāsaṅgaho ekassa dinnopi sabbesaṃ dinno hotīti dasseti. Pavāraṇāsaṅgahe dinne satīti yojanā. Āgantukāti saṭṭhivassāpi āgantukā. Tesanti dinnapavāraṇāsaṅgahānaṃ. Antarāpīti komudiyā cātumāsiniyā antarāpi.

241. Regarding "a certain comfortable dwelling": here, what is meant by "a comfortable dwelling" is explained as "either nascent serenity or nascent insight." By this, he shows that because one dwells comfortably by means of nascent serenity and insight, it is called a "comfortable dwelling." Regarding "we will be excluded": here, as to why they will be excluded from this comfortable dwelling, it is said, "due to the state of not having fixed places for night or day stays, and so on." Here, "due to the state of not having fixed places for day stays, and so on" is the cause, and the connection is with "being unable." By the word "and so on," not having fixed walking paths and the like are included. By "he rejects the giving of consent," he shows the negation of the statement "all must gather in one place." "Hi" means truly, or because. The interpretation is: in these three cases, the giving of consent is not proper; therefore, he rejects it. The interpretation is: this, called the acceptance of Pavāraṇā, should not be given. The interpretation is: let there be even a single person who is an obtainer of nascent serenity and insight. By "it must be given even to one," he shows that this acceptance of Pavāraṇā, when given to one, is given to all. The interpretation is: when the acceptance of Pavāraṇā has been given. "Newcomers" means that even those of sixty years' standing are newcomers. "Of them" means of those to whom the acceptance of Pavāraṇā has been given. "Even in between" means even in the interval before the Komudī Cātumāsinī.

Iti pavāraṇākkhandhakavaṇṇanāya yojanā samattā.

Thus ends the explanation of the construction of the commentary on the Pavāraṇā Chapter.

5. Cammakkhandhakaṃ

5. The Chapter on Hides

147. Soṇakoḷivisavatthukathā

147. The Story of Soṇa Koḷivīsa

242. Cammakkhandhake [M 0.0331][V 2.0001] issariyādhipaccanti ettha issarassa bhāvo issariyaṃ, adhipatino bhāvo ādhipaccaṃ, issariyañca ādhipaccañca, tehi samannāgataṃ issariyādhipaccanti atthaṃ dassento āha “issarabhāvena ca adhipatibhāvena ca samannāgata”nti. “Rājabhāva”nti iminā rajjanti ettha rañño bhāvo rajjanti vacanatthaṃ dasseti. “Raññā kattabbakicca”nti iminā rañño idaṃ rajjanti vacanatthaṃ dasseti. “Koḷivīsoti gotta”nti idaṃ aṭṭhakathāvādavasena vuttaṃ[V 2.0002], apadāne pana tassa jātakkhaṇe pitarā koṭivīsadhanassa dinnattā “koḷivīso nāmā”ti vuttaṃ. Vuttañhi tattha

242. In the Chapter on Hides, regarding "lordship and dominion": here, the state of a lord (issara) is lordship (issariyaṃ), the state of a master (adhipati) is dominion (ādhipaccaṃ); "lordship and dominion" is that which is endowed with both. Showing this meaning, he says, "endowed with the state of a lord and the state of a master." By "the state of a king," he shows the etymological meaning of "kingship" (rajjaṃ) as "the state of a king." By "duties to be performed by a king," he shows the etymological meaning of "kingship" (rajjaṃ) as "that which belongs to the king." "Koḷivīsa is the clan name": this is said according to the view of the commentaries, but in the Apadāna it is said that because at the moment of his birth he was given wealth of twenty crores by his father, he was named "Koḷivīsa." For it is stated there:

“Jātaputtassa me sutvā, pitu chando ayaṃ ahu;

Dadāmahaṃ kumārassa, vīsakoṭī anūnakā”ti.

"Upon hearing of me, his newborn son, this was my father’s wish: ‘I shall give the boy twenty crores without deduction.’"

Iminā pāḷinayena “koṭivīso”ti vattabbe “cakkavāḷa”ntiādīsu viya ṭakārassa ḷakāraṃ katvā koḷivīsoti vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Añjanavaṇṇānīti añjanassa vaṇṇo viya vaṇṇo etesanti añjanavaṇṇāni. Lomāni jātāni hontīti sambandho. Soti soṇo. Ṭhapesi kirāti sambandho. Tehīti asītisahassapurisehi. Paṇṇasālanti paṇṇena chāditaṃ, tena ca parikkhittaṃ sālaṃ. Uṇṇapāvāraṇanti uṇṇamayaṃ uttarāsaṅgaṃ. Pādapuñchanikanti pādaṃ puñchati sodheti anenāti pādapuñchaniyaṃ, tadeva pādapuñchanikaṃ. Sabbevāti soṇena saha asītisahassapurisā eva. Tassa cāti soṇassa ca. Pubbayogoti pubbūpāyo.

By this textual principle, it should be understood that although "koṭivīsa" ought to be said, "koḷivīsa" is said by changing the letter "ṭa" to "ḷa," as in "cakkavāḷa" and other such cases. "Of the color of collyrium" (añjanavaṇṇāni) means their color is like the color of collyrium (añjana). The connection is "hairs have grown." "He" means Soṇa. The connection is "it is said that he placed." "By them" means by the eighty thousand men. "A leaf-hut" means a hall covered and surrounded by leaves. "A woolen cloak" means an upper garment made of wool. "A foot-wiper" (pādapuñchanika) is that by which one wipes or cleans the feet, hence "pādapuñchaniyaṃ," which is the same as "pādapuñchanika." "All" means Soṇa together with the eighty thousand men. "And of him" means of Soṇa. "Past connection" means past means.

Asītigāmikasahassānīti ettha gāmesu vasantīti gāmikā, tesaṃ asītisahassāni asītigāmikasahassānīti atthaṃ dassento āha “tesū”tiādi. Tattha “kulaputtāna”nti iminā vasantyatthe pavattassa [M 0.0332] ṇikapaccayassa sarūpaṃ dasseti. “Asītisahassānī”ti iminā saddantaropi asītisahassasaddānaṃ samāsabhāvaṃ dasseti. Kenacidevāti ettha “kenaci ivā”ti padavibhāgaṃ katvā dakāro padasandhimatto, ivasaddo upamatthoti āha “kenaci karaṇīyena viyā”ti. Atha vā “na panā”tiādinā evaphalassa dassitattā “kenaci evā”ti padacchedaṃ katvā evatthopi yujjatevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Assāti bimbisārarañño. Tassāti soṇassa. Dassanāya aññatra kiñci karaṇīyaṃ na atthīti yojanā. Rājāti bimbisāro rājā, sannipātāpesīti sambandho. Diṭṭhadhammike attheti ettha diṭṭhadhammasaddo idhalokattho, ikasaddo hitatthe pavattoti āha “idhalokahite”ti. “Amhāka”nti iminā “so no bhagavā”ti ettha nosaddo amhasaddakāriyoti dasseti. Amhākaṃ so bhagavāti yojanā. Samparāyiketi paralokahite.

Regarding "eighty thousand villagers": here, showing the meaning that because they dwell in villages they are "villagers" (gāmikā), and eighty thousand of them are "eighty thousand villagers" (asītigāmikasahassāni), he says, "among them," and so on. Therein, by "of clansmen," he shows the form of the suffix -ṇika, which is used in the sense of "dwelling." By "eighty thousand," he shows that the word "eighty thousand" can form a compound with another word. Regarding "kenacideva": here, dividing the words as "kenaci iva" (by some, as it were), the letter "d" is merely for euphonic conjunction, and the word "iva" has the meaning of comparison; thus he says, "as if by some duty." Alternatively, because the result is shown by "but not..." and so on, it should be understood that by dividing the words as "kenaci eva" (by some indeed), the meaning of "indeed" is also suitable. "Of him" (assa) means of King Bimbisāra. "Of him" (tassa) means of Soṇa. The construction is: "apart from seeing him, there was no other duty." "The king" means King Bimbisāra; the connection is with "had them assembled." Regarding "for the goal in the present life" (diṭṭhadhammike atthe): here, the word "diṭṭhadhamma" has the meaning of "this world," and the suffix "-ika" is used in the sense of "benefit"; thus he says, "for the benefit in this world." By "of us" (amhākaṃ), he shows that here in the phrase "that Blessed One of us" (so no bhagavā), the word "no" performs the function of the word "amha." The construction is "that Blessed One is ours" (amhākaṃ so bhagavā). "In the future life" (samparāyike) means for the benefit in the next world.

“Jānāpemī”ti iminā “paṭivedemī”ti ettha vidadhātuyā ñāṇatthaṃ dasseti. Paṭikāya nimujjitvāti ettha paṭikāsaddo aḍḍhendupāsāṇavācakoti āha “aḍḍhacandapāsāṇe”ti. So hi paṭati aḍḍhabhāvaṃ gacchatīti paṭikāti vuccati. Paṭikāsaddoyaṃ attharaṇavisesepi vattati. Yassa [V 2.0003] dānīti ettha yasaddassa visayaṃ dassento āha “tesaṃ hitakaraṇīyatthassā”ti. Iminā ayaṃ yaṃsaddo na taṃsaddāpekkhoti dasseti. Atha vā yassāti yo assa. Assa tesaṃ hitakaraṇīyatthassa yo kālo atthi, taṃ kālaṃ bhagavā jānātīti yojanā. Tesanti asītigāmikasahassānaṃ. Pacchāyāyanti ettha pakāro paccantatthavācakoti āha “vihārapaccante chāyāya”nti. Sammanāharantīti saṃ punappunaṃ manasāgataṃ abhimukhaṃ harantīti atthaṃ dassento āha “punappunaṃ manasikarontī”ti. “Pasādavasenā”ti iminā “kodhavasenā”tiādīni paṭikkhipati. “Puna visiṭṭhatara”nti iminā bhiyyoso mattāyāti nipātassa atthaṃ dasseti.

By 'I make known,' he shows that in 'I declare,' the root vid has the meaning of knowing. Regarding 'having plunged into the paṭikā,' here the word paṭikā denotes a half-moon stone; thus he said, 'on the half-moon stone.' For it splits and becomes half, hence it is called a paṭikā. This word paṭikā is also used for a particular kind of covering. Regarding 'For whose sake now,' indicating the scope of the word 'whose,' he said, 'for the purpose of benefiting them.' By this, it is shown that this word 'whose' does not depend on the word 'that.' Alternatively, yassā is yo assa. The construction is: the Blessed One knows that time which exists for the purpose of their benefit. 'Of them' refers to the eighty thousand villagers. Regarding pacchāyāyaṃ, here the prefix pa- denotes the farthest end; thus he said, 'in the shade at the monastery's boundary.' Regarding sammanāharanti, showing the meaning 'they repeatedly bring to mind what is mentally present,' he said, 'they reflect again and again.' By 'out of confidence,' he rejects alternatives like 'out of anger,' and so on. By 'again more distinguished,' he shows the meaning of the particle in bhiyyoso mattāya (to a greater degree).

Soṇassa pabbajjākathā

The Story of Soṇa's Going Forth

243. “Makkhito”ti [M 0.0333] iminā phurati vipphārati byāpetīti phuṭoti vutte phuradhātuyā vipphāraṇaṃ nāma makkhitatthoti dasseti. Yatthāti yasmiṃ ṭhāne. Iminā gāvo āhananti etthāti gavāghātananti atthaṃ dassebhi. Tantissareti tantiyā guṇassa sare. Vādanakusaloti vādane kusalo. Kharamucchitāti kharena mucchitā. “Sarasampannā”ti iminā saro etissamatthīti saravatī, vīṇāti dasseti. Kammaññāti ettha kammasaddato khamatthe ññapaccayoti āha “kammakkhamā”ti. Mandamucchanāti mandena mucchanā. Same guṇeti ettha samo nāma majjhimo, guṇo nāma mukhyato vīṇāya jiyā, upacārato saroti āha “majjhime sare”ti. Vīriyasamathanti ettha vīriyañca samatho cāti atthaṃ paṭikkhipanto āha “vīriyasampayuttaṃ samatha”nti. Iminā vīriyena sampayuttaṃ samathaṃ vīriyasamathanti dasseti. “Vīriyaṃ samathena yojehī”ti iminā vīriyena samathaṃ yojehīti atthopi dassitoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Indriyānañca samatanti ettha saddhādīni pañcindriyāneva gahetabbāni, na aññānīti dassento āha “saddhādīnaṃ indriyāna”nti. “Samabhāva”nti iminā tāpaccayo bhāvatthe hotīti dasseti. Tatthāti “indriyānaṃ samata”ntipāṭhe, saddhādīsu indriyesu vā. Tattha ca nimittaṃ gaṇhāhīti ettha bhāvenabhāvalakkhaṇe thapaccayo hotīti āha “tasmiṃ samathe satī”ti. Ādāse sati mukhabimbena kattubhūtena uppajjitabbaṃ iva, tasmiṃ samathe sati yena nimittena kattubhūtena uppajjitabbanti yojanā. Samathassa nimittaṃ samathanimittaṃ, indriyānaṃ samabhāvo. Eseva nayo sesesupi. Samathanimittādīni cattāri ekasesena vā sāmaññaniddesena vā “nimitta”nti vuccati.

243. Regarding Makkhito, it shows that when phuṭo is said, meaning 'it touches, it spreads, it pervades,' the spreading of the root phur has the meaning of being smeared. Yatthāti means 'in which place.' By this, it is shown that 'a place where cows are struck' (gavāghātana) is derived from 'cows are struck here' (gāvo āhananti ettha). Tantissareti refers to the sound of the string. Vādanakusaloti means 'skilled in playing.' Kharamucchitāti means 'sounded harshly.' By Sarasampannā, it shows that saravatī means 'it possesses sound,' referring to a lute (vīṇā). Here, regarding Kammaññā, it says that the suffix -ñña from the word kamma is in the sense of 'fit for,' hence it is said kammakkhamā (fit for work). Mandamucchanāti means 'sounded softly.' Here, regarding Same guṇeti, sama means middle, and guṇa primarily means the string of the lute, and figuratively the sound; hence, it is said majjhime sare (in the middle sound). Here, regarding Vīriyasamatha, rejecting the meaning 'energy and calm,' it says vīriyasampayuttaṃ samatha (calm associated with energy). By this, it shows that calm associated with energy is called vīriyasamatha. It should be understood that by 'yoke energy with calm,' the meaning 'yoke calm with energy' is also shown. Here, regarding Indriyānañca samataṃ, showing that only the five faculties beginning with faith should be taken, not others, it says saddhādīnaṃ indriyānaṃ (of the faculties beginning with faith). By Samabhāva, it shows that the suffix -tā is in the sense of 'state.' Here, regarding tatthāti in the reading indriyānaṃ samataṃ, or in the faculties such as faith. Here, regarding Tattha ca nimittaṃ gaṇhāhīti (and grasp the sign there), it says that the suffix -tha is in the sense of a locative absolute (bhāvenabhāvalakkhaṇa), hence it says tasmiṃ samathe sati (when that calm exists). Just as when there is a mirror, a reflection of the face should arise as the agent, so when that calm exists, the sign by which something arises as the agent—this is the connection. The sign of calm (samathanimitta) is the balanced state of the faculties. The same method applies to the rest. The four—samathanimitta and so on—are called 'sign' (nimitta), either by ellipsis (ekasesa) or by generic designation.

244. Aññaṃ [V 2.0004] byākareyyanti ettha aññaṃ byākaronto attānaṃ “arahā aha”nti jānāpetīti āha “arahā aha”nti jānāpeyya”nti. Cha ṭhānānīti ettha ṭhānasaddo kāraṇatthoti āha “cha kāraṇānī”ti[M 0.0334]. “Paṭivijjhitvā”tiādinā adhimuttoti padassa adhippāyatthaṃ dasseti. Saddattho pana adhimuccatīti adhimuttoti daṭṭhabbo. Arahattaṃ vuccatīti sambandho. Hīti vitthāro. Asammohotīti ettha ākāratthavācako itisaddo pubbapadesupi yojetvā “nekkhamaṃ iti vuccatī”tiādinā yojanā kātabbā.

244. Regarding 'should declare another,' here, because by declaring another one makes oneself known as 'I am an Arahant,' he said, 'should make known, "I am an Arahant."' Regarding 'six bases,' here, because the word 'base' (ṭhāna) has the meaning of 'cause,' he said, 'six causes.' By 'having penetrated,' and so on, he shows the intended meaning of the word adhimutto. But the literal meaning should be understood as: 'he is resolved' (adhimuccati), hence adhimutto. The connection is: 'Arahantship is said.' Hī is for detail. Regarding asammoho ti, here the particle iti, which expresses manner, should be connected with the preceding terms as well, and the construction should be made as in 'renunciation is thus called,' and so on.

“Paṭivedharahita”nti iminā kevalaṃ saddhāmattakanti ettha mattasaddassa nivattetabbatthaṃ dasseti. Paṭivedhapaññāyāti maggapaññāya. “Asammissa”nti iminā kevalasaddassa asammissatthaṃ dasseti. Paṭicayanti ettha paṭisaddo anupacchinnattho, cidhātu vaḍḍhanatthoti āha “punappunaṃ karaṇena vaḍḍhi”nti, maggapaṭivedhena vītarāgattāyevāti sambandho. Tanninnamānasoyevāti tasmiṃ phalasamāpattivihāre ninnamānaso eva.

By 'devoid of penetration,' he shows what is to be excluded by the word matta in 'merely faith alone.' 'By the wisdom of penetration' means 'by the wisdom of the path.' By 'unmixed,' he shows that the word kevala has the meaning of 'unmixed.' Regarding paṭicayanti, here the prefix paṭi- has the meaning of 'uninterrupted,' and the root ci has the meaning of 'growth'; thus he said, 'growth through repeated doing.' The connection is: precisely because of being free from lust through the penetration of the path. Tanninnamānaso yeva means 'with mind inclined solely towards that abiding in the attainment of fruition.'

Lābhasakkārasilokanti ettha labhanaṃ lābho, suṭṭhu karaṇaṃ sakkāro, silokanaṃ vaṇṇabhaṇanaṃ siloko, lābho ca sakkāro ca siloko ca lābhasakkārasilokanti atthaṃ dassento āha “catupaccayalābhañcā”tiādi. Tesaṃyevāti catunnaṃ paccayānameva. “Sīlañca vatañcā”ti iminā sīlabbatantipadassa dvandavākyaṃ dasseti.

Regarding lābhasakkārasiloka, here, 'getting' is lābha (gain), 'doing well' is sakkāra (honor), 'praising, speaking of qualities' is siloka (fame). Showing the meaning that 'gain and honor and fame' is lābhasakkārasiloka, he said, 'and the gain of the four requisites,' and so on. Tesaṃ yeva means 'of just the four requisites.' By 'both virtue and observance,' he shows the analysis of the dvandva compound sīlabbata.

Bhusasaddassa kaliṅgaratthaṃ paṭikkhipanto āha “balavanto”ti “khīṇāsavassā”ti iminā nevassāti ettha tasaddassa visayaṃ dasseti. “Gahetvā”ti iminā pariyādiyantīti ettha paripubbaāpubbadādhātuyā gahaṇatthaṃ dasseti. Hīti saccaṃ. Kilesā karontīti sambandho. Tesanti kilesānaṃ. Āneñjappattanti ettha iñjanaṃ kampanaṃ iñjaṃ, na iñjaṃ aneñjaṃ, tameva āneñjaṃ, taṃ pattanti āneñjappattanti atthaṃ dassento āha “acalanappatta”nti. Vayañcāti casaddo avuttasampiṇḍanatthoti āha “vayampi uppādampī”ti.

Rejecting the meaning 'chaff' for the word bhusa, he said, 'powerful.' By 'of one whose taints are destroyed,' he shows the scope of the pronoun ta in nevassa. By 'having taken,' he shows that in pariyādiyanti, the root dā with the prefixes pari- and ā- has the meaning of 'taking.' Hī means 'truly.' The connection is: 'the defilements do.' Tesaṃ means 'of the defilements.' Regarding āneñjappatta, here, showing the meaning: 'shaking' is iñjanaṃ or iñjaṃ (movement); 'not movement' is aneñjaṃ (unmoving); that very aneñjaṃ is āneñjaṃ; 'attained that' is āneñjappatta, he said, 'attained the unshakeable.' Regarding vayañca, the particle ca is for including what is unsaid; thus he said, 'both cessation and arising.'

Upādānakkhayassāti ettha upādānakkhayaṃ adhimuttassāti dassento āha “upayogatthe sāmivacana”nti. “Uppādañca vayañcā”ti iminā āyatanuppādanti [M 0.0335] ettha uppādasaddena vayopi avinābhāvato gahetabboti dasseti. Sammāti nipāto ñāyatthoti āha “hetunā nayenā”ti. Santacittassāti ettha santasaddassa khedādīsupi pavattattā idha nibbutatthe vattatīti āha “nibbutacittassā”ti. Anunayapaṭighehīti anu punappunaṃ ārammaṇe cittaṃ netīti anunayo, [V 2.0005] rāgo, ārammaṇe paṭihaññatīti paṭigho, doso, anunayo ca paṭigho ca anunayapaṭighā, tehi. Iṭṭhe anunayo, aniṭṭhe paṭigho hotīti sambandho daṭṭhabbo.

Regarding upādānakkhayassa (of the destruction of clinging), showing that it means 'of one intent on' the destruction of clinging, he said, 'the genitive case is in the sense of relation (upayoga).' By 'both arising and cessation,' he shows that here, regarding āyatanuppāda (arising of the sense bases), by the word uppāda (arising), vaya (cessation) should also be taken due to their inseparability. Sammā is a particle in the sense of 'rightly'; thus he said, 'by cause and method.' Regarding santacittassa (of one with a tranquil mind), since the word santa also occurs in contexts like 'weariness,' he said nibbutacittassa (of one with a cooled mind) because here it is used in the sense of 'extinguished' (nibbuta). Regarding anunayapaṭighehi (by attachment and aversion): anunayo is so called because it repeatedly leads the mind towards an object, which is lust; paṭigha is so called because it is repelled by an object, which is aversion. Anunayapaṭighā refers to both attachment and aversion; 'by them.' The connection should be seen as: attachment towards the desirable and aversion towards the undesirable.

148. Diguṇādiupāhanapaṭikkhepakathā

148. The Discourse on the Rejection of Double-Layered Sandals and Other Footwear

245. Aññaṃ byākarontīti ettha aññasaddo sabbanāmasuddhanāmavasena duvidho. Tesu idha suddhanāmaṃ, taṃ pana bāle ca dārake ca arahatte ca pavattati, idha pana arahatteti dassento āha “arahattaṃ byākarontī”ti. Yenāti sabhāvena. Arahāti ñāyatīti arahāiti attho ñāyati. Soti sabhāvo. Suttavaṇṇanātoyevāti aṅguttaraṭṭhakathāto eva. Na upanītoti na upari nīto. Ekacce moghapurisāti ekaccesaddo aññepariyāyo, moghasaddo tucchavevacanoti āha “aññe pana tucchapurisā”ti. “Hasamānā viyā”ti iminā hasamānakaṃ maññeti ettha maññesaddo viyatthoti dasseti. Asantamevāti avijjamānaṃyeva. Ekapalāsikanti ettha palāsasaddo paṇṇavācako. Paṭalaṃ nāma paṇṇaṃ viya hoti, tasmā “ekapaṭala”nti vuttaṃ. Asītisakaṭavāheti ettha asīti padaṃ sakaṭapadena sambandhaṃ katvā asītisakaṭehi vahitabbeti attho daṭṭhabbo. “Dve sakaṭabhārā eko vāho”ti iminā vāhānaṃ cattālīsabhāvaṃ dasseti. Sattahatthikañca anīkanti ettha anīkassa sarūpaṃ dassento āha “cha hatthiniyo cā”tiādi. Sattannaṃ hatthīnaṃ samūho sattahatthikaṃ. Sattaanīkattā ekūnapaññāsahatthino honti. Tesu satta hatthino, dvācattālīsa [M 0.0336] hatthiniyo honti. Dviguṇāti ettha guṇasaddo paṭalatthoti āha “dvipaṭalā”ti. Guṇaṅguṇūpāhanāti ettha dviguṇatiguṇānaṃ visuṃ gahitattā pārisesato guṇaṅguṇabhāvaṃ dassento āha “catupaṭalato paṭṭhāya vuccatī”ti. Guṇaṅguṇūpāhanāti paṭalapaṭalā upāhanā, bahupaṭalā upāhanāti attho. Ukārena saha yojetvā gakāro sajjhāyitabbo ca likhitabbo ca. Idāni potthakesu pana ukāro na dissati.

245. Regarding 'declaring another' (aññaṃ byākaronti), here the word 'añña' is twofold, as a pronoun and as a pure noun. Among these, here it is a pure noun, and it applies to fools, children, and arahants. Here, indicating arahantship, it is said, 'declaring arahantship.' Regarding 'by which' (yena), it means 'by its nature' (sabhāvena). Regarding 'arahant' (arahā), it means 'is understood as worthy' (ñāyatīti arahā); thus the meaning is understood. That (so) is its nature. Regarding 'as in the Sutta commentary' (suttavaṇṇanātoyeva), it means 'as in the Aṅguttara commentary itself' (aṅguttaraṭṭhakathāto eva). Regarding 'not brought up' (na upanīto), it means 'not brought above' (na upari nīto). Regarding 'some foolish men' (ekacce moghapurisā), the word 'ekacce' is a synonym for 'aññe' (others), and the word 'mogha' is a synonym for 'tuccha' (empty); hence, it is said, 'others, empty men' (aññe pana tucchapurisā). By 'as if laughing' (hasamānā viyā), it shows that here the word 'maññeti' is in the sense of 'viya' (as if). Regarding 'nonexistent indeed' (asantameva), it means 'simply not existing' (avijjamānaṃyeva). Regarding 'one palāsa' (ekapalāsikaṃ), here the word 'palāsa' refers to a leaf (paṇṇa). A 'paṭala' is like a leaf; therefore, it is called 'one paṭala' (ekapaṭalaṃ). Regarding 'eighty cartloads' (asītisakaṭavāha), here the word 'eighty' (asīti) should be connected with the word 'cart' (sakaṭa), and the meaning should be understood as 'to be carried by eighty carts' (asītisakaṭehi vahitabbeti). By 'two cartloads are one haul' (dve sakaṭabhārā eko vāho), it indicates that there are forty hauls. Regarding 'seven elephants and a troop' (sattahatthikañca anīkaṃ), here, to show the form of a troop, it is said, 'and six female elephants' (cha hatthiniyo cā), etc. A group of seven elephants is called 'sattahatthikaṃ.' Being seven troops, there are forty-nine elephants. Among them, seven are male elephants and forty-two are female elephants. Regarding 'double' (dviguṇā), here the word 'guṇa' means 'layer' (paṭala); hence, it is said, 'two layers' (dvipaṭalā). Regarding 'guṇaṅguṇūpāhanā' (sandals with layers upon layers), here, because 'double' (dviguṇa) and 'triple' (tiguṇa) are taken separately, to show the remaining aspect of being 'layer upon layer' (guṇaṅguṇa), it is said, 'starting from four layers, it is called' (catupaṭalato paṭṭhāya vuccati). The meaning of 'guṇaṅguṇūpāhanā' is 'sandals with layers upon layers' (paṭalapaṭalā upāhanā), that is, 'sandals with many layers' (bahupaṭalā upāhanā). The letter 'ga' should be recited and written together with the vowel 'u'. Now, however, the vowel 'u' is not seen in the books.

149. Sabbanīlikādipaṭikkhepakathā

149. The Discourse on the Rejection of All-Blue Sandals and So Forth

246. Sabbāva nīlikāti sabbāva upāhanāyo nīlikā, sabbaṭṭhānesu nīlametāsanti sabbanīlikātipi kātabbo. Tattha cāti tesu nīlikādīsu ca. Ummārapupphassa vaṇṇo viya vaṇṇo etissāti ummārapupphavaṇṇā. Evaṃ sesesupi. Addāriṭṭhakavaṇṇāti ettha addoti allo. Ariṭṭhoti pheṇilarukkho vā kāko vā, tasmā addo allo ariṭṭho pheṇilarukkho, kāko vāti addāriṭṭho, tadeva addāriṭṭhako, addāriṭṭhakassa vaṇṇo viya vaṇṇo etissāti addāriṭṭhakavaṇṇā[V 2.0006]. Etāsūti sabbanīlikādīsu. Puñchitvāti parimajjitvā. Appamattakenāpīti pisaddo sambhāvane. Sabbanīlādike bhinne kā nāma kathāti attho.

246. Regarding 'all-blue' (sabbāva nīlikā), it means 'all sandals are blue' (sabbāva upāhanāyo nīlikā); it should also be understood as 'they are blue in all places' (sabbaṭṭhānesu nīlametāsaṃ), hence 'all-blue' (sabbanīlikā). Regarding 'and there' (tattha ca), it means 'and among those blue sandals and so forth' (tesu nīlikādīsu ca). Regarding 'ummārapupphavaṇṇā' (the color of the ummāra flower), it means 'its color is like the color of the ummāra flower' (ummārapupphassa vaṇṇo viya vaṇṇo etissā). Similarly for the rest. Regarding 'addāriṭṭhakavaṇṇā' (the color of the addāriṭṭhaka), here 'addo' means 'allo' (wet). 'Ariṭṭho' is either the soap-nut tree (pheṇilarukkho) or a crow (kāko). Therefore, 'addāriṭṭho' means a wet soap-nut tree or a wet crow; that itself is 'addāriṭṭhako'. Its color is like the color of the addāriṭṭhaka, hence 'addāriṭṭhakavaṇṇā'. Regarding 'among these' (etāsu), it means 'among all the all-blue sandals and so forth' (sabbanīlikādīsu). Regarding 'having wiped' (puñchitvā), it means 'having cleaned' (parimajjitvā). Regarding 'even with a small amount' (appamattakenāpi), the particle 'pi' is used for possibility. The meaning is: When all-blue sandals and so forth are broken, what is there to say?

“Yāsaṃ vaddhāyeva nīlā”ti iminā nīlakā vaddhikā etāsanti nīlakavaddhikāti chaṭṭhībāhiratthasamāsaṃ dasseti. Vaddhikāti ca naddhi. Sā hi upāhanatalato vaddhayatīti vaddhikāti ca upāhanatalaṃ bandhati imāyāti vaddhikāti ca vuccati. Sabbatthāti sabbesu pītakavaddhikādīsu. Etāyopīti nīlakavaddhikādikā upāhanāyopi. Taleti upāhanāya tale. “Khallakaṃ bandhitvā”ti iminā khallakena bandhitabbāti khallakabaddhāti vacanatthaṃ dasseti. Yonakaupāhanāti yonakajātīnaṃ manussānaṃ upāhanā. Paliguṇṭhetvāti parisamantato veṭhetvā. “Upari…pe… jaṅgha”nti iminā puṭabaddhato visesaṃ dasseti. Tūlapicunāti tūlasaṅkhātena picunā. “Tittirapattasadisā”ti iminā tittirassa [M 0.0337] pattaṃ viya tittirapattikāti vacanatthaṃ dasseti. Tittiroti ca eko sakuṇaviseso. Kaṇṇikaṭṭhāneti dvinnaṃ vaddhikānaṃ ekato samāgamaṭṭhāne. “Meṇḍa…pe… katā”ti iminā meṇḍassa visāṇena sadisā vaddhikā etāsanti meṇḍavisāṇavaddhikāti vacanatthaṃ dasseti. Tathevāti yathā meṇḍaajasiṅgasaṇṭhāne vaddhe yojetvā katā, tathevāti attho. “Vicchikā…pe… katā”ti iminā vicchikāya aḷo vicchikāḷo, so viya vaddhikā etāsanti vicchikāḷikāti vacanatthaṃ dasseti. Aḷasaddo “aḷacchinno”tiādīsu (mahāva. 119) aṅguṭṭhavācako, idha pana naṅguṭṭhavācako, tasmā vuttaṃ “naṅguṭṭhasaṇṭhāne”ti. Talesūti upāhanāya talesu. “Mora…pe… sibbikā”ti iminā morapiñchehi parisamantato, parikkhipitvā vā sibbitā morapiñchaparisibbitāti vacanatthaṃ dasseti. Citrā upāhanāyoti ettha citrasaddo vicitratthoti āha “vicitrā”ti. Etāsūti khallakabaddhādīsu. Vaḷañjetabbāti paribhuñjitabbā. Vaḷaji paribhogeti dhātupāṭho (saddanītidhātumālāyaṃ 15 jakārantadhātu). Tālujo tatiyo. Tesu panāti khallakādīsu pana. Sati santesūti yojanā. Sīhacammena parikkhipitabbāti sīhacammaparikkhatāti vacanatthaṃ dassento āha “pariyantesū”tiādi. Pakkhibiḷāloti tuliyo. So hi pakkhayuttattā ca biḷālamukhasadisamukhattā ca pakkhibiḷāloti vuccati. Iminā luvakacammaparikkhatāti ettha luvakasaddo pakkhibiḷālapariyāyoti dasseti. “Ulūkacammaparikkhatā”tipi pāṭho. Etāsupīti sīhacammaparikkhatādīsupi. Yā kāci upāhanāyoti sambandho.

By 'those whose bindings are blue' (yāsaṃ vaddhāyeva nīlā), it indicates the meaning of 'nīlakavaddhikā' (blue-bound) as 'those whose bindings are blue' (nīlakā vaddhikā etāsaṃ), showing a sixth-case external compound. And 'vaddhikā' (binding) is a fastening (naddhi). For it is called 'vaddhikā' because it grows (vaddhayati) from the sole of the sandal, and it is called 'vaddhikā' because the sole of the sandal is bound by it. Regarding 'in all cases' (sabbattha), it means 'in all instances, such as yellow bindings and so forth' (sabbesu pītakavaddhikādīsu). Regarding 'even these' (etāyopi), it means 'even blue-bound sandals and so forth' (nīlakavaddhikādikā upāhanāyopi). Regarding 'on the sole' (tale), it means 'on the sole of the sandal' (upāhanāya tale). By 'having bound with a leather strip' (khallakaṃ bandhitvā), it indicates the meaning of the term 'khallakabaddhā' (leather-strip-bound) as 'to be bound with a leather strip' (khallakena bandhitabbā). Regarding 'Yona footwear' (yonakaupāhanā), it means 'the footwear of people of the Yona race' (yonakajātīnaṃ manussānaṃ upāhanā). Regarding 'having wrapped around' (paliguṇṭhetvā), it means 'having encircled on all sides' (parisamantato veṭhetvā). By 'above... up to the shin' (upari…pe… jaṅghaṃ), it indicates the distinction from being bound in a bundle (puṭabaddhato). Regarding 'with cotton wool' (tūlapicunā), it means 'with cotton, which is called picu' (tūlasaṅkhātena picunā). By 'like a partridge’s feather' (tittirapattasadisā), it indicates the meaning of 'tittirapattikā' (partridge-feathered) as 'like the feather of a partridge' (tittirassa pattaṃ viya). And 'tittiro' is a specific type of bird. Regarding 'at the joining place' (kaṇṇikaṭṭhāne), it means 'at the place where two bindings meet together' (dvinnaṃ vaddhikānaṃ ekato samāgamaṭṭhāne). By 'made like a ram’s horn' (meṇḍa…pe… katā), it indicates the meaning of 'meṇḍavisāṇavaddhikā' (ram-horn-bound) as 'those whose bindings are like a ram’s horn' (meṇḍassa visāṇena sadisā vaddhikā etāsaṃ). Regarding 'similarly' (tatheva), the meaning is 'just as they are made by fitting bindings in the shape of a ram’s or goat’s horn, so too here.' By 'made like a scorpion’s sting' (vicchikā…pe… katā), it indicates the meaning of 'vicchikāḷikā' (scorpion-sting-bound) as 'those whose bindings are like a scorpion’s sting (vicchikāḷo), which is the sting of a scorpion' (vicchikāya aḷo). The word 'aḷa' in phrases like 'aḷacchinno' (Mahāva. 119) refers to a finger or toe, but here it refers to a tail; therefore, it is stated 'in the shape of a tail' (naṅguṭṭhasaṇṭhāne). Regarding 'on the soles' (talesu), it means 'on the soles of the sandal' (upāhanāya talesu). By 'stitched with peacock feathers' (mora…pe… sibbikā), it indicates the meaning of 'morapiñchaparisibbitā' (stitched all around with peacock feathers) as 'stitched all around with peacock feathers, or covered and stitched' (morapiñchehi parisamantato, parikkhipitvā vā sibbitā). Regarding 'variegated footwear' (citrā upāhanāyo), here the word 'citra' means 'multicolored' (vicitra); hence, it is said, 'multicolor' (vicitrā). Regarding 'among these' (etāsu), it means 'among leather-strip-bound sandals and so forth' (khallakabaddhādīsu). Regarding 'should be used' (vaḷañjetabbā), it means 'should be worn' (paribhuñjitabbā). The Dhātupāṭha states 'vaḷaji' means 'to use' (paribhoge) (in Saddanīti’s Dhātumālā, the 15th root ending in 'ja'). 'Tālujo' is the third. Regarding 'among these' (tesu pana), it means 'among leather-strip-bound sandals and so forth' (khallakādīsu pana). The connection is 'when present, being present' (sati santesu). Regarding 'should be encircled with lion skin' (sīhacammena parikkhipitabbā), to indicate the meaning of 'sīhacammaparikkhatā' (lion-skin-covered), it is said, 'around the edges' (pariyantesu), etc. Regarding 'pakkhibiḷālo', it means 'a flying squirrel' (tuliyo). For it is called 'pakkhibiḷālo' because it is adorned with feathers (pakkhayuttattā) and has a face resembling a cat’s face (biḷālamukhasadisamukhattā). By this, it shows that in 'luvakacammaparikkhatā' (covered with luvaka skin), the word 'luvaka' is synonymous with 'pakkhibiḷālo'. The reading 'covered with owl skin' (ulūkacammaparikkhatā) is also found. Regarding 'among these too' (etāsupi), it means 'among lion-skin-covered sandals and so forth' (sīhacammaparikkhatādīsupi). The connection is 'whatever footwear' (yā kāci upāhanāyo).

247. Omukkanti ettha avatyūpasaggassa viyogatthaṃ dassento āha “paṭimuñcitvā apanīta”nti. Purāṇaṃ guṇaṅguṇūpāhananti attho.

247. Regarding 'omukkaṃ' (removed), here, to show the meaning of separation of the prefix 'ava', it is said, 'having released and removed' (paṭimuñcitvā apanītaṃ). The meaning is 'old sandals with layers upon layers' (purāṇaṃ guṇaṅguṇūpāhanaṃ).

151. Ajjhārāme upāhanapaṭikkhepakathā

151. The Discourse on the Prohibition of Footwear Within the Monastery

248. “Yena [V 2.0007] sippenā”tiādinā abhi adhikaṃ jīvanti anenāti abhijīvanaṃ, kiṃtaṃ? Sippanti atthaṃ dasseti. Tassāti sippassa[M 0.0338]. Idhāti imasmiṃ sāsane. Yaṃsaddo vacanavipallāsoti āha “ye tumhe”ti. Hīti saccaṃ. Yaṃnipātoti yaṃiti nipāto yadisaddassa atthe pavattatīti yojanā. Ācariyā evāti evasaddena ācariyamattabhāvaṃ paṭikkhipati. Hīti saccaṃ. Soti avassiko. Tanti chabbassaṃ. Nissāya vacchatīti avassikassa catuvassakāle chabbassassa dasavassikattā taṃ nissāya vasati. Upajjhāyamattaṃ dassento āha “upajjhāyassā”tiādi. Mahantatarāti attano vuḍḍhatarā. Upajjhāyassa mattaṃ pamāṇametesanti upajjhāyamattā.

248. 'By which craft,' and so on—by this they live excessively, hence 'abhijīvana' (excessive livelihood). What is that? It indicates the meaning of 'craft.' 'Of that' means of the craft. 'Here' means in this dispensation. The word 'yaṃ' is a change of wording; hence, it is said, 'ye tumhe (you who).' 'Hī' means truly. The particle 'yaṃ' functions in the sense of the word 'yadi' (if); thus is the connection. 'Teachers indeed'—by the word 'eva,' it rejects the mere status of a teacher. 'Hī' means truly. 'So' means he is an avassika. 'That' means six years. 'He lives depending on it'—because for an avassika of four years, a monk of six years has the status of a monk of ten years, he lives in dependence on that. Showing the measure of a preceptor, it is said, 'of the preceptor,' and so on. 'Greater' means more senior than oneself. 'Their measure is the measure of a preceptor'—thus they are 'of the measure of a preceptor'.

249. Pādato nikkhantena khīlasadisena maṃsena pavatto ābādho pādakhīlābādhoti vacanatthaṃ dassento āha “pādato”tiādi. Pādato nikkhantanti sambandho.

249. To explain the meaning of the term 'foot-stake ailment' as 'the ailment that occurs from flesh like a stake emerging from the foot,' it is said, 'from the foot,' and so on. The connection is 'emerged from the foot'.

251. Tiṇapādukātiādīsu tiṇena katā pādukā tiṇapādukāti vacanatthādiṃ dassento āha “yena kenaci tiṇenā”tiādi. Taṃ suviññeyyameva. “Bhūmiyaṃ suppatiṭṭhitāti”ādinā na saṅkamitabbāti asaṅkamanīyāti atthaṃ dasseti.

251. In 'grass sandals,' and so on, explaining the meaning of the term 'grass sandals' as 'sandals made of grass,' he says, 'by any kind of grass,' and so on. That is easily understandable. By 'well-fixed on the ground,' and so on, he indicates the meaning that it should not be moved, that is, 'immovable.'

252. Aṅgajātenevāti attano aṅgajātena eva. Aṅgajātanti gāvīnaṃ aṅgajātaṃ. Ogāhetvāti ettha otyūpasaggo daḷhatthoti āha “daḷhaṃ gahetvā”ti.

252. 'By his own organ of generation' means just by his own organ of generation. 'Organ of generation' means the organ of generation of cows. In 'having plunged into,' here the prefix 'o' has the meaning of firmness; therefore, he says, 'having firmly grasped.'

153. Yānādipaṭikkhepakathā

153. The Discourse on the Prohibition of Conveyances, and so on.

253. Itthiyuttenāti ettha rūḷīvasena dhenupi itthī nāmāti āha “dhenuyuttenā”ti. Purisantarenāti ettha puriso eva antaro añño etthāti purisantaraṃ yānaṃ. Purisantaro nāma atthato sārathīti āha “purisasārathinā”ti, yānenāti yojanā. Gaṅgāmahiyāyāti ettha gaṅgā ca mahī ca gaṅgāmahī, tattha kīḷikā gaṅgāmahiyāti atthaṃ dassento āha “gaṅgāmahīkīḷikāyā”ti. Tattha hi itthipurisā yānehi udakakīḷaṃ kīḷanti. Purisayuttaṃ [M 0.0339] hatthavaṭṭakanti ettha “anujānāmi bhikkhave purisayuttañca hatthavaṭṭakañcā”ti dassento āha “etthā”tiādi. Tattha purisayuttanti purisena yujjitabbanti purisayuttaṃ yānaṃ. Hatthavaṭṭakanti hatthena [V 2.0008] vaṭṭetabbanti hatthavaṭṭakaṃ yānaṃ. Yānugghātenāti yānassa ullaṅghitvā gamanena. Hanadhātu hi gatyattho. Tamatthaṃ dassento āha “yānaṃ abhiruhantassā”tiādi. “Tappaccayā”ti iminā yānugghātenāti ettha hetvatthe karaṇavacananti dasseti. Pīṭhakasivikanti pīṭhena saha kataṃ sivikaṃ. Paṭapoṭalikanti paṭamayaṃ poṭalikaṃ.

253. 'Itthiyuttena' (yoked with a woman): Here, according to common usage, even a cow is called a woman, hence it is said, 'dhenuyuttena' (yoked with a cow). 'Purisantarena' (with a man as intermediary): Here, a man is indeed the intermediary, another in this case; hence, a vehicle with a man as intermediary. 'Purisantara' means, in essence, the charioteer, hence it is said, 'purisasārathinā' (with a man as charioteer). This connects with 'yānena' (by means of a vehicle). 'Gaṅgāmahiyāya' (on the Ganges-earth): Here, the Ganges and the earth are 'Gaṅgāmahī,' and the play there is 'Gaṅgāmahī'; explaining this meaning, he says, 'gaṅgāmahīkīḷikāya' (in the Ganges-earth play). For there, men and women play water-sports with vehicles. 'Purisayuttaṃ hatthavaṭṭakaṃ' (a vehicle yoked with men and a hand-turned vehicle): Here, to indicate 'I allow, monks, a vehicle yoked with men and a hand-turned vehicle,' it is said, 'here,' and so on. There, 'purisayuttaṃ' means that which is yoked with a man; hence, a vehicle yoked with a man. 'Hatthavaṭṭakaṃ' means that which is turned by hand; hence, a hand-turned vehicle. 'Yānugghātena' means by passing over the vehicle. The root 'han' indeed has the meaning of going. To indicate that meaning, it is said, 'of one mounting the vehicle,' and so on. By 'tappaccayā' (due to that cause), it is shown that in 'yānugghātena,' the instrumental case is used in the sense of reason or cause. 'Pīṭhakasivikaṃ' (a palanquin with a seat): a palanquin made with a seat. 'Paṭapoṭalikaṃ' (a cloth bundle): a bundle made of cloth.

154. Uccāsayanamahāsayanapaṭikkhepakathā

154. The Discourse on the Prohibition of High and Large Beds.

254. Uccaṃ āsayanaṃ uccāsayanaṃ. Mahantaṃ āsayanaṃ mahāsayanaṃ. Āsandiādīsu evaṃ vinicchayo veditabboti yojanā. Pamāṇātikkantāsananti dīghāsanaṃ. Tañhi āgamma sadati nisīdatīti ettha, āyataṃ vā suṭṭhuṃ dadātīti āsandīti vuccati. Vāḷarūpānīti sīhabyagghādivāḷarūpāni. Pādesu vāḷarūpāni paricchinditvā aṅkīyati lakkhīyatīti pallaṅko. Gonakoti gavati dīghalomehi uggacchati etthāti gonako. Kojavoti kuyaṃ bhūmiyaṃ javati gacchatīti kojavo. Tassāti gonakassa. Lomāni caturaṅgulādhikāni honti kirāti yojanā. Vānacitrauṇṇāmayattharaṇoti vānena sibbanena sañjātaṃ citrarūpametthāti vānacitraṃ, uṇṇāya nibbatto uṇṇāmayo, soyeva attharaṇo uṇṇāmayattharaṇo, vānacitrañca taṃ uṇṇāmayattharaṇo ceti vānacitrauṇṇāmayattharaṇo. Setattharaṇoti setatthikehi sevīyatīti soto, soyeva attharaṇo setattharaṇo. Iminā atthena paṭati setabhāvaṃ gacchatīti paṭikāti kātabbaṃ. Paṭikāsaddoyaṃ aḍḍhendupāsāṇepi pavattati. Ghanapupphakoti ghanaṃ kathinaṃ pupphametthāti ghanapupphako. Iminā ghanapupphasaṅkhātaṃ paṭalamettha atthīti paṭalikāti dasseti. Soti attharaṇo. Āmalakapaṭoti āmalakapupphaṃ dassetvā kato paṭo. Tūlikāti tūlaṃ pūretvā [M 0.0340] katā tūlikā. Vikatikāti sīhabyagghādirūpehi (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.15) vicittākārena karīyatīti vikatikā. Dīghanikāyaṭṭhakathāyaṃ “uddalomīti ubhatodasaṃ uṇṇāmayattharaṇaṃ. Ekantalomīti ekatodasaṃ uṇṇāmayattharaṇa”nti vuttaṃ. Idha pana “uddalomīti ekato uggatalomaṃ uṇṇāmayattharaṇaṃ, ekantalomīti ubhato uggatalomaṃ uṇṇāmayattharaṇa”nti vuttaṃ. Tasmā dve aṭṭhakathāyo aññamaññaṃ visadisā honti. Ettha dīghanikāyaṭṭhakathānayena vacanatthaṃ karissāmi. Uṭṭhitaṃ dvīhi pakkhehi, dvīsu vā dasāsaṅkhātaṃ lomametthāti uddalomī. Niggahitāgamaṃ katvā “undalomī”tipi pāṭho, ayamevattho. Ekasmiṃ ante dasāsaṅkhātaṃ lomametthāti ekantalomīti. Koseyyakaṭṭissamayanti ettha koseyyanti kosiyasuttaṃ. Kaṭṭissanti kaṭṭissanāmakaṃ vākaṃ. Iminā koseyyañca kaṭṭissañca kaṭṭissānīti virūpekasesaṃ katvā kaṭṭissehi [V 2.0009] pakataṃ attharaṇaṃ kaṭṭissanti atthaṃ dasseti. Suddhakoseyyanti ratanaaparisibbitaṃ suddhakoseyyaṃ. Iminā suddhakaṭṭissampi vaṭṭatīti dasseti.

254. A high bed is a high bed. A large bed is a large bed. In the case of couches, and so on, the determination should be understood in this way—this is the connection. A seat exceeding the measure is a long seat. Because one lies down or sits upon it, or because it is extended or gives well, therefore it is called a couch ('āsandī'). 'Animal-shaped' means animal shapes like lions and tigers. A bed ('pallaṅka') is so called because animal shapes are cut out on its legs and marked or distinguished. 'Gonaka' means that in which long hairs grow upwards. 'Kojava' means that which moves or goes on the ground. 'Of that' refers to the gonaka. The explanation is that the hairs are, it is said, more than four fingers long. 'Vānacitrauṇṇāmayattharaṇa' (a woolen coverlet with variegated designs): 'vānacitra' means a variegated design arising from weaving; 'uṇṇāmaya' means made of wool; that itself is the 'woolen coverlet' (uṇṇāmayattharaṇa); and 'vānacitra' and that 'uṇṇāmayattharaṇa' together form 'vānacitrauṇṇāmayattharaṇa.' 'Setattharaṇa' (a white coverlet): it is resorted to by those desiring white; that itself is the 'white coverlet.' By this meaning, 'paṭikā' should be understood as that which extends and becomes white. The word 'paṭikā' also applies to a half-moon stone. 'Ghanapupphaka' (thickly flowered): means that in which there are thick, hard flowers. By this, he shows that there is a layer called 'thickly flowered,' therefore it is called 'paṭalikā.' That is a coverlet. 'Āmalakapaṭa' (an āmalaka cloth): a cloth made displaying āmalaka flowers. 'Tūlikā' (a cushion): a cushion made by filling it with cotton. 'Vikatikā' (a variegated coverlet): is made in a variegated way with shapes of lions, tigers, etc. In the Dīghanikāya commentary, it is said: 'Uddalomī means a woolen coverlet with a fringe on both sides. Ekantalomī means a woolen coverlet with a fringe on one side.' Here, however, it is said: 'Uddalomī means a woolen coverlet with hair standing up on one side. Ekantalomī means a woolen coverlet with hair standing up on both sides.' Therefore, the two commentaries are mutually contradictory. Here, I will give the meaning according to the Dīghanikāya commentary. 'Uddalomī' means that in which the hair called the fringe stands up on two sides. With the insertion of a niggahita, the reading is also 'undalomī'; this has the same meaning. 'Ekantalomī' means that in which the hair called the fringe is on one end. In 'Koseyyakaṭṭissamaya' (made of silk and bark cloth): here, 'koseyya' means silk thread; 'kaṭṭissa' is a kind of bark cloth called kaṭṭissa. By this, having made a virūpekasesa compound 'koseyyañca kaṭṭissañca kaṭṭissānīti,' he shows the meaning of 'kaṭṭissa' as a coverlet made from kaṭṭissas. 'Suddhakoseyya' (pure silk) means pure silk unadorned with jewels. By this, he shows that pure kaṭṭissa is also allowable.

Soḷasa nāṭakitthiyo ṭhatvā naccaṃ karonti etthāti kuttakanti atthaṃ dassento āha “soḷasanna”ntiādi. Ajinacammehīti ajinamigacammehi, kataiti sambandho. Paveṇīti dupaṭṭatipaṭṭādīhi paraṃparavasena katattā “paveṇī”ti vuccati. Ajinacammāni hi sukhumatarāni, tasmā dupaṭṭatipaṭṭādīni katvā paveṇivasena katāni. Tasmā vuttaṃ “ajinapaveṇī”ti. “Kadalimigacammaṃ nāmā”ti iminā tassa cammaṃ kadalimigaiti gahetabbaṃ uttarapadalopavasena vā upacārena vāti dasseti. Pavarasaddo uttamatthoti āha “uttamapaccattharaṇa”nti. Tanti kadalimigapavarapaccattharaṇaṃ. Sauttaracchadanti ettha sakāro sahasaddakāriyoti dassento āha “saha uttaracchadenā”ti. “Uparī”ti iminā uttarasaddassa seṭṭhādayo nivatteti. “Saddhi”nti iminā sahasaddassa tulyatthaṃ nivatteti. “Seta…pe… na vaṭṭatī”ti iminā rattavitānaṃ heṭṭhā kappiyapaccattharaṇe satipi na vaṭṭatīti dasseti[M 0.0341]. Kasmā? Rattavitānassa akappiyattā. Ubhatolohitakūpadhānanti ettha ubhasarūpaṃ dassetuṃ vuttaṃ “sīsūpadhānañca pādūpadhānañcā”ti. Sīso upagantvā tiṭṭhati etthāti upadhānaṃ, upa bhusaṃ vā sukhaṃ dhāretīti upadhānaṃ, bibbohanaṃ. Sace pamāṇayuttaṃ, taṃ upadhānaṃ vaṭṭatīti yojanā.

Sixteen dancing girls stand and dance here; hence, it is called a 'kuttaka'—thus the meaning is shown by the phrase 'soḷasanna,' and so on. 'Ajinacammehi' (with Ajina hides): with the hides of Ajina deer; 'kata' is the connection. 'Paveṇī' (a long rug): it is called 'paveṇī' because it is made in succession with layers like two-layered and three-layered ones, and so on. The hides of Ajina deer are very fine, so they are made into two-layered and three-layered ones, and so on, and arranged in succession. Therefore, it is said, 'ajinapaveṇī' (a long rug of Ajina hides). By the phrase 'kadalimigacammaṃ nāma' (named kadalimiga hide), it is shown that its hide should be understood as 'kadalimiga,' either by elision of the latter word or by metaphorical usage. The word 'pavara' means supreme; hence, it is said, 'uttamapaccattharaṇa' (supreme coverlet). 'That' refers to the supreme coverlet made of kadalimiga hide. 'Sauttaracchada' (with an upper covering): here, showing that the syllable 'sa' functions like the word 'saha,' it is said, 'saha uttaracchadena' (together with an upper covering). 'Uparī' (above): by this, the meanings of superiority, and so on, of the word 'uttara' are negated. 'Saddhi' (together): by this, the meaning of sameness of the word 'saha' is negated. 'White…and so on…is not permissible': by this, it is shown that even if there is a proper coverlet beneath a red canopy, it is not permissible. Why? Because the red canopy itself is improper. 'Ubhatolohitakūpadhāna' (a pillow red on both sides): here, to show both forms, it is said, 'sīsūpadhānañca pādūpadhānañca' (a head-pillow and a foot-pillow). 'Upadhāna' (a pillow) means that which is placed near the head, or that which provides great comfort; it is a cushion. If it is of the proper size, then that pillow is permissible—this is the interpretation.

155. Sabbacammapaṭikkhepādikathā

155. Account of the Rejection of All Hides, etc.

255. Dīpipotakoti dīpipoto viyāti dīpipotako vaccho. Bhittidaṇḍakādīsūti bhittisambandhesu daṇḍakādīsu. Ādisaddena bhittithambhādayo saṅgaṇhāti.

255. The term 'dīpipotako' means a calf that is like a young leopard. In 'bhittidaṇḍakādīsu' (among the sticks, etc., connected to walls), it means among the sticks, etc., connected to walls. By the word 'ādi' (etc.), wall pillars and the like are included.

256. Yo na sakkoti anupāhano gāmaṃ pavisituṃ, so gilāno nāmāti yojanā.

256. The explanation is: 'He who is unable to enter a village without sandals is called sick.'

157. Soṇakuṭikaṇṇavatthukathā

157. The Story of Soṇakuṭikaṇṇa.

257. Etenāti “kuraraghare”ti pāṭhena. Assāti mahākaccānassa. Papātanāmaketi yasmā mahātaṭo ettha atthi, tasmā papātanāmako hoti. Etenāti “papātake pabbate”ti pāṭhena. Assāti mahākaccānassa. Koṭiagghanakaṃ piḷandhanaṃ kaṇṇe etassatthīti kuṭikaṇṇoti vacanatthaṃ dassento āha “koṭiagghanakaṃ panā”tiādi. Piḷandhati anenāti piḷandhanaṃ, alaṅkāro[V 2.0010]. Dantajo catutthakkharo. “Pasādajanaka”nti iminā pasādaṃ janetīti pāsādikoti vacanatthaṃ dasseti. Pasādanīyanti pasāditabbaṃ, pasādituṃ arahanti attho. Atthavacananti attho vuccati anenāti atthavacanaṃ. Pāḷiyaṃ idāni potthakesu “pasādanīya”nti pāṭho natthi. “Pāsādika”ntipadassa pubbe “dassanīya”nti pāṭhoyeva atthi. Uttamadamathasamathantiettha damathasaddassa ñāṇatthañca indriyasaṃvaratthañca samathasaddassa samādhatthañca cittūpasamatthañca dassento āha “uttamaṃ damathañcā”tiādi. Casaddena dvandavākyaṃ dasseti. Visūkāyikavipphanditānanti visūkāya paṭipakkhāya pavattānaṃ diṭṭhicittasaṅkhātānaṃ vividhacalanānaṃ. “Vīriyindriya”nti iminā yatindriyanti ettha yatasaddo vīriyavācakoti [M 0.0342] dasseti. Nāganti ettha natthi āgu pāpametassāti nāgoti vacanatthaṃ dassento āha “āguvirahita”nti kiṃ divasato paṭṭhāyāti āha “mama pabbajjādivasato paṭṭhāyā”ti. Kaṇhā mattikā uttari etthāti kaṇhuttarāti atthaṃ dassento āha “kaṇhamattikuttarā”ti. “Uparī”ti iminā uttarasaddassa atthaṃ dasseti. “Gunnaṃ khurehī”ti iminā gunnaṃ khurakaṇṭakasadisattā gokaṇṭakā nāmāti dasseti. Te gokaṇṭake rakkhitunti sambandho. Evaṃ kharā bhūmi hotīti yojanā. Etehīti eragūādīhi catūhi tiṇehi. Tanti eragūtiṇaṃ. Tenāti moragūtiṇena. Jantussa vaṇṇoti sambandho. Senāsanaṃ paññapesīti ettha kiṃ nāma senāsanaṃ paññapesīti āha “bhisiṃ vā kaṭasārakaṃ vā paññapesī”ti. Paññapetvā ca pana soṇassa ārocesi. Kiṃ ārocesīti āha “āvuso”tiādi. Satthā vasitukāmoti sambandho.

257. By this, that is, by the reading 'kuraraghare'. 'Assa' refers to Mahākaccāna. It is called Papāta because there is a great cliff here; therefore, it is named Papāta. By this, that is, by the reading 'papātake pabbate'. 'Assa' refers to Mahākaccāna. Showing the meaning of 'kuṭikaṇṇa' as 'he has an ornament worth a crore in his ear,' he says, 'koṭiagghanakaṃ panā,' and so on. 'Piḷandhana' is that by which one adorns oneself; it is an ornament. The fourth letter is dental. By 'pasādajanaka' (inspiring confidence), he shows the meaning of 'pāsādika' as that which inspires confidence. 'Pasādanīya' means that which should be inspired with confidence, that which is worthy of inspiring confidence. 'Atthavacanaṃ' means: the meaning is spoken by this. Now in the Pāli manuscripts, the reading 'pasādanīya' does not exist. Before the word 'pāsādika,' only the reading 'dassanīya' existed. Here, to show the meaning of the word 'damatha' as knowledge and restraint of the senses, and the meaning of the word 'samatha' as concentration and calming of the mind, he says: 'the highest damatha and…,' and so on. The particle 'ca' indicates a dvandva phrase. 'Visūkāyikavipphanditāni' refers to the various agitations, designated as views and thoughts, that arise in opposition to the proper course. By 'vīriyindriya' (the faculty of energy), he shows that in 'yatindriya' (one whose faculties are restrained), the word 'yata' means energy. Regarding 'nāga', showing the meaning 'there is no evil (āgu) for him,' he says 'free from evil.' When asked, 'From what day onwards?' he says, 'From the day of my ordination onwards.' Explaining 'kaṇhuttarā' as 'black earth is superior (uttara) here,' he says 'kaṇhamattikuttarā.' By 'uparī' (above), he shows the meaning of the word 'uttara.' By 'gunnaṃ khurehī' (by the hooves of cattle), he shows that because they are like the hoof-thorns of cattle, they are called 'gokaṇṭaka' (caltrops). The connection is: 'protected by those caltrops.' Thus, the ground is rough—this is the construction. 'Etehi' (by these) refers to the four grasses beginning with eragū. 'Taṃ' (that) refers to eragū grass. 'Tena' (by that) refers to moragū grass. The connection is: 'the color of the creature.' Regarding 'Senāsanaṃ paññapesī' (he prepared a lodging), when asked, 'What kind of lodging did he prepare?' he says, 'He prepared either a mattress or a straw mat.' And having prepared it, he informed Soṇa. What did he inform him of? He says, 'Friend,' and so on. The connection is: 'The Teacher wishes to stay.'

258. “Tassa soṇassā”ti iminā paṭibhātu tanti ettha “ta”ntipadaṃ sāmyatthe upayogavacananti dasseti. Tanti tava. Aṭṭhakavaggikānīti aṭṭhapamāṇo, aṭṭhasamūho vā vaggo etesanti aṭṭhakavaggikāni. Kāmasuttādīni (su. ni. 772 ādayo) soḷasa suttāni. Yoti puggalo, samannāgatoti sambandho. Ariyopīti pisaddo na kevalaṃ sucisamannāgatoyeva pāpe na ramati, atha kho ariyopīti dasseti. “Paṭibhātu ta”nti pāṭhato yāva “sucīti vutta”nti pāṭhā kesuciyeva aṭṭhakathāpotthakesu atthi. Ayaṃ khvassāti ettha assasaddo ākhyātoti āha “bhaveyyā”ti. Paridassesīti pañca varāni paricchinditvā dassesi. Yaṃ vacanaṃ me upajjhāyo jānāpeti, tassa vacanassa ayaṃ kālo bhaveyyāti yojanā.

258. By 'Tassa soṇassā' (of that Soṇa), he shows that here, in 'paṭibhātu taṃ' (let it occur to you), the word 'taṃ' is a usage in the sense of the genitive. 'Taṃ' means 'tava' (your). 'Aṭṭhakavaggikāni': these are called Aṭṭhakavaggikāni because their section (vagga) is of eight in measure or is an eightfold collection. These are the sixteen suttas beginning with the Kāmasutta (Snp 772, etc.). 'Yo' (who) refers to a person; the connection is with 'samannāgato' (endowed with). By 'ariyopi' (even the noble one), the particle 'pi' shows that not only one endowed with purity does not delight in evil, but also the noble one. The reading from 'Paṭibhātu taṃ' up to 'sucīti vuttaṃ' is found only in some commentary manuscripts. In 'Ayaṃ khvassa' (now this would be), he says that the word 'assa' here is a verb meaning 'bhaveyyā' (it would be). 'Paridassesi' (he showed the boundaries): he defined and showed the five boons. The construction is: 'This would be the time for the word that my preceptor makes known to me.'

259. Vinayadharapañcamenāti ettha upajjhāyapañcamenāti atthaṃ paṭikkhipanto āha “anussāvanācariyapañcamenā”ti. Upāhanakosakoti upāhanāya pakkhipanokāso kosako. Eḷakacammaajacammesu akappiyaṃ nāma natthi. Migacamme pana kiñci vaṭṭati, na kiñci vaṭṭati[V 2.0011][M 0.0343]. Taṃ vibhajitvā dassento āha “migacamme”tiādi. Etesaṃyevāti eṇimigādīnaṃ channameva. Aññesaṃ panāti chahi migehi avasesānaṃ pana. Tesaṃ cammaṃ na vaṭṭatīti sambandho.

259. Regarding 'Vinayadharapañcamena' (with a Vinaya expert as the fifth), rejecting the meaning 'with the preceptor as the fifth', he says 'with the recitation teacher as the fifth'. 'Upāhanakosaka': a 'kosaka' (case) is a place for putting a shoe. Among sheepskin and goatskin, there is nothing impermissible. But regarding the hide of wild animals, some is allowable, and some is not. Distinguishing and showing this, he says, 'regarding the hide of wild animals…,' and so on. 'Etesaṃyeva' (only of these) refers to only these six, namely, antelope, deer, etc. But 'aññesaṃ' (of others) refers to the remaining animals apart from these six. The connection is: 'Their hide is not allowable.'

Gāthāyaṃ makkaṭo ca kāḷasīho ca sarabho ca kadalimigo ca keci ye vāḷamigā atthi, te cāti yojanā. Tesanti makkaṭādīnaṃ.

In the verse, the monkey, the black lion, the sarabha, and the plantain deer, as well as any other wild animals that exist, they too—this is the construction. 'Tesaṃ' refers to the monkey and the others.

Tatthāti gāthāya, makkaṭādīsu vā. “Sīhabyagghaacchataracchā”ti iminā vāḷamigānaṃ sarūpaṃ dasseti. Ettakāyeva vāḷamigāti āha “na kevala”ntiādi. Etesaṃyevāti sīhabyagghaacchataracchānameva. Na cammaṃ na vaṭṭatīti sambandho. Yesanti channaṃ eṇimigādīnaṃ. Teti cha eṇimigādike. Hi saccaṃ sabbesaṃ etesaṃ vāḷamigānaṃ cammaṃ na vaṭṭatīti yojanā. Āharitvā vā na dinnanti āharitvā vā hatthe vā pādamūle vā ṭhapetvā na dinnaṃ. “Gaṇanaṃ na upetī”ti iminā gaṇanaṃ upagacchatīti gaṇanūpaganti atthaṃ dasseti. Adhiṭṭhitañcāti adhiṭṭhitaṃ pana. Yadāti yasmiṃ kāle. Tatoti kālato.

'Tattha' (there) refers to in the verse, or among monkeys and the like. By 'Sīhabyagghaacchataracchā' (lions, tigers, bears, hyenas), he shows the nature of wild animals. When asked 'Are only these wild animals?', he says 'not only…,' and so on. 'Etesaṃyeva' (only of these) refers to only lions, tigers, bears, and hyenas. The connection is: 'It is not that their hide is not allowable.' 'Yesaṃ' (of which) refers to the six, such as antelope and deer. 'Te' (those) refers to the six, such as antelope and deer. Indeed, truly, the construction is that the hide of all these wild animals is not allowable. 'Āharitvā vā na dinnaṃ' (even if brought, not given) means that even if brought and placed in the hand or at the foot, it is not given. By 'Gaṇanaṃ na upeti' (it does not enter into the count), he shows the meaning of 'gaṇanūpaga' as 'that which enters into the count.' 'Adhiṭṭhitañca' (and what is determined) means 'adhiṭṭhitaṃ pana' (but what is determined). 'Yadā' (when) means 'at which time.' 'Tato' (thence) means 'from that time.'

Iti cammakkhandhakavaṇṇanāya yojanā samattā.

Thus the explanation in the commentary on the Chapter on Hides is concluded.

6. Bhesajjakkhandhakaṃ

6. The Chapter on Medicaments

160. Pañcabhesajjādikathā

160. The Discourse on the Five Medicines and so on

260. Bhesajjakkhandhake saradakāle uppanno sāradikoti atthaṃ dassento āha “saradakāle uppannenā”ti. “Pittābādhenā”ti iminā ābādhassa sarūpaṃ dasseti. Pittābādhassa kāraṇaṃ vitthārento āha “tasmiṃ hī”tiādi. Tenāti hetunā. Tesanti bhikkhūnaṃ. Koṭṭhabbhantaragatanti koṭṭhassa abbhantaraṃ gataṃ. Antassa anto pavisanaṃ hotīti adhippāyo. Āhāratthanti āhārassa kiccaṃ, āhārena vā kattabbaṃ kiccaṃ.

260. In the Chapter on Medicaments, explaining the meaning of 'sāradika' as 'arisen in the autumn season,' he says: 'by that which has arisen in the autumn season.' By 'pittābādhena' (due to a disorder of the bile), he indicates the nature of the illness. Elaborating on the cause of the disorder of the bile, he says: 'for in that…' and so on. 'Tena' means 'for that reason' (hetunā). 'Tesaṃ' means 'of them,' referring to the monks. 'Koṭṭhabbhantaragataṃ' means 'gone into the interior of the abdomen.' The intention is that it enters the innermost part of the intestines. 'Āhāratthaṃ' means 'for the purpose of food,' that is, the function of food, or the function to be performed by food.

261. Nacchādentīti tāni bhesajjāni bhojanāni nacchādenti. Kasmā? Bhojanānaṃ ajīraṇattā[V 2.0012]. Iti imamatthaṃ dassento āha “na [M 0.0344] jīrantī”ti. Nacchādattā na vātarogaṃ paṭippassambhetuṃ sakkonti. Ettha ca “na jīrantī”ti iminā nacchādanassa kāraṇaṃ dasseti. “Na vāta…pe… sakkontī”ti iminā tasseva phalaṃ dassetīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. “Siniddhānī”ti iminā sinihantīti senehikānīti atthaṃ dasseti. Bhattacchannakenāti ettha bhattassa acchannakaṃ nāma bhattassa arocikaṃ bhattassa ruciyā anuppādakanti āha “bhattārocakenā”ti.

261. 'Nacchādenti' means those medicines do not cover the foods. Why? Because the foods are undigested. To explain this meaning, he says: 'na jīranti' (they do not digest). Because they do not cover, they cannot pacify wind disorders. Here, by 'na jīranti' he indicates the reason for not covering. By 'Na vāta…pe… sakkonti' (they cannot… wind, etc.), he shows the result of that; this should be understood. By 'Siniddhāni' (oily), he shows the meaning of 'senehikāni' as 'they are oily'. Regarding 'bhattacchannakena', here 'bhattassa acchannakaṃ' means that which causes disrelish for food, that which does not produce an appetite for food; thus he says 'bhattārocakena' (with that which causes disrelish for food).

262. Acchavasantiādīsu vinicchayo veditabboti yojanā. Pāḷiyaṃ “paṭiggahitaṃ nippakkaṃ saṃsaṭṭha”nti padānaṃ kiriyāvisesanaṃ katvā “paribhuñjitu”nti padena sambandhitabbabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ vuttaṃ “kāle paṭiggahitanti ādīsū”tiādi. Telaparibhogena paribhuñjitunti ettha kittakaṃ kālaṃ telaparibhogena paribhuñjitabbanti āha “sattāhakāla”nti.

262. The construction is that the decision should be known regarding 'acchavasanti' and so on. In the Pāli text, to show that the words 'paṭiggahitaṃ nippakkaṃ saṃsaṭṭhaṃ' (received, uncooked, mixed) are made into adverbs and should be connected with the word 'paribhuñjituṃ' (to consume), it is said: 'kāle paṭiggahitaṃ' (received at the proper time) and so on. Regarding the phrase 'telaparibhogena paribhuñjituṃ' (to consume with the use of oil), when asked for how long one should consume with the use of oil, he says 'sattāhakālaṃ' (for a period of seven days).

161. Mūlādibhesajjakathā

161. The Discourse on Root Medicines and so on

263. Mūlabhesajjādivinicchayopīti pisaddo acchavasantiādīsu vinicchayaṃ apekkhati. Idhāti bhesajjakkhandhake. Yaṃ yanti vinicchayaṃ. Pisanasilāti pisati etthāti pisanā, sāyeva silāti pisanasilā. Iminā acalaṃ hutvā nisīdatīti nisadoti atthaṃ dasseti. Pisanapotakoti pisati anenāti pisano, soyeva potakoti pisanapotako, iminā nisadato potakoti nisadapotakoti atthaṃ dasseti. Hiṅgujātiyoti hiṅgukulāni.

263. In 'Mūlabhesajjādivinicchayopi,' the particle 'pi' relates to the decision regarding 'acchavasanti' and so on. 'Idha' means in the Chapter on Medicaments. 'Yaṃ yaṃ' means the decision. 'Pisanasilā' means 'it is ground here,' therefore 'pisanā'; that itself is a stone, hence 'pisanasilā.' By this, it shows the meaning of 'nisada' as 'it sits immovably.' 'Pisanapotaka' means 'one grinds with this,' therefore 'pisano'; that itself is a 'potaka,' hence 'pisanapotaka.' By this, it shows the meaning of 'nisadapotaka' as 'a sitting pestle.' 'Hiṅgujātiyo' means the species of hiṅgu.

Sāmuddanti ettha samudde santiṭṭhatīti sāmuddanti vacanatthaṃ dassento āha “samuddatīre”tiādi. “Tīre”ti iminā samuddeti ettha sattamīvibhattiyā samīpatthe pavattabhāvaṃ dasseti. Pakatiloṇanti sabhāvaloṇaṃ, na dabbasambhārehi saddhiṃ pacitanti attho. “Pabbate uṭṭhahatī”ti iminā sindhunāmake pabbate uṭṭhahatīti sindhavanti atthaṃ dasseti. Ubbito bhūmito īrati uggacchatīti ubbiranti vacanatthaṃ dassento [M 0.0345] āha “bhūmito aṅkuraṃ uṭṭhahatī”ti. Iminā aṭṭhakathānayena oṭṭhajo tatiyakkharoyeva yujjati, potthakesu pana catutthakkharoyeva dissati. “Ubbhida”ntipi pāṭho. Bilanti koṭṭhāso. Tasmā dabbasambhārehi bilehi saddhiṃ pacitaṃ bilanti atthaṃ dassento āha “dabbasambhārehi saddhiṃ pacita”nti. Abhidhāne pana (abhidhāne 461 gāthāyaṃ) “bilāla”nti pāṭho atthi. Tanti bilaṃ.

Here, regarding 'sāmuddaṃ,' to show the etymological meaning 'it exists in the sea, therefore it is sāmuddaṃ,' he said 'samuddatīre' and so on. By 'tīre,' he shows that here the locative case in 'samudde' is used in the sense of proximity. 'Pakatiloṇaṃ' means natural salt; the meaning is that it is not cooked with ingredients. By 'it arises from the mountain,' he shows the meaning of 'sindhavaṃ' as 'it arises from the mountain named Sindhu.' To show the etymological meaning of 'ubbiraṃ' as 'it is stirred up from the ground, it goes up,' he said 'a sprout arises from the ground.' According to this commentarial method, the third labial consonant is appropriate, but in the manuscripts, the fourth labial consonant is seen. 'Ubbhida' is also a reading. 'Bilaṃ' means a portion. Therefore, to show the meaning of 'bilaṃ' as 'cooked with ingredients in portions,' he said 'cooked with ingredients.' In the Abhidhānappadīpikā, however, (in verse 461) the reading 'bilāla' is found. 'Taṃ' means 'bilaṃ'.

264. Assādīnaṃ [V 2.0013] kāyagandho viya kassaci kāyagandho hotīti yojanā. Tassāpīti bhikkhunopi. Pisaddena kaṇḍuvābādhabhikkhuādayopi sampiṇḍeti. Chakaṇasaddassa assādīnaṃ malepi pavattanato vuttaṃ “gomaya”nti. Pākatikacuṇṇampīti apakkarajanacuṇṇampi. Etampīti pākatikacuṇṇampi.

264. The connection is: just as there is the body odor of horses and so on, so too is there the body odor of someone. 'Tassāpi' means 'of a bhikkhunī also.' By the particle 'pi,' bhikkhus with an itching disease and others are also included. Because the word 'chakaṇa' also applies to the excrement of horses and so on, 'gomaya' is stated.
