Kenābhatanti taṃ paṭhamaṃ pārājikaṃ kena ābhataṃ, iti saṅkhepatthoti yojanā.

Thus, having shown the method of explanation by way of showing the object, now, showing another method of explanation by way of showing the instrument, he says ‘apicā’tiādi (moreover, etc.). By the word ‘pubbenivāsādīhi’tiādi (by recollection of past lives, etc.), since the divine eye is to be taken separately, the powers of psychic potency, divine ear, and knowledge of others’ minds should be understood. By these words, he shows that the five mundane higher knowledges are indeed the instruments of the two words ‘jānatā’ (knowing) and ‘passatā’ (seeing). ‘Tīhi vijjāhi’ (by the three knowledges) means by the three knowledges known as recollection of past lives, the divine eye, and the knowledge of the destruction of the taints. ‘Chahi vā pana abhiññāhi’ (or by the six higher knowledges) means by the six higher knowledges, which are the five mundane higher knowledges together with the knowledge of the destruction of the taints. ‘Sabbatthā’ (in all respects) means in all three times and in all five knowable phenomena. ‘Samantacakkhunā’ (with the all-seeing eye) means with the all-seeing eye, which is the unobstructed knowledge of omniscience. ‘Paññāya’ (by wisdom) means by the wisdom of omniscience. ‘Tirokuṭṭādi’ (through walls, etc.)—by the word ‘ādi’ (etc.), it includes through mountains and so forth. ‘Maṃsacakkhunā’ (with the fleshly eye) means with the sensitive eye. ‘Paṭivedhapaññāya’ (by penetrative wisdom) means by the wisdom of the path. ‘Desanāpaññāya’ (by the wisdom of teaching) means by the wisdom of omniscience. For in essence, the wisdom of teaching is indeed the wisdom of omniscience. Hence it is said: ‘By the radiance of that wisdom, he set in motion the discourse on the Abhidhamma path for the gods’ (DhsA. 5). By these words, he shows the possibility of the instrument for the two words, separately according to their contexts. ‘Arahatā’ (by the Arahant) means because he has destroyed enemies and spokes (of the wheel of existence), and because he is worthy of offerings, etc., he is an Arahant. ‘Sammāsambuddhena’ (by the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One) means because he has fully awakened to all phenomena by himself, he is the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. The connection is ‘tena bhagavatā’ (by that Blessed One). ‘Kenābhatanti’ (by whom was it brought?) means by whom was that first Pārājika brought? This is the concise meaning—thus is the connection.

2. Pucchāvisajjane pana evamattho veditabboti yojanā. Yaṃ tena…pe… pārājikanti idaṃ padaṃ paccuddharaṇamattamevāti sambandho. Patiuddharaṇamattameva, na atthadassananti attho. Etthāti etesu padesu. Ekā paññattīti ekā paṭhamapaññatti. Anupaññattiyoti pacchā ṭhapitā paññattiyo.

2. In the question and answer, however, the meaning should be understood thus—this is the connection. The connection is that the phrase ‘yaṃ tena…pe… pārājikaṃ’ (that which by him… etc…. entails defeat) is merely for recollection. The meaning is that it is merely for recollection, not for showing the meaning. ‘Ettha’ (here) means in these passages. ‘Ekā paññatti’ (one promulgation) means the one, first promulgation. ‘Anupaññattiyo’ (subsequent promulgations) means promulgations established later.

Ettāvatāti ettakena “ekā paññatti, dve anupaññattiyo”ti vacanamattena vissajjitā hontīti sambandho. Tatiyaṃ pucchanti sambandho. Kasmā anuppannapaññatti tasmiṃ natthīti āha “ayaṃ hī”tiādi. Tattha hi yasmā aññatra natthi, tasmā natthīti yojanā. “Anuppanne dose paññattā”ti iminā anuppanne dose paññapetabbāti anuppannapaññattīti vacanatthaṃ dasseti. Sāti anuppannapaññatti. Tasmāti yasmā aññatra natthi, tasmā. Sabbatthapaññattīti ettha sabbasmiṃ padese paññatti sabbatthapaññattīti aluttasamāsaṃ dassento āha “majjhimadese cevā”tiādi. “Majjhimadese ceva paccantimajanapadesu cā”ti iminā “sabbatthā”ti padassa sarūpaṃ dasseti. Padesapaññattiṃ apanetvā sabbatthapaññattiṃ pārisesanayena dassento āha “vinayadharapañcamenā”tiādi[M 0.0550]. Tattha vinayadharapañcamenāti anussāvanācariyapañcamena. Etthevāti majjhimadeseyeva. Etehīti catūhi sikkhāpadehi. Sesānīti catūhi sikkhāpadehi sesāni.

The connection is that by just this much—by the mere statement ‘ekā paññatti, dve anupaññattiyo’ (one promulgation, two subsequent promulgations)—they are answered. They ask the third question—this is the connection. Why is there no promulgation for an unarisen fault therein? He says ‘ayaṃ hī’tiādi (for this, etc.). Here, the explanation is: because it does not exist elsewhere, therefore it does not exist. By ‘anuppanne dose paññattā’ (promulgated for an unarisen fault), he shows the verbal meaning that ‘anuppannapaññatti’ (promulgation for an unarisen fault) means that which should be promulgated for an unarisen fault. ‘Sā’ (that) means the promulgation for an unarisen fault. ‘Tasmā’ (therefore) means because it does not exist elsewhere, therefore. Regarding ‘sabbatthapaññatti’ (universal promulgation), here, showing that ‘promulgation in every region is a universal promulgation’ is an unelided compound, he says ‘majjhimadese cevā’tiādi (in the Middle Country, etc.). By ‘majjhimadese ceva paccantimajanapadesu cā’ (in the Middle Country and in the border regions), he indicates the form of the word ‘sabbatthā’ (everywhere). Excluding regional promulgations, he shows the universal promulgation by the method of residue, saying ‘vinayadharapañcamenā’tiādi (with a Vinaya expert as the fifth, etc.). Here, ‘vinayadharapañcamena’ (with a Vinaya expert as the fifth) means with a recitation teacher as the fifth. ‘Ettheva’ (just here) means only in the Middle Country. ‘Etehi’ (by these) means by these four training rules. ‘Sesāni’ (the rest) means the rest, apart from the four training rules.

Sādhāraṇapaññattīti [V 2.0184] ettha sādhāraṇā nāma bhikkhubhikkhunīnamevāti āha “bhikkhūnañceva bhikkhunīnañcā”ti. Idaṃ panāti paṭhamapārājikaṃ pana, paññattanti sambandho. Vinītakathāmattamevāti vinītavatthupakāsakaṃ kathāmattameva. Tāsanti bhikkhunīnaṃ. Byañjanamattamevāti “sādhāraṇā”ti ca “ubhato”ti ca byañjanamattameva. Etthāti sādhāraṇapaññattiubhatopaññattipade.

Regarding ‘sādhāraṇapaññatti’ (common promulgation), here, he says that ‘sādhāraṇā’ (common) means for both bhikkhus and bhikkhunīs, as stated: ‘bhikkhūnañceva bhikkhunīnañcā’ (for both bhikkhus and bhikkhunīs). ‘Idaṃ pana’ (but this) means the first Pārājika. The connection is ‘paññattaṃ’ (is promulgated). ‘Vinītakathāmattameva’ (merely an account of the disciplined) means merely an account revealing the subject matter of the disciplined. ‘Tāsaṃ’ (of them) refers to the bhikkhunīs. ‘Byañjanamattameva’ (merely the expression) means that ‘sādhāraṇā’ (common) and ‘ubhato’ (for both) are merely the wording. ‘Ettha’ (here) means in the terms ‘sādhāraṇapaññatti’ (common promulgation) and ‘ubhatopaññatti’ (promulgation for both).

“Nidāne anupaviṭṭha”nti iminā “nidānogadha”nti padassa sattamīsamāsañca ogadhasaddassa anupaviṭṭhatthañca dasseti. Ogāḷho hutvā dharati tiṭṭhatīti ogadhaṃ. Nanu nidānogadhe sati “paṭhamena uddesenā”ti vattabbaṃ, kasmā “dutiyena uddesenā”ti vuttanti āha “nidānogadha”nti. Nidānapariyāpannampi samānanti nidānapariyāpannaṃ samānampīti yojanā. Pisaddo garahattho, pageva dutiye uddese pariyāpanneti dasseti. “Sīlavipattiādīna”nti vacanaṃ vitthārento āha “paṭhamā hī”tiādi.

By ‘Nidāne anupaviṭṭha’ (entered into the cause), he shows both the seventh-case compound of the word ‘nidānogadha’ and that the word ‘ogadha’ has the meaning of ‘entered into.’ Having plunged in, it is held and remains; thus it is ‘ogadha.’ Now, since it is immersed in the cause, should it not be said ‘by the first recitation’? Why then is it said ‘by the second recitation’? He says, ‘nidānogadha.’ The construction for ‘Nidānapariyāpannampi samānaṃ’ is ‘nidānapariyāpannaṃ samānaṃ pi’ (even while being included in the cause). The particle ‘pi’ has the meaning of censure, showing that it is all the more included in the second recitation. Expounding on the statement ‘of the failure in virtue, etc.,’ he says, ‘paṭhamā hī’tiādi (the first, indeed, etc.).

Dvaṅgikenāti kāyacittasaṅkhātena dvaṅgikena. Nanu “ekena samuṭṭhānenā”ti vuttattā “kāyatoyevā”ti vattabbaṃ, atha kasmā “kāyato ca cittato ca samuṭṭhātī”ti vuttanti āha “ettha hī”tiādi. Etthāti “ekena samuṭṭhānenā”ti vacane. Cittanti sevanacittaṃ. Āpannosīti tvaṃ āpanno asīti yojanā. Āma āpannomhīti āma ahaṃ āpanno amhīti yojanā. Tāvadevāti tasmiṃ paṭijānakkhaṇeyeva. Taṃ puggalanti pārājikamāpannaṃ taṃ puggalaṃ. Tappaccayāti tassa pārājikamāpannassa kāraṇā. “Na katamena samathena sammatī”ti yaṃ pana vacanaṃ vuttanti yojanā. Tanti vacanaṃ, vuttanti sambandho.

‘Dvaṅgikena’ (with two parts) means with the two parts consisting of body and mind. But since it is said, ‘ekena samuṭṭhānena’ (arising from one source), should it not be said, ‘kāyato yeva’ (from the body alone)? Why then is it said, ‘it arises from both body and mind’? He says, ‘ettha hī’tiādi (here, indeed, etc.). ‘Ettha’ (here) refers to the statement ‘ekena samuṭṭhānena’ (arising from one source). ‘Cittaṃ’ (mind) refers to the mind engaged in the act. The construction for ‘Āpannosi’ (you have transgressed) is ‘tvaṃ āpanno asi’ (you are one who has transgressed). The construction for ‘Āma āpannomhi’ (yes, I have transgressed) is ‘āma ahaṃ āpanno amhi’ (yes, I am one who has transgressed). ‘Tāvadeva’ (at that very moment) means right at the moment of acknowledging. ‘Taṃ puggalaṃ’ (that person) refers to that person who has committed a pārājika offense. ‘Tappaccayā’ (because of that) means for the reason of that person having committed a pārājika offense. As for the statement, ‘Na katamena samathena sammati’ (By which settlement is it not settled?), the connection is to the word ‘vuttaṃ’ (is said). ‘Taṃ’ (that) refers to the statement; the connection is to ‘vuttaṃ’ (is said).

Vuttamātikā paññattīti vuttamātikāsaṅkhātā paññatti vinayo nāmāti yojanā. Mātikā hi yasmā paññapīyati saṅkhepena ṭhapīyati, pakāraṃ jānāpeti vā, tasmā paññattīti vuccati. “Padabhājanaṃ vuccatī”ti [M 0.0551] iminā vitthārena bhājiyati etāyāti vibhattīti dasseti. Vītikkamoti kāyavācāvītikkamo. So hi na saṃvarati kāyavācaṃ na pidahatīti asaṃvaroti vuccati. Yesaṃ vattatīti ettha vattatikiriyāya kattāraṃ dassento āha “vinayapiṭakañca aṭṭhakathā cā”ti. Paguṇāti vācuggatā. Teti te puggalā, dhārentīti sambandho. Hīti saccaṃ, yasmā vā. Etassāti paṭhamapārājikassa. Kenābhatanti ettha bharadhātuyā dhāraṇaposanatthesu (pāṇinī 108 dhātupāṭhe) dhāraṇatthaṃ dassento āha “kena ānīta”nti[V 2.0185]. “Paramparāya ānīta”nti iminā paramparābhatanti padassa tatiyāsamāsaṃ dasseti. Athavā “kenābhata”nti pucchāya anurūpaṃ yakāralopavasena vākyanti dasseti.

The construction for ‘Vuttamātikā paññatti’ (the stated matrix is a designation) is: the designation known as the stated matrix is called the Vinaya. For the matrix is designated, established in brief, or makes known the manner; therefore, it is called a designation. By ‘padabhājanaṃ vuccati’ (it is called word-analysis), he shows that ‘vibhatti’ means ‘by this it is analyzed in detail.’ ‘Vītikkamo’ (transgression) means transgression of body and speech. For one who does not restrain body and speech, does not suppress them, is called ‘asaṃvaro’ (unrestrained). Regarding ‘yesaṃ vattati’ (for whom it applies), here, to show the agent of the verb ‘vattati,’ he says, ‘vinayapiṭakañca aṭṭhakathā cā’ (the Vinaya Piṭaka and the commentaries). ‘Paguṇā’ (familiar) means fluent in speech. The connection for ‘te’ (they) is to ‘te puggalā’ (those persons) and ‘dhārenti’ (they bear). ‘Hi’ means truly, or because. ‘Etassa’ (of this) refers to the first pārājika. Regarding ‘Kenābhataṃ?’ (By whom was it brought?), here, showing the meaning of ‘bearing’ for the root ‘bhar’ (which has the meanings of ‘bearing’ and ‘nourishing,’ as in Pāṇini’s Dhātupāṭha, 108), he says, ‘kena ānītaṃ?’ (by whom was it brought?). By ‘paramparāya ānītaṃ’ (brought down through tradition), he shows that the word ‘paramparābhataṃ’ is an instrumental compound. Alternatively, he shows that the sentence is suitable for the question ‘kenābhataṃ?’ through the elision of the letter ‘ya’.

3. Upāli dāsako cevātiādikā gāthāyo kimatthaṃ kehi ṭhapitāti āha “idānī”tiādi. Tanti paraṃ paraṃ. Tatthāti tāsu gāthāsu. Yanti vacanaṃ. Iminā nayenāti paṭhamapārājikassa pucchāvisajjane vuttena iminā nayena.

3. Regarding the verses beginning ‘Upāli dāsako ceva’ (Upāli, Dāsaka, and so on), for what purpose and by whom were they established? He says, ‘idānī’tiādi (now, etc.). ‘Taṃ’ (that) means in unbroken succession. ‘Tattha’ (there) refers to in those verses. ‘Yaṃ’ (which) refers to the expression. ‘Iminā nayena’ (in this way) means in this way, as stated in the question and answer regarding the first pārājika.

Iti mahāvibhaṅge paññattivāravaṇṇanāya yojanā samattā.

Thus, the explanation of the commentary on the section of designations in the Mahāvibhaṅga is complete.

Katāpattivārādivaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Section on Committed Offenses, and so on.

157. Itoti paññattivārato, paraṃ vuttā satta vārā uttānatthā evāti yojanā. Katāpattivāroti “katāpattī”ti padena lakkhito vāro. Eseva nayo sesesupi. Tadanantaroti tesaṃ sattannaṃ vārānaṃ anantare vutto. Samuccayavāroti saṃ ekato āpattivipattiādayo uciyanti sampiṇḍiyanti etthāti samuccayo, soyeva vāro samuccayavāro.

157. ‘From this’ means from the section on designations; the construction is that the seven sections stated thereafter are indeed clear in meaning. ‘The section on committed offenses’ means the section signified by the word ‘committed offense.’ This same method applies to the rest as well. ‘Immediately after that’ means that which is stated immediately after those seven sections. ‘The section on combinations’ is so called because offenses, misfortunes, and so forth are heaped and collected together therein; therefore, it is the combination section.

188. Tatoti tehi aṭṭhahi vārehi, paraṃ vuttāti sambandho. Paccayavasena vutto eko paññattivāroti yojanā. Paccayavasenāti paccayasaddassa vasena. Tassāti paccayassa. Tepīti aṭṭha [M 0.0552] vārāpi. Itītiādi nigamanaṃ. Tatoti mahāvibhaṅgato, paraṃ āgatāti sambandho. Evaṃ ime dvattiṃsa vārāti yojanā. Hīti saccaṃ, yasmā vā. Etthāti dvattiṃsavāresu.

188. ‘From that’ means from those eight sections; ‘stated thereafter’ is the connection. The construction is ‘one section on designations is stated based on conditions.’ ‘Based on conditions’ means based on the word ‘condition.’ ‘Of that’ refers to the condition. ‘Those too’ means the eight sections also. ‘Thus’ and so on is the conclusion. ‘From that’ means from the Mahāvibhaṅga; ‘have come thereafter’ is the connection. The construction is ‘thus these thirty-two sections.’ ‘Indeed’ means truly, or because. ‘Here’ refers to within these thirty-two sections.

Samuṭṭhānasīsavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Principal Origins.

257. Tadanantarāyāti tesaṃ dvattiṃsavārānaṃ anantaraṃ vuttāya samuṭṭhānakathāya evamattho veditabboti yojanā. Anattā iti nicchitāti anattātveva vinicchitā. Iminā anattā iti nicchayāti ettha cidhātuyā vinicchayatthaṃ dasseti. “Aniccākārādīhī”ti iminā sabhāgadhammānanti ettha aniccākārādīhi samāno bhāgo etesanti sabhāgā, teyeva dhammā sabhāgadhammāti vacanatthaṃ dasseti. Nāmamattampīti aniccādināmamattampi. Pisaddena pageva nāmiko aniccādisabhāvoti dasseti. Na paññāyatīti na khāyati. Iminā na nāyatīti ettha ñādhātuyā khāyanatthaṃ dasseti. Dukkhahāninti ettha dukkhaṃ jahātīti dukkhahānīti dassento [V 2.0186] āha “dukkhaghātana”nti. Dukkhaṃ hanatīti dukkhaghātano, saddhammo, taṃ. “Khandhakā yā ca mātikā”ti vattabbe sukhuccāraṇatthāya rassavasena pāṭho atthīti āha “khandhakā ya ca mātikā”ti. Samuṭṭhānaṃ niyatokatanti (saṃ. ni. 1.216) ettha “samuṭṭhānaṃ niyatakata”nti vattabbe “parosahassa”ntiādīsu viya okārāgamavasena “samuṭṭhānaniyatokata”nti vuttanti āha “samuṭṭhānaṃ niyatakata”nti. Etenāti “samuṭṭhānaṃ niyatokata”nti pāṭhena. Paccetabboti pati etabbo, paṭimukhaṃ ñātabboti attho. Aññehīti tīhi sikkhāpadehi aññehi sikkhāpadehi.

257. ‘Immediately after that’—the construction is that this meaning should be understood for the discourse on origination stated immediately after those thirty-two sections. ‘“Not-self” is determined’ means it is definitively determined as ‘not-self’ indeed. By this, he shows the meaning of ‘ascertaining’ for the root `ci` in ‘`anattā iti nicchayāti`.’ By ‘by way of impermanence, etc.,’ he shows the meaning of the word `sabhāgadhammā` (similar phenomena) here, which is: ‘they have a similar part by way of the aspects of impermanence, etc., therefore they are similar, and those very phenomena are similar phenomena.’ ‘Mere name’ means even the mere name of impermanence, etc. The particle `pi` indicates that the nature of impermanence, etc., is indeed merely nominal. ‘Does not appear’ means it is not manifest. By this, he shows the meaning of ‘manifestation’ for the root `ñā` in ‘`na nāyatīti`.’ In ‘abandoning suffering,’ showing that `dukkhahānīti` means ‘one abandons suffering,’ he says, ‘the destruction of suffering.’ ‘Destroying suffering’ means the destroyer of suffering, that is, the true Dhamma; that. In ‘the Khandhakas and the Mātikā,’ he says that although it should be said thus, for ease of pronunciation, there is a shorter reading, ‘`khandhakā ya ca mātikā`.’ In ‘origination is fixedly made’ (Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.216), he says that although it should be said ‘`samuṭṭhānaṃ niyatakata`,’ it is stated as ‘`samuṭṭhānaniyatokata`’ by way of the addition of the `o` sound, as in ‘`parosahassa`’ and so on, and he says ‘`samuṭṭhānaṃ niyatakata`.’ ‘By this’ means by the reading ‘`samuṭṭhānaṃ niyatokata`.’ ‘To be recognized’ means ‘to be approached;’ the meaning is ‘to be known face-to-face.’ ‘Others’ means other training rules apart from the three training rules.

Tatthāti sambhedanidānavacanesu. Sambhedavacanena paccetabbanti sambandho. Hīti saccaṃ. Tāni tīṇi sikkhāpadāni ṭhapetvāti sambandho. Paññattidesasaṅkhātanti paññattiṭṭhānabhūtadesasaṅkhātaṃ. “Imāni tīṇī”ti iminā “dissantī”ti kiriyāya kattāraṃ dasseti. “Paññāyantī”ti iminā disadhātuyā khāyanatthaṃ dasseti. Tatthāti samuṭṭhānaniyamasambhedanidānasaṅkhātesu [M 0.0553] tīsu, niddhāraṇe bhummaṃ. Itaraṃ panāti samuṭṭhānaniyamasambhedehi aññaṃ pana.

‘Therein’ refers to the expressions of combination and cause. ‘To be recognized’ is the connection with the expression ‘combination.’ ‘Indeed’ means truly. ‘Excepting those three training rules’ is the connection. ‘Reckoned as a place of designation’ means reckoned as a place that has become the location of designation. By ‘these three,’ he shows the agent of the verb ‘are seen.’ By ‘are manifested,’ he shows the meaning of ‘manifestation’ for the root `dis`. ‘Therein’ refers to among the three reckoned as origination, fixed rule, and combination-cause; the locative is for determination. ‘The remainder, however,’ means that which is other than origination, fixed rule, and combination.

Āḷavīti āḷaviyaṃ. Sakkesu bhaggesu cāti ettha janapadanāmattā bahuvacanavasena vuttaṃ.

‘Āḷavī’ means in Āḷavī. In ‘among the Sakyans and Bhaggas,’ it is stated in the plural because they are merely names of peoples.

Dvīsu vibhaṅgesu paññattaṃ yaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ uddisantīti yojanā. “Vibhaṅgesū”ti iminā vibhaṅgeti ettha sukāralopoti dasseti. Tassāti sikkhāpadassa. Yathāñāyanti yuttiyā anurūpaṃ. Tanti samuṭṭhānaṃ. Me suṇāthāti mama santikā suṇātha. Itīti ayamattho.

The construction is ‘they recite the training rule that is designated in the two Vibhaṅgas.’ By ‘in the Vibhaṅgas,’ he shows that the `su` syllable is elided here in `vibhaṅge`. ‘Of that’ refers to the training rule. ‘According to reason’ means suitable in accordance with justification. ‘That’ refers to the origination. ‘Listen to me’ means listen from my presence. ‘Thus’ means this is the meaning.

Kathinanti paṭhamakathinasamuṭṭhānaṃ. Ananuññātāya saddhinti ananuññātasamuṭṭhānena saddhiṃ. Sadisā idha dissareti ettha idhasaddo atthapakaraṇavasena ubhatovibhaṅgavisayoti āha “idha ubhatovibhaṅge”ti. “Sadisānī”ti iminā sadisāti ettha nikārassākārādeso dassito. “Dissantī”ti iminā dissareti ettha antisaddassa rekāro (niruttidīpaniyaṃ 570 sute) dassito.

‘Kathina’ means the origination of the first Kathina rule. ‘With the unpermitted’ means together with the origination of the unpermitted rule. In ‘similar ones are seen here,’ he says that the word `idha` (here) has the scope of both Vibhaṅgas according to the context, as stated: ‘here in both Vibhaṅgas.’ By ‘similar ones’ (`sadisāni`), it is shown that in `sadisā`, the `ā` is a substitute for the `ni` sound. By ‘are seen’ (`dissanti`), it is shown that the `r` is a substitute for the suffix `anti` in `dissare` (as in Niruttidīpanī, verse 570).

Samuṭṭhānasīso

The Principal Origins

Paṭhamapārājikasamuṭṭhānavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Arising of the First Pārājika.

258. Kimatthaṃ [V 2.0187] “methunaṃ sukkasaṃsaggo”tiādivacanaṃ vuttanti āha “idānī”tiādi. Tattha tatthāti “methunaṃ sukkasaṃsaggo”tiādivacane. Samuṭṭhānasīsanti samuṭṭhānānaṃ, samuṭṭhānesu vā sīsaṃ. Sesānīti paṭhamapārājikato sesāni pañcasattati sikkhāpadāni. Tenāti paṭhamapārājikena. “Sukkasaṃsaggo”tiādivacanaṃ saṃvaṇṇento āha “tatthā”tiādi. Tattha tatthāti “sukkasaṃsaggo”tiādivacane.

258. For what purpose is the statement 'sexual intercourse, contact with semen,' and so forth, stated? He says, 'now,' and so on. 'Therein, therein' means in the statement 'sexual intercourse, contact with semen,' and so on. 'The head of origins' means the head of the origins, or the chief among the origins. 'The rest' means the remaining seventy-five training rules apart from the first pārājika. 'By that' means by the first pārājika. Explaining the statement 'contact with semen,' and so on, he says, 'therein,' and so on. 'Therein, therein' means in the statement 'contact with semen,' and so on.

Khuddakavaṇṇanāvasāneti khuddakaṭṭhakathāya avasāne.

‘At the conclusion of the Explanation of the Minor Texts’ means at the conclusion of the Commentary on the Minor Texts.

Liṅgavipariyāyoti liṅgavipallāso. Kāyamānasikā katāti ettha kāyamānasesu pavattā kāyamānasikāti vutte samuṭṭhānāti āha “kāyacittasamuṭṭhānā katā”ti.

‘Change of gender’ means inversion of gender. In the phrase ‘bodily and mental are done,’ ‘bodily and mental’ refers to that which occurs in the body and mind; regarding the arisings, it is said, ‘done as arising from body and mind.’

Dutiyapārājikasamuṭṭhānavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Arising of the Second Pārājika.

259. Idaṃ [M 0.0554] samuṭṭhānaṃ ekaṃ samuṭṭhānasīsanti sambandho. “Adinnādāna”nti iminā adinnanti ettha samudāyanāme ekadesavohāroti dasseti. Sesānīti dutiyapārājikato sesāni ekūnasattati sikkhāpadāni. Tenāti dutiyapārājikena. Tatthāti “viggahuttarī”tiādivacane. Viggahuttarītiādipadānaṃ byañjane ādaramakatvā atthameva dassetuṃ vuttaṃ “manussaviggahauttarimanussadhammasikkhāpadānī”ti. Aniyatā dutiyikāti āpattiṃ apekkhitvā pāḷiyaṃ itthiliṅgavasena vuttaṃ, aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana sikkhāpadaṃ apekkhitvā napuṃsakaliṅgavasena dutiyanti vuttaṃ.

259. This origin is one head of origins—this is the connection. By 'taking what is not given,' he shows that in 'not given' here, it is a case of using a part to refer to the whole in a collective name. ‘The rest’ means the remaining sixty-nine training rules apart from the second pārājika. ‘By that’ means by the second pārājika. ‘Therein’ means in the statement beginning 'disputes and so on.' The expression 'disputes and so on' is stated to show only the meaning without regard for the letters, as in 'training rules concerning human disputes and superhuman states.' ‘The second of the uncertain rules’ is stated in the feminine gender in the Pāli text with reference to the offense, but in the commentary, it is referred to as 'the second' in the neuter gender with reference to the training rule.

Samuṭṭhānā tikā katāti ettha “tikasamuṭṭhānā”ti vattabbe padavipariyāyavasena kakārassa dīghavasena samuṭṭhānā tikāti vuttanti dassento āha “tikasamuṭṭhānā katā”ti.

In ‘the arisings are made threefold,’ showing that when ‘of threefold arising’ should be said, it is instead stated as ‘the arisings are threefold’ by reversing the word order and lengthening the vowel of ‘ka,’ he says ‘made of threefold arising.’

Sañcarittasamuṭṭhānavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Arising of Acting as a Go-between.

260. “Sañcarī”ti [V 2.0188] idaṃ tāva sañcarittaṃ nāma ekasamuṭṭhānasīsaṃ, sesāni tena sadisāni.

260. ‘Acting as a go-between’—this, to begin with, is called acting as a go-between, having a single origin as its head; the rest are similar to it.

Vibhaṅge āgatena “riñcantī”ti (pārā. 576) padena eḷakalomadhovāpanasikkhāpadaṃ upalakkhitvā vuttanti āha “vibhaṅge riñcanti uddesanti āgata”nti.

It is stated having signified the training rule about having wool washed by the word 'riñcanti' (pārā. 576) that has come in the Vibhaṅga, thus he says: 'in the Vibhaṅga, “riñcanti” has come in the recitation.'

“Yāva dvārakosā aggaḷaṭṭhapanāya” iti (pāci. 135-136) ca “aññātikāya bhikkhuniyā cīvaraṃ dadeyya”iti (pāci. 169) ca “cīvaraṃ sibbeyya”iti (pāci. 176-177) ca vuttasikkhāpadattayanti yojanā.

‘Up to the door socket for setting the bolt’ (Pāc. 135-136), ‘and should give a robe to a bhikkhunī who is not a relative’ (Pāc. 169), and ‘should sew a robe’ (Pāc. 176-177)—the construction is that these are the three training rules stated.

“Samaṇacīvarena cā”ti evaṃ vacanaṃ vuttanti sambandho. “Samaṇacīvaraṃ dadeyyā”ti idaṃ (pāci. 917) vacanaṃ sandhāyāti sambandho.

‘And with a monk's robe’—this phrase is stated thus—this is the connection. This phrase ‘should give a monk's robe’ (Pāc. 917) is intended—this is the connection.

Samanubhāsanāsamuṭṭhānavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Arising of Formal Proclamation.

261. Bhedanti [M 0.0555] idaṃ samanubhāsanaṃ nāma ekaṃ samuṭṭhānasīsaṃ, sesāni tena sadisāni.

261. 'Division'—this is called the formal act of proclamation, one head of arising; the rest are similar to this.

Kathinasamuṭṭhānavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Arising of the Kaṭhina

262. Ubbhatanti idaṃ kathinasamuṭṭhānaṃ nāma ekaṃ samuṭṭhānasīsaṃ, sesāni tena sadisāni.

262. 'Withdrawn'—this is called the arising of the kaṭhina, one head of arising; the rest are similar to it.

Āvasathena saddhinti āvasathasaddena saddhiṃ.

'With lodging' means together with the word 'lodging'.

Eḷakalomasamuṭṭhānavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Arising of Sheep's Wool

263. “Eḷakalomā”ti idaṃ eḷakalomasamuṭṭhānaṃ nāma ekaṃ samuṭṭhānasīsaṃ. Itoti yathāvuttato. Pāḷinti mātikāpāḷiṃ. Virajjhitvāti pubbāparato virādhetvā. Yathāti yenākārena[V 2.0189]. Panasaddo anuggahattho. Kiñcāpi likhanti, pana tathāpīti yojanā. Evanti tathākārena. Atthānukkamoti atthassa anukkamo.

263. 'Sheep's wool'—this is called the arising of sheep's wool, one head of arising. 'From this' means as has been stated. 'The Pāḷi' means the matrix Pāḷi. 'Having failed' means having failed in sequence, both before and after. 'As' means in whatever manner. The word 'pana' is for emphasis. 'Although they write, yet even so'—this is the construction. 'Thus' means in that manner. 'Order of meaning' means the order of the meaning.

“Abhikkhukāvā sena cā”ti etaṃ vacanaṃ vuttanti sambandho. “Abhikkhuke āvāse vassaṃ vaseyyā”ti (pāci. 1047) idaṃ vacanaṃ sandhāyāti sambandho. “Bhikkhunī”tiādinā vuttānīti sambandho. Ādisaddena “sikkhamānā ca sāmaṇerī gihiniyā”ti pāṭhaṃ saṅgaṇhāti.

The phrase 'and in a residence without monks' is spoken—this is the connection. 'One should spend the rains residence in a dwelling without monks' (Pāc. 1047)—this statement is intended; this is the connection. 'A nun', and so forth, are spoken—this is the connection. By the word 'etc.' it includes the text: 'a female probationer, a female novice, and a laywoman'.

Padasodhammasamuṭṭhānavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Arising of Offenses by Step

264. Padanti idaṃ padasodhammasamuṭṭhānaṃ nāma ekaṃ samuṭṭhānasīsaṃ, sesāni tena sadisāni. “Tathā atthaṅgatena cā”ti etaṃ vacanaṃ vuttanti sambandho. “Atthaṅgate sūriye ovadeyyā”ti (pāci. 154-155) idaṃ vacanaṃ sandhāyāti sambandho. Anokāso ca…pe… sandhāya vuttanti (pāci. 1219-1221) etthāpi eseva nayo.

264. 'Step'—this is called the arising of offenses by step, one head of arising; the rest are similar to it. 'And likewise when it has set'—this statement is spoken; this is the connection. 'One should advise when the sun has set' (Pāc. 154-155)—this statement is intended; this is the connection. And 'Unsuitable occasion'... etc. ... spoken with reference to (Pāc. 1219-1221)—here too, this is the method.

Addhānasamuṭṭhānavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Arising of the Journey

265. Addhānanti [M 0.0556] idaṃ addhānasamuṭṭhānaṃ nāma ekaṃ samuṭṭhānasīsaṃ, sesāni tena sadisāni.

265. 'Journey'—this is called the arising of the journey, one head of arising; the rest are similar to it.

Theyyasatthasamuṭṭhānavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Arising of a Band of Thieves

266. Theyyasatthanti idaṃ theyyasatthasamuṭṭhānaṃ nāma ekaṃ samuṭṭhānasīsaṃ, sesāni tena sadisāni. “Byūhena sattamā”ti idaṃ vacanaṃ vuttanti yojanā. Tadanantaramevāti tassa sikkhāpadassa anantarameva, “āgata”iti sambandho.

266. 'A band of thieves'—this is called the arising of a band of thieves, one head of arising; the rest are similar to it. 'Seventh with the troop formation'—this statement is spoken; this is the construction. 'Immediately after that' means immediately after that training rule; 'has come' is the connection.

Dhammadesanāsamuṭṭhānavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Arising of the Dhamma Teaching

267. Dhammadesanāsamuṭṭhāne samuṭṭhānasīsaṃ natthi, sabbāni ekadasa sikkhāpadāni sampiṇḍetvā dhammadesanāsamuṭṭhānānīti vuttāni. Evantiādi nigamanaṃ. Tesanti tesaṃ sikkhāpadānaṃ[V 2.0190]. Sambhinnasamuṭṭhānanti saṃsaggasamuṭṭhānaṃ. Tividhanti bhūtārocanacorivuṭṭhāpanaananuññātasamuṭṭhānavasena tippakāraṃ. Tanti niyatasamuṭṭhānaṃ, hotīti sambandho. Puna tanti niyatasamuṭṭhānaṃ, dassetunti sambandho. Puna tanti vacanaṃ. Nettidhammānulomikanti ettha kāyavācaṃ neti vinetīti netti, kāyavācaṃ neti vineti ettha, etāyāti vā netti. Dhammoti pāḷi. Sā hi yasmā atthaṃ dhāreti, tasmā dhammoti vuccati. Nettiyeva dhammo nettidhammo, tassa anulomikaṃ nettidhammānulomikaṃ. Tena vuttaṃ “vinayapāḷidhammassa anuloma”nti.

267. In the arising of the Dhamma teaching, there is no head of arising; all eleven training rules are grouped together and called 'the arisings of the Dhamma teaching'. 'Thus', etc., is the conclusion. 'Of those' means of those training rules. 'Mixed arising' means the arising of association. 'Threefold' means of three kinds: by way of the arising from reporting what is true, the arising from rehabilitating a thief, and the arising from what is not permitted. 'That' means a fixed arising; 'is' is the connection. Again, 'that' means a fixed arising; 'they show' is the connection. Again, 'that' is the word. Regarding 'in accordance with the guide and the Dhamma': here, 'guide' (netti) is that which guides or disciplines body and speech, or it is that by which one guides or disciplines body and speech. 'Dhamma' means the Pāḷi text. Because it bears (dhāreti) the meaning, it is called 'dhamma'. The guide itself is the Dhamma, hence 'guide-Dhamma' (nettidhammo). That which is in accordance with it is 'in accordance with the guide and the Dhamma' (nettidhammānulomikaṃ). Therefore it is said: 'in accordance with the Dhamma of the Vinaya Pāḷi'.

Iti samuṭṭhānasīsavaṇṇanāya yojanā samattā.

Thus ends the analysis of the explanation of the heads of arising.

Antarapeyyāla katipucchāvāravaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Intermediate Sections and Question Sections

271. Idāni vuttoti sambandho. “Idānī”ti padena sambandhattā vuttoti ettha tapaccayo paccuppannakālikoti daṭṭhabbo.

271. 'Now spoken' is the connection. Because of the connection with the word 'now', the suffix 'ta' in 'spoken' should be understood here as referring to the present time.

Tatthāti [M 0.0557] mātikāyaṃ, pucchāsu vā. Āgatāpattipucchāti āgatāpattiyā pucchā. Hīti visesajotako, hi visesaṃ vakkhāmīti attho. Etthāti “kati āpattikkhandhā”ti dutiyapade. “Rāsivasenā”ti iminā khandhasaddassa rāsatthaṃ dasseti. Vinītavatthūnīti ettha vinītasaddo vinayapariyāyoti āha “vinayapucchā”ti. Nanu vinītavinayasaddānaṃ saddato nānattā atthatopi nānaṃ, kasmā pana “vinayapucchā”ti vuttanti āha “vinītaṃ…pe… eka”nti. Idanti padattayaṃ. Atthato ekanti atthatoyeva ekaṃ, na saddato. Vinītavatthūnīti āpattivinayakāraṇattā vinītavatthūni. Yesūti agāravesu. Satīti santesu. Ettha ca yesu sati āpattiyo na honti, asati hontīti vākyampi avuttasiddhinayena gahetabbaṃ. Yesūti gāravesu. Teti agāravagārave. Yasmā pana natthīti sambandho. Vipattibhāvapucchāti vipattibhāvassa pucchā. Pucchiyati imāyāti pucchā. Vivādamūlāni anuvādamūlānīti imā pucchāyo mūlapucchāti sambandho. Potthakesu “imānī”ti nikārena saha pāṭho atthi, so apāṭhoyeva. Mūlapucchāti pucchiyanti imāhīti pucchā, mūlānaṃ pucchā mūlapucchā. “Adhikaraṇa”ntiādīsu [V 2.0191] “vuttaṃ” iti sambandho. Tesaṃyevāti adhikaraṇānaṃyeva. Ayamettha mātikā.

'Therein' means in the matrix, or in the questions. 'Question on offenses that have come' means a question about an offense that has come. 'Hi' is an illuminator of distinction; the meaning is, 'for I will state the distinction.' 'Here' means in the second phrase, 'how many aggregates of offenses?' By 'by way of a heap', it shows the meaning 'heap' for the word 'aggregate'. Regarding 'settled matters' (vinītavatthūni): here, it says the word 'settled' (vinīta) is a synonym for 'discipline' (vinaya), hence 'a question about discipline' (vinayapucchā). But is it not so that since the words 'vinīta' and 'vinaya' differ in form, they also differ in meaning? Why then is it called 'vinayapucchā'? It is said, 'vinīta... etc. ... one.' This is three words. In meaning it is one, not in form. 'Settled matters' are so called because they are the cause for the settling of offenses. 'In which' means in cases of disrespect. 'Being' means when they exist. And here, the sentence 'offenses do not arise when these are present, but arise when they are absent' should be understood by the principle of what is established though unstated. 'In which' means in cases of respect. 'Those' means disrespect and respect. The connection is 'because there is not'. 'Question on the state of failure' means a question about the state of failure. 'Question' (pucchā) is that by which one questions. 'Roots of dispute, roots of accusation'—these questions are root questions; this is the connection. In the books, there is a reading 'imāni' with the 'ni' syllable, but that is not a correct reading. 'Root question' (mūlapucchā) is that by which one questions about roots, hence 'a question of roots'. In 'legal issues', etc., 'it is said' is the connection. 'Of those very' means of those very legal issues. This is the matrix here.

Niddese mātikāyāti pātimokkhe. Vibhaṅgeti padabhājaniyaṃ, āgatavasena vuttāti yojanā. Ayamettha niddeso.

In the exposition, 'of the matrix' means of the Pātimokkha. 'Analysis' means the word-by-word explanation; it is spoken according to tradition—this is the construction. This is the exposition here.

Paṭiniddese āratītiādipadānaṃ vacanatthaṃ dassento āha “ārakā”tiādi. Tattha “ārakā”ti iminā āratīti ettha āupasaggassa atthaṃ dasseti. Etehīti āpattikkhandhehi, ārakāti sambandho. “Ramatī”ti iminā tipaccayo katvatthe hotīti dasseti. Ratīti ramanaṃ. Iminā tipaccayo bhāvatthepi hotīti dasseti. Vināti etehi āpattikkhandhehi vinā. Iminā viratīti ettha vityūpasaggassa atthaṃ dasseti. Paccekanti pati ekaṃ, paṭisaddo vicchatthajotako, visuṃ visunti attho. Iminā paṭiviratīti ettha paṭityūpasaggassa atthaṃ dasseti. Virati paṭiviratīti etthāpi tipaccayo bhāvatthepi veditabbo[M 0.0558]. Veranti anatthakarattā viramitabbanti viraṃ, tadeva veraṃ, rāgādiakusaladhammā. Te hi verahetuttā veranti vuccanti. Etāyāti viratiyā. Iminā akiriyāti ettha ririyapaccayo karaṇatthe hotīti dasseti. Yaṃ āpattikkhandhakaraṇanti yojanā. Tassāti āpattikkhandhakaraṇassa. Paṭipakkhatoti viruddhabhāvato. Iminā akaraṇanti ettha akāro viruddhatthoti dasseti. Āpattikkhandhaajjhāpattiyāti āpattikkhandhānaṃ atikkamitvā āpajjanassa. “Velanato”ti iminā velatīti velā, velanaṃ vā velāti vacanatthe dasseti. Niyyānanti maggaṃ. Maggo hi nibbānaṃ ārammaṇakaraṇavasena yāti gacchatīti niyyānanti vuccati. “Bandhatī”ti iminā sidhātuyā bandhanatthaṃ dasseti. “Nivāretī”ti iminā bandhadhātuyā adhippāyatthaṃ. Etanti “setū”ti nāmaṃ. Taṃ setunti āpattikkhandhasaṅkhātaṃ taṃ setuṃ. Ettha kesuci potthakesu “so setū”ti ca “etāya paññattiyā”ti ca pāṭho atthi, so apāṭhoyeva.

In the detailed explanation, showing the meaning of the words beginning with 'āratī,' it is said, 'ārakā,' and so on. Therein, by 'ārakā,' it shows the meaning of the prefix 'ā' in 'āratī.' 'Etehi' refers to the groups of offenses; 'ārakā' is the connection. By 'ramatī,' it shows that the suffix 'ti' has the meaning of the agent. 'Ratī' is delighting. By this, it shows that the suffix 'ti' can also have the meaning of an abstract noun. 'Vinā' means without these groups of offenses. By this, it shows the meaning of the prefix 'vi' in 'viratī.' 'Paccekam' means 'pati ekaṃ' (to each one); the word 'paṭi' indicates distribution, meaning 'severally' or 'separately.' By this, it shows the meaning of the prefix 'paṭi' in 'paṭiviratī.' In 'virati' and 'paṭiviratī' also, the suffix 'ti' should be understood as having the meaning of an abstract noun. 'Vera' means what should be abstained from because it is harmful—hence 'viraṃ,' which is the same as 'veraṃ,' referring to unwholesome states such as lust. For they are called 'vera' because they are a cause of enmity. 'Etāya' refers to this abstinence. By this, it shows that in 'akiriyā,' the suffix '-iriya' has the instrumental meaning. The construction is 'the doing of the groups of offenses.' 'Tassa' refers to the doing of the groups of offenses. 'Paṭipakkhato' means from the state of opposition. By this, it shows that the negative prefix 'a' in 'akaraṇa' conveys the meaning of opposition. 'Āpattikkhandhaajjhāpattiyā' means the transgressing of the groups of offenses. By 'velanato,' it shows the verbal derivation of 'velā' from 'velati' or 'velanaṃ.' 'Niyyāna' means the path. The path is called 'niyyāna' because it goes (yāti) toward Nibbāna by making it the object. By 'bandhatī,' it shows the meaning of binding from the root 'si.' By 'nivāretī,' it shows the intended meaning of the root 'bandh.' 'Etam' is the name 'setu.' 'Taṃ setum' refers to that 'setu,' which is reckoned as the groups of offenses. Here, in some books, there are readings such as 'so setū' and 'etāya paññattiyā,' but these are indeed incorrect readings.

Buddhe agāravādīsu evaṃ vinicchayo veditabboti yojanā. Yoti yo koci, na gacchatītiādīsu sambandho. Dharamāneti tiṭṭhamāne, saṃvijjamāneti attho. Upaṭṭhānanti upaṭṭhānaṭṭhānaṃ, upaṭṭhānatthaṃ vā. Etassāti yassa kassaci gahaṭṭhassa vā pabbajitassa vā. Dhammassavananti dhammassavanaṭṭhānaṃ, dhammassavanatthaṃ vā. Dhammassavanagganti dhammassavanaṃ gaṇhanti etthāti dhammassavanaggo, dhammasavanamaṇḍapo. Atha vā dhammassavanaṃ gaṇhātīti dhammassavanaggo, dhammassavanaṭṭhāne [V 2.0192] samāgamajano, taṃ dhammassavanaggaṃ. Cittīkāranti apacāyanākāraṃ. Vikkhitto vā anādaro vā hutvā nisīdatīti yojanā. Kāyapāgabbiyanti bhusaṃ garati aññe pīḷeti anenāti pagabbo, atimāno, oṭṭhajo tatiyakkharo. Pagabbassa bhāvo pāgabbiyaṃ, kāyena pāgabbiyaṃ kāyapāgabbiyaṃ (vajira. ṭī. parivāra 271; sārattha. ṭī. parivāra 3.271; vi. vi. ṭī. parivāra 2.271 saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 2.2.146; a. ni. aṭṭha. 3.6.82-84; su. ni. aṭṭha. 1.144), kāyānācāraṃ. Tisso sikkhāti adhisīlasikkhādikā tisso sikkhā. Pamajjanaṃ pamādo[M 0.0559], sativippavāsoti āha “pamāde ca sativippavāse”ti. Āmisapaṭisandhāranti āmisena attano, paresañca antarassa paṭisandahanaṃ āmisapaṭisandhāro, tathā dhammapaṭisandhāro.

The connection is that in those who are disrespectful to the Buddha, the determination should be understood thus. 'Yo' refers to whoever; the connection is as in 'does not go,' etc. 'Dharamāne' means standing, existing, or being present. 'Upaṭṭhāna' means the place of attendance, or for the purpose of attendance. 'Etassa' refers to anyone, whether a householder or a monastic. 'Dhammassavana' means the place for hearing the Dhamma, or for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma. 'Dhammassavanagga' means that where the Dhamma teaching is received, hence 'dhammassavanagga,' a Dhamma-listening hall. Or, 'dhammassavanagga' refers to one who receives the Dhamma teaching, or the assembly gathered at the place for hearing the Dhamma; that is 'dhammassavanagga.' 'Cittīkāra' means the manner of reverence. The connection is: 'sits being distracted or disrespectful.' 'Kāyapāgabbiya' refers to 'pagabba,' one who greatly scorns and oppresses others by this; it is excessive pride, the third letter of the labial class. The state of being 'pagabba' is 'pāgabbiya'; bodily arrogance is 'kāyapāgabbiya' (bodily misconduct). 'Tisso sikkhā' refers to the three trainings beginning with the higher training in morality. 'Pamajjana' is negligence; 'sativippavāsa' means loss of mindfulness, as stated: 'in negligence and loss of mindfulness.' 'Āmisapaṭisandhāra' means the connecting of the gap between oneself and others through material means; similarly, 'dhammapaṭisandhāra' means connecting through the Dhamma.

272. Sattharipi agāravotiādīnaṃ atthoti sambandho. “Anīcavuttī”tiādinā appatissoti padassa adhippāyatthaṃ dasseti, saddattho panevaṃ veditabbo, paṭimukhaṃ ādarena satthuvacanaṃ asuṇanto appatisso nāmāti. Ajjhattaṃ vāti ettha niyakajjhattādīsu catūsu niyakajjhattabhāvañca sattamīvibhattiyā amādesabhāvañca dassento āha “attano santāne vā”ti. “Attano pakkhe vā”ti iminā attano cittasantāneti atthaṃ paṭikkhipati. Tatra tumheti ettha tasaddassa visayaṃ dassento āha “tasmiṃ ajjhattabahiddhābhede”ti. Saparasantāneti attaparasantāne. Pahānāyāti ettha hādhātuyā karaṇañca āyasaddassa tadatthabhāvañca dassento āha “mettābhāvanādīhi nayehi pahānattha”nti. Mettābhāvanādīhītiādisaddena karuṇābhāvanādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Tanti vivādamūlaṃ. “Appavattibhāvāyā”ti iminā anavassavāyāti ettha avapubba sudhātuyā pavattanatthaṃ dasseti.

272. The connection is the meaning of 'Sattharipi agāravo' (disrespectful even to the Teacher), and so on. By 'anīcavuttī,' etc., it shows the intended meaning of the word 'appatisso,' but the literal meaning should be understood thus: one who does not listen respectfully to the Teacher's words is called 'appatisso.' Regarding 'ajjhattaṃ vā' (or internally)—here, showing both the state of being one's own internal state among the four kinds beginning with that, and that the '-am' ending is not a substitute for the locative case, it says, 'attano santāne vā' (or in one's own continuum). By 'attano pakkhe vā' (or on one's own side), it rejects the meaning of 'in one's own mental continuum.' Regarding 'tatra tumhe' (there you)—here, showing the scope of the word 'ta,' it says, 'in that distinction between internal and external.' 'Saparasantāne' means in one's own and others' continua. Regarding 'pahānāya' (for abandoning)—here, showing both the instrumentality of the root 'hā' and that the suffix 'āya' has that meaning, it says, 'for the purpose of abandoning through methods like the development of loving-kindness.' By 'mettābhāvanādīhi' (by the development of loving-kindness, etc.), the word 'etc.' includes the development of compassion, etc. 'Tam' (that) is the root of dispute. By 'appavattibhāvāya' (for the state of non-arising), it shows that in 'anavassavāya' (for non-flowing), the root 'su' with the prefix 'ava' has the meaning of 'pavattana' (arising/flowing).

Sandiṭṭhiparāmāsīti ettha sassa attano idaṃ saṃ, saṃ diṭṭhiṃ parato āmasatīti sandiṭṭhiparāmāsīti dassento āha “sakameva diṭṭhiṃ parāmasatī”ti. “Ya”ntiādinā parāmasanākāraṃ dasseti. Ādhānaggāhīti ettha ābhuso ṭhiyate ādhānanti vacanatthena ādhānasaddo daḷhapariyāyoti āha “daḷhaggāhī”ti. Daḷhaṃ gaṇhātīti daḷhaggāhī.

Regarding 'sandiṭṭhiparāmāsī' (one who clings to his own view): here, 'saṃ' means 'one's own' (sassa attano idaṃ saṃ). Showing that 'sandiṭṭhiparāmāsī' is one who 'clings to his own view in preference to others' (saṃ diṭṭhiṃ parato āmasati), it is said, 'he clings only to his own view' (sakameva diṭṭhiṃ parāmasati). By 'ya' and so on, the manner of clinging is shown. Regarding 'ādhānaggāhī' (one who grasps firmly): here, by the verbal derivation of 'ādhāna' as 'that which is repeatedly established' (ābhuso ṭhiyate ādhānaṃ), the word 'ādhāna' is a synonym for 'firm' (daḷhapariyāya), thus it is said, 'one who grasps firmly' (daḷhaggāhī). He grasps firmly, thus 'daḷhaggāhī'.

273. Anuvādamūlaniddeso kiñcāpi samānoti yojanā. Atha khoti tathā samānopi, ayamettha visesoti sambandho. Vivadantānaṃ puggalānanti yojanā. Tathā vivadantāti tenākārena vivadantā, anuvadantīti sambandho. “Asukaṃ nāma vipattiṃ āpanno”ti vuttamevatthaṃ āpattiyā sallakkhetvā dassento āha “pārājikaṃ āpannosī”tiādi[M 0.0560][V 2.0193]. Etthāti anuvādamūle. Visesoti vivādamūlato viseso. Vivadantānaṃ kodhūpanāhādīni vivādamūlāni, anuvadantānaṃ anuvādamūlānīti vuttaṃ hoti.

273. The connection is: the explanation of the root of accusation, 'even though it is similar.' But even though it is similar in that way, the connection is: 'this is the distinction here.' The connection is: 'of persons who dispute.' 'Thus disputing' means disputing in that manner; the connection is 'they accuse.' Having marked with an offense the very matter that was stated as 'he has fallen into such-and-such misfortune,' showing this, he says, 'You have committed a pārājika offense,' and so on. Here, in the root of accusation, the distinction is a distinction from the root of dispute. For those who dispute, anger, resentment, and so on are the roots of dispute; for those who accuse, the roots of accusation—thus it is said.

274. Mettaṃ kāyakammaṃ nāmāti ettha mettā etassatthīti mettaṃ, kāyakammaṃ, mettacittasahagataṃ kāyakammanti vuttaṃ hoti. Tena vuttaṃ “mettacittena kataṃ kāyakamma”nti. Sammukhaparammukhānaṃ vitthāraṃ dassento āha “tatthā”tiādi. Tattha tatthāti tesu sammukhaparammukhesu. Kāyakammaṃ nāmāti mettaṃ kāyakammaṃ nāma. Therānaṃ dānaiti sambandho. Ubhayehipīti navakattherehipi. Tesūti navakattheresu. Avamaññanti avamānaṃ. Attano dunnikkhittānaṃ paṭisāmanaṃ viya paṭisāmananti yojanā. “Mettākāyakammasaṅkhāto”ti iminā ayampi dhammoti ettha dhammasarūpaṃ dasseti. Pisaddo upari vakkhamāne dhamme apekkhati. “Saritabbo”ti iminā anīyasaddo kammavācakoti dasseti. Satijanakoti sabrahmacārīnaṃ satijanako. Tassa padassa adhippāyaṃ dassento āha “yo na”ntiādi. Tattha yoti puggalo. Nanti mettaṃ kāyakammaṃ. Taṃ puggalaṃ anussarantīti sambandho. Yesanti sabrahmacārīnaṃ. Teti sabrahmacārino. Pasannacittā hutvāti sambandho. “Piyaṃ karotī”ti iminā piyakaraṇoti padassa piyaṃ karotīti piyakaraṇoti vacanatthaṃ dasseti. Eseva nayo garukaraṇoti etthāpi. “Saṅgahetabbabhāvāyā”ti iminā saṅgahāyāti padassa bhāvappadhānakammaniddesabhāvaṃ dasseti. Saṅgahetabboti saṅgaho, tadatthāya. Tehīti sabrahmacārīhi. “Samaggabhāvāyā”ti iminā samaggassa bhāvo sāmaggīti vacanatthaṃ dasseti.

274. Regarding 'mettaṃ kāyakammaṃ nāma' (loving bodily action): here, 'mettaṃ' means 'having loving-kindness' (mettā etassatthīti mettaṃ), and 'kāyakammaṃ' means 'bodily action accompanied by a mind of loving-kindness' (mettacittasahagataṃ kāyakammaṃ). Therefore, it is said, 'bodily action done with a mind of loving-kindness' (mettacittena kataṃ kāyakammaṃ). To elaborate on 'face-to-face' and 'behind-the-back', he says, 'in this regard' and so on. 'In this regard' (Tattha tattha) refers to those situations of face-to-face and behind-the-back. Regarding 'kāyakammaṃ nāma' (bodily action): it is 'loving bodily action' (mettaṃ kāyakammaṃ nāma). 'The elders' gift' (therānaṃ dānaṃ)—this is the connection. 'By both' (ubhayehipi) means also by the newly ordained monks (navakattherehi). 'Among them' (tesu) refers to the newly ordained monks (navakattheresu). 'Avamaññanti' means contempt (avamānaṃ). The connection is 'attending to' (paṭisāmanaṃ) like 'attending to one's own things badly put away' (attano dunnikkhittānaṃ paṭisāmanaṃ viya). By 'designated as loving bodily action' (mettākāyakammasaṅkhāto), the nature of this Dhamma is also indicated here. The particle 'pi' refers to the Dhamma to be discussed subsequently. By 'saritabbo' (should be recollected), it is shown that the suffix 'anīya' denotes the passive voice (kammavācako). 'Satijanako' means 'a generator of mindfulness for fellow practitioners' (sabrahmacārīnaṃ satijanako). To explain the meaning of that phrase, he says, 'one who... it' (yo naṃ) and so on. Here, 'yo' refers to a person (puggalo). 'Naṃ' refers to loving bodily action (mettaṃ kāyakammaṃ). The connection is 'they recollect that person' (taṃ puggalaṃ anussaranti). 'Yesaṃ' refers to fellow practitioners (sabrahmacārīnaṃ). 'Te' refers to fellow practitioners (sabrahmacārino). The connection is 'having become pleased in mind' (pasannacittā hutvā). By 'piyaṃ karoti' (one makes dear), he shows the verbal meaning of the word 'piyakaraṇa' as 'one makes dear, thus it is piyakaraṇa'. The same method applies to 'garukaraṇa' (making respected). By 'saṅgahetabbabhāvāya' (for the sake of being included), he shows that the word 'saṅgahāya' (for inclusion) is a statement of the action where the state is primary (bhāvappadhānakammaniddesabhāvaṃ). 'That which is to be included' (saṅgahetabbo) is 'inclusion' (saṅgaho); for that purpose (tadatthāya). 'Tehi' means 'by fellow practitioners' (sabrahmacārīhi). By 'samaggabhāvāya' (for the sake of harmony), he shows the verbal meaning of 'sāmaggī' (harmony) as 'the state of being harmonious' (samaggassa bhāvo).

Paggayha vacananti paggahetvā vacanaṃ. Vihāreti ādhāre bhummaṃ, there asanteti yojanā. Tanti theraṃ kadā āgamissati nukhoti yojanā. Mamāyanavacananti mamāyanākārena pavattaṃ vacanaṃ. Mettāsinehasiniddhānīti mettāsaṅkhātena sinehena sinehitāni. Nayanānīti cakkhūni. “Appābādho”ti iminā arogoti padasseva atthaṃ [M 0.0561] dasseti. Niccābādhena vā arogo, āgantukābādhena appābādho, ajjhattābādhena vā arogo, bahiddhābādhena appābādho, kāyābādhena vā arogo, cittābādhena appābādho. Samannāharaṇanti punappunaṃ manasikaraṇaṃ.

Regarding 'paggayha vacanaṃ' (taking up the word): it means 'having taken up the word' (paggahetvā vacanaṃ). Regarding 'vihāreti' (he dwells): it is in the locative case (bhummaṃ) indicating the support (ādhāre); the connection is 'when the elder is not present' (there asante). The connection is 'when will that elder come?' (taṃ theraṃ kadā āgamissati nu kho). Regarding 'mamāyanavacanaṃ' (speech expressing 'mine'): it means 'speech proceeding in the manner of "mine"' (mamāyanākārena pavattaṃ vacanaṃ). Regarding 'mettāsinehasiniddhāni' (moistened with the affection of loving-kindness): it means 'moistened by the affection designated as loving-kindness' (mettāsaṅkhātena sinehena sinehitāni). 'Nayanāni' means 'eyes' (cakkhūni). By 'appābādho' (of few ailments), he shows the meaning of the word 'arogo' (healthy). Or, 'arogo' (healthy) is in respect to constant ailments, while 'appābādho' (of few ailments) is in respect to adventitious ailments. Or, 'arogo' is in respect to internal ailments, while 'appābādho' is in respect to external ailments. Or, 'arogo' is in respect to bodily ailments, while 'appābādho' is in respect to mental ailments. 'Samannāharaṇaṃ' (attending) means 'repeatedly paying attention' (punappunaṃ manasikaraṇaṃ).

Na puggalaṃ paṭivibhajitvā bhuñjatīti yojanā. Tadatthaṃ vitthārento āha “yo hī”tiādi. Tattha yoti puggalo, bhuñjatīti sambandho. “Ettakaṃ…pe… bhuñjissāmī”ti iminā āmisapaṭivibhattabhogibhāvaṃ dasseti. “Ettakaṃ vā asukassa ca…pe… bhuñjissāmī”ti iminā puggalapaṭivibhattabhogibhāvaṃ dasseti. Ayanti puggalo. Ābhatanti gāmādito [V 2.0194] ānītaṃ. Adātumpīti pisaddena dātumpi vaṭṭatīti dasseti. Dānañhi nāma na kassaci vāritaṃ. Sabbesanti dussīlasīlavantānaṃ. Vuttanti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 2.141; ma. ni. aṭṭha. 2.492; a. ni. aṭṭha. 3.6.11) vuttaṃ. Viceyyāti vicinitvā. Dātumpīti pisaddena avicinitvā sāmaññato dātumpi vaṭṭatīti sampiṇḍeti. Nanu evaṃ sati puggalavibhāgo kato nāma hoti, kasmā viceyya dātuṃ vaṭṭatīti āha “na hī”tiādi. Hīti yasmā. Eteti gilānādayo. Idaṃ padaṃ vicinitvāti pade kammaṃ, “dentenā”ti pade sampadānaṃ. Hīti saccaṃ. Iti ayanti iti manasikatvā ayaṃ sāraṇīyadhammapūrako.

The connection is 'he does not consume by dividing according to individuals' (na puggalaṃ paṭivibhajitvā bhuñjati). Expanding on that meaning, he says, 'for whoever' (yo hi) and so on. Here, 'yo' refers to a person (puggalo), and 'bhuñjati' (consumes) is the connection. By 'so much... I will consume' (ettakaṃ...pe... bhuñjissāmi), he shows the state of enjoying material goods by dividing them (āmisapaṭivibhattabhogibhāvaṃ). By 'so much for so-and-so... I will consume' (ettakaṃ vā asukassa ca...pe... bhuñjissāmi), he shows the state of enjoying by dividing among individuals (puggalapaṭivibhattabhogibhāvaṃ). 'This one' (ayaṃ) refers to a person (puggalo). 'Brought' (ābhatam) means 'brought from the village or elsewhere' (gāmādito ānītaṃ). By the particle 'pi' in 'adātuṃpi' (even not to give), he shows that giving is also appropriate (dātuṃpi vaṭṭati). For giving is not prohibited to anyone. Regarding 'sabbesaṃ' (to all): it means 'to the immoral and the virtuous' (dussīlasīlavantānaṃ). Regarding 'vuttaṃ' (stated): it means 'stated in the commentary' (aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ) (Dī. Ni. Aṭṭha. 2.141; Ma. Ni. Aṭṭha. 2.492; A. Ni. Aṭṭha. 3.6.11). Regarding 'viceyya' (having discerned): it means 'having discerned' (vicinitvā). By the particle 'pi' in 'dātuṃpi' (even to give), he concludes that giving in a general way, even without discerning, is also appropriate (avicinitvā sāmaññato dātumpi vaṭṭati). Now, if that is the case, a division by individuals is indeed made, is it not? Why then is it said to be appropriate to give after discerning? He says, 'for not' (na hi) and so on. Regarding 'hi': it means 'because' (yasmā). 'Ete' refers to the sick and so on (gilānādayo). This term is the object (kammaṃ) in the word 'vicinitvā'; in relation to the word 'dentena' (by the giver), it is the recipient (sampadānaṃ). Regarding 'hi': it means 'truly' (saccaṃ). 'Iti ayaṃ' (thus this one) means 'thus considering, this one is a fulfiller of the states that are to be remembered' (iti manasikatvā ayaṃ sāraṇīyadhammapūrako).

Akhaṇḍānītiādīsu paṭhamaṃ tāva khaṇḍachiddasabalakammāsāni dassetvā tesaṃ paṭipakkhavasena akhaṇḍādīni dassento āha “yassā”tiādi. Tattha yassāti bhikkhussa, sikkhāpadaṃ bhinnanti sambandho. Sattasu āpattikkhandhesūti ādhāre bhummaṃ, sikkhāpadanti sambandho. Āpattiñhi paṭicca sikkhāpadassa paññattattā āpatti tassa visayo hoti. Ādimhi vā ante vāti sikkhāpadānaṃ ādimhi vā ante vā. Vāsaddo aniyamavikappattho. Sikkhāpade bhinne āpattisambhavato vuttaṃ “sikkhāpadaṃ bhinna”nti. Khaṇḍaṃ nāmāti chinnaṃ nāma. Vemajjheti sikkhāpadānaṃ vemajjhe. Bhinnanti sikkhāpadaṃ bhinnaṃ. Chiddaṃ nāmāti vivaraṃ nāma. Dve tīṇi sikkhāpadānīti sambandho. Sabalaṃ nāmāti citraṃ nāma. Bhinnānīti sikkhāpadāni bhinnāni. Kammāsaṃ nāmāti vicitraṃ nāma. Ettha [M 0.0562] ca ekasmiṃ ṭhāne ekena visabhāgavaṇṇena citraṃ sabalaṃ nāma, nānāṭhāne nānāvaṇṇena vicitraṃ kammāsaṃ nāmāti ayametesaṃ viseso. Khaṇḍādīnaṃ viparivattanavasena akhaṇḍādīni dassento āha “yassa panā”tiādi. Abhinnānisīlānīti abhinnāni sikkhāpadasīlāni. Tāni panāti sīlāni pana. “Etānī”ti padaṃ padālaṅkāramattaṃ. Bhujissabhāvakaraṇatoti taṇhādāsabyato mocetvā bhujissakaraṇabhāvato. Iminā “bhujissabhāvakaraṇānī”ti vattabbe uttarapadalopavasena evaṃ vuttanti dasseti. Bhujissānīti vuccantīti sambandho. Viññūhīti buddhādīhi sappurisehi. Upacārasamādhiṃ appanāsamādhiṃ vāti ettha vāsaddo samuccayattho. Upacārasamādhiñca appanāsamādhiṃ cāti hi attho. “Saṃvattayantī”ti iminā samādhisaṃvattanikānīti ettha anīyasaddo bahulaṃ kattuvācakoti dasseti. Sīlasāmaññagatoti ettha samānassa bhāvo sāmaññaṃ, taṃ gatoti sāmaññagato, sīlena sāmaññagato sīlasāmaññagato, hutvā viharatīti yojanā. Tena vuttaṃ “samānabhāvūpagatasīlo viharatī”ti.

In the section beginning with 'unbroken' (akhaṇḍāni) and so on, first, having shown the broken (khaṇḍa), perforated (chidda), spotted (sabala), and mottled (kammāsa), he then shows their opposites, the unbroken (akhaṇḍa) and so on, saying 'of whom' (yassa) and so on. Here, 'yassa' refers to a monk (bhikkhussa), and the connection is 'the training rule is broken' (sikkhāpadaṃ bhinnaṃ). Regarding 'in the seven classes of offenses' (sattasu āpattikkhandhesu): this is the locative case indicating the support (ādhāre bhummaṃ), and the connection is 'the training rule' (sikkhāpadaṃ). For since a training rule is laid down in dependence on an offense, the offense is its scope. Regarding 'at the beginning or at the end' (ādimhi vā ante vā): it means 'at the beginning or at the end of the training rules' (sikkhāpadānaṃ ādimhi vā ante vā). The word 'vā' (or) has the meaning of indefiniteness or alternative. Because an offense occurs when a training rule is broken, it is said, 'the training rule is broken' (sikkhāpadaṃ bhinnaṃ). 'Broken' (khaṇḍaṃ nāma) means 'severed' (chinnaṃ nāma). 'In between' (vemajjhe) means 'in between the training rules' (sikkhāpadānaṃ vemajjhe). 'Broken' (bhinnaṃ) means 'the training rule is broken' (sikkhāpadaṃ bhinnaṃ). 'Perforated' (chiddaṃ nāma) means 'a gap' (vivaraṃ nāma). The connection is 'two or three training rules' (dve tīṇi sikkhāpadāni). 'Spotted' (sabalaṃ nāma) means 'variegated' (citraṃ nāma). 'Broken' (bhinnāni) means 'the training rules are broken' (sikkhāpadāni bhinnāni). 'Mottled' (kammāsaṃ nāma) means 'diverse' (vicitraṃ nāma). Here, the distinction between them is this: 'spotted' (sabala) means variegated with a single contrasting color in one place, while 'mottled' (kammāsa) means diverse with various colors in various places. By reversing the terms 'broken' and so on, he shows the unbroken and so on, saying 'but of whom' (yassa pana) and so on. Regarding 'unbroken virtues' (abhinnāni sīlāni): it means 'unbroken training-rule virtues' (abhinnāni sikkhāpadasīlāni). 'Tāni pana' refers to those virtues. The word 'etāni' (these) is merely a stylistic ornament (padālaṅkāramattaṃ). Regarding 'because they make one free' (bhujissabhāvakaraṇato): it means 'because they make one free by liberating from the slavery of craving' (taṇhādāsabyato mocetvā bhujissakaraṇabhāvato). By this, he shows that when 'bhujissabhāvakaraṇāni' (making one free) should be said, it is said thus by way of elision of the latter part of the compound (uttarapadalopavasena). The connection is 'they are called free' (bhujissāni ti vuccanti). Regarding 'by the wise' (viññūhi): it means 'by noble persons such as the Buddhas' (buddhādīhi sappurisehi). Regarding 'either access concentration or absorption concentration' (upacārasamādhiṃ appanāsamādhiṃ vā): here, the word 'vā' (or) has a collective meaning (samuccayattho). Indeed, the meaning is 'both access concentration and absorption concentration' (upacārasamādhiñca appanāsamādhiṃ ca). By 'they lead to' (saṃvattayanti), he shows that in 'leading to concentration' (samādhisaṃvattanikāni), the suffix 'anīya' frequently functions as an agentive (kattuvācako). Regarding 'endowed with the commonality of virtue' (sīlasāmaññagato): here, the state of being equal is 'commonality' (sāmaññaṃ); 'gone to that' (taṃ gato) is 'endowed with commonality' (sāmaññagato); 'endowed with commonality by virtue' (sīlena sāmaññagato) is 'endowed with the commonality of virtue' (sīlasāmaññagato). The connection is 'having become so, he dwells' (hutvā viharati). Therefore, it is said, 'he dwells having attained a state of equality in virtue' (samānabhāvūpagatasīlo viharati).

Yāyaṃ [V 2.0195] diṭṭhīti ettha “diṭṭhī”ti sāmaññagatassāpi saddassa “ariyā”ti saddantarasannidhānena visesavisayattā sammādiṭṭhīti āha “maggasampayuttā sammādiṭṭhī”ti. “Maggasampayuttā”ti iminā lokiyasammādiṭṭhiṃ paṭikkhipati. Niddosāti visuddhattā, uttamattā vā niddosā. Iminā ariyasaddo niddosatthavācako anipphannapāṭipadikoti dasseti. Niyyātīti nibbānaṃ yāti. Iminā anīyasaddo bahulaṃ kattuvācakoti dasseti. Yo tathākārī hoti, takkarassāti yojanā. Tathākārīti tāya maggasampayuttāya sammādiṭṭhiyā kārī hoti. Iminā tāya sammādiṭṭhiyā karotīti takkaroti vacanatthaṃ dasseti. Dukkhakkhayāyāti ettha khīyanaṃ khayo, dukkhassa khayo dukkhakkhayo, tadatthāyāti dassento āha “sabbadukkhassa khayattha”nti. Sesanti vuttavacanato sesaṃ vacanaṃ.

Regarding 'yāyaṃ diṭṭhī' (this view): here, although the word 'diṭṭhī' (view) is general, due to the proximity of the other word 'ariyā' (noble), it has a specific scope; thus, it is said to be 'right view associated with the path' (maggasampayuttā sammādiṭṭhī). By 'associated with the path' (maggasampayuttā), he rejects mundane right view. Regarding 'niddosā' (faultless): it is faultless because it is pure (visuddhattā) or because it is supreme (uttamattā). By this, it is shown that the word 'ariyā' conveys the meaning of 'faultless' and is an underived nominal stem. Regarding 'niyyāti' (it leads out): it means 'it goes to Nibbāna' (nibbānaṃ yāti). By this, it is shown that the word 'anīya' frequently functions as an agentive. The connection is: 'for one who does so' (takkarassa) means 'for one who acts accordingly' (yo tathākārī hoti). 'One who acts accordingly' (tathākārī) means 'one who acts by means of that right view associated with the path.' By this, he shows the meaning of the expression 'takkara' is 'one acts by means of that right view' (tāya sammādiṭṭhiyā karoti). Regarding 'dukkhakkhayāya' (for the destruction of suffering): here, 'destruction' (khayo) is the state of ceasing (khīyanaṃ); the destruction of suffering is 'dukkhakkhayo'. To show that it is 'for that purpose' (tadatthāya), he says, 'for the destruction of all suffering' (sabbadukkhassa khayatthaṃ). 'The rest' (sesaṃ) means 'the remaining statement from what has been said'.

Iti katipucchāvāravaṇṇanāya yojanā samattā.

Thus, the explanation of the Section of Several Questions is completed.

Khandhakapucchāvāro

The Section of Questions Concerning the Khandhakas

Pucchāvissajjanāvaṇṇanā

Exposition of Questions and Answers

320. Upasampadakkhandhakanti [M 0.0563] mahākhandhakaṃ. “Nidānena ca niddesena ca saddhi”nti iminā saha nidānenāti sanidānaṃ, saha niddesenāti saniddesanti vacanatthaṃ dasseti. Ettha nidānenāti sikkhāpadapaññattidesasaṅkhātena nidānena. Niddesenāti puggalādiniddesena. Tatthāti upasampadakkhandhake. Samukkaṭṭhapadānanti ettha samukkaṭṭhasaddo uttamapariyāyoti āha “uttamānī”ti. Padānīti “na bhikkhave ūnavīsativasso puggalo upasampādetabbo”ti (pāci. 402-403; mahāva. 124) ādinā nayena vuttāni padāni. Imehi padehi “samukkaṭṭhāni padāni samukkaṭṭhapadānī”ti vacanatthaṃ dasseti. Itīti ayamattho. Kasmā panettha “samukkaṭṭhapadānaṃ kati āpattiyo”ti padānameva sāmivasena niddeso kato, nanu āpattiyo nāma puggalānaññeva hontīti āha “yena yena hī”tiādi. Hīti yasmā. Yena yena padena paññattāti sambandho. Sā sāti āpatti. Dve āpattiyoti ettha dvinnaṃ āpattīnaṃ sarūpaṃ dassento āha “pācittiyaṃ, dukkaṭa”nti.

320. The Upasampadā Khandhaka is the Mahākhandhaka. By this phrase “with the origin and with the explanation,” he shows the meaning of the words “sanidāna” as “with the origin” and “saniddesa” as “with the explanation.” Here, “by origin” means by the origin consisting of the description of the enactment of the training rules. “By explanation” means by the explanation of individuals and so forth. There, in the Upasampadā Khandhaka, concerning “samukkaṭṭhapadāni,” here the word “samukkaṭṭha” is a synonym for “supreme,” thus he said “supreme.” “Padāni” refers to the words spoken in the manner of “Monks, a person under twenty years of age should not be ordained” (Pāci. 402-403; Mahāva. 124) and so forth. By these words, he shows the meaning of “samukkaṭṭhapadāni” as “supreme words.” Thus, this is the meaning. But why here is the explanation given generally only in terms of the words “how many offenses are there in the supreme words,” when surely offenses belong only to individuals? He says: “because, by whatever…” and so forth. “Hī” means “because.” The connection is “by whatever word it is enacted.” “Sā” means that offense. Concerning “two offenses,” here, showing the nature of the two offenses, he says: “a pācittiya, a dukkaṭa.”

Nassanteteti [V 2.0196] nassantu ete. Vinassanteteti vinassantu ete bhikkhūti attho. Tehīti bhikkhūhi. Vadatoti vadantānaṃ. Sesesu uposathakaraṇesūti sambandho. “Dukkaṭāpattiyevā”ti iminā ekā āpattīti ettha atthapakaraṇādivasena dukkaṭāpattiyevāti dasseti.

“Nassantete” means “let them be destroyed.” “Vinassantete” means “let these monks be utterly destroyed.” “Tehi” means “by the monks.” “Vadato” means “of those who are speaking.” The connection is “in the remaining Uposatha observances.” By this phrase “only a dukkaṭa offense,” he shows that here, in the sense of “one offense,” it is only a dukkaṭa offense, by way of meaning, context, and so forth.

Pavāraṇakkhandhakepīti pisaddo uposathakkhandhakaṃ apekkhati.

In “In the Pavāraṇā Khandhaka too,” the word “pi” refers back to the Uposatha Khandhaka.

Cammasaṃyuttepīti cammena saṃyuttaṃ katvā desite khandhakepi, cammakkhandhakepīti attho. Pisaddo pavāraṇakkhandhakaṃ apekkhati. Bhesajjakkhandhakepīti pisaddo cammakkhandhakaṃ apekkhati. Samantāti aṅgajātassa samantato.

“In the Cammasaṃyutta too” means in the Khandhaka taught as connected with leather, that is, in the Camma Khandhaka too. The word “pi” refers to the Pavāraṇā Khandhaka. In “In the Bhesajjakkhandhaka too,” the word “pi” refers to the Camma Khandhaka. “Samantā” means “all around the sexual organ.”

Tatthāti [M 0.0564] kathinakkhandhake. Cīvarasaṃyutteti cīvarakkhandhake.

“Tattha” means in the Kathina Khandhaka. “Cīvarasaṃyutte” means in the Cīvara Khandhaka.

Campeyyaketi campeyyakkhandhake. Samuccayakkhandhakesupīti pisaddo campeyyakkhandhakaṃ apekkhati.

“Campeyyake” means in the Campeyya Khandhaka. In “In the Samuccaya Khandhakas too,” the word “pi” refers to the Campeyya Khandhaka.

Samathakkhandhake imā dve āpattiyo hontīti yojanā. Eseva nayo sesesupi. Khuddakavatthuketi khuddakavatthukkhandhake. Garubhaṇḍavissajjaneti garubhaṇḍassa vissajjane.

The construction is: “In the Samatha Khandhaka, these two offenses occur.” This same method applies to the rest as well. “Khuddakavatthuke” means in the Khuddakavatthu Khandhaka. “Garubhaṇḍavissajjane” means in the relinquishing of heavy goods.

Saṅghabhedeti saṅghabhedakkhandhake. “Samācāraṃ pucchissanti vutte vattakkhandhake”ti iminā samācārasaddena vattakkhandhakaṃ gahetabbanti dasseti. Sāti dukkaṭāpatti. “Tathā”ti padena “ekā dukkaṭāpattiyevā”ti padaṃ atidisati. “Pātimokkhaṭṭhapane”ti iminā pāḷiyaṃ ṭhapanaṃ pucchissanti ettha “pātimokkha”ntiādipadassa lopaṃ dasseti. Pañcasatikasattasatikesūti pañcasatikakkhandhakasattasatikakkhandhakesu. Āropitoti ettha rupadhātuyā dvikammikattā, nyādigaṇattā ca “dhammo”ti padhānakammameva vuttaṃ, na “saṅgaha”nti apadhānakammaṃ. Tena vuttaṃ “dhammo saṅgaha”nti. Tatthāti pañcasatikasattasatikesu.

“Saṅghabhede” means in the Saṅghabheda Khandhaka. By the statement, “When ‘they will ask about conduct’ is said, it refers to the Vattakkhandhaka,” he shows that the Vattakkhandhaka is to be understood by the word “samācāra.” “Sā” refers to a dukkaṭa offense. By the word “tathā,” he extends the phrase “only one dukkaṭa offense.” By this phrase “in the suspension of the Pātimokkha,” he indicates the omission of the word “Pātimokkha” and so forth in the Pāli phrase “they will ask about the suspension.” “In the five-hundred and seven-hundred” means in the Pañcasatika Khandhaka and the Sattasatika Khandhaka. Concerning “āropito” (imputed), here, because the root “rup” is ditransitive and belongs to the nyādi group, only the primary object “the Dhamma” is stated, not the secondary object “the inclusion.” Therefore, it is said “the Dhamma, the inclusion.” “Tattha” means in the five-hundred and seven-hundred Khandhakas.

Iti khandhakapucchāvaṇṇanāya yojanā samattā.

Thus concludes the explanation of the commentary on the questions concerning the Khandhakas.

Ekuttarikanayo

The Method of Increasing by One

Ekuttarikanayo ekakavāravaṇṇanā

The Method of Increasing by One: Exposition of the Section of Ones

321. Evaṃ [V 2.0197] khandhakapucchāya vaṇṇanaṃ katvā idāni ekuttarikanayassa taṃ karonto āha “āpatti…pe… naye”ti. Tattha ekuttarikanaye evaṃ vinicchayo veditabboti yojanā. “Cha āpattisamuṭṭhānānī”ti iminā samuṭṭhānāni āpattiṃ karontīti atthena āpattikarā nāmāti dasseti. Etesanti channaṃ āpattisamuṭṭhānānaṃ. Hīti yasmā, āpajjatīti [M 0.0565] sambandho. Sikkhāpade cāti mātikāsikkhāpade ca. Lahukā āpattīti ettha appasāvajjattā na lahukā nāma hoti, lahukena pana vinayakammenāti āha “lahukena vinayakammena visujjhanato”ti. Pañcavidhāti thullaccayādivasena pañcapakārā. Kenacīti lahukena vā garukena vā kenaci ākārena. Saṃvijjati gihibhāvato avaseso samaṇabhāvo etissāti sāvasesā, paṭipakkhavasena anavasesā. Dve āpattikkhandhāti pārājikasaṅghādisesavasena dve āpattikkhandhā.

321. Having thus made the exposition of the questions on the Khandhakas, now, making it for the Ekuttarika method, he says: “offense… etc. … in the method.” The construction is: “Here, in the Ekuttarika method, the determination should be understood thus.” By this phrase “six origins of offenses,” he shows that these origins are called “offense-makers” in the sense that they cause offenses. “Etesaṃ” means of these six origins of offenses. “Hī” means “because,” and the connection is “one commits.” “And in the training rule” means and in the fundamental training rule. Concerning “a light offense,” here, it is not called “light” due to its small fault, but because it is purified by a light disciplinary action, thus he says: “because of purification by a light disciplinary action.” “Fivefold” means five kinds by way of thullaccaya and so forth. “By any” means by any manner, whether light or heavy. “Sāvasesā” means “with remainder,” because for one who commits this, a remainder of the monastic state, as distinct from the state of a householder, still exists; “anavasesā” (without remainder) is to be understood in the opposite way. “Two aggregates of offenses” means two aggregates of offenses by way of pārājika and saṅghādisesa.

“Karontī”ti iminā antarāyikāti ettha ṇikapaccayassa atthaṃ dasseti. Antarāyikā āpattiyo sabbathā antarāyikā hontīti āha “antarāyikaṃ āpannassāpī”tiādi. Desetvā suddhipattassāti sambandho. Lokavajjāti lokehi vajjetabbā. Paṇṇattivajjāti bhagavato paṇṇattiyā vajjetabbā. Yanti yaṃ āpattiṃ āpajjatīti sambandho. Karontoti kiriyamānato. Ettha hi mānasaddassa antādeso. Iminā karaṇaṃ kiriyanti bhāvatthaṃ dasseti. Āpajjatīti puggalo āpajjati. Sā āpatti kiriyato samuṭṭhitā nāmāti yojanā. Kā āpatti viyāti āha “pārājikāpatti viyā”ti. Eseva nayo anantaravākyesupi.

By this word “karonti” (they make), he shows the meaning of the affix “ṇika” here in “antarāyikā” (obstructive). He says that obstructive offenses are obstructive in every way, thus: “even for one who has fallen into an obstructive offense” and so forth. The connection is “for one who has attained purity after having confessed.” “Lokavajjā” (blameworthy in the world) means it should be avoided by worldly people. “Paṇṇattivajjā” (blameworthy by enactment) means it should be avoided according to the Blessed One’s enactment. “Yaṃ” is connected with “whatever offense one commits.” “Karonto” (doing) means “because it is being done.” Here, indeed, there is a substitution for the ending of the suffix “māna.” By this, he shows the abstract meaning of “karaṇa” (doing) is “kiriya” (action). “Āpajjati” means “a person commits.” The construction is: “that offense is named as arising from the act.” “What offense is it like?” He says: “like a pārājika offense.” This same method applies to the subsequent statements as well.

Pubbāpattīti ettha pubbasaddo paṭhamatthoti āha “paṭhamaṃ āpannāpattī”ti. “Āpannā”ti padena majjhelopaṃ dasseti. Pacchā āpannāpattīti vattabhedadukkaṭāpatti. Mūlavisuddhiyāti mūle kāyaci āpattiyā amissattā visuddhiyā āpattiyā. Kurundiyaṃ vuttanti sambandho. Idampīti [V 2.0198] kurundiyaṃ vuttavacanampi. Pisaddena purimaṃ mahāaṭṭhakathāvacanaṃ apekkhati. Ekena pariyāyenāti ekena kāraṇena.

Concerning “pubbāpatti,” here, he says that the word “pubba” means “first,” thus: “the first offense committed.” By the word “āpannā,” he shows the elision of the middle syllable. “Pacchā āpannāpatti” (later committed offense) refers to a dukkaṭa offense for breaking an observance. “Mūlavisuddhiyā” (by fundamental purity) means by the purity of an offense due to its non-association with any offense at the root. The connection is “it is stated in the Kurundī.” “Idampi” means also this statement stated in the Kurundī. By the word “pi,” it refers to the previous statement of the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā. “Ekena pariyāyena” means “by one reason.”

Yāti āpatti, desitā hotīti sambandho. Ayaṃ desitā gaṇanūpikā nāmāti yojanā. Yā desitā hoti, ayaṃ agaṇanūpikā nāmāti yojanā. Saussāhenevāti punapi āpajjissāmīti saha ussāheneva. Hīti saccaṃ, yasmā vā. “Gaṇanaṃ na upetī”ti [M 0.0566] iminā gaṇanaṃ na upagacchatīti agaṇanūpikāti vacanatthaṃ dasseti. Aṭṭhame vatthusmiṃ pūraṇeti sambandho. Idaṃ pāḷiyaṃ aṭṭhavatthukapūraṇavasena bhikkhunīnaṃ āgatattā bhikkhuniyo sandhāya vuttaṃ. Bhikkhūnampi dutiyapārājikaṭṭhāne labbhatiyeva.

The connection is: 'The offense is gone, it is declared.' The construction is: 'This declared one is called gaṇanūpikā (counting expedient).' The construction is: 'That which is declared is called agaṇanūpikā (non-counting expedient).' Saussāheneva means 'with effort indeed,' thinking, 'I will offend again.' Hī means 'truly,' or 'because.' By this phrase, 'it does not approach counting,' it shows the meaning of agaṇanūpikā as 'it does not come under counting.' The connection is 'completion in the eighth instance.' This, having come in the Pāli by way of the completion of the eight instances for nuns, is stated with reference to nuns. For monks too, it is indeed obtained in the context of the second pārājika offense.

Thullavajjāti ettha thullaṃ vajjaṃ etissāti thullavajjāti dassento āha “thulladose paññattā”ti. Yā ca dhammikassa paṭissavassa asaccāpane āpatti atthi, sā ca gihipaṭisaṃyuttāti yojanā. Pañcānantariyakammāpattīti pañcahi ānantariyakammehi āpannā pārājikāpatti. Sudinnattherādīti ādisaddena dhaniyattherādayo saṅgaṇhāti. Ādikammikoti ādikammaṃ karonto, tasmiṃ niyutto vā. Makkaṭisamaṇādīti ādisaddena vajjiputtakādayo saṅgaṇhāti. Yo kadāci karahaci āpattiṃ āpajjati, so adhiccāpattiko nāmāti yojanā. Paratopi eseva nayo.

Concerning thullavajjā, here, showing that it is thullavajjā because 'a grave fault belongs to this one,' he says: 'declared as a grave fault.' The construction is: 'And that offense which exists for the non-fulfillment of a lawful promise, that too is connected with a householder.' Pañcānantariyakammāpatti means a pārājika offense incurred through the five immediate actions. Sudinnattherādi (Elder Sudinna and so forth) means by the word 'and so forth,' he includes Elder Dhaniya and others. Ādikammiko (initial worker) means one who does the initial work, or one assigned to it. Makkaṭisamaṇādi (Monkey ascetic and so forth) means by the word 'and so forth,' he includes the Vajjiputtakas and others. The construction is: 'One who commits an offense occasionally is called adhiccāpattiko (an occasional offender).' The same method applies further on as well.

“Codetī”ti iminā codetīti codakoti vacanatthaṃ dasseti. “Codito”ti iminā coditabboti cudito, soyeva cuditakoti vacanatthaṃ dasseti. Pañcadasasūti pātimokkhaṭṭhapanakkhandhake vuttesu pañcadasadhammesu. Tenāti adhammacodakena, coditoti sambandho. Pātimokkhaṭṭhapanakkhandhake (cūḷava. 401) vutte sacce ca akuppe ca atiṭṭhantopi adhammacuditakoyeva nāma, so pana dhammacodakena coditeyeva kuppanto adhammacuditako nāma, adhammacodakena codite pana kuppantopi adhammacuditako nāma na hoti, tasmā idha na vutto. “Samannāgato”ti iminā niyatā etassa santīti niyatoti vacanatthaṃ dasseti.

By this word codeti (accuses), it shows the meaning of codaka (accuser) as 'one who accuses.' By this word codito (accused), it shows the meaning of cudita as 'one who should be accused,' and that very one is cuditaka. Pañcadasasu (in the fifteen) means among the fifteen things stated in the Pātimokkhaṭṭhapana Khandhaka. Tena (by him) means by the unlawful accuser; the connection is 'accused.' In the Pātimokkhaṭṭhapana Khandhaka (Cūḷavagga 401), it is stated that even one who does not remain steadfast in truth and the unshakeable is called an adhammacuditaka (unlawfully accused). But he who becomes agitated when accused by a lawful accuser is called an adhammacuditaka. However, one who becomes agitated when accused by an unlawful accuser is not called an adhammacuditaka; therefore, it is not mentioned here. By this word samannāgato (possessed), it shows the meaning of niyata (resolute) as 'certitudes exist for him.'

Āpajjituṃ bhabbāti bhabbāpattikā. Kenaci kammena akatopi anukkhittakoyeva nāma, so pana ukkhittakoti saṅkābhāvato idha na vutto. Ayanti tajjanīyādikammakato bhikkhu. Hīti yasmā, na kopetīti sambandho. Liṅgadaṇḍakammasaṃvāsanāsanāhīti liṅganāsanena [M 0.0567] ca daṇḍakammanāsanena ca saṃvāsanāsanena ca. Yenāti bhikkhunā. Soti nānāsaṃvāsako. Dvinnaṃ nānāsaṃvāsakānaṃ [V 2.0199] viseso heṭṭhā (pāci. aṭṭha. 428) vuttoyeva. Ṭhapanaṃ jānitabbanti ettha kiṃ ṭhapanaṃ nāmāti āha “pātimokkhaṭṭhapana”nti.

They are capable of committing an offense, thus they are bhabbāpattikā (liable to offenses). Even one upon whom no formal act has been done is still called 'not suspended'; but here, since there is no suspicion of his being suspended, it is not stated. This refers to a bhikkhu who has been subjected to a formal act of censure or the like. Hī means 'because,' and the connection is with 'he does not get angry.' Liṅgadaṇḍakammasaṃvāsanāsanāhi means by the removal of the sign, by the removal of the punishment-act, and by the removal of communion. Yena refers to the bhikkhu. So means one who is in non-communion. The distinction between the two types of those in non-communion is indeed explained below (Pācittiya Commentary 428). Regarding 'The suspension should be known,' here, asking, 'What is called suspension?' he says, 'the suspension of the Pātimokkha.'

Iti ekakavāravaṇṇanāya yojanā samattā.

Thus, the analysis in the commentary on the section of single items is completed.

Ekuttarikanayo dukavāravaṇṇanā

The Method of Numerical Progression: The Commentary on the Section of Pairs.

322. Dukesu acittakā āpattīti sambandho. Bhūtārocanāpattīti pācittiyāpatti. Abhūtārocanāpattīti pārājikathullaccayāpatti. Padasodhammādikātiādisaddena uttarichapañcavācā saṅgahitā. Mañcapīṭhādīnantiādisaddena bhisiādayo saṅgaṇhāti. Anāpucchāgamanādīsūti ādisaddena anuddharitvā gamanaṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Sapuggaloti so attasaṅkhāto puggalo sapuggalo. Parapuggaloti paro puggalo parapuggalo. Garukanti saṅghādisesaṃ. Lahukanti pācittiyaṃ. Puna garukanti pārājikaṃ. Puna lahukanti pācittiyameva.

322. The connection is: In the pairs, the offense is unintentional. The offense of truthful reporting is a pācittiya offense. The offense of false reporting is a pārājika or thullaccaya offense. By the word ādi in padasodhammādikāti, the six or five further statements are included. By the word ādi in mañcapīṭhādīnanti, items like cushions and so forth are included. By the word ādi in anāpucchāgamanādīsu, going without having put away the bedding is included. Sapuggala means one's own person is sapuggala. Parapuggala means another person is parapuggala. Garuka refers to a saṅghādisesa offense. Lahuka refers to a pācittiya offense. Again, garuka refers to a pārājika offense. Again, lahuka refers to a pācittiya offense indeed.
